argument_text: He added that in passing through channels these letters may have been lost and that this possibility constitutes the chief reason for the initiation of the tracer letter.
explanation: This provides a reason (letters may have been lost in channels) leading to a conclusion/action (initiation of the tracer letter). The causal connector “constitutes the chief reason” makes the argumentative structure explicit.
main_claim: The tracer letter was initiated because the original applications may have been lost in channels.

argument_text: Second Bomb Group Headquarters, according to Colonel Robert K. Martin, commanding officer, recently initiated a tracer letter through military channels to the War Department in order to determine whether former members of the 463rd Bombardment Group, the 99th Bombardment Group, and the 301st Bombardment Group during the period between the 22nd of March and VE day will be authorized to wear the Central Europe battle star and get the five points that goes with it. Previous verbal attempts have been made and failed.
explanation: The juxtaposition of the action (initiated a tracer letter) with the statement that “Previous verbal attempts have been made and failed” implies a reason: because prior attempts failed, the unit escalated to a formal tracer letter to achieve authorization. The reasoning is suggested, not explicitly linked with “therefore.”
main_claim: A tracer letter was necessary because earlier verbal efforts to resolve the award status failed.

argument_text: Colonel Martin was definite in pointing out that these three bombardment groups of the former Fifth Wing which did not receive the battle star had sent letters of application to the theater commander at the proper time; however, authorization of the award was never received.
explanation: The contrastive “however” sets up a norm: timely applications should lead to authorization; the fact that no authorization was received implies an irregularity or error that needs correction. The text suggests a claim of procedural failure without stating it outright.
main_claim: Despite timely applications, no authorization was received, indicating a procedural failure that warrants corrective action.

argument_text: "The reason for the tracer letter," Colonel Martin said, "is to determine whether the award was ever issued to the three groups. If the battle star was not awarded, it will depend on the Theater Command whether, on the strength of the records we have from the files of Fifth Wing, the battle star can still be obtained."
explanation: The second sentence implies that existing Fifth Wing records provide a substantive basis for awarding the battle star if it was not previously granted, presenting evidentiary strength as the rationale for possible approval. The conclusion (that the star can be obtained) is conditional and framed as dependent on the records’ strength, making the argumentative thrust implicit.
main_claim: If the battle star was not previously awarded, the strength of Fifth Wing records could justify obtaining it, subject to Theater Command’s decision.

argument_text:
After Jerry's picture was printed in last week's Occupator, Lou Cook of AES cut the picture out of all the copies of the paper he could lay his hands on, and distributed them among the kids standing on the streets of Foggia. He promised "molti presentes" for any one who found Jerry.

In Tuesday morning, two grimy little guys came up to the radio station and told Cookie that they had found the dog.
explanation: The passage narrates a sequence: dissemination of the dog's picture and a promised reward are followed by kids reporting they found the dog. The juxtaposition implies a causal argument that distributing the pictures and offering a reward led to the recovery. The causal connection is suggested rather than stated, making it implicit.
main_claim: Publicizing the missing dog with pictures and promising a reward led to the dog's being found and reported.

argument_text: Investigation proved that it was Jerry, and he was brought back to his owner, Sgt. Thorsfelt, and his buddy, Ace.
explanation: This sentence uses the evidential term "proved" to connect a premise (an investigation's findings) to a conclusion (the dog was Jerry), followed by an action based on that conclusion (he was brought back). The structure explicitly presents evidence leading to a conclusion.
main_claim: The investigation established that the found dog was indeed Jerry, warranting his return to the owner.

argument_text: The AES personnel were so glad to see the dog again that they contributed a carton of cigarettes, molti candy, and chewing gum to the two kids who found the dog.
explanation: The causal connector "so...that" explicitly links the premise (their being very glad) to the conclusion/action (they contributed goods), presenting a reasoned justification for the contribution.
main_claim: Because they were very glad to recover the dog, AES personnel gave gifts to the kids who found him.

argument_text: Your AES Foggia Goes Off The Air To Change Its Kilos
explanation: The headline presents a claim with a stated reason/purpose: the station "goes off the air" in order "to change its kilos" (kilos = kilocycles/frequency). The purpose clause functions as a premise justifying the action, forming an explicit argument structure (X will happen to achieve Y).
main_claim: AES Foggia will go off the air in order to change its broadcast frequency.

argument_text: The Army Expeditionary Station in Foggia will go off the air, Friday, December 21st, as requested in a letter from General Ridgeway, Commanding General, MTOUSA, in order to change its frequency.
explanation: This sentence gives the action (going off the air on a specific date) and provides two explicit reasons: it was requested by an authoritative source (General Ridgeway) and it is for the purpose of changing frequency. These premises explicitly support and justify the conclusion/action.
main_claim: The station will go off the air on December 21st because an order requested it and to change its frequency.

argument_text: Keep tuned to your AES Foggia for further information.
explanation: This is a directive that implies a reason: listeners ought to stay tuned because more information will be provided. The benefit of receiving “further information” functions as an unstated premise supporting the recommendation, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Listeners should keep tuned to AES Foggia because it will provide further information.

argument_text:
"Peace" Brother?

Tokyo (CNS) — The Japs have chosen names for 2 new brands of domestic cigarets. The names: "Corona" and "Peace".
explanation: The headline’s rhetorical question "Peace Brother?" combined with the derogatory term "Japs" frames the subsequent factual report about naming a cigarette "Peace" as ironic or hypocritical. This framing implies skepticism about the sincerity or appropriateness of Japan invoking "Peace" so soon after the war. The premises (they named a cigarette "Peace") are presented to support the implied conclusion (this is mockable or insincere), signaled by ironic tone and evaluative framing rather than explicit reasoning.
main_claim: Japan’s choice to name a cigarette brand “Peace” is ironic and unconvincing, implying insincerity about peace.

argument_text: Washington (CNS) — The USA is still growing. Latest reports from the Census Bureau show the nation’s population has climbed 8 million since 1940, and now has passed the 140 million mark.
explanation: The first sentence states a claim (“The USA is still growing.”). The second sentence provides evidence from Census Bureau reports that the population increased by 8 million since 1940 and surpassed 140 million, which functions as premises supporting the conclusion that the population is growing.
main_claim: The USA is still growing.

argument_text: That great big wonderful bird, The Stork, has been responsible for lots of cigars these days. Into the office came Sgt Walter Powell, 20th Squadron, Motor Pool Dispatcher, with a cigar and a really beaming face to tell us about the fact that Dedria, a brand new baby daughter came to his house. Lt. Gerhardt J. Gliege, Professor of Business Law at the Fortress Institute and Co-Pilot, is the proud pappy of eight and a half pounds Carolyn Jean. Lt. Gliege is passing out the Calvert at the 49th Squadron.
explanation: The opening causal claim (“The Stork... has been responsible for lots of cigars these days”) is supported by successive instances of new fathers distributing cigars/Calvert, functioning as evidence. The argument is implicit because the text does not explicitly say “there are many cigars because several babies were born,” but it lists cases to suggest that births are causing widespread cigar-giving.
main_claim: Recent births have been causing many celebratory cigars to be handed out.

argument_text: "Yes, gentlemen, the boy weighs nine pounds, the mother is doing fine, and my kid can lick your kid..."
explanation: This is a boast that implies a conclusion (his child is tougher than others) using premises about the baby’s weight and well-being; the link between “nine pounds” and “can lick your kid” is an implied causal/indicative rationale rather than an explicit argument structure.
main_claim: My child is tougher than other men’s children.

argument_text:
Captain Joseph T. Guzek has succeeded Lt. Colonel Herbert H. Kerr, who has been transferred to Caserta to be Deputy Surgeon of MTOUSA.

A native of Olyphant, Pennsylvania, Captain Guzek was a member of the 37th General Hospital when it was organized at the King's County Hospital at Brooklyn in January 1943. On July 7, 1943 he landed with the unit in Casablanca. Since that time he has been stationed at Naples, Padua, Mantona and then to the 55th Station Hospital Unit at Pisa. He accompanied them when the Hospital was transferred to Foggia. Captain Guzek is a specialist in ophthalmology.
explanation: The passage lists Guzek’s succession and then marshals his credentials (founding member of a hospital unit, overseas landings, multiple postings, specialty training) in a way that implicitly justifies or endorses his appointment as commanding officer. The evaluative stance is implied through selective inclusion of achievements and experience, which function as premises supporting the unstated conclusion that he is well-qualified and that the leadership change is appropriate.
main_claim: Captain Joseph T. Guzek is a well-qualified and appropriate choice to command the 55th Station Hospital.

argument_text: The other day we just happened to wend our way into that sanctum of the local gendarmes known as the "Local Precinct" and discovered to our utter surprise and confusion that these masters of the local traffic problems are just as you and me. Just as in every other group of men the main point of conversation is "redeployment." The boys with 57 and 56 points were thinking and talking of what a wonderful Christmas this would be if they should be fortunate enough to make it home on time; while giving encouragement to those about to depart, the low pointers would "bat away" at their destiny in Foggia. Some of the M.P.'s had a few new rumors and all had the hope of the States in March.
explanation: This passage advances the claim that the local MPs are ordinary people with the same concerns as others. The evaluative conclusion “are just as you and me” is supported implicitly by observations about their conversations and hopes (focus on redeployment, point totals, Christmas at home, hopes for March). The causal/illustrative link is implied rather than stated with explicit “because,” making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: The local MPs are just like everyone else, as shown by their shared preoccupation with redeployment and hopes of going home.

argument_text: The reason for the change is, of course, to make life just a bit more pleasant and comfortable for the boys who, of necessity, must wear that authoritative and displeased look.
explanation: This sentence states a conclusion about the purpose of the change (to make life more pleasant/comfortable) and provides a reason (their necessarily unpleasant, authoritative role), forming a clear premise-to-conclusion justification.
main_claim: The move is intended to make life more pleasant and comfortable for the MPs/security personnel because their job compels them to maintain an authoritative, displeased demeanor.

argument_text: They will have their mess hall located right in the billets, and it will be open twenty-four hours a day for snacks and coffee for the men while the feeding hours on meals will stretch over a two hour period to insure that no man is forced to miss a meal.
explanation: The sentence provides premises (on-site mess hall; 24-hour snacks; extended meal periods) leading to an explicit purpose/conclusion (to ensure no one misses a meal), forming a direct causal-teleological argument.
main_claim: The on-site mess hall with 24-hour access and extended meal periods will ensure that no man is forced to miss a meal.

argument_text: from the way the plans are laid out at present the boys should have a pretty good time while they “sweat it out” in Foggia.
explanation: This evaluative claim infers a positive outcome (having a good time) from the previously listed amenities (day rooms, bar, food access). The argument is implied by the contrast between “sweat it out” and “pretty good time,” suggesting that the facilities mitigate hardships.
main_claim: Given the planned amenities, the men are likely to have a relatively enjoyable time in Foggia.

argument_text: I wonder if, with these inducements, the Provost Marshall hadn’t better get set to receive a number of new applications for his unit; or would you just rather get a job as mail clerk in your own squadron?
explanation: The rhetorical question implies that the offered perks will attract new applicants, contrasting this with the alternative of choosing a more comfortable mail clerk position. The inducements are presented as reasons for increased applications; the question format and contrast signal the implied conclusion.
main_claim: The new inducements will likely increase applications to the Provost Marshal’s unit.

argument_text: The men around 1898th have a vague suspicion that either their Battalion is an exception or that the old army saying about first sgt's is wrong. Without exception the four first Sergeants in the Battalion have been among the best liked men in their companies. Two of them Sgt. Stokes of Company "C", and Sgt. Paschell of Hq & Sv Company have already left for home while Sgt. Woods of Company "A" and Sgt. Williams of Company "B" both expect to be home by Christmas.
explanation: This passage advances a claim that contradicts an “old army saying” about first sergeants (typically that they are disliked). The reasoning is: if all four first sergeants in this battalion are among the best liked men, then either this unit is an exception or the saying is wrong. The evaluative language (“best liked”) and the explicit contrast with the “old army saying” signal an argument; the conclusion is implied via the alternatives rather than asserted as a single declarative claim.
main_claim: The old army saying that first sergeants are disliked does not hold in the 1898th (i.e., either the battalion is an exception or the saying is wrong).

argument_text: At first the high pointers (above 49) could not understand why the low pointers (below 50, poor fellows) kept standing in front of mirrors shouting orders at themselves or strutted up and down as if they ruled the entire area. The high pointers thought they were trying to be section eight's, that being about the only way some of them will ever get out of the army, until one low pointer broke down and confessed that all the low pointers were practicing to be first sergeants since all the present ones are leaving soon, that explained everything....
explanation: This passage offers an explanation for observed behavior (low pointers acting like bosses). The initial hypothesis (they’re trying for section eight) is rejected in light of new evidence (a confession that they’re practicing to be first sergeants because current first sergeants are leaving). The causal connector “that explained everything” signals an explicit inference from premises to conclusion.
main_claim: The low pointers’ strutting and self-commanding was because they were practicing to become first sergeants, not trying to get section-eight discharges.

argument_text: When he went up he had 56 points when he returned he only had 54. Such is the fortune or life, James!
explanation: The passage presents a factual premise (his points decreased from 56 to 54 during the trip) immediately followed by an evaluative generalization ("Such is the fortune or life"), implying a conclusion that life/fortune is capricious or unfair. The argument is implicit because it relies on juxtaposition and evaluative framing rather than explicit connectors (e.g., "therefore") to infer a general claim from the specific incident.
main_claim: Life’s fortunes are capricious, as illustrated by James losing two points during his trip.

argument_text: The fire, caused by the explosion of a can of gasoline left near the stove, was qickly extinguished with no casualties and minor damage to the wood-work.
explanation: This sentence asserts a specific causal relationship: a can of gasoline left near the stove exploded and caused the fire. The structure presents the premise (explosion of a gasoline can left near the stove) leading to the conclusion (this caused the fire). The additional details about outcomes do not change the central explicit causal claim.
main_claim: The fire was caused by the explosion of a gasoline can left near the stove.

argument_text: Sgt. Francis Peo, non-com in charges was on the scene immediately, and the station was open for business two hours later.
explanation: The juxtaposition of immediate response and rapid reopening implies a positive evaluation of the response and that disruption and damage were minimal. The premises (immediate presence of Sgt. Peo; reopening within two hours) support the implied conclusion that the incident was efficiently handled and not serious. The conclusion is not directly stated, making it implicit.
main_claim: The station’s prompt and effective response ensured minimal disruption and swift resumption of services.

argument_text:
Gino Bagano, was seriously beaten by two American soldiers in an incident that nearly caused a riot Sunday night. The M.P.'s were called at 2015 hours to an off-limits bar in the alley-way one block south of the MP Station. Mr. Bagano was found seriously injured, but the soldiers had disappeared.

Shortly after, a crowd of civilians gathered in front of BOQ 20.
explanation: This passage advances a causal claim that the assault "nearly caused a riot." The subsequent details—MPs called, serious injury, and a crowd gathering shortly after—function as implicit premises supporting that causal conclusion. The argument relies on temporal sequencing and outcome framing (crowd formation) to suggest that the incident led to near-riot conditions, without explicitly laying out a formal premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The assault by the soldiers precipitated conditions that nearly caused a riot.

argument_text: Mr. Bagano was found seriously injured, but the soldiers had disappeared.
explanation: The contrastive "but" frames the disappearance of the soldiers against the discovery of the injured victim, implying evasion or consciousness of guilt. This functions as an implicit argument that the soldiers fled to avoid accountability, using contrast as the cue rather than an explicit statement of culpable flight.
main_claim: The soldiers fled the scene to avoid responsibility for the assault.

argument_text: They claimed that the culprits had escaped through the building, and that they were waiting for them to come out again.
explanation: This sentence presents a reason-action linkage: premise (culprits escaped through the building) leading to the conclusion/decision (therefore they were waiting for them to come out again). The connective "and that" ties the rationale to the resultant behavior, forming an explicit argument justifying the crowd's waiting.
main_claim: The crowd waited because they believed the culprits had escaped into the building and would come out again.

argument_text:
The Group Information and Education office had spent two weeks of its time and the labor of an artist, two interpreters, and three carpenters to prepare a bulletin board for the local Italians. The board had fourteen posters with pictures of life in the United States cut from American magazines, and explanations beneath were in Italian.

That night it rained hard in Foggia, and the next morning the monument was only a memory. The pictures had washed off and the ink had run down into lacy unintelligible twirls.
explanation: This passage juxtaposes significant effort and resources invested with the immediate destruction of the product by rain. The implied reasoning is that the project was futile or wasteful because it was not durable enough to survive normal weather, so the investment did not achieve lasting impact. The evaluative conclusion is not stated but suggested by the narrative contrast.
main_claim: The bulletin board project was a futile use of time and labor because it quickly disintegrated in the rain.

argument_text: When finally erected, it was a huge success. Young and old crowded around to read about life in the States. Little dogs, however, still thought it was a latrine.
explanation: The contrast marker “however” undercuts the claim of “huge success” by immediately noting dogs treated it as a latrine, implying design, placement, or appropriateness problems. The implicit argument is that the proclaimed success is questionable or incomplete given this undermining evidence.
main_claim: The supposed success of the bulletin board was compromised, suggesting it was not as well-conceived or effective as claimed.

argument_text: As the house-like structure was being carried through the streets the local populace didn’t know what to think. Some one suggested a new outdoor latrine. Every few yards the fourteen men paused to rest, and little kids gathered around quoting prices on the wood.
explanation: This sequence uses reported reactions (latrine suggestion, children pricing the wood) to imply a mismatch between the intended cultural-educational purpose and local perceptions/needs (utility or material value). The argument is suggested through framing and selective detail, not stated directly.
main_claim: The project did not align with local perceptions or needs, as people saw it as a latrine or raw materials rather than an educational monument.

argument_text: One minute of silence, please.
explanation: This rhetorical request evokes mourning for the “monument,” implying it has effectively died or failed; it functions as an evaluative conclusion to the preceding narrative of collapse. The argument is conveyed through tone and implication rather than explicit premises.
main_claim: The bulletin board’s demise merits lament, implying the project ended in failure.

argument_text: The new styles caused a veritable sensation, not to mention the chic young things who were wearing them.
explanation: This presents a positive evaluation of the show and implies a reason: the event was sensational because of both the styles and the attractive models. The phrase “not to mention” functions as a justificatory cue linking the perceived sensation to contributing causes (styles and those wearing them), forming an implicit premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The show was highly exciting and impactful because of the new styles and the chic young women modeling them.

argument_text: The show opened novelly for the usually "ultra" conservative gathering, when a service-man (person who has served with our boys overseas) suggested to the entrepreneur, Mlle. Marie Dolliver, the particular styles he would like to see his wife wear when he sees her again.
explanation: The sentence advances the claim that the opening was novel, supporting it with a contrast: the gathering is “usually ‘ultra’ conservative” but this time a serviceman publicly suggested styles. The contrast between typical conservatism and the unusual suggestion serves as a premise that justifies the conclusion of novelty.
main_claim: The opening was unusually novel because, unlike the typically ultra-conservative tone, a serviceman openly proposed styles for his wife.

argument_text: To offset the blushing laughter of the audience, Charleen (who else), opened the show, shimmered gracefully onto the plush stage with an opaque (damn it) white nightie.
explanation: The phrase “To offset” posits a causal-rhetorical purpose: Charleen’s entrance in a specific outfit served to counterbalance the audience’s embarrassed laughter. This implies a claim about the function/effectiveness of the entrance (premise: there was blushing laughter; action: Charleen’s appearance; implied conclusion: it offset the mood).
main_claim: Charleen’s graceful entrance in a white nightie was intended to and did counter the audience’s embarrassed laughter.

argument_text: It had the ruffled hem hand bodice that is the rage of Italy.
explanation: By asserting the feature is “the rage of Italy,” the text appeals to popularity/fashion authority to imply that the design is desirable or commendable. The implicit reasoning is that what is widely fashionable is good/appropriate, thus endorsing the garment.
main_claim: The garment’s ruffled hem and bodice are desirable because they are currently highly fashionable in Italy.

argument_text: Women will play, you know. Tennis, too. Thus, out bounced Miss My Reynolds and Miss Peg Starney in blue and white play-suits (still for tennis) with their shorts held up by colorful scarfs.
explanation: This provides a clear premise-conclusion sequence with the connective “Thus.” Premise: women will play tennis; Conclusion: therefore, the show features tennis play-suits. The “thus” explicitly marks the justificatory link between the claim about women’s activities and the appropriateness of displaying playwear.
main_claim: Because women play tennis, it makes sense to include tennis play-suits in the show.

argument_text: One of the audience asked to borrow the scarf.
explanation: This anecdote functions as implied evidence that the accessory was attractive or desirable; audience behavior is used to suggest approval or desirability of the scarves, supporting an evaluative stance without stating it directly.
main_claim: The colorful scarf was appealing and desirable, as evidenced by an audience member asking to borrow it.

argument_text:
Making the long trip through winding narrow mountain roads a party of Foggia’s Christmas-spirited folk journeyed almost a hundred and fifty miles on Monday to obtain Christmas trees for the Enlisted Men’s Red Cross, the 55th Station Hospital, and the 20th Bombardment Squadron.

The convoy of six trucks, guided by Program Director Joseph Hamilton, and Gino Santoro both of the Red Cross EM Club, left Foggia early, travelled about 15 miles out the Manfredonia Road, then turned north-ward to the mountains and the Umbrian Forest. Extremely difficult road conditions and biting cold weather were encountered. The convoy was halted many times for reassem-bly in the heavy fog or the purpose of pushing out vehicles stuck in snow fifteen inches deep.
explanation: The passage labels the group as “Christmas-spirited” and immediately provides evidence of arduous travel and harsh conditions to obtain trees. The evaluative label functions as a conclusion implied by the actions described; the details of distance, fog, and deep snow serve as premises indicating dedication. This is an argument by character inference: because they undertook a difficult mission for communal benefit, they exemplify the “Christmas spirit.”
main_claim: The group’s difficult journey to secure Christmas trees shows they exemplify the Christmas spirit.

argument_text: Members of the 55th Station Hospital group, who were collecting forty trees and decorations for the ward of their hospital and also the Foggia civilian hospital, included Miss Virginia Woolfolk of the Red Cross, Chaplain J. S. Bouson, Captain J. W. Kitchen, Lt. E. W. Wilson, First Sergeant T. P. Elder, Sergeant J. B. Ferguson and Pfc. M. E. Dennis. Captain Kitchen will act as Santa Claus in the affair at the Foggia Hospital on the afternoon of December 24, when he will present Christmas stockings and packages to the 200 patients. Arrangements have been made by Captain Joseph T. Guzek, new C. O. of the hospital and Executive Chairman of their Christmas Committee. Miss Woolfolk, along with Captain Frances Everett, chief nurse, are co-vice-chairmen of this hard working unit.
explanation: The text concludes with the evaluative phrase “this hard working unit” after listing concrete activities and organizational roles (collecting trees and decorations, planning a Santa event, making arrangements, committee leadership). The preceding details function as premises supporting the evaluative conclusion that the unit is hardworking.
main_claim: The 55th Station Hospital group is a hardworking unit.

argument_text: A warming fire was offered to the cold travellers by hospitable members of E. M. E. S. 7622, an isolated RAF radar unit of thirty men stationed in that wilderness of the Umbrian Forest. The party had a chance to dry and thaw before starting the trip back.
explanation: Calling the radar unit “hospitable” is an evaluative claim, supported by the specific helpful action of offering a warming fire to cold travelers. The action serves as the premise that justifies the characterization of hospitality.
main_claim: The RAF radar unit members were hospitable.

argument_text:
After getting the trees and a sufficient number of spruce boughs and
holly, and notwithstanding many difficulties, including two flat tires, vehicles again stuck in the snow, a 2½ ton truck sliding off an icy shoulder of the road, and biting cold, the final descent from the mountains was made in the darkness.
Foggia will have trees for Christmas 1945!
explanation: The passage lists obstacles overcome (premises) and then triumphantly asserts the outcome that the city will have trees. The causal/contrastive phrasing “notwithstanding many difficulties” implies that overcoming these challenges led to the successful result. The exclamatory conclusion signals the claim grounded in the preceding evidence.
main_claim: Despite many difficulties, the party’s efforts ensured that Foggia will have Christmas trees.

argument_text: As soon as official word was released that the (Group was going to move Somewhere soon, all sorts of rumors began flying, most of them “proving” that we were going home. Every one had is own private reason for believing that, and although nothing official confirmed that wild hope, we heard some pretty good stories.
explanation: This passage contrasts abundant rumors with the lack of official confirmation, using evaluative language (“wild hope”) to imply that the rumors are unreliable. The premise is that nothing official has confirmed the claim of going home; the implied conclusion is that these rumors shouldn’t be believed.
main_claim: The rumors that we are going home are unfounded because there is no official confirmation.

argument_text: One lucky person who gets mail from home told us that his second cousin (on his father’s side) wrote that he expects to arrive in Europe soon to replace high point Air Corps men. This fine second cousin has five points.
explanation: The anecdote is presented with irony to undercut the credibility of the rumor: a distant relative with only five points claiming he will replace high-point men is weak evidence. The implicit conclusion is that such hearsay does not support the belief that the unit is going home.
main_claim: Hearsay from a distant, low-point relative is not credible evidence that we are going home.

argument_text: An even better rumor was from an anonymous correspondent who works in the supply rooms. He told us that a huge consignment of toilet paper was rerouted to the States. The assumption was, therefore, that as soon as the available paper stock runs out we shall be forced to follow the consignment.
explanation: This passage presents a premise (toilet paper consignment rerouted to the States) and an explicit inference signaled by “therefore” leading to a conclusion (we will have to follow the consignment home when paper runs out). Although framed humorously as a “rumor,” it contains a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Because toilet paper was rerouted to the States, once our stock runs out we will be forced to go home.

argument_text: Using that last one as the basis of our dreams, we have petitioned the mess halls to leave a little more soap on the mess-gear.
explanation: This is a recommendation/action justified by the prior causal claim: if the toilet paper shortage would force them home, then increasing conditions that deplete or necessitate paper (via soapy mess-gear causing digestive issues) advances that goal. The implicit conclusion is that they should take this step to hasten going home.
main_claim: We should encourage leaving more soap on mess gear to help bring about the paper shortage that will send us home.

argument_text:
1. It is our belief that the G.I.’s of this area do not
   agree with a certain article in last Saturdays’ Occu-
   pator-the one about the AES Cookie program.
2. In our own personal survey, we have yet to find
   one, repeat, one, Cookie fan.
explanation: This presents a clear claim (that local G.I.s do not agree with the AES Cookie article) supported by a stated reason/evidence (a personal survey found no Cookie fans). The structure is premise (survey result) leading to conclusion (disagreement with the article), making it an explicit argument.
main_claim: The G.I.s of the area do not agree with the Occupator’s article about the AES Cookie program.

argument_text:
3. We suggest that in the future that the Occupator
   check all such stories before they are sent to press,
   and that they be written by someone other than a
   friend of the one concerned.
explanation: This is a prescriptive recommendation implying underlying reasons: the prior article was insufficiently checked and biased (written by a friend), and given the preceding dissatisfaction, such processes should change. The rationale is not fully spelled out in this sentence but is suggested by the evaluative framing and recommendation, thus it is an implicit argument.
main_claim: The Occupator should fact-check such stories before publication and have them written by someone not personally connected to the subject.

argument_text:
The first lesson any would-be journalist learns is that a news-story consists, as Caesar's Gaul, in three parts. First, the lead which summarizes the story, then the development of all the pertinent facts, and finally a conclusion.

Now, as an object lesson on how not to write a news-story, let us consider the item on the Barber and the Ten Cent Tip.
explanation: The passage first states a normative standard for news writing (premise: a proper news story has a lead, development of facts, and a conclusion), then immediately frames the referenced item as “an object lesson on how not to write” (conclusion). The evaluative conclusion is implied by juxtaposing the standard with the item, without explicit connective language.
main_claim: The “Barber and the Ten Cent Tip” piece serves as an example of how not to write a news story because it fails to meet basic journalistic structure.

argument_text: The lead we cannot discuss since there was none worthy of the name.
explanation: This is a concise argument: conclusion—there is no lead to discuss—supported by the stated reason that there was “none worthy of the name.” The because-since structure makes the premise-to-conclusion relation explicit.
main_claim: The article lacked a proper lead.

argument_text: We can assume that the author's heart bleeds over the fate of the barbers of Italy. All this well and good, for everyone should have a hobby in these trying times. Therefore, he should know first that all wages are determined by AFHQ and local custom. This is true of all civilians employed by Allied organizations.
explanation: Amid sarcasm about the author’s sympathies, the writer asserts that wages are determined by AFHQ and local custom (and that this is generally true), implying the conclusion that the original article’s treatment of wages was misinformed and that the author ought to have known this. The critique is implied rather than explicitly stated as “therefore the article was wrong.”
main_claim: Wages for civilian barbers are set by AFHQ and local custom, a fact the original writer should have known.

argument_text: The fact that non-administrative Red Cross personnel do not know what wages the barbers receive or that their wages are higher than that paid to barbers in extraneous. The manner in which that issue was brought into the article indicates a kind of displeasure at female Red Cross personnel.
explanation: The author claims that the referenced information is extraneous (irrelevant) and infers from how it was presented that the original piece displays displeasure toward female Red Cross staff. The reasoning is implied: irrelevant details suggest bias rather than informing the central issue.
main_claim: The mention of Red Cross personnel’s wage knowledge and comparisons was irrelevant and signals a bias against female Red Cross personnel.

argument_text: First, he should check with the civilian labor unit of his own organization regarding the MTOUSA directives regarding wages of civilian personnel. Two, he should have talked to authoritative Red Cross people who could have given him the facts regarding the supplies, the space, and the costs of running a barbershop in their installations.
explanation: The passage makes concrete recommendations (what the writer should have done) and provides a reason for the second recommendation (“who could have given him the facts”), indicating that consulting proper authorities yields necessary factual grounding.
main_claim: The writer should have consulted the civilian labor unit and authoritative Red Cross sources to obtain the relevant facts before writing.

argument_text: What other lessons can we derive from this little gem, lessons that can be passed on to your other contributors? First, I would impress on their minds to secure and to know all the facts making sure that what they write is not verbalized emotion, and two, write clearly and logically and, what is most important, both the editor's and writer's responsibility to the truth.
explanation: The author recommends practices (secure facts, avoid emotional writing, write clearly and logically, uphold responsibility to truth) implying that these are necessary to good journalism and that the criticized article failed at them. The normative stance and implied causal link to quality make it an argument.
main_claim: Contributors ought to gather all facts, avoid emotional writing, write clearly and logically, and uphold responsibility to the truth.

argument_text: (Ed's Note: We heartily agree, but you must excuse us. You see we were brought up on the Chicago Tribune, Washington Herald-Times, and the New York Daily News)
explanation: The editors ask for an excuse and give a reason—their journalistic upbringing on certain newspapers—implying that their background explains or mitigates their approach. The causal mitigation is suggested rather than argued in detail.
main_claim: The editors should be excused for their editorial approach because their journalistic background shaped their style.

argument_text: You feel that Italians are underpaid and have difficulty supporting themselves on their wages. No one in his right mind would dispute that.
explanation: This passage advances agreement with the claim that Italians are underpaid by appealing to presumed universal consensus (“No one in his right mind would dispute that”). The premise (it is beyond dispute) implicitly supports the conclusion (the claim should be accepted). The argument is implicit because it relies on evaluative language and an appeal to common sense rather than explicit evidence.
main_claim: Italians are underpaid and have difficulty supporting themselves on their wages.

argument_text: You feel that Red Cross workers are overpaid. That is open to dispute. I earn 225 dollars per month (not 175 dollars), yet if I were to explain the details of my job I think you would agree that I am not being overpaid.
explanation: This argues against the blanket claim that Red Cross workers are overpaid by offering a counterexample: the writer’s own salary and implied demanding job details. The contrastive “yet” signals a rebuttal. The support is implicit because the “details” are not provided; the reasoning relies on the suggestion that job responsibilities justify the pay, thereby making the overpaid claim disputable.
main_claim: The claim that Red Cross workers are overpaid is disputable, and at least in my case the pay is not excessive.

argument_text: Your article implies that Red Cross is starving its civilian workers, is indifferent to the situation of the Italians just as long as Red Cross is well paid. That's not true. Surely you know that the wage scale for Italians is set by the Army and not Red Cross. And do you think that Red Cross girl really would have objected if you had given the barber a larger tip?
explanation: This refutes the article’s implied accusation by providing reasons: the Army sets Italian wage scales (thereby undermining blame placed on the Red Cross) and a rhetorical question suggesting a Red Cross worker would not oppose a larger tip (undercutting the idea of indifference or obstruction). The main claim (“That’s not true”) is explicitly supported by causal/attributional correction and a rhetorical question.
main_claim: The article’s implication that the Red Cross mistreats civilians and is indifferent to Italians’ situation is false.

argument_text: Your article confuses two issues. If you feel that Italians are underpaid why not write about that. And if you feel that Red Cross is overpaid, or incompetent, or callous in its attitude toward the Italians by all means let's have an article about that, giving facts and figures. But let's not confuse the issues.
explanation: This argues for separating distinct topics and providing evidence. Premises: there are two distinct issues (Italian wages vs. Red Cross behavior/pay); therefore the conclusion is that the editor should address them separately and support claims with facts and figures and “not confuse the issues.” The directives and contrastive framing make the reasoning explicit.
main_claim: The editor should not conflate Italian wage issues with criticisms of the Red Cross and should treat each with evidence.

argument_text: (Again the Editor: The article, The Barber and The Ten Cent Tip, only endeavored to show the inflationary state and high cost of living in Foggia. That and only that was our purpose).
explanation: The editor asserts the article’s sole purpose (to show inflation and high living costs), implicitly rebutting the accusation of issue confusion or anti–Red Cross intent. The conclusion about purpose is stated and justified by the claim that the article “only endeavored” to show that.
main_claim: The sole purpose of the earlier article was to illustrate inflation and the high cost of living in Foggia.

argument_text: It is for us, the living rather to be dedicated here to the unfinished work which they who fought here have thus far so nobly advanced.
explanation: This urges the living to dedicate themselves to finishing the work. The justification is embedded: those who fought have nobly advanced that work, implying a duty to continue it. The causal/ought relationship is implied rather than stated with an explicit “because.”
main_claim: The living should dedicate themselves to completing the unfinished work advanced by those who fought.

argument_text: It is rather for us to be here dedicated to the great task remaining before us — that from these honored dead we take increased devotion to that cause for which they gave the last full measure of devotion;
explanation: This advocates increased devotion to a cause, with the premise that the honored dead gave their lives for it. The moral obligation is implied: because they sacrificed fully, we ought to heighten our dedication. The argument relies on evaluative and normative language rather than explicit logical connectors.
main_claim: We should increase our devotion to the cause for which the honored dead sacrificed their lives.

argument_text: that we here highly resolve that these dead shall not have died in vain;
explanation: This is a normative commitment implying an obligation to act so that the sacrifices have meaningful consequences. The premise—that the dead’s sacrifice should have purpose—supports the conclusion that we must resolve to ensure it was not in vain, though the reasoning is not spelled out with explicit premises.
main_claim: We must resolve to ensure that the fallen did not die in vain.

argument_text: that this nation, under God, shall have a new birth of freedom;
explanation: This projects a desired outcome tied to the call for dedication and resolve. It implies that by our renewed dedication, the nation will experience a revitalization of freedom. The causal link between our actions and this outcome is suggested, not explicitly argued.
main_claim: Our renewed dedication should lead to a new birth of freedom for the nation.

argument_text: and that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.
explanation: This presents a goal that democratic government endure, implying that our dedication and resolve are necessary to secure its survival. The underlying premise—that our actions can prevent the perishing of such government—is assumed rather than explicitly defended.
main_claim: We must ensure that democratic self-government endures and does not perish.

argument_text: Two ex-GIs of this war and 2 vets of the last, all appearing on the radio program Information Please, were asked what a "Hershey Bar" is. None of them knew.
explanation: This reports that four veterans, including two regular panelists and two WWII veterans, were unable to answer what a “Hershey Bar” is. The implied conclusion is that the term is obscure or not widely recognized, supported by the premise that even presumably knowledgeable or experienced individuals did not know it. The argument is implicit because the conclusion (“it’s obscure/not widely known”) is suggested rather than stated.
main_claim: The term “Hershey Bar” is not widely known or easily recognized.

argument_text: You may be in good company if you too don’t know, but anyway, here’s the answer: A Hershey Bar, named for the Selective Service director, is a gold sleeve insignia denoting 6 months overseas duty.
explanation: The editor reassures readers that not knowing the term is acceptable (“in good company”), implicitly arguing that ignorance here is understandable or common. This relies on the prior report that even notable veterans didn’t know. The evaluative reassurance functions as a conclusion, with the earlier anecdote serving as unstated support.
main_claim: Readers shouldn’t feel bad about not knowing what a “Hershey Bar” is because many others don’t know it either.

argument_text:
The POE went into high gear, like this:

The transport was ordered to put in at Halifax, the nearest port.
The Navy transport, Patrick, was directed to intercept the Army transport to help out.
The Patrick readied a supply of rations, rigged breeches buoys, and was all set for the transfer.
explanation: The sequence frames a problem-response narrative using evaluative wording ("went into high gear") and a list of coordinated actions, implying a claim about the POE’s speed and effectiveness. Although no explicit conclusion is stated, the premise set (multiple rapid, appropriate measures) supports the implicit conclusion that the POE responded efficiently and competently.
main_claim: The POE responded swiftly and effectively to the reported emergency.

argument_text: The transport was ordered to put in at Halifax, the nearest port.
explanation: The phrase "the nearest port" functions as a reason justifying the order to put in at Halifax; proximity is presented as the rationale for the decision. This implies an argument from expediency/efficiency: because Halifax is nearest, it was the appropriate destination.
main_claim: Ordering the transport to put in at Halifax was justified because it was the nearest port.

argument_text: The Navy transport, Patrick, was directed to intercept the Army transport to help out.
explanation: The infinitive phrase "to help out" provides a purpose-based justification for the directive, implying that interception was warranted as a means of providing assistance. The premise (interception would help) supports the conclusion (therefore it was directed to intercept).
main_claim: Directing the Patrick to intercept was warranted in order to provide assistance.

argument_text: Hours later the POE got another radio message from the Army vessel. It said: "Never mind. We found the food."
explanation: The punchline supplies new information that negates the initial premise of an emergency, implying that the preceding mobilization was unnecessary and that the initial report was mistaken. The causal/evaluative implication is that the alarm was unfounded due to an internal oversight (they had the food all along).
main_claim: The earlier emergency was unfounded because the vessel had not actually run out of food.

argument_text: Declaring that the rate of demobilization was twice the peak reached after World War I, the War Department announced that 3,114,000 of the 8,300,000 men in the Army on VE-Day had been discharged through Nov 16.
explanation: This presents a comparative claim about the current demobilization rate (twice the WWI peak) and immediately provides a quantitative figure as supporting evidence. The logical structure is: the current number of discharges is very large within a short post-VE-Day window, therefore the rate exceeds, by a factor of two, the earlier peak after WWI. The argument is implicit because it relies on the reader to infer the rate comparison from totals and timeframe rather than stating a formal premise-conclusion connection.
main_claim: The current Army demobilization rate is twice the highest rate reached after World War I.

argument_text: Since VE-Day more soldiers have been discharged than were in the AEF, the WD said, recalling that on Nov 11, 1918 the Army had 1,929,760 men overseas out of a total strength of 3,673,888.
explanation: This sentence explicitly advances the claim that the number discharged since VE-Day exceeds the size of the AEF, and it supplies numerical premises (AEF overseas and total strength figures) to support the comparison. The marker “Since VE-Day more soldiers have been discharged than were in the AEF” is a clear comparative conclusion grounded in the recalled figures.
main_claim: More soldiers have been discharged since VE-Day than the number who served in the AEF during World War I.

argument_text: The WD said that discharges were now running “for ahead of the rate planned” and declared that 1,270,000 soldiers became civilians in October, with discharge figures contemplated at 1,200,000 in November and more than a million in December.
explanation: This asserts a conclusion—that discharges are running far ahead of plan—and pairs it with monthly discharge counts and projections as evidence. The reasoning is that high actual and projected monthly numbers indicate performance beyond planned rates. It’s implicit because it does not detail the planned target figures; instead, it relies on the juxtaposition of stated outcomes with the evaluative claim “far ahead of the rate planned.”
main_claim: Army discharges are running far ahead of the planned rate.

argument_text: The constant redeployment of allied troops from this area has forced the Flagella Theater to limit its matinees from seven days a weeks to three. The Ensa Theater and The Little very rarely get sufficient attendance in the afternoons to have them maintain their matinee performances. It is unfortunate that these movie houses cannot be put to use in crowded Foggia. At night these same movie houses rarely play to capacity. This condition is due to the excellent facilities offered by the bars and clubs in the military units, the diminishing number of personnel and the tendancy of many clubs to feature movies every night as part of their program. Let’s quit hoarding on these movies houses by returning The Ensa and The Little to the civilian population.
explanation: The passage presents multiple premises (low attendance at matinees and nights, troop redeployment, competing entertainment facilities, fewer personnel, clubs showing films nightly) that lead to a clear conclusion/recommendation: stop “hoarding” and return the theaters to civilians. The inferential structure supports the policy claim with causal and factual considerations.
main_claim: The Ensa and The Little should be returned to the civilian population instead of being kept for military use.

argument_text: It is unfortunate that these movie houses cannot be put to use in crowded Foggia.
explanation: The evaluative term “unfortunate” and the phrase “cannot be put to use” imply a normative stance: the theaters ought to be used by (or for) the public in a crowded city, and the current situation is undesirable. The argument is implicit because the “ought” is suggested rather than stated.
main_claim: The current underuse of these theaters in crowded Foggia is undesirable and they should be put to better use.

argument_text: That in itself would be an excellant Christmas present to Foggia!
explanation: This rhetorical claim implies that returning the theaters to civilians would significantly benefit the city. The positive framing (“Christmas present”) signals a value judgment that supports the recommendation without restating premises.
main_claim: Returning the theaters to civilians would meaningfully benefit Foggia.

argument_text: One of the truest tests that any group of people can pass who desire democracy is the ability to maintain a government by law. The tendancy of an individual or group of individuals to take the law in their own hands is either a weakness of the people themselves or of the efficiency of the police who are maintained to uphold the law.
explanation: This passage advances a normative standard (democracy requires maintaining government by law) and a causal attribution (vigilantism indicates weakness in the people or police). It implies the conclusion that communities should uphold the rule of law and not take the law into their own hands, using evaluative language and diagnostic reasoning rather than explicit premise-conclusion markers.
main_claim: A people who desire democracy must uphold government by law and avoid taking the law into their own hands, which signals societal or police weakness.

argument_text: The other day two drunken soldiers walked into an off-limits bar and assaulted a civilian. A group of friends of the civilian attempted to take the law into their own hands by trying to apprehend these two soldiers who by their conduct are a disgrace to the uniform they wear.
explanation: The descriptive first sentence provides factual premises (drunkenness, entering an off-limits bar, assault), and the second delivers a normative judgment (“are a disgrace to the uniform they wear”). The evaluation is justified by the cited conduct, forming an argument through evaluative inference rather than explicit connective terms.
main_claim: The soldiers’ conduct disgraced the uniform they wear.

argument_text: Yet, at the same time that very group of civilians who attempted to apprehend the soldiers were guilty of the intent to commit the same act which then they had accused the soldiers.
explanation: This sentence argues that because the civilians attempted to apprehend the soldiers, they were thereby guilty of intending the same wrongful act they accused the soldiers of; the contrastive marker “Yet” signals a conclusion drawn from the preceding facts.
main_claim: The civilians were themselves guilty of intending the same wrongdoing they accused the soldiers of.

argument_text: The law of the mob can never find any justice in their acts.
explanation: This categorical judgment concludes that mob action is inherently unjust, drawing on the preceding example as implied evidence; it is a normative claim without explicit premises stated in this sentence.
main_claim: Mob justice is inherently unjust.

argument_text: Such conduct has its place in the Nazi State. It has no justification for existence here.
explanation: This is an argument by contrast/association: aligning mob conduct with the Nazi State implies it is incompatible with the present society and therefore unjustified. The evaluative and oppositional framing implies the conclusion without explicit logical connectors.
main_claim: Mob-style conduct is unacceptable and unjustified in our society.

argument_text: There is still about a couple of weeks left to help in bringing Christmas to the unfortunate children of Foggia.
explanation: This sentence urges readers to help; the evaluative phrasing “to help” and reference to “unfortunate children” implies a normative conclusion that readers ought to act. The stated premise is that there is still time (“a couple of weeks left”), which functions as a reason enabling or motivating the implied call to help.
main_claim: Readers should help bring Christmas to the unfortunate children of Foggia.

argument_text: Many of you have packages that you are getting from home. There are still a couple of PX days of candy and soap that you could bring to the EM Red Cross.
explanation: This passage presents reasons (you have incoming packages; there are PX days to obtain candy and soap) leading to a recommendation (“you could bring to the EM Red Cross”). The structure provides premises that support the action-oriented conclusion to donate items.
main_claim: You should bring candy, soap, and other items to the EM Red Cross for donation.

argument_text: You yourself will not have a Christmas tree when you wake up in the morning of December 25th. All of us will feel a little sad and a great deal homesick, but the thought that a lot of young hearts are going to be very warm and happy thanks to you will bring a smile to your lips and a lot of warmth to your heart as you lie in bed Christmas morning.
explanation: This contrasts anticipated sadness and homesickness with a promised emotional benefit derived from making children happy “thanks to you,” implying that donating will alleviate personal sorrow. The conclusion (you ought to help/donate) is implied via motivational appeal rather than stated directly, using evaluative language and causal attribution (“thanks to you” leading to warmth and a smile).
main_claim: By helping make local children happy at Christmas, you will feel better despite your own homesickness, so you should contribute.

argument_text: The debate in the House of Commons was more successful in demonstrating the alarm and despondency that had been generated in all sections of the community by the atomic bomb than in providing workable suggestions for dealing with it.
explanation: This evaluative comparison implies a claim that the debate failed to produce solutions, supported by the contrast with its success in showing alarm. The argumentative cue is the comparative framing “more successful … than,” which presupposes a judgment about effectiveness without laying out formal premises.
main_claim: The Commons debate revealed public alarm but failed to yield workable responses to the atomic bomb.

argument_text: The minor problem is whether the secret should be entrusted to Russia, and the answer that different people will give ought logically to turn on the opinions they form of the likelihood that giving the Russians the secret (supposing it to be really a secret) would make them any easier to live with. Withholding it from them appears to have contributed to the deterioration of international relations in the last three months—but it does not necessarily follow that to give it to them would make them any sweeter.
explanation: This presents a decision rule (premise: the answer should depend on whether sharing would improve relations) and evidence (withholding worsened relations) but argues to the conclusion that sharing does not necessarily improve relations. The “does not necessarily follow” indicates explicit argumentative structure countering a presumed inference.
main_claim: Even if withholding has worsened relations with Russia, it does not follow that sharing the atomic secret would improve them.

argument_text: It is noticeable that the closer one approaches to the men—of every party—who have the responsibility of actually negotiating with the Russians and who would therefore be most anxious to snatch at any chance that exists of making their task easier, the greater is their apparent reluctance to share the secret. The outsider will be tempted to observe that the policy of withholding the secret is most obviously incompatible with the theory of mutual confidence and unanimous agreement among the Big Three upon which—and upon which alone—the structure of the United Nations is founded. Mr Bevin's policy of withholding the secret until the U.N.O. is strong enough to hold it is self-contradictory.
explanation: Premise 1: Those most engaged in negotiations are reluctant to share. Premise 2: Withholding is incompatible with the United Nations’ foundation of mutual confidence. Conclusion: Bevin’s policy is self-contradictory. The passage explicitly links premises to the evaluative conclusion of contradiction.
main_claim: Withholding the atomic secret contradicts the UN’s premise of mutual confidence, making Bevin’s policy self-contradictory.

argument_text: First, the atom bomb is quite capable of destroying the human race within the lifetime of the present generation—or if not of destroying the human race at least of so shattering all social and economic organisation that homo sapiens would be thrust back nearly to his biological infancy.
explanation: This asserts a high-stakes consequence to justify urgency in policy thinking; the claim is advanced without detailed premises in this sentence, relying on the evaluative and predictive framing to imply the seriousness as a reason for subsequent conclusions.
main_claim: The atomic bomb could annihilate humanity or collapse civilization within the current generation.

argument_text: Secondly, it would appear to be impossible to separate the warlike and the peaceful uses of atomic energy—or at least to separate them sufficiently to prevent one and permit the other.
explanation: This is a policy-relevant claim about inseparability of uses; it advances a stance without explicit supporting evidence here, functioning as a premise for later arguments against internationalisation and regulation.
main_claim: Peaceful and military applications of atomic energy cannot be effectively separated.

argument_text: Thirdly, though the atom bomb will make the next war far more horrible, it may have the effect of delaying it. Modern wars do not begin by accident or because somebody's gun happens to go off. They start because some head of a State thinks he will win, thinks he himself won't be badly hurt in the process of winning. That is what Hitler thought in 1939—and how nearly right he was! Though the atom bomb makes it easier to win very quickly if the victim has no atom rockets, it makes it impossible, so long as the victim has no atom rockets, it makes it impossible, so long as the victim has any power of retaliation, for the aggressor to believe that he will be unscathed. Thus, so long as non-aggressive nations (naming no names) keep themselves fairly well supplied with atomic rockets, it is possible that a precarious equilibrium peace might be maintained balance of power may be the best hope for this generation.
explanation: Premises: Leaders start wars when they expect to win without being hurt; Hitler example; atomic retaliation makes safety unlikely for aggressors. Conclusion: Deterrence via mutual atomic capability may delay war and sustain a precarious balance. The “thus” signals inference.
main_claim: Mutual atomic deterrence could delay war and sustain a precarious balance of power for this generation.

argument_text: But, fourthly, the balance can hardly be maintained for ever. All historical experience shows that sooner or later the aggressor convinces himself he has a chance. And if war once starts atom bombs will be used from the first moment. The fact that the poison gas horror weapons of the last war were not used in this war for fear of retaliation is a misleading analogy. Poison gas is neither a decisive weapon. In the next major war it will be compulsory for the aggressor to win in the first week for fear of his opponent's atom bombs; and therefore he must use them himself.
explanation: Premises: Historical tendency of aggressors to believe they can win; poison gas is a poor analogy because it wasn’t decisive; need for rapid victory under atomic threat. Conclusion: If war occurs, atomic bombs will be used immediately. The “therefore” marks the inference.
main_claim: If a major war breaks out, atomic weapons will be used from the outset because aggressors must seek immediate victory.

argument_text: Fifthly, the atom bomb finally upsets the balance between the offence and the defence. In the old days the time needed for the victims under attack to mobilise for defence was not significantly longer than the time the aggressor needed to win. The balance began to shift as soon as war was industrialised; in 1940 defence required five years while the attack merely did the job in three weeks. Now the period for winning is to be measured in hours. It follows that no nation, however innocent, can afford to disarm.
explanation: Historical timeline comparisons are premises showing accelerating offensive advantage; conclusion: disarmament is unaffordable. “It follows that” indicates explicit inference.
main_claim: Given the offensive dominance of atomic warfare, no nation can afford to disarm.

argument_text: The primary conclusions to be drawn from the evidence are therefore, first, that the atom bomb cannot be abolished; secondly, that it is difficult to the point of impossibility to police any restriction in the use of the nuclear fission to peaceful ends; and, thirdly, that it is certain to be used if ever a third major war breaks out.
explanation: Summative inferences (“to be drawn,” “therefore”) present three conclusions derived from prior points regarding deterrence, inseparability, offensive advantage, and historical patterns.
main_claim: The bomb cannot be abolished, restrictions cannot be effectively policed, and atomic weapons will certainly be used if another major war occurs.

argument_text: These conclusions show that the favourite doctrine of the moment, that secret should be "internationalised" by being entrusted to the custody of a security council of united nations, is merely a piece of escapism. Indeed it embodies a double fallacy. In the first place "internationalising" the secret does not render it harmless; if the use of nuclear fission for peaceful purposes is to be permitted all over the world, any aggressor could quickly and easily possess himself of atomic bombs; and so long as that possibility existed no other nation could possibly afford to be without the means of retaliation. And, secondly, to hand the secret to a security council is not to internationalise it at all, but to hand it over to eleven highly nationalist sovereign states.
explanation: Premises: Internationalisation wouldn’t remove danger because peaceful use enables quick weaponisation; and a security council is still a set of sovereign national states. Conclusion: The internationalisation doctrine is escapist and fallacious. “These conclusions show,” “double fallacy,” and enumerated reasons make the structure explicit.
main_claim: Entrusting the atomic secret to a UN security council is misguided because it neither neutralizes the danger nor truly internationalizes control.

argument_text: Much the same objections apply to the proposals that the nations should agree to pool all their armed forces in an international police force, for as long as national governments retained sufficient sovereignty to engage in secret projects, a bold aggressor could destroy the international police force as well as his enemies by one unannounced blow. Indeed, logic leads straight to the ultimate conclusion that the only way in which the atom bomb can be abolished is by abolishing the sovereign state - by abolishing it so completely and creating a world state so all-powerful that no lesser unit can pursue any secret project involving more than five or six persons. A local authority in Britain or France could not engage in a conspiracy to make atom bombs in its power station and until all national governments are reduced to that level there will be no peace.
explanation: Premise: As long as sovereign states can act secretly, an aggressor could annihilate an international police force with a surprise strike. Conclusion 1: Pooling forces is inadequate. Conclusion 2: Only abolishing sovereign states in favor of a powerful world state prevents secret atomic projects and brings peace. The “for,” “Indeed, logic leads straight,” and example about local authority function as explicit reasoning.
main_claim: Because sovereign states can secretly prepare surprise atomic attacks, only a powerful world state that eliminates such sovereignty can prevent atomic war and secure peace.

argument_text: It is hardly necessary to devote any words to proving how impossible the creation of a world state is. Logic and reason may commend it; but it offends every one of those instincts which are the biological means of the preservation of the species. Even to get it on to an agenda for international discussion would be a triumph of mid over instinct for which the human species is a very long way indeed from being ready.
explanation: Premises: A world state offends entrenched preservation instincts; people are far from ready to prioritize reason over instinct. Conclusion: Creating a world state is (currently) impossible. The contrast “Logic and reason … but it offends” and the readiness claim support the impossibility judgment.
main_claim: Despite rational appeal, establishing a world state is presently impossible because it contradicts deep human instincts and readiness.

argument_text: Or so it has seemed hitherto. Public opinion, it has so often and so rightly been said, would not tolerate it. But perhaps the public, after it has brooded on the atomic bomb for a little longer and has realised how sharp the choice is between a world state and destruction, will change its mind.
explanation: This challenges the prior consensus by suggesting that awareness of existential stakes could shift public opinion. The reasoning is implied: increased understanding of the stark choice will motivate acceptance. Cues: “perhaps,” “after … realised how sharp the choice is.”
main_claim: Public opinion may shift to accept a world state once the existential stakes of the atomic bomb are fully appreciated.

argument_text: The only way of knowing is to find out, to ask the people to stand up and be counted.
explanation: This is a prescriptive conclusion (poll or consult the public) derived from the uncertainty about public opinion; it proposes a method as the logical means to resolve uncertainty (“only way”).
main_claim: We should directly gauge public opinion by asking people to declare their views.

argument_text: has a long history of successful engagements behind it, according to Lt W. B. Snyder, Officer-In-Charge.
explanation: This advances a claim (the band has a long history of successful engagements) and provides a premise by appeal to authority (Lt. Snyder’s statement) to support it. The structure is explicit: conclusion is asserted and justified by citing an authority.
main_claim: The band has a long history of successful engagements.

argument_text: to have this fine aggregation of musicians transferred to Foggia
explanation: The evaluative phrase “fine aggregation of musicians” implies the claim that the band is of high quality; the surrounding context of arranging a transfer underscores their perceived value. The argument is implicit because the evaluation is not accompanied by explicit reasons in this phrase, but it signals a positive judgment.
main_claim: The band is a high-quality group of musicians.

argument_text: The following night the entire group played at the dance at the Officer's Club as a swing band "rockin the joint to jumpin feet."
explanation: This sentence implies that the band’s performance was exciting and successful, using audience reaction (“jumpin feet”) as evidence. It’s an implicit argument because the positive evaluation is conveyed through idiomatic description rather than an explicit claim-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The band delivered a highly exciting and successful swing performance at the Officer’s Club.

argument_text: The band has within its fold many fine musicians with considerable pre-war experience.
explanation: This asserts that the band contains “many fine musicians,” and links their quality to “considerable pre-war experience,” implying that experience is a reason for judging them fine. The causal link is implied rather than laid out deductively, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: The band is strong because it includes many fine musicians with substantial pre-war experience.

argument_text: Sergeant De Grazia formerly played the saxophone-clarinet position in Henry Busse's popular combination. Teddy Powell's hot unit is represented by the band's drummer, Corporal Bert Morris, who leads the rhythm section for the Second Bomb boys.
explanation: By listing members’ notable prior associations (Henry Busse, Teddy Powell) and current leadership roles, the passage implies that the band’s caliber is high. The premise is the members’ prestigious backgrounds; the implied conclusion is the band’s quality. The argument is implicit because the evaluative conclusion is suggested, not stated.
main_claim: The band is of high quality because its members have prestigious professional backgrounds and leadership roles.

argument_text: According to Corporal Rowe Scott, Sax-man, "Rex is really a post-war threat to the swooner field. He's the Dick Haymes type."
explanation: This quoted statement presents a clear claim (Rex is a serious contender in the crooner/swooner field) and provides a supporting premise by analogy/comparison (“He’s the Dick Haymes type”) and an appeal to the speaker’s authority as a band member. The structure is explicit: conclusion plus supporting comparison.
main_claim: Vocalist Rex Bowman is a serious post-war contender among crooners.

argument_text: The band members stated that they would like some additional members in the group. A pianist for the swing combo is especially wanted.
explanation: This expresses a preference/need, implying the claim that the band is not complete and would benefit from additional members, especially a pianist. The recommendation (“especially wanted”) functions as a normative cue indicating an underlying argument about improving the band’s capability.
main_claim: The band needs additional personnel, particularly a pianist for the swing combo, to improve or complete its lineup.

argument_text: The Court will rule on a 2-year argument whether or not the Post Office Department can revoke Esquire's second-class mailing permit on the basis that it isn't "information of a public character."
explanation: This passage reports a specific argumentative structure: the claimed conclusion is that the Post Office Department can revoke Esquire's second-class mailing permit, and the stated premise is that Esquire is not "information of a public character." The phrase "on the basis that" signals a premise-to-conclusion relation, making the argument explicit, even though it is presented as a disputed claim under review.
main_claim: The Post Office Department can revoke Esquire's second-class mailing permit because Esquire is not "information of a public character."

argument_text:
Heat Finally Comes To Officers Club

New florescent lights and a new heating system has finally been installed at the Second Bomb Group’s Officers Club bar according to an announcement made by 1st Lt. Gorman D. Howell, Mess Officer of the club. Every Sunday night they will feature a Buffet Supper with orchestra music following the supper. A new snack bar has been opened for the mornings featuring coffee, toast, jam and cake from 0900 to 1100 hours. In the evening the snack bar will present a variety of toasted sandwiches from 2030 to 2300 hours.
explanation: The piece enumerates improvements (heat, lighting) and amenities (buffet with orchestra, snack bar offerings and hours) using positive framing (e.g., “finally”), which functions as selective, favorable evidence to imply that the Officers Club is now attractive and worth visiting; although no explicit recommendation is stated, the promotional tone and details serve as premises for the implied conclusion that personnel should attend/use the club.
main_claim: Personnel should visit and make use of the Officers Club because it now has improved heating and lighting and offers food, music, and convenient snack bar hours.

argument_text: 7:30 - Wrapping party (This is the big event of the week - as we hope to get up half our quota of packages 1500 - done up on the 19th)
explanation: The passage advances a claim ("This is the big event of the week") and provides a reason introduced by "as" (they hope to complete half of the 1500-package quota on the 19th). The reasoning links the significance of the event to its expected productivity, forming a clear premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The wrapping party is the big event of the week.

argument_text: 429th football team had a big party at the Embassy Club the other night. Only casualty reported was the bump on the cranium that Bill Gray received when he slid down the bannister head first. I wonder what makes coca-cola so potent these days. You should have seen the mean rumba Johnson was doing (swivel hips himself). And such a big boy.
explanation: The writer juxtaposes rowdy/over-the-top behavior (a head-first slide ending in a bump, an unusually “mean” rumba) with the rhetorical question about “what makes coca-cola so potent these days.” The insinuation is that the Coca-Cola was unusually strong (perhaps spiked), causing the antics. The conclusion is implied via rhetorical question and contextual evidence of behavior.
main_claim: The Coca-Cola at the party was unusually potent (likely spiked), which contributed to the rowdy behavior.
