argument_text: Speaking of Lowe, if you were in the snack bar Monday night you were probably overwhelmed by the powerful aroma. Tex and friend Bob were up in Ann’s room concocting various new perfumes from her collection.
explanation: This provides an explicit causal explanation: people were overwhelmed by a strong smell because Tex and Bob were concocting perfumes upstairs. The second sentence supplies the cause for the effect described in the first.
main_claim: The powerful aroma in the snack bar was caused by Tex and Bob mixing perfumes in Ann’s room.

argument_text:
The following anecdote goes to prove that water is the staff of life. The other morning at breakfast at the EM Hqs Mess Bob Olivigni after downing two fried eggs and a couple of slices of toast asked the waiter for a glass of water.

Result: he received two more eggs and toast. Again after eating this serving, he asked for a glass of water. Instead another helping of toast and two eggs appeared at his place. Being stuffed to a super-saturation point he walked out of the mess hall gasping with thirst because he was afraid to ask for a glass of water. He absolutely could not eat two more eggs and toast!
explanation: The passage announces a claim (“water is the staff of life”) and presents an anecdote as evidence: repeated attempts to obtain water only produced more food, leaving Bob too full and thirsty, demonstrating the indispensability of water. The narrative functions as premises supporting the general conclusion.
main_claim: Water is essential, as shown by Bob’s inability to get any without being overfed, leaving him desperately thirsty.

argument_text: As a result of a whistle census, it is agreed that Saturday night’s fashion show was a hit.
explanation: The phrase “as a result of a whistle census” provides evidence (audience whistles as a proxy for approval) leading to the conclusion that the show “was a hit.” This is an explicit inference from observed reactions to evaluative judgment.
main_claim: Saturday night’s fashion show was a success, as evidenced by the audience’s whistles.

argument_text: The introduction by those two wits, of course, Blondie Burns and Schnicklefritz Hooper was to be commended.
explanation: This is an evaluative claim recommending commendation. The justification is implied by calling them “two wits” and the context of the successful event, suggesting their introduction was entertaining and meritorious, though no explicit premises are stated.
main_claim: Blondie Burns and Schnicklefritz Hooper deserve commendation for their introduction at the fashion show.

argument_text: Congratulations also to Irene and home bound Todd for the appropriate and beautiful music they played.
explanation: The statement recommends congratulations and provides evaluative descriptors (“appropriate and beautiful music”) as the implicit reason. The argument is that their music merits praise because of its qualities.
main_claim: Irene and Todd deserve congratulations because the music they played was appropriate and beautiful.

argument_text: 20th Sqdn loses a good man from its basketball team since Jess Hannon has decided to play football with the All-Star team.
explanation: This sentence uses “since” to state the premise (Hannon decided to play football) that supports the conclusion (the 20th Squadron’s basketball team loses a good player). It asserts both a causal relation and an evaluative assessment of Hannon’s value.
main_claim: The 20th Squadron’s basketball team suffers a significant loss because Jess Hannon switched to the All-Star football team.

argument_text:
DONUT CLUSTERS

Donut clusters awarded to:
...that gifted South African-Jim Wilson.
...the great lover-Don Heitzman.
...the blond bombshell-Cliff Modell.
explanation: These awards imply the recipients deserve “donut clusters,” with the attached epithets serving as humorous justifications (premises) for the commendations. The evaluative act (awarding) is supported by the noted qualities.
main_claim: Wilson, Heitzman, and Modell deserve “donut clusters” in light of their highlighted qualities.

argument_text: Spurs to Jim Pancresi for those famous boots.
explanation: The preposition “for” supplies an explicit reason: Pancresi should get “spurs” because of his famous boots, forming a straightforward premise-to-conclusion link.
main_claim: Jim Pancresi merits spurs because he has those famous boots.

argument_text: Carnations to Gelinas on being reelected to a coveted post.
explanation: The sentence presents a commendation and offers the reason explicitly: Gelinas was reelected to a coveted position; therefore, carnations are due.
main_claim: Gelinas deserves carnations in recognition of being reelected to a coveted post.

argument_text: Although the "Split Arrow Club" will probably have closed its doors due to consolidation of Squadrons by the time this column goes to press, it was one of the most delightfully unpretentious night spots in Foggia. The Renzulli Orchestra, the sisters Dal Cin, and Angelina Menduni provided three nights of entertainment; American whiskey was on hand for the opening; decorations were tastefully simple; and the drinks were expertly mixed.
explanation: This advances an evaluative conclusion (“one of the most delightfully unpretentious night spots”) supported by concrete premises (quality entertainment, availability of American whiskey, simple decorations, well-mixed drinks). The listed features function as reasons for the overall assessment.
main_claim: The Split Arrow Club was one of the most delightfully unpretentious night spots in Foggia.

argument_text: The complete renovation of the building was accomplished in record time by club manager T/Sgt Eddie Cohan, who is apt to be seen tearing his hair any day now because the results of his labors were available for so short a time.
explanation: This sentence gives a predicted reaction (“apt to be seen tearing his hair”) and a causal premise introduced by “because” (his rapid renovation yielded results that were available only briefly). The structure is a clear premise-conclusion link.
main_claim: Eddie Cohan is likely to be very frustrated because his rapid renovation was enjoyed for only a short time.

argument_text: He can take some comfort in the thought that the loss will be equally felt by all discerning dypsos who must inevitably lament the loss of such thoroughly congenial surroundings in which to indulge in their favorite indoor sport.
explanation: This asserts that the closure is a shared loss and will be lamented, implying the reason that the club provided “thoroughly congenial surroundings” for drinking. The causal/evaluative language (“must inevitably lament,” “congenial”) signals a claim supported by implied premises about the club’s quality.
main_claim: The club’s closure will be widely and keenly felt because it deprived drinkers of especially congenial surroundings.

argument_text: The 20th Squadron Enlisted Men's Club located on the third floor of the 20th Squadron barrack is open to all Group personnel and is the right spot for those who like comparative privacy for their drinking, their dice games, their ping pong, and that card game that goes on into the night. Hence the thirsty man can indulge in the bar without the risk of being lured into chasing the galloping dominoes unless he crosses the hall to the dice room, and the man who takes his poker seriously is spared the torture of having an inebriate proffer advise on how that hand "ought to have been played." Club manager is S/Sgt Seymour Pechter, and entertainment is provided three nights a week by a different local unit each week.
explanation: This passage argues that the 20th Squadron Club is “the right spot” for those preferring privacy, with explicit reasoning signaled by “Hence.” The separation of activities (bar vs. dice room) and avoidance of unwanted advice are premises supporting the suitability claim; additional details (open to all, scheduled entertainment) bolster it.
main_claim: The 20th Squadron Enlisted Men’s Club is the best choice for those who want comparatively private, well-organized drinking and gaming.

argument_text: To say that he leaves reluctantly would be untrue, but it would be equally ridiculous to say that he leaves without nostalgia.
explanation: Through a contrast that rejects two extremes, the writer implies a nuanced stance: he is not reluctant to leave, yet he does feel nostalgia. The evaluative terms (“untrue,” “ridiculous”) implicitly justify the middle-ground claim by dismissing opposing characterizations.
main_claim: The correspondent departs without reluctance but with genuine nostalgia.

argument_text: Foggia boasts a new program, “Musical Alarm Clock” for the early risers among us.
explanation: The evaluative verb "boasts" implies that the new program is a positive addition worth pride, and the phrase "for the early risers among us" frames it as useful to a specific audience. This suggests a claim of value (the program is beneficial/noteworthy) without stating it explicitly.
main_claim: The new “Musical Alarm Clock” program is a noteworthy and beneficial addition for early risers in Foggia.

argument_text: The music which begins at six thirty and lasts until eight o’clock, is interrupted only by the early morning news and title announcements.
explanation: The use of "only" highlights minimal interruptions as a positive feature, implying the program offers a desirable, largely continuous music block, which serves listeners' preferences. The claim of desirability is implied rather than stated.
main_claim: The program’s mostly uninterrupted music format is a desirable feature for listeners.

argument_text: Having no pre-war announcing experience, Jack Bowman is a newcomer to the broadcasting field, but not to radio. Before coming overseas he trained as a radio and radar mechanic.
explanation: The concessive structure ("but not to radio") and the credentialing detail about training function to counterbalance the lack of announcing experience, implicitly arguing that Bowman is nonetheless qualified for broadcasting work.
main_claim: Despite lacking pre-war announcing experience, Bowman is qualified for broadcasting due to his radio and radar training.

argument_text: He applied to Lt. John Barry, then officer-in-charge of the station, for an announcing position. Lt. Barry felt that his rich deep voice was adequately suited to the job, and Bowman immediately stepped into the “Top of the Morning” spot where he has been until now.
explanation: This presents a clear rationale: premise—Bowman has a "rich deep voice" adequately suited to the job—leading to the outcome that he was placed in the announcer role. The suitability of his voice is offered as the reason for the decision.
main_claim: Bowman was suitable for and thus appointed to the announcer position because his rich, deep voice fit the job.

argument_text: The joy and gladness which traditionally surround this great feast are dimmed by the grim thought that many of our comrades have died for the principles of democracy we cherish and are willing to share with all nations.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal structure: the main claim is that the season’s joy is “dimmed,” and the reason offered is that comrades have died for democratic principles. The “because”-type linkage is explicit (“dimmed by the grim thought that…”), making the premise (sacrifice for democracy) support the conclusion (muted joy).
main_claim: The joy of Christmas is diminished because many comrades died for cherished democratic principles.

argument_text: The war is over, and friend and foe alike are deeply grateful for that, but there are still a few diehards left, and in a few isolated spots, man is still letting his brother's blood. May the prayer of each one of us on this Christmas be for complete peace with justice to all, for the impoverished multitudes suffering in the aftermath of war, and for those who have died on the field of battle.
explanation: The passage advances a recommendation about what our prayers should focus on, supported by premises: although the war is over and appreciated, violence persists and many suffer. The “but” contrast sets up the need, and the normative recommendation (“May the prayer… be for…”) is justified by the ongoing bloodshed and suffering.
main_claim: Our Christmas prayers should focus on complete peace with justice and on those suffering and fallen because violence and hardship persist despite the war’s end.

argument_text: Christmas is a holiday of merrymaking in normal times, but in its unfamiliar cloak of "Occupation," it is difficult to carry on the old customs and feel that the day means everything it did in former years.
explanation: This sentence uses a contrastive structure (“but”) to argue that occupation conditions (premise) make it difficult to maintain traditional customs and feelings (conclusion). The causal implication is explicit: the “unfamiliar cloak of ‘Occupation’” leads to the difficulty.
main_claim: Due to the conditions of occupation, it is difficult to continue traditional Christmas customs and feelings.

argument_text: We can, however, rededicate ourselves to the teachings of Him whose birthday we celebrate, and whose mission was to bring peace on earth to men of goodwill. We can translate that teaching into action by being generous with our time, our goods, and assistance to help cheer the innocent victims of war that surround us.
explanation: This recommends a course of action (be generous to aid war victims) grounded in an appeal to religious teachings about peace. The normative “we can” functions as an exhortation implying “we ought,” and the phrase “to help cheer the innocent victims of war” provides a purpose/benefit as justification. The moral premise (teachings about peace and goodwill) is invoked to support the recommendation, making the argumentative link implicit rather than formally stated.
main_claim: We should act on Christian teachings by generously helping the innocent victims of war around us.

argument_text: "This year many of us are far from our homes with all their pleasant associations. Yet, great though the distance may be, there is no barrier of time or space which is able to break the bond of love."
explanation: The passage advances a claim that love endures despite physical separation. The contrastive marker "Yet" sets up a reasoning move from the premise (being far from home) to the conclusion (distance cannot break the bond of love). The argument is implicit because the inferential link is suggested rather than laid out as formal premises supporting a stated conclusion.
main_claim: Distance cannot break the enduring bond of love between those far from home and their loved ones.

argument_text: "It is with true gratitude that we stand at this present place in the world's long history. The events of these past few years have again vindicated the truth of the Christmas message. Bigotry, hatred, intolerance, and greed bring only confusion into the world; the spirit of goodwill brings peace and the presence of God."
explanation: This sequence presents a clear argumentative structure: it asserts that recent events vindicate the Christmas message, and provides supporting premises via causal generalizations—vices lead to confusion whereas goodwill leads to peace and God's presence. These reasons support the conclusion that the Christmas message is true and grounds the expressed gratitude.
main_claim: Recent events confirm the truth of the Christmas message that goodwill leads to peace and God’s presence, while bigotry and greed produce only confusion.

argument_text: "Wise is the man who kneels in humility before the manger crib; wise is he who hears the truth of the Angel's Song "I bring you good tidings of great joy, unto you is born a Saviour which is Christ, the Lord.""
explanation: The evaluative term "Wise" functions normatively, implying that one ought to kneel in humility and heed the Angel’s message. The appeal to religious authority (the Angel’s Song) serves as an implicit reason for the recommended attitudes and actions. The argument is implicit because the prescriptive conclusion (one should do these things) is suggested rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: It is wise—and therefore to be emulated—to approach Christ with humility and to heed the Angel’s message.

argument_text: The observance of Christmas this year is not a cessation of hostilities on a battle front for a few brief hours; it is the sustained peace of dearly bought victory.
explanation: This contrasts two interpretations of Christmas observance (temporary truce versus lasting peace) and asserts the latter as true. The premise is implied: the war has ended in victory, hence peace is sustained, not momentary. The lack of explicit “because” makes it an implicit argument supported by the wartime context.
main_claim: This year’s Christmas signifies lasting peace achieved through victory rather than a brief wartime truce.

argument_text: God has indeed blessed us with peace. Shall we preserve it with "good will toward men"?
explanation: The rhetorical question presupposes an affirmative answer and implies a normative conclusion: we ought to preserve peace by practicing goodwill. The first sentence provides the premise (we have peace as a blessing), leading to the implied obligation in the question.
main_claim: We should preserve the peace by practicing goodwill toward others.

argument_text: True, we are away from home—some for their third Christmas; others for the first. All of us would like to be back with those we love around the Christmas tree, the dinner table, and in the Church of our dearest recollection. But Christmas is a spirit that can no more be confined to any one place than it can be selfishly enjoyed. It is the embodiment of the Christ, who is everywhere, and of whom it was written: "He went about doing good."
explanation: This passage acknowledges the desire to be home, then argues that Christmas transcends place and selfish enjoyment because it is a universal, Christ-embodied spirit associated with doing good. The implied conclusion is that meaningful celebration is possible even away from home.
main_claim: Even far from home, one can truly celebrate Christmas because it is a universal, unconfined spirit centered on doing good.

argument_text: We shall have a wonderful Christmas in proportion as we possess in our hearts the spirit of Him written of by the prophet: "Unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and... His name shall be called WONDERFUL."
explanation: This states a causal/conditional relation: the degree of a “wonderful Christmas” depends on possessing the Christlike spirit. The quoted scripture functions as support for what that spirit is, linking the premise to the outcome.
main_claim: The more we embody Christ’s spirit in our hearts, the more wonderful our Christmas will be.

argument_text: No other time of the year is so universally looked forward to with as much anticipation as Christmas. Therefore, it is fitting and proper that although we may be far from our homes and loved ones, we enter the spirit of the season and enjoy to the fullest, A Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year.
explanation: The first sentence offers a premise (Christmas is uniquely anticipated). The “Therefore” draws a normative conclusion: despite being away from home, we ought to fully enter the season’s spirit and enjoy it.
main_claim: Because Christmas is uniquely anticipated, it is appropriate to fully embrace and enjoy it even when away from home.

argument_text: At this most joyous and festive season, it is gratifying to witness the unselfishness of members of this squadron in helping to share a little of their abundance with so many less fortunate.
explanation: The sentence praises squadron members’ unselfishness, citing their sharing with the less fortunate as evidence. The implied reasoning is that acts of sharing indicate unselfish character, supporting the evaluative claim.
main_claim: The squadron members are unselfish, as shown by their sharing with the less fortunate.

argument_text: When it comes to ambitious plans for Christmas, the 55th Station Hospital has them. From the CO to the POWs, everyone in the place has the Christmas spirit. In the workshop in the basement, officers, nurses, detachment men, and patients have been turning out presents for the poor of Foggia. Little sheepskin boots are being made from salvage flying jackets. Wooden toys come from packing crates and scrap plywood. Across the hall in the Red Cross rooms, "stained glass" windows are being made from transparent paper. Crepe paper and tinsel made from radar "chaff" is all over the place, lending an air of festive confusion.
explanation: The opening claim that the hospital has “ambitious plans” is supported by a list of concrete activities (making boots, toys, decorations). The inference is implied via accumulation of evidence rather than an explicit “because,” signaling an implicit argument that these activities demonstrate ambition and widespread Christmas spirit.
main_claim: The 55th Station Hospital has ambitious plans for Christmas and a pervasive Christmas spirit.

argument_text: A walk up the main stairs and through the wards confirms the impression of holiday spirit. The staircase is decorated from top to bottom with Christmas greens and paper. In each room is a tree brought in from the mountains. The patients in each ward have been making their own decorations for the rooms and the trees with whatever material is available. The hospital's officers and nurses have been spending their evenings wrapping packages to be distributed at the civilian hospital in Foggia. There are boxes full of gay Christmas stockings for their children's party at the hospital.
explanation: The phrase “confirms the impression of holiday spirit” explicitly frames the subsequent details (decorations, trees, package-wrapping, stockings) as evidence verifying a claim about the presence of holiday spirit throughout the hospital.
main_claim: The hospital genuinely exhibits a strong holiday spirit.

argument_text: All over the building all of the time is the ARC Asst. Field Director, Miss Virginia Woolfolk. She isn't the chairman of the Christmas Committee; that is being ably handled by CO Capt. J. T. Guzek. What she does is act as the sparkplug for the whole affair.
explanation: The passage implies that because Woolfolk is omnipresent and active, she serves as the motivating force (“sparkplug”) for the program, even though she is not the formal chair. The evaluative term “ably” also advances a claim about Guzek’s competence. The argument relies on descriptive evidence (her constant presence) and evaluative language to support the role attribution.
main_claim: Despite not being the chair, Woolfolk is the driving motivator of the Christmas effort, while Guzek handles the formal leadership competently.

argument_text: Actually, the whole program is too big to give the credit to any one person. It's the unit working together.
explanation: This presents a reason (“the whole program is too big”) leading to a conclusion (“credit” should not go to one person; instead, it’s collective effort). The causal relation is explicit, making this a clear argument about teamwork over individual credit.
main_claim: The Christmas program’s success is due to unit-wide teamwork rather than any single individual.

argument_text: All of it seems to point to the fact that Christmas in Foggia doesn't have to be dreary at all.
explanation: The phrase “seems to point to the fact” explicitly signals an inference drawn from prior reported activities and decorations: because of the hospital’s efforts, the general outlook for Christmas in Foggia need not be dreary.
main_claim: Given these preparations and efforts, Christmas in Foggia need not be dreary.

argument_text: The first time that we can look forward to a return to home, civilian job, and to our normal way of life that makes for the contentment and prosperity of man.
explanation: This sentence advances a normative claim that returning to a “normal way of life” is good because it “makes for the contentment and prosperity of man.” The relative clause functions as a reason supporting why looking forward to return is warranted. The argument structure is implicit: premise (normal life yields contentment and prosperity) implies the conclusion (we should look forward to returning to it).
main_claim: We should look forward to returning to normal civilian life because it promotes human contentment and prosperity.

argument_text: It is difficult for us to thoroughly enjoy this Christmas without the snow, the trees, and the atmosphere of America. And yet, here, there is for us an opportunity to demonstrate the true purpose of this yuletide season and in doing so enjoy Christmas.
explanation: This passage uses a contrast (“And yet”) to argue that despite missing familiar American holiday elements (premise), one can still enjoy Christmas by demonstrating its true purpose (implied prescription), leading to the conclusion that enjoyment is possible through meaning rather than ambiance. The reasoning is implicit through concessive structure rather than explicit logical markers.
main_claim: Despite lacking American holiday atmosphere, we can still enjoy Christmas here by focusing on and demonstrating its true purpose.

argument_text: During this holiday we can give ourselves to the task of making the teachings of Our Lord a living thing by our charity to those more unfortunate than we, by extending goodwill toward all men.
explanation: This is a recommendation/ought-claim framed as “we can,” implying that one should make religious teachings “a living thing” via charity and goodwill. The implicit argument is that practicing charity and goodwill is the way to embody those teachings, thus prescribing specific actions as justified by the goal of living the teachings.
main_claim: We should embody the teachings of Our Lord during the holiday by practicing charity and extending goodwill toward all.

argument_text: The first time that we can look forward to a return to home, civilian job and to our normal way of life that makes for the contentment and prosperity of man.
explanation: This sentence presents a positive evaluation of the “normal way of life” as something that “makes for the contentment and prosperity of man,” which functions as a reason for why returning to it is desirable and something to “look forward to.” The premise (normal life produces contentment and prosperity) supports the implied conclusion (returning to normal life is good/desirable and thus worth anticipating). The argument is implicit because the normative conclusion is suggested rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: Returning to a normal civilian life is desirable because it brings contentment and prosperity.

argument_text: It is difficult for us to thoroughly enjoy this Christmas without the snow, the trees, and the atmosphere of America. And yet, here, there is for us an opportunity to demonstrate the true purpose of this yuletide season and, in doing so, enjoy Christmas. During this holiday we can give ourselves to the task of making the teachings of Our Lord a living thing by our charity to those more unfortunate than we, by extending goodwill toward all men.
explanation: This passage contrasts the lack of familiar American Christmas elements (premise: it’s difficult to enjoy Christmas without them) with a proposed means to enjoy Christmas nonetheless (premise: we can demonstrate the true purpose of the season by living out charity and goodwill). The implied conclusion is a recommendation: we should give ourselves to acts of charity and goodwill because that embodies the season’s true purpose and will enable us to enjoy Christmas even abroad. The conclusion is not stated as an explicit “therefore,” making it an implicit argument supported by contrastive framing and a practical “ought.”
main_claim: We should practice charity and goodwill during the holiday to live the season’s true purpose and thereby enjoy Christmas despite being far from American traditions.

argument_text: When asked how they looked, the loser could only say that they had "an Ox Blood tinge on the usual brown and were of the well-known, often seen, often sold GI type." Finding the shoes was, of course, a snap. Oh, sure!
explanation: This uses irony and contrast to argue that with such a vague, generic description, it is unrealistic to expect the MPs to find the stolen shoes. The sarcastic "of course" and "Oh, sure!" signal that the implied conclusion is the opposite: it was not a “snap.” The premise (generic description) supports the conclusion (complaint/expectation is unreasonable or futile).
main_claim: It is unreasonable to expect MPs to recover stolen items when the complainant provides only a vague, generic description.

argument_text: All he wanted was transportation home. Of course, the MP station is known to have all the transportation in town at its beck and call. At least a dozen of the local celebrants come into the station during the week and request, if not demand, a ride home.
explanation: The passage uses sarcasm (“Of course… at its beck and call”) and exemplification (many celebrants demand rides) to imply that MPs are not a taxi service and that such demands are inappropriate. The implicit claim is normative: people shouldn’t expect or demand rides from the MP station.
main_claim: MPs should not be treated as a taxi service and people should not expect or demand rides from the MP station.

argument_text: The men of the force complain of only a few things. Most prominent among these things is, however, their complaint on unnecessary griping and moaning. Of course, they do a good deal themselves, but they hate to have it brought into their business. When a small job can be done in the line of duty to make things just a bit better for the poor old GI, they are only too glad to do so, but they aren't the motor pool, the Foggia electric system, or the local dispensary. They are there to help in time when help is needed. Like the doctor's, their job is preventive as well as curative.
explanation: This sequence contrasts what MPs are willing and able to do (small tasks within duty; help when needed; preventive and curative roles) with what they are not (not the motor pool, electric system, or dispensary). From these premises it implies a normative conclusion: stop bringing unnecessary complaints and misdirected service requests to the MPs. The argument relies on evaluative language (“unnecessary griping”), role delineation, and contrast to imply the “ought.”
main_claim: People should refrain from bringing unnecessary complaints and service requests to MPs because their role is to provide needed assistance within their duty, not to replace other services.

argument_text: Believe Who? You pays yer money and you takes yer choice!
explanation: This headline frames two contradictory letters and suggests that credibility is a matter of reader choice, implying that the accounts conflict and that no authoritative resolution is provided. The evaluative idiom “you pays your money and you takes your choice” insinuates that both sides are being offered as equally selectable, thereby making an implicit claim about the equivalence or indecisiveness of the evidence.
main_claim: Readers must decide for themselves which conflicting account to believe because the evidence presented supports opposing conclusions.

argument_text:
"Dear Editor, As an inhabitant of the 7th Depot for the past six days, I believe I am qualified in making the following remarks. I have been treated with courtesy and consideration ever since I first arrived. Living quarters are excellent. Heat and electric lights are plentiful. Bed, mattress, sheets, and pillows are the best I've had in Italy outside of a hospital. The PX and recreational facilities are numerous.

This is in answer to the statements made against the depot. If persons who criticize this depot would have lived in the old 7th depot (race track) as I did from October '44 to March '45, they would not complain, believe me. I have nothing but praise for it now. Pfc. BOB L. DOLL R. D." (From "The Stars and Stripes", Nov. 29, 1945)
explanation: The writer presents premises drawn from personal experience (courtesy, good living quarters, ample heat and light, high-quality bedding, numerous facilities) to support the conclusion that the 7th Depot is praiseworthy now and that criticisms are unwarranted. The explicit conditional—“If persons who criticize this depot would have lived in the old 7th depot... they would not complain”—strengthens the argument by contrasting present conditions with worse past conditions, thus directly countering critics. The opening claim of qualification (“I believe I am qualified”) is an argument from ethos supporting the credibility of the subsequent evaluation.
main_claim: Current conditions at the 7th Depot are good and criticisms of it are unjustified.

argument_text:
Dear Editor, Just a few lines to let you know that it has been just three days since I have been away from the Group, and in the three days, I haven't had my clothes off once. I even slept in them because we have lived and are still living in G— D— —d holey tents without stoves, and without lights, and believe me, I definitely expect to sleep with all my clothes on until I get out of these cold tents.

Reference is now made to the question of food. My reply is "What food?" I haven't seen anything that resembles food since I left Headquarters. Outside of the aforestated, everything is fine and dandy. This, I must admit, is the worst conditions I have ever had since I have been in the Army considering that the war has been over for some time and that conditions were supposed to have improved. My only remaining incentive is that eventually, I will be placed on a boat and returned to the states. Well, what more can I say other than it is not fit for a kennel, but we hardened veterans have to contend with it. (NAME WITHHELD)
explanation: The writer lists concrete deprivations (holey tents, no stoves or lights, sleeping in clothes, lack of food) as premises to support the evaluative conclusion that conditions are unacceptable—“the worst … since I have been in the Army” and “not fit for a kennel.” The reference to the war being over and conditions “supposed to have improved” adds a normative premise that current hardship is especially unacceptable postwar, reinforcing the conclusion that the situation merits complaint.
main_claim: The current living conditions are intolerable and unfit, especially given that the war is over and conditions should have improved.

argument_text: Maybe what they put back was number 4, maybe it was ball-bearings. It was big stuff though, and they figured it would be a good persuader for a duck or goose to stop flying and make itself available for a duck dinner.
explanation: This passage reports the hunters’ reasoning: using larger shot (“big stuff”) will cause ducks/geese to stop flying and thus be obtainable for dinner. The premise (larger shot) is presented as the causal means to the conclusion (more effective at bringing down birds). The causal language (“would be a good persuader… to stop flying”) makes the argument explicit.
main_claim: Using larger shot will more effectively bring down ducks and geese for dinner.

argument_text: Ahh, the Candelaro Swamps—duck hunter's paradise! Quiet glens, glassy waters, silence but for the soft bleat of the foraging goose, and close by, the azure blue of Lake Salso. Yes, that is exactly what the small print says in the lower left corner of the travel folder.
explanation: The lyrical description is undercut by the final sentence attributing it to “the small print… of the travel folder,” cueing irony. The contrast implies the claim that the brochure’s idyllic portrayal is marketing copy rather than reality. The argumentative cue is the ironic framing that signals skepticism.
main_claim: The brochure’s idyllic description of the Candelaro Swamps should not be taken as reality.

argument_text: If they only had a retriever! Meat on the table—but no retriever.
explanation: This implies a counterfactual causal claim: having a retriever would have yielded meat on the table by retrieving downed birds. The omission of a retriever is presented as the reason for not securing the ducks, making it an implicit argument via causal insinuation and contrastive framing.
main_claim: Lacking a retriever prevented the hunters from bringing home the birds they shot.

argument_text: Then, inspired, it turned away on a 45-degree angle. Realizing that he had maneuverability over the faster jeep, he did some desperate broken field running and got away.
explanation: This is a causal explanation: the fox escaped because it had greater maneuverability than the jeep, allowing evasive “broken field running.” The premise (maneuverability advantage) directly supports the conclusion (it got away), making the reasoning explicit.
main_claim: The fox escaped because its superior maneuverability allowed it to evade the faster jeep.

argument_text: The jeep, in a moment of compassion for the quarry-less hunters, slammed its windshield against a whippoorwill, proving that all the uses for this little vehicle have not been discovered by any means.
explanation: Despite humorous personification, the sentence makes an explicit inferential claim: the event (jeep hitting a bird) “proves” that jeeps have undiscovered uses. The use of “proving that” signals a conclusion drawn from the incident.
main_claim: The incident shows that jeeps have unexpected, not-yet-discovered uses.

argument_text: Ed's Note: The same hunters had better luck Friday Morning, December 21 by bagging ten geese and five ducks. They brought them home too.
explanation: The note asserts “had better luck” and provides evidence (“by bagging ten geese and five ducks” and successfully bringing them home). The structure explicitly links the outcome (bagging many birds) as the basis for the evaluative conclusion (better luck).
main_claim: The hunters’ later success in bagging and bringing home many birds shows they had better luck on December 21.

argument_text: Although Congress has not been officially notified, the duration plus six months period has come to an end for American troops in Foggia. Starting last Monday, the cries of "Here" and "Present" have been echoing through the vacant lots near military establishments. The morning roll call has returned to the Soldier's Day.
explanation: This passage implies that, regardless of formal Congressional action, the practical reality (the return of roll call) means the "duration plus six months" period is over. The evaluative framing "Although Congress has not been officially notified" contrasts official inaction with on-the-ground facts, suggesting a conclusion about the period’s end. The premises (roll call has returned; soldiers are answering "Here"/"Present") support the implied claim of de facto termination.
main_claim: The "duration plus six months" period has effectively ended in practice even if Congress has not officially acknowledged it.

argument_text: As a result of the new order that makes it necessary for all soldiers to be on the alert for the hour of reveille, the demand for timepieces has necessitated a quick revision of the price scale in Foggia's illegal trading market.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal chain: the new order (premise) increases demand for timepieces (intermediate premise), which necessitates a price increase in the illegal market (conclusion). The phrase "As a result" signals explicit argumentative structure.
main_claim: The new roll call order has driven up watch prices in Foggia’s illegal market.

argument_text: The Rest Camp Section has been swamped with requests to return to Switzerland to buy watches for their own use. Sgt Fields of Paris fame told your reporter that due to impending bad weather, it will be necessary to cut down on the local quota, thus forcing individuals to buy their watches here.
explanation: These sentences argue that because bad weather will reduce the local quota for trips, soldiers will be compelled to buy watches locally. The premises (high demand; impending bad weather; quota cut) lead to the conclusion ("thus forcing" local purchases). Causal connectors ("due to," "thus") make the argument explicit.
main_claim: Impending bad weather will reduce travel quotas and thereby force soldiers to purchase watches locally.

argument_text: At the meeting last night, a resolution was passed pledging all married men to eliminate the morning kisses in order to enable them to make the roll call.
explanation: This presents a policy recommendation justified by a purpose: eliminating morning kisses (action) is needed "in order to" make roll call (goal). The instrumental rationale provides an explicit premise-conclusion relation.
main_claim: Married men should eliminate morning kisses so they can make roll call on time.

argument_text:
Night Clubs To Suffer

Our Roving Dipso Reporter has noted that many men are leaving the bars earlier these nights.
explanation: The headline asserts a negative outcome for nightclubs, and the observation that men leave earlier functions as supporting evidence. The causal link (earlier departures lead to reduced business) is implied rather than stated, relying on a presupposed understanding of nightclub revenue patterns.
main_claim: Nightclubs will be hurt because men are leaving bars earlier due to the new order.

argument_text: At the meeting of the Council of The Big Three at a local Vino Shop, 'Vino' Grapieoli gave a new angle to the roll call. "As I see it," The Vino says, "the ladies of Washington are at it again. First of all, we get this new roll call order, and then we see that the Drys are holding a get together in Washington complaining about the amount of alcohol being consumed. To me, it looks like those Generals in Washington are attending 'real' tea parties these days."
explanation: This is a sarcastic chain of insinuations linking the new roll call order and temperance activists ("the Drys") to suggest that Washington generals are aligned with or influenced by prohibitionist sentiment. The juxtaposition and the phrase "looks like" imply causation/political alignment without stating it explicitly, using irony to advance the claim.
main_claim: Washington military leaders are aligning with temperance pressures, using measures like the new roll call to curb soldiers’ drinking.

argument_text: “Yeah, I saw Eddie about five minutes ago. He was sitting at the bar. On the bar, he had a picture of his wife, and he was drinking toasts to her. That's been going on for hours. There's a big sag in the bar. Bad taste, very bad taste.”
explanation: The speaker evaluates Eddie’s public toasting as “bad taste,” implying a normative claim that such behavior is inappropriate. The premises are that Eddie has been toasting for hours with his wife’s picture on the bar, causing a “big sag,” suggesting disruption or excessive display. The evaluative conclusion (“Bad taste”) is not logically derived explicitly but is inferred from these contextual cues, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Eddie’s prolonged public toasting with his wife’s photo is in bad taste.

argument_text:
“Don't you like it?”
“Not in Italy. They shoot at you here.”
explanation: The conclusion is that he does not like flying in Italy, supported by the explicit reason that “they shoot at you here.” This is a straightforward premise-to-conclusion structure: danger (being shot at) is given as the reason for dislike.
main_claim: He does not like flying in Italy because it is dangerous.

argument_text: “Look, Sis,” he said, talking right into her face. “When we come to Rome, we don't come to talk combat. We come here for other things.”
explanation: The speaker asserts a norm about the purpose of leave in Rome: not discussing combat but pursuing “other things.” The argumentative force is that conversation should avoid combat topics, justified implicitly by the purpose of leave (relaxation/pleasure). The premise (purpose of coming to Rome) is used to justify the conclusion (don’t talk about combat), but the linkage is suggested rather than spelled out.
main_claim: Conversations during Rome leave should avoid combat because leave is for other pursuits.

argument_text: “I'm human too. Don't you think that I get lonely sometimes? Don't you think we miss our families too? Just because we don't get shot at doesn't mean that we don't work hard.”
explanation: The WAC advances the conclusion that non-combat personnel (like herself) also work hard and suffer loneliness/longing for family. Premises include her shared humanity and experiences of loneliness and missing family. She explicitly refutes a potential inference (“just because we don't get shot at”) leading to a clear argumentative structure.
main_claim: Non-combat personnel also work hard and endure emotional hardships.

argument_text: “You see Lew and Eddie?” He didn't wait for an answer. “Do you know how many men are on a bomber crew?” The ice in the glass was clinking as his hand shook. “There are ten! Ten, Sis. But on my crew, there are only three now. Three, Sis. Now, how much do you want to talk about combat?”
explanation: The speaker argues that discussing combat is inappropriate or unwelcome, supporting this conclusion with explicit evidence: heavy crew losses (only three left of ten). The loss serves as reason to avoid the topic of combat, forming a clear premise-conclusion relationship.
main_claim: Given the severe losses on his crew, he does not want to talk about combat.

“My wife—you know, Kitty—my wife, she likes that song. They don't have any right to play that song. Jeez Charley, not tonight... not that song.”
explanation: Eddie claims the orchestra should stop playing “White Christmas” and asserts they have no right to play it, providing a personal reason: the song is tied to his wife and causes him pain. The implied normative conclusion is that, given his emotional harm, the song ought not be played here/now. The premises (personal association, distress) are used implicitly to support a prescriptive claim.
main_claim: The orchestra should not play “White Christmas” here tonight because it causes Eddie personal anguish.

argument_text: We have tried hard to be very good all year long and have worked hard. This year there is only one little thing we would like. Could you please bring us back those happy mornings without reveille? We will work hard if you do and probably work better than if we had to stand out in the cold to have our name called. That isn't much to ask, but we don't need much while we are waiting to go home.
explanation: The passage advances a recommendation (bring back mornings without reveille) and provides reasons: they have worked hard; they will work hard (and even better) without having to stand in the cold for roll call; the request is small given they are waiting to go home. The conclusion is explicitly stated as a request, and the premises are given to justify it.
main_claim: Reveille/roll call should be removed so that personnel can work better and avoid standing in the cold.

argument_text: Since you seemed to be so concerned about the kind of Christmas that the Italians are going to have, how about doing a little worrying for us poor misfortunates who have to spend Christmas here.
explanation: This sentence argues that the editor should also show concern for U.S. personnel, using the premise that the editor has been concerned about Italians’ Christmas and the fact that soldiers must spend Christmas there. It concludes with a direct recommendation to worry about them as well.
main_claim: The editor should show concern for the soldiers’ Christmas, not only for Italians.

argument_text: As long as we got to stay here, we might as well have a good time. The least Uncle Sam can do is to send over rations of whiskey for military personnel here. What kind of a Christmas will it be without eggnog and what is eggnog without whiskey? A lot of officers and soldiers in Foggia would appreciate that kind of a Christmas gift.
explanation: The passage argues that Uncle Sam should send whiskey rations. Premises include that they must stay and should enjoy themselves, that Christmas customs (eggnog) require whiskey, and that many personnel would appreciate it. The conclusion is explicitly stated as “The least Uncle Sam can do is to send over rations of whiskey.”
main_claim: The military should provide whiskey rations to personnel in Foggia for Christmas.

argument_text: Don't get me wrong about these parties for the children of Foggia. I, myself, have contributed my candy rations and have also put a lot of money in the Christmas fund boxes.
explanation: This functions as a rebuttal to an anticipated objection that asking for whiskey is selfish or anti-Italian. By asserting his own contributions to local children and funds, the writer implies that advocating for whiskey does not conflict with supporting Italians. The conclusion is implied rather than directly stated.
main_claim: Requesting whiskey rations does not mean the writer opposes or neglects aid to Italian children.

argument_text: (Ed's Note: We regret to say that there are no authorized whiskey rations to this theater of operations. Blame it on the Dry Lobby in Washington.)
explanation: The editor assigns causal responsibility for the lack of whiskey rations to the “Dry Lobby in Washington.” The passage presents the fact of no authorized rations and then implies the cause (“Blame it on the Dry Lobby”) without supplying evidence, making the causal argument implicit.
main_claim: The absence of authorized whiskey rations is due to the Dry Lobby in Washington.

argument_text: It is with deep appreciation that we read the article in the 3rd issue of the "FOGGIA OCCUPATOR" concerning the schools of Foggia. First, because it demonstrates that the Allies are aware of the existence of a problem, and then because it gives the teachers a moral satisfaction to know there is an understanding on the part of the Allied authorities of the unfavorable conditions under which they work daily.
explanation: The writer offers a clear conclusion—deep appreciation for the article—and provides two stated reasons: (1) it shows Allied awareness of the problem, and (2) it gives teachers moral satisfaction through recognized understanding of their unfavorable working conditions. The presence of “because” and the ordered “First… and then…” signals a standard premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The article is deserving of deep appreciation because it shows Allied awareness of the schools’ problems and gives teachers moral satisfaction.

argument_text: We know that it is the school which molds the generations of tomorrow. We know too, that only from the schools of today can emerge renewed and stronger bonds of friendship and understanding between Italy and the Allies. We are grateful, therefore, for all that you may do for the schools of Foggia, knowing that your help will have an effect on the souls, not only of the students and teachers, but of all the citizens of Foggia.
explanation: The passage states premises about the role of schools in shaping future generations and strengthening bonds between Italy and the Allies, then uses “therefore” to draw a conclusion of gratitude for Allied help, further supported by the predicted broad positive effects of such help. This is a clear argumentative chain linking reasons to a conclusion.
main_claim: Allied assistance to Foggia’s schools is valuable and warranted, as schools shape future generations, foster Allied-Italian understanding, and positively affect the whole community.

argument_text: We parked our jeep, and this kid asked to watch it. I thought we ought to let him watch it since it was locked anyway.
explanation: This contains a clear conclusion supported by a stated reason. Conclusion: they ought to let the kid watch the jeep. Premise: the jeep was locked anyway, implying low risk and thus permitting the decision. The cue "since" marks the premise-conclusion relation.
main_claim: We ought to let the kid watch the jeep because the jeep is locked anyway.

argument_text: I was watching a disgusted GI cuss out a signorina and was wondering what would have happened to our girls in South Africa if the Jerries or Japs had won the war. I guess I was feeling sorry for the women at the same time.
explanation: This passage implies a normative stance: soldiers should empathize with local women and not mistreat them. The counterfactual about “our girls” if the enemy had won functions as a moral analogy, suggesting that seeing one’s own women in a similar situation justifies sympathy toward the Italian women. The evaluative reaction (“feeling sorry for the women”) signals the implied conclusion without stating it directly.
main_claim: Soldiers should feel empathy toward local women and avoid mistreating them, as imagining our own women under enemy victory shows why sympathy is warranted.

argument_text: Have you ever thought how rich you are? Rich not necessarily in the material things of life, but rich in the Spirit of America. It is not a thing that you can pack and put away or a thing that you can pull off the tree like an apple. It is richer, finer, greater, and more important than anything else in the world. It springs from the earth that was cultivated by the blood of the American Revolutionary Army. It comes from an earth nourished and loved by free men. It is in the songs that Americans write for free souls and not in the servitude of despots and dictators.
explanation: The passage advances the claim that readers possess a special non-material wealth—the Spirit of America—that is supremely valuable and rooted in freedom and sacrifice. The premises include contrasts (not material but spiritual), superlative evaluations (“more important than anything else”), and causal attributions to historical struggle and freedom. The argument is implicit because it does not state a formal conclusion but strongly suggests the evaluative claim through descriptive and laudatory language.
main_claim: You are truly rich because you possess the supremely valuable Spirit of America grounded in freedom and sacrifice.

argument_text: You see this Spirit when our people go to their own churches, the church of their wish, to pray to God. You see this Spirit when citizens go to the polls to select their government representatives.
explanation: This passage identifies empirical indicators of the Spirit (freedom of religion and democratic voting) to support an implicit claim about what constitutes or evidences that Spirit. The use of examples functions as premises for the inferred conclusion that these practices manifest the Spirit and, by implication, are valuable. It is implicit because the conclusion is suggested rather than stated.
main_claim: The Spirit of America is manifest in freedom of worship and democratic voting.

argument_text: It is the same spirit that permits a man to write and say as his conscience dictates and not be tossed into jail, stoned, or shot. A great richness is this spirit which makes every man a king in his own castle—his own.
explanation: The passage explicitly links the Spirit to freedom of expression and personal sovereignty, and concludes evaluatively that this spirit is a “great richness.” The causal attribution (“permits”) and the value judgment form a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The Spirit of America, which ensures free expression and personal sovereignty, is a great richness.

argument_text: Yes, that is the Spirit of America. Sometimes we selfishly misuse it. Many times we ignore it. But for just this time, sit down and think about it. It is yours, and you can give it to anyone you choose, and at the same time increase the amount you have. That is the greatness of this Spirit. Every time you give some of it, your own increases in proportion.
explanation: This contains a direct recommendation (sit down and think; give it to anyone) supported by a reason: giving the Spirit increases one’s own share. The structure presents premises (you can give it and it increases) leading to a conclusion about what one ought to do.
main_claim: You should reflect on and share the Spirit of America because giving it increases your own share.

argument_text: For example, suppose you taught school back in the States. The principles of your profession were guided by the Spirit of America. All you have to do is make a friend of an Italian school teacher in Foggia. Tell the teacher about our schools, the progressive teaching methods we have. The rights any child, be he rich or poor, has to attend school.
explanation: This recommends that American teachers share educational practices and values with Italian teachers. The normative conclusion (you ought to befriend and inform) is implied by assertions about the Spirit guiding teaching and by directives. The argument is implicit because it relies on the presupposed value of sharing these principles rather than stating a formal conclusion.
main_claim: American teachers should share U.S. educational principles and methods with Italian teachers in Foggia.

argument_text: You, Sergeant Jones. Give one month of your America—the America of crop rotation, animal husbandry, the right to own one's own land. Give that spirit to some farmer on the Manfredonia Road.
explanation: This is a directive urging Sergeant Jones to share agricultural knowledge and property-rights values with local farmers. The justification is implied by invoking the content of “your America” (practices and rights), suggesting benefit to the recipient. The conclusion (he should do this) is not spelled out as a premise-conclusion chain but is implied by the imperative and framing.
main_claim: Sergeant Jones should share American agricultural practices and land-rights values with a local farmer.

argument_text: You, Corporal Smith, who have worked with your hands on so many engines. Tell these young men about tools. Tell them how to preserve them, how to use them. Tell them of the wonders they create!
explanation: The passage urges a skilled mechanic to teach locals about tools and their use, implying it is beneficial and aligned with the Spirit of America. The imperative structure conveys the normative claim without explicitly stating reasons beyond assumed benefits.
main_claim: Corporal Smith should teach local youth about tools, their care, and their creative potential.

argument_text: You, Sergeant Russell, who have the love of sport and competition. Create in these young bodies and minds the will to win, the right to play, the spirit of true sportsmanship. What a wonderful gift is in your possession.
explanation: This recommends fostering sportsmanship and competitive spirit among youth, supported by the evaluative statement that the addressee possesses a “wonderful gift,” implying it ought to be shared. The conclusion is implied via exhortation and value language.
main_claim: Sergeant Russell should instill in local youth the will to win, the right to play, and true sportsmanship because he holds a valuable gift.

argument_text: You, Chaplain, teach these people the Love of God. Make them understand that no man is greater or wiser than his Creator.
explanation: Imperatives urge the Chaplain to teach religious values, presupposing that spreading such beliefs is good and needed. The normative claim is implied through commands rather than argued explicitly.
main_claim: The Chaplain should teach locals the love of God and human humility before the Creator.

argument_text: You, Doctor, invite the men of medicine to your laboratory. Tell them of the wonders of Science. Show them what free minds have created the world over.
explanation: This exhorts a doctor to share scientific knowledge and demonstrate achievements of free inquiry, implying that doing so is beneficial and aligned with American ideals. The conclusion is implied via directives and value-laden phrasing.
main_claim: The Doctor should share scientific knowledge with local medical men and showcase what free minds have achieved.

argument_text: You, Mr. Citizen of America, walk with head high. Stop Mr. Foggia on the street and tell him: "Friend, study the platforms of the political parties in Italy. Join the one you think is the one that you want. Express your will at the polls by the ballot, never by the bullet."
explanation: This passage explicitly advocates democratic political engagement and nonviolence, with clear directives supported by reasons embedded in the content (study platforms, choose freely, use ballots not bullets). The logical structure presents a normative conclusion with practical steps as supporting rationale.
main_claim: American citizens should encourage Italians to engage in informed, peaceful democratic participation, choosing parties freely and voting rather than using violence.

argument_text: What a wonderful gift is in your possession. Give the next month of your America.
explanation: The evaluative statement (“wonderful gift”) functions as a reason to perform the directive (“Give the next month of your America”). The argument is implicit because it relies on the value claim to justify the action without an explicit premise-conclusion format.
main_claim: Because you possess a wonderful gift, you should spend the next month sharing your America.

argument_text: To say, as many uninformed persons do, that the meeting was a failure and therefore that the Western Powers and the USSR will come to conflict is not only unintelligent but misguided.
explanation: This evaluative statement rejects a prevalent conclusion (that the meeting was a failure leading to conflict) without yet laying out explicit premises; it implies that such a conclusion ignores relevant facts and reasoning to be presented. The cues “uninformed,” “unintelligent,” and “misguided” mark a normative stance and suggest the claim is wrong because it lacks factual grounding.
main_claim: It is misguided to conclude from the meeting that it was a failure and that the Western Powers and the USSR will come into conflict.

argument_text:
The first mistake made at the meeting was that the Council adopted the procedure decided upon at Potsdam for the drafting of treaties. The Potsdam declaration stated that, "for the discharge of each of these tasks, the Council will be composed of members representing those states which were signatory to the terms of surrender imposed upon the enemy state concerned..."

When France and China were added to the Big Three as members of the Council of Foreign Ministers, the Big Three followed a wrong analogy. If it was the intention of the Big Three to model the Council of Foreign Ministers on the Security Council of the United Nations, they should have included not only the five permanent members but also the six non-permanent members, all of which are to be middle or small-sized nations.
explanation: The passage asserts a conclusion (“first mistake”) and supports it with premises: the Potsdam procedure restricts participation to surrender-signatories; adding only France and China is a “wrong analogy”; if modeling on the UN Security Council, inclusion should extend to non-permanent members as well. The conditional “If it was the intention…” provides the rationale linking procedure choice to the claim of error.
main_claim: Adopting the Potsdam-based procedure and adding only France and China was a mistake because, if the Council was to be modeled on the UN Security Council, it should also have included the non-permanent members.

argument_text: From the Soviet point of view, the participation of France and China was undesirable since, in their opinion, they had made no important contribution to the defeat of Germany. When the United States and Britain refused to accept this view, the meeting reached a deadlock, and the compromise solutions offered by Mr. Byrnes and Mr. Bevin failed to break this stalemate.
explanation: The passage presents a causal chain: Soviet objection to France and China; US/UK refusal to accept that objection; resulting deadlock not resolved by compromises. The premises explicitly lead to the conclusion about why the meeting stalemated.
main_claim: The refusal by the United States and Britain to accept the Soviet objection to France and China’s participation caused a deadlock that compromises failed to resolve.

argument_text:
From the time of the Dumbarton Oaks Conference, the USSR has expected the Big Three, which are charged with the responsibility of keeping the peace, to use the machinery of the United Nations for the purpose of fulfilling their responsibility.

This concept of international organization is based on the premise that the Big Three will take the leadership in constructing the peace. This is not a democratic concept, if by democracy we understand the equality of all nations. But this concept has already been accepted by the United States and Great Britain when they decided the veto power in the Big Three.
explanation: The argument claims that although the Big Three leadership concept is not “democratic,” it is nonetheless established and accepted, as shown by the veto power decision. Premises: USSR expectation of Big Three-led use of UN machinery; leadership premise; acknowledgment of its non-democratic nature; acceptance evidenced by veto power. The contrastive “But” ties acceptance to the main claim.
main_claim: The Big Three leadership model, though not democratic in the sense of equal nations, has been accepted—evidenced by the veto power—and thus underpins USSR expectations about using UN machinery.

argument_text: Another reason for the difference in opinion between Russia and the Western Powers lies in the fact that the former has another meaning for the word democracy than the latter. In the Anglo-Saxon world, democracy means individual liberty guaranteed by law and a government responsive to the wish of the people. For the Russians, the test of democracy is whether there is an equality of social and economic opportunity guaranteed by the State and safeguards against individual accumulations of land, wealth, and special anti-Fascist forces. The rights of man are defended by a one-party system which includes all the progressive-minded people and by an absolute suppression of all other parties either left or right.
explanation: The passage offers an explanatory argument: differences in definitions of “democracy” account for disagreements. It supports the claim by detailing contrasting conceptions (individual liberties vs. state-guaranteed socioeconomic equality and one-party system) as premises explaining divergent positions.
main_claim: Divergent definitions of democracy between Russia and the Western Powers help explain their differences of opinion.

argument_text: By that reasoning, the Russians would have the Big Three say the last word on all proposals affecting world security, while the United States and Great Britain would consult with the smaller powers.
explanation: This sentence draws an inference from prior premises (“that reasoning” about differing democratic concepts) to a concrete policy implication: Russians favor Big Three final authority, whereas US/UK favor consultation with smaller powers. The structure is inferential and explicit.
main_claim: Given their respective conceptions, Russia favors Big Three final authority on world security while the US and UK favor consulting smaller powers.

argument_text: The above are two tangible pieces of ideological outlook that are making for temporary division between the powers.
explanation: The sentence concludes that the two previously described ideological factors are causing temporary division. It references earlier premises and draws a causal conclusion, making the argumentative structure explicit.
main_claim: Those two ideological outlooks are currently causing a temporary division among the powers.

argument_text:
However, there are a number of intangibles which should be considered when weighing the results of the Council of Foreign Ministers. The Russians seem to suspect a tendency on the part of the Western Powers to unite and they have hinted at their fear of a Western bloc.

The USSR still feels isolated at international conferences. They fear that their allies will resume the attitude of hostility current prior to 1941, since their military aid is no longer needed. They disapprove of the United States' use of the atom bomb as a political weapon.
explanation: The passage advances an implicit causal-explanatory argument: beyond ideological factors, intangible perceptions (suspicion of a Western bloc, isolation, fear of renewed hostility, disapproval of atom-bomb politics) should factor into assessments of outcomes. The recommendation to “consider” these and the causal attributions imply that these intangibles influence divisions and the Council’s results, though the ultimate conclusion is not spelled out.
main_claim: Intangible factors such as Soviet suspicions, isolation, fears, and disapproval of U.S. atomic policy should be considered because they significantly shape the Council’s outcomes and East–West tensions.

argument_text: Despite all this, all the powers genuinely desire a system of world security, and should that desire be negated by the emergence of an anti-Soviet bloc, then we shall have tragedy on a world scale; tragedy which will make all mankind victims of hunger, chaos, and despair.
explanation: This is an explicit conditional warning: premise that all powers desire world security; conclusion that if an anti-Soviet bloc negates that desire, catastrophic global consequences will follow. The “should… then…” structure signals a clear argument form.
main_claim: If an anti-Soviet bloc emerges and undermines the shared desire for world security, it will lead to worldwide tragedy of hunger, chaos, and despair.

argument_text: The announcement that the U.S. has been selected as the permanent site of the United Nations Assembly provides literal proof that America has at last earned a position in international affairs which is commensurate with her avowed responsibilities.
explanation: This sentence presents evidence (the selection of the U.S. as the permanent site of the UN Assembly) to support a conclusion (that America has earned an international position matching its responsibilities). The causal/evidential phrasing “provides literal proof” makes the argument structure explicit.
main_claim: America has earned an international position commensurate with its avowed responsibilities, as evidenced by being chosen as the UN’s permanent site.

argument_text:
Many of us may become vain and overbearing upon receipt of this great honor. Others may feel that we have forced the world to accept our leadership by dint of sheer power.
If such impressions are projected into our foreign policy, the trust placed in our hands by the United Nations Organization will be imperiled and our hopes for a real peace, shattered.
explanation: The passage warns that certain attitudes (vanity; belief that leadership was forced) will, if carried into foreign policy, cause negative outcomes (imperiled trust; shattered hopes for peace). The conditional “If such impressions… the trust… will be imperiled” lays out premises leading to a clear conclusion.
main_claim: Allowing vanity or coercive self-conceptions to shape U.S. foreign policy will undermine UN trust in the U.S. and jeopardize hopes for peace.

argument_text: For the first time in history, there exists a nation which can place international security above its private interests, and which is strong enough to establish and enforce that security. If we prove, our sincerity will not be questioned. It is not questioned now. The world looks to us. We cannot turn our backs; we must not retreat.
explanation: The sequence asserts U.S. capacity and perceived sincerity, then concludes with a normative directive not to “turn our backs” or “retreat.” The conclusion is supported by premises about unique capability and global expectations (“The world looks to us”), but the inferential link is implied rather than formally stated; the phrase “If we prove” is also syntactically incomplete, increasing ambiguity.
main_claim: The United States must not retreat from its international responsibilities and leadership.

argument_text: If America is to house the capital of the world, then let us remember that we must stand together as citizens of the world, prepared to accept our new duties and responsibilities.
explanation: This is a conditional ought-claim: given the premise (America will house the world’s capital), the conclusion follows about what Americans ought to do (stand together as global citizens and accept new duties). The “If… then…” construction makes the argumentative structure explicit.
main_claim: Given that America will host the UN, Americans must unite as global citizens and accept new duties and responsibilities.

argument_text: The Italian Presepe is without Santa Claus or Xmas trees or gifts (which are instead distributed on January 6, on the Epiphany Holiday) but with the same issue: to amuse children, on the "Child's" holiday all over the world, under all skies.
explanation: This sentence presents a contrastive structure: despite lacking certain common Christmas elements (premise), the Presepe serves the same function (conclusion) of amusing children globally. The "but" signals the argumentative move from contrasting features to an asserted equivalence of purpose.
main_claim: Even without Santa, trees, or gifts at Christmas, the Italian Presepe serves the same purpose of amusing children worldwide.

argument_text: And on Christmas day, the first one with peace again, we will send also to Italian boys a Merry Christmas, I mean, a "Buon Natale!"
explanation: This is a recommendation framed as a collective intention. The phrase "the first one with peace again" functions as a reason, implying that because peace has returned after war, it is appropriate to extend Christmas greetings to Italian boys. The causal/normative link is implied rather than spelled out, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Because this is the first peaceful Christmas after the war, we should extend Merry Christmas greetings to Italian boys.

argument_text: Replacements Everyone will be pleased to hear that the supply department has a new form. It is to be used for those nice new replacements who come overseas with five points and under. The form will be a tag, distributed to all regular members of this organization and will read, "This is Mine." The first person to spot a replacement will be entitled to tag him and go home in his place.
explanation: The passage, in satirical tone, proposes a “policy” whereby any regular member who spots a low-point replacement can tag him and go home in his stead. While framed humorously as a “new form,” it advances a normative recommendation: replacements should enable current members to demobilize. The implicit reasoning is: (1) new replacements with very low points are arriving; (2) current members want to go home; therefore (3) a system allowing immediate swap (“This is Mine” tag) would be desirable/justified and would please everyone. Cues indicating implicitness include irony (“nice new replacements”), the exaggerated mechanism (a literal tag), and the claim that “everyone will be pleased,” which presupposes the desirability of the outcome rather than arguing for it explicitly.
main_claim: Regular members should be able to tag newly arrived low-point replacements and go home in their place.

argument_text: Band Bils Frank De Grazia and his new Second Bomb orchestra have been seen all about town the past week, and the guys, both alligators and long-hairs, have voiced hearty approval.
explanation: The passage presents evidence (wide visibility and “hearty approval” from diverse listeners) that implies an evaluative conclusion about the orchestra’s quality/popularity. The evaluative phrase “voiced hearty approval” functions as support for the implied claim that the band is well-received/good, without explicitly stating that conclusion.
main_claim: The orchestra is popular/well-received because many people across tastes voiced hearty approval.

argument_text: The orchestra splits up into two units for night-clubbing, and that way they covered all the high spots in town during the past week.
explanation: This sentence provides a causal structure: splitting into two units (premise) led to covering “all the high spots” (conclusion). The phrase “that way” signals an explicit reasoning link between action and outcome.
main_claim: Splitting into two units enabled the orchestra to cover all the high spots in town.

argument_text: The orchestra is putting out an appeal for a pianist. They need two to cover all their engagements, and Cpl "Wear Hall" Roberts is doing overtime on the ivories right now.
explanation: The passage asserts a need (conclusion) and provides reasons: numerous engagements require two pianists and the current pianist is overworked. The necessity (“need two”) is justified by workload and scheduling demands, forming a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The orchestra needs additional pianists (two) to meet their engagements because the current workload is too heavy.

argument_text: It was the turn-table under the influence, not Jack Early. The dial said 78 revolutions per. A quick count determined that it was spinning at 58 on that particular morning.
explanation: This passage asserts a clear conclusion (the turn-table was at fault, not the announcer) and immediately provides factual support (the turntable was spinning at 58 instead of the intended 78 RPM). The premises directly explain the anomalous audio and justify the conclusion.
main_claim: The strange broadcast sound was caused by a malfunctioning, slow-spinning turntable, not by Jack Early being impaired.

argument_text: He said, "What would the men in this Group rather do — go without a woman for a week or go without eating for a week?"
explanation: This rhetorical question functions as an argument: it presupposes that men would choose to forego sex rather than food, implying that hunger outweighs sex. The conclusion (hunger instinct is stronger) is suggested rather than stated, with the expected answer serving as the supporting premise.
main_claim: The hunger instinct is stronger than the sex instinct.

argument_text: The statement seemed conclusive until someone asked him to which mess-hall he was referring.
explanation: This sentence undercuts the prior argument by implying that the quality of the mess-hall food can reverse the expected preference, thereby weakening the claim that hunger is always stronger than sex. The irony and contextual insinuation serve as the implicit premise.
main_claim: The supposed conclusiveness of the hunger-over-sex claim is questionable because preferences may change if the food is bad.

argument_text: The 49th Squadron Communications Department has requested that we publish a notice for information leading to the arrest of someone who stole their ground station. It's not funny, either!
explanation: The evaluative statement “It’s not funny” paired with the report of a serious theft implies a normative claim: this theft should be treated seriously and the culprit apprehended. The seriousness of stealing a ground station functions as the implicit premise supporting that stance.
