main_claim: The theft of the ground station is serious and should be treated as such, with efforts made to find and arrest the culprit.

argument_text:
The Smile Did It

That young lady with the beautiful smile is Miss Wilbur Strange of Sumter, South Carolina, who won the Red Cross Sweetheart Photograph Contest. Below, we see Sgt. Elbert E. Morgan, 529th ASG, looking on as Capt. Joseph O'Neil announces him over AES, Foggia as the owner of the winning picture, Tuesday night at the Red Cross EM Club.
explanation: The headline “The Smile Did It” coupled with the description “the beautiful smile” and the report that she “won the ... Contest” implies a causal explanation: she won because of her smile. The evaluative language and framing function as premises supporting the implicit conclusion about why she won, even though no explicit argument markers (like “because”) are present.
main_claim: Miss Wilbur Strange won the Red Cross Sweetheart Photograph Contest because of her beautiful smile.

argument_text:
At the Gym

"A"-League pre-tournament game limbers up teams as the date of the first tournament match approaches.
explanation: The sentence asserts a causal/purposive relationship: the pre-tournament game serves to “limber up” teams, with the approaching tournament date as contextual justification. This implies an argument that holding such a game is beneficial preparation for the upcoming tournament, though it is presented as a descriptive statement rather than an explicit recommendation.
main_claim: Pre-tournament games help prepare (“limber up”) teams for the forthcoming tournament as its start date approaches.

argument_text: All pugilists or guys who want to batter someone's nose on general principles can do it legally by arranging a boxing match at the Second Bomb gym. John Russel opened the way this week when he completed work on the new boxing ring in the gym.
explanation: This passage advances the claim that legal boxing at the gym is now available, with the implied premise that the completion of the new ring enables this legality and opportunity. The causal connection is suggested rather than stated with “because,” making it an implicit argument: the completion of the ring “opened the way,” therefore those who want to fight can do so legally at this venue.
main_claim: Legal opportunities to box at the Second Bomb gym are now available because the new ring has been completed.

argument_text: The posts and ropes have adequate padding, and the ropes are good and springy.
explanation: By emphasizing adequacy of padding and the springiness of the ropes, the passage implicitly argues that the ring is safe and suitable for boxing. The evaluative term “adequate” and positive description serve as reasons supporting the unstated conclusion about safety/fitness.
main_claim: The boxing ring is safe and suitable for use.

argument_text: If enough entries appear for open competition, Russel intends to start a tournament, for which there is already one contender. Howard Price, an Australian welterweight, fought his way to fame last year, and if anyone thinks they can beat him, Price is available.
explanation: This passage implies that people should enter the competition: the conditional promise of a tournament and the presence of a notable contender (Howard Price) function as reasons to join. The appeal rests on desirability (a tournament) and challenge/prestige (facing a famed boxer), signaling a persuasive argument without explicit “should” wording.
main_claim: Prospective boxers should enter so a tournament can be held and potentially challenge the notable contender Howard Price.

argument_text: For a tournament, there are all the training facilities that one can expect to find outside of Stillman's, New York. Two punching bags mounted on wooden stands have recently been erected, and punching gloves go with them. There are also skipping ropes, and hot showers run until 2000 hours.
explanation: The first sentence makes a strong evaluative claim about the comprehensiveness/quality of training facilities, and the subsequent sentences list concrete evidence (punching bags, gloves, skipping ropes, hot showers) that directly supports the claim. This provides an explicit argument structure: assertion followed by specific supporting details.
main_claim: The gym has comprehensive, high-quality training facilities suitable for a tournament.

argument_text: There are also skipping ropes, and hot showers run until 2000 hours. Russel is currently appealing to the British Town Major to have the water facilities continue until 2200 hours.
explanation: The mention of current shower hours followed by Russel’s appeal implies a normative claim that the facilities ought to stay open later. The action of appealing functions as evidence of the perceived need; the structure suggests “because showers currently close at 2000, they should be extended to 2200,” even though the “should” is not explicitly stated.
main_claim: The gym’s water facilities should remain open until 2200 hours instead of 2000.

argument_text: Anyone who feels qualified to instruct boxers should contact Russel.
explanation: This directive implies a need for boxing instructors and urges qualified individuals to volunteer. The “should” signals a recommendation/ought-claim; the preceding context about facilities and a prospective tournament serves as background reasons, making this an implicit persuasive argument.
main_claim: Qualified individuals ought to volunteer as boxing instructors by contacting Russel.

argument_text: Russel requested that we give special mention to "Miss Santa Claus," Virginia Woolfolk (ARC), who added many of those gifts to the ones Russel provided.
explanation: The sentence advances a normative recommendation (to give special mention) and includes a justificatory clause (“who added many of those gifts”), which functions as the reason. The causal link is implied rather than signaled with an explicit connector like “because,” making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: The paper should give special mention to Virginia Woolfolk.

argument_text: Ave Maria, gentle maid, Oh hearken to our supplication, For Thou alone canst render aid. Through Thee a world would gain salvation. We sleep secure in Thy affection, And free from evil's dark design. O Virgin, ever give protection, And guard and keep us always Thine. Ave Maria...
explanation: This passage uses explicit causal markers (“For,” “Through Thee”) to argue that Mary alone can render aid and bring salvation; therefore, the supplicants are secure and ask her to protect and keep them. The premises (“Thou alone canst render aid,” “Through Thee a world would gain salvation”) support the conclusion/request for ongoing protection.
main_claim: Mary alone can render aid and thus should protect and keep the supplicants as her own.

argument_text: Ave Maria, purest maid. Because Thy wings enfold our sorrow, We waken safe and undismayed To greet with fortitude the morrow.
explanation: The explicit connector “Because” presents the premise (Mary’s comforting protection) leading to the conclusion that “we waken safe and undismayed” and can face tomorrow with fortitude.
main_claim: We awaken safe and undismayed to face tomorrow because Mary enfolds our sorrow.

argument_text: Thy smile illumines darkest places; It heals the wounds of all mankind. O Mother, see our upturned faces Fulfill each wish Thou has divined. Ave Maria...
explanation: The lines provide evaluative premises about Mary’s healing and illuminating power, followed by a petition “Fulfill each wish...” The implied argument is that because Mary heals and brings light, she ought to answer petitions. The normative request relies on the preceding attributions as reasons.
main_claim: Because Mary heals and illuminates humanity, she should fulfill the supplicants’ wishes.

argument_text: Ave Maria, stainless maid. All demons, seeing Thee, must perish; Thy virtue pierces through their shade. A light whose beams we ever cherish. We take our lives unto the altar; In thankfulness we seek Thy shrine. O grant that we may never falter As faithful children, ever Thine. Ave Maria...
explanation: The passage attributes power over demons and great virtue to Mary and presents devotion (“we take our lives unto the altar... we seek Thy shrine”) as reasons for the petition “O grant that we may never falter.” The conclusion (grant perseverance) is supported by the implied premises of Mary’s power and the supplicants’ devotion.
main_claim: Given Mary’s power and the supplicants’ devoted gratitude, she should grant that they never falter.

argument_text:
O come, all ye faithful, joyful and triumphant, O come ye, O come ye to Bethlehem; Come and behold Him, born the King of angels;

(After each verse) O come, let us adore Him, O come, let us adore Him, O come, let us adore Him, Christ the Lord.
explanation: This is a call to action (come, behold, adore) justified by the reason “born the King of angels.” The imperative plus stated status of the child implies the argument that because He is the King of angels (Christ the Lord), one ought to come and adore Him.
main_claim: Because Christ is born the King of angels, the faithful should come to Bethlehem and adore Him.

argument_text: Sing, choirs of angels, sing in exultation, Sing all, ye citizens of heaven above; Glory to God in the highest;
explanation: Commands to sing in exultation are paired with “Glory to God in the highest,” implying the reason for the action: God’s supreme glory warrants exaltant praise. The evaluative claim functions as the premise for the imperative.
main_claim: Because God merits the highest glory, angels and citizens of heaven should sing in exultation.

argument_text: Yea, Lord we greet Thee, born this happy morning; Jesus, to Thee be glory giv'n; Word of the Father, now in flesh appearing;
explanation: The attribution “Word of the Father, now in flesh appearing” provides the theological reason for the evaluative/normative claims “to Thee be glory giv’n” and the greeting; the incarnation justifies giving Jesus glory and greeting Him.
main_claim: Because Jesus is the incarnate Word of the Father, He should be greeted and given glory.

argument_text: Deck the halls with boughs of holly, Fa la la la la, la la la la. 'Tis the season to be jolly, Fa la la la la, la la la la.
explanation: The imperative “Deck the halls...” is justified by the seasonal claim “’Tis the season to be jolly,” implying that the festive season provides reason to decorate accordingly.
main_claim: Since it is the season to be jolly, people should deck the halls with holly.

argument_text: Sing we joyous all together, Fa la la la la, la la la la. Heedless of the wind and weather. Fa la la la la, la la la la.
explanation: An exhortation to “Sing we joyous all together” is strengthened by the directive “Heedless of the wind and weather,” implying that external conditions are not sufficient reasons to refrain; thus one should sing regardless of weather.
main_claim: We should all sing joyfully together regardless of the wind and weather.

argument_text: Fast away the old year passes, Fa la la la, la la la la la. Hail the new, ye lads and lasses, Fa la la la la, la la la la.
explanation: The call to “Hail the new” is implicitly justified by the observation that “the old year passes,” implying that the transition of the year is a reason to celebrate the new one.
main_claim: Because the old year is passing, people should hail the new year.

argument_text: The Foggia Post Exchange expects an increasing amount of unrationed goods according to PX Officers Lt. Don DeVogelier and Lt. Henry Skeele.
explanation: This presents a forward-looking claim (increasing unrationed goods) and cites officers as the source. The reliance on named officials functions as an argument from authority: the audience is invited to accept the expectation because PX officers say so. The argumentative structure is implicit because no explicit connective like “therefore” is used; the credibility cue is the attribution to officers.
main_claim: There will be an increasing amount of unrationed goods at the PX.

argument_text: Cigarette smokers will be happy to know that the backlog supply of Chesterfields is about gone. January’s rations will offer more variety of choice.
explanation: The first sentence provides a premise (the backlog of a single brand, Chesterfields, is nearly gone), and the second asserts a conclusion (January rations will have more variety). The causal link (less backlog of one brand implies greater variety) is implied through juxtaposition and evaluative framing (“will be happy to know”), not stated with explicit logical connectors.
main_claim: January cigarette rations will have more variety because the Chesterfield backlog is nearly gone.

argument_text:
The PX has been hit by redeployment, as has every other organization in Foggia. In December three of the GI staff were redeployed but were replaced by T/Sgt. Calvin Purvis and S/Sgt. Thomas Pare, who are both from the Second Bomb Group.

Business continues as usual.
explanation: These sentences supply premises (redeployment affected the PX; three GI staff left; replacements were obtained) and then assert a conclusion (“Business continues as usual.”). The adversative “but were replaced” signals a compensating reason supporting operational continuity. The conclusion is presented as a consequence of the replacements, though the inference is implicit.
main_claim: Despite redeployment, the PX’s operations are unaffected because departed staff were replaced.

argument_text: The closest we came in comparison was a B-24. We believe we're safe in making that statement because most of us in this area happen to be B-17 devotees.
explanation: This presents a conclusion supported by a stated reason. Conclusion: the armored car most closely resembles a B-24. Premise: the authors are B-17 devotees, implying they would be biased toward calling it a B-17, so choosing B-24 indicates confidence. The connective "because" makes the argument structure explicit.
main_claim: The armored car most closely resembles a B-24, and this judgment is reliable despite the authors’ B-17 preference.

argument_text: Later in the week we saw the car in action and to put it in the vernacular, "it really travels." Especially with the Provost Marshal, Lt. Murphy at the controls.
explanation: This links an observation (seeing the car in action) to an evaluative conclusion ("it really travels," meaning it is fast). The second sentence adds an intensifying qualifier that when Lt. Murphy drives, its speed is even more evident, implying causal attribution. The observation functions as the premise supporting the speed claim.
main_claim: The armored car is very fast, particularly when Lt. Murphy is driving it.

argument_text: Being a past master at receiving grunts from officers, we knew enough to accept this to mean "no".
explanation: There is an inferential move from a general premise (their extensive experience interpreting officers’ grunts) to a specific conclusion (the grunt here meant “no”). The causal/justificatory relation is explicit: their experience justifies the interpretation.
main_claim: Based on their prior experience, the officer’s grunt should be interpreted as a refusal.

argument_text:
Attention Beer Guzzlers!

The new armoured-cars recently acquired by the Foggia MP Station have made the MP’s so happy that they have decided to give away two cases of beer to the two men suggesting the best names for them.
explanation: The vocative “Attention Beer Guzzlers!” targets beer enthusiasts, and the announcement of “two cases of beer” for the best names functions as an incentive. Together they imply a persuasive claim: if you like beer, you should enter the naming contest to try to win beer. The conclusion (enter the contest) is suggested rather than stated, making it an implicit argument driven by audience targeting and incentive framing.
main_claim: Beer lovers should enter the naming contest to try to win beer.

argument_text: All they will need are names to suit their personalities. Stroll down to the MP Station and gaze upon them for inspiration.
explanation: This is a recommendation supported by a reason: the imperative “Stroll down … and gaze upon them” is justified by “for inspiration,” and the prior sentence establishes that names should “suit their personalities.” The structure gives a clear premise (seeing the cars will inspire suitable names) leading to a conclusion (you should go look at them).
main_claim: You should visit the MP Station to look at the cars because seeing them will inspire suitable names.

argument_text: Two men of the Twentieth squadron, Sgt. James E. Elliot and Sgt. Ralph B. Brown, were victims Sunday December 23rd, of what is believed to be an accidental shooting.
explanation: This advances the claim that the shooting was accidental. The phrasing “what is believed to be” signals reliance on an (unspecified) authoritative assessment, implying that readers should accept non-intentionality. The argument is implicit because no explicit reasons are provided; instead, the credibility of unnamed beliefs serves as an implied premise supporting the conclusion that the shooting was accidental.
main_claim: The shooting was accidental rather than intentional.

argument_text: it is the opinion of the doctors that Sgt. Elliot will carry no permanent disability from his wound.
explanation: This is an argument from expert authority: the premise is that medical professionals hold the opinion, and the conclusion is that Elliot will not have permanent disability. The structure explicitly invokes expert judgment as the reason to accept the claim.
main_claim: Sgt. Elliot will not suffer any permanent disability from his wound.

argument_text: Rumours of other shootings in the Foggia area are unfounded.
explanation: This asserts a conclusion that counters circulating claims. The implicit support comes from the article’s framing (“Some Facts”) and preceding specific, verified details about the single incident, suggesting that official information does not substantiate any additional shootings; thus, other rumors lack basis. The argument is implicit because the premises are not spelled out as reasons within the same sentence.
main_claim: There were no additional shootings in the Foggia area beyond the reported incident.

argument_text:
The Red Cross barbers are no longer paying rent to ARC. This was revealed by Miss Mary Doliver, the director of the EM Red Cross Club. At the same time, she emphasised, they are receiving all their supplies free of charge.

The individual barbers said that the money previously used for rent will be divided among them equally.

Thank you, nice people. —ESC
explanation: The passage presents premises that the barbers pay no rent and receive supplies free, and that they will keep the former rent money by dividing it among themselves. The concluding line “Thank you, nice people” is ironic/sarcastic, signaling a negative evaluation. Together, these cues imply the claim that the barbers are behaving selfishly or ungratefully by pocketing benefits rather than passing them on (e.g., to customers or the community). The argument is implicit because the conclusion is not stated directly but inferred from the contrast and sarcasm.
main_claim: The Red Cross barbers are acting selfishly by keeping the rent savings for themselves despite receiving free support.

argument_text: Arsonist At Work?
explanation: This is a rhetorical question that implies a claim rather than asking for information. The framing insinuates that the incident involved arson, cueing readers to interpret the subsequent narrative as evidence. The implicitness comes from the interrogative form and suggestive title rather than a direct assertion with explicit premises.
main_claim: An arsonist was involved in the incident described.

argument_text:
He walks into the heater room; turns gas up three turns past maximum; retires to bathroom to wait.

Scene: heater room. Time: twenty minutes later.

Man walks into heater room; sees, to his horror that an inch of an odorous liquid lines floor of heater room; dives towards furiously burning heater. There is an explosion. Man retreats.
explanation: The sequencing and causal cues (“turns gas up three turns past maximum” followed by “There is an explosion”) imply that the man’s deliberate over-adjustment of the gas created a dangerous condition that led to the explosion. This functions as an argument by narrative implication: it provides premises (reckless adjustment, flammable conditions, explosion) supporting the conclusion of responsibility/recklessness akin to arson, without explicitly stating it.
main_claim: The man’s reckless tampering with the heater’s gas setting caused the dangerous explosion and implies culpability.

argument_text: All is serene. The heater is burning gently. Inscribed upon the soot in the wall are the following words, "Arsonist Currie did it!"
explanation: The quoted inscription advances a clear claim of blame (“Currie did it”), but as presented it relies on the surrounding narrative as its support, making the argumentative structure implicit. The juxtaposition of calm aftermath with an accusatory inscription implies a conclusion about responsibility without laying out explicit premises within this sentence.
main_claim: Currie is responsible for the incident, characterized as arson.

argument_text: Due to the foresight of the ARC girls there was plenty of food on hand and no one went away hungry.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal premise (“Due to the foresight of the ARC girls”) leading to an outcome (“there was plenty of food on hand and no one went away hungry”). It explicitly argues that the ARC girls’ foresight ensured sufficient food and satisfaction.
main_claim: The ARC girls’ foresight ensured there was enough food so that no one went hungry.

argument_text: All present had a good time even if Santa never did come down the cardboard chimney.
explanation: The concessive structure (“even if”) contrasts an expected festive element (Santa appearing) with the reported outcome (everyone had a good time), implying that the event’s success did not depend on Santa’s appearance. The argument is implicit because it suggests, rather than states, that enjoyment came from other factors.
main_claim: The event was enjoyable despite the absence of a Santa appearance, showing that such theatrics were unnecessary for a good time.

argument_text: All who wished to attend the breakfast had been requested to sign up before. As it happened thirty men signed up and one hundred twenty arrived at the club expecting breakfast.
explanation: The juxtaposition of a prior request to sign up with the large disparity between sign-ups (30) and attendees (120) implies that the sign-up process was disregarded or unreliable. The argument is inferred from the contrast rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: The sign-up request was not effectively followed, making the sign-up an unreliable indicator of attendance.

argument_text: Oh Girls What Wonders You Do To Our Morale
explanation: This headline advances a positive evaluative claim that the presence/actions of the girls significantly improve morale. The passage itself contains no explicit premises, but in context it frames the subsequent descriptions (girls in civilian clothes, passing out donuts) as supporting evidence. The stance is signaled by expressive language (“What Wonders”) that implies a conclusion rather than arguing it explicitly.
main_claim: The girls greatly boost the morale of those present.

argument_text: The old fashioned carol sing at the EM Red Cross Club on Christmas Eve was a great success. Miss Mary Dolliver played the piano and led the singing with her usual vivacity. British, and South Africans mingled their voices with the soprano of the choir of Italian orphan boys. They had just finished singing for the broadcast of Dicken’s Christmas Carol but took time out from their ice cream to sing, “Jingle Bells”.
explanation: The first sentence states an evaluative conclusion (“was a great success”), and the following sentences provide descriptive details that function as implicit premises (energetic leadership, multinational participation, additional willing singing despite other engagements) that support the success judgment. The argument structure is implicit because causal connectors like “because” are not used, yet evidence is presented to justify the conclusion.
main_claim: The Christmas Eve carol sing at the EM Red Cross Club was highly successful.

argument_text: The ARC girls, all in civilian dresses (wow!) circulated around passing out donuts. It was hard to say which gave the biggest boost to morale: the singing or the girls in civilian clothes.
explanation: The second sentence asserts a comparative evaluative claim about morale-boosting effects, implying that both the singing and the girls in civilian clothes significantly raised morale. The prior sentence functions as contextual evidence (girls’ attire and action of passing out donuts) that supports the implied effect. The argument is implicit because the conclusion is suggested through comparison rather than laid out with explicit premises.
main_claim: Both the singing and the girls in civilian clothes substantially boosted morale, to the point that it’s hard to say which helped more.

argument_text: Few departments the size of group communications operate in as noiseless a manner. For the functions of this department are such as to remain unnoticed until they cease to function.
explanation: This presents a clear premise-conclusion structure signaled by "For." The main claim is that group communications operates very quietly; the supporting reason is that its functions are inherently unnoticed unless they fail, which explains the perceived noiselessness.
main_claim: Group communications operates more noiselessly than comparable departments because its functions go unnoticed unless they break down.

argument_text: Whenever a new order appears on the bulletin board, whenever you make a telephone call, whenever a radio-operator calls the ground the functions of this department are being used.
explanation: By listing ubiquitous activities and asserting that the department's functions are used in each, the passage implies a claim about the department's pervasive role and importance. The examples function as evidence, but no explicit conclusion marker is used, making it implicit.
main_claim: The group communications department’s functions are integral and in constant use across many routine activities.

argument_text: First, it was planned to write one article on the entire department. It was soon discovered that the functions of Group Communications are too diverse. So the three main subdivisions will be covered in three separate articles.
explanation: The passage states a decision and justifies it: because the department’s functions are "too diverse," therefore the coverage will be split into three articles. The conclusion is explicitly introduced by "So."
main_claim: Because the department’s functions are too diverse, the coverage will be split into three separate articles on its subdivisions.

argument_text: Few departments the size of group communications operate in as noiseless a manner. For the functions of this department are such as to remain unnoticed until they cease to function.
explanation: This is an argument: the first sentence makes a comparative claim about the department’s “noiseless” operation; the second sentence, introduced by “For,” provides the reason—its functions remain unnoticed unless they fail—which supports the conclusion that it operates noiselessly.
main_claim: Group Communications operates unusually noiselessly because its functions go unnoticed unless they stop working.

argument_text: First, it was planned to write one article on the entire department. It was soon discovered that the functions of Group Communications are too diverse. So the three main subdivisions will be covered in three separate articles.
explanation: This sequence offers a reasoned justification for a decision: the initial plan (one article) changed because the functions are “too diverse,” thus leading to the conclusion (stated with “So”) to cover the subdivisions in three separate articles.
main_claim: Because the department’s functions are too diverse, the coverage will be split into three separate articles rather than one.

argument_text: This is attached to another teletype machine of a late model and has an interesting use. If all the machines are operating full blast and there is another message to be sent, someone starts punching it out upon the perforator. This produces a tape with a series of little holes in it. As soon as the message can be transmitted, the tape is put into the "reperforator", a switch is thrown and the machine proceeds to send the original message automatically and without mistakes.
explanation: The passage advances an evaluative claim that the perforator’s use is “interesting,” implicitly justified by functional advantages described: it lets operators queue messages during peak load and later transmit them “automatically and without mistakes.” The reasons (queuing capability and error-free automation) support the positive evaluation, even though the conclusion is not stated in a formal argumentative structure.
main_claim: The perforator’s function is valuable/interesting because it enables queued, automatic, and error-free transmission when machines are busy.

argument_text: The perforator has another interesting ability. We watched a message coming through. It read thus, "When girls are young they like to kiss. When they grow up they do like this." If you’d like to find out what happens after that, drop in to the teletype room sometime.
explanation: This passage attempts to persuade readers to visit the teletype room. It provides a teaser (an incomplete, suggestive message) and then issues a conditional recommendation: “If you’d like to find out… drop in.” The implied argument is that curiosity or desire to know the continuation provides a reason to visit, even though the imperative is framed as an invitation rather than an explicit ought-statement.
main_claim: You should visit the teletype room if you want to find out the rest of the tantalizing message.

argument_text: The conversation divulged nothing, however, as his office is classified as “secret” even now that the war is over.
explanation: This sentence provides a conclusion ("The conversation divulged nothing") and an explicit reason ("as his office is classified as 'secret'"), forming a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The conversation revealed nothing because the office remains classified as secret.

argument_text: At the beginning of the war, a large number of men applied for jobs in the cryptography department. Lt. Taaffe believes it is because the science has long held an aura of mystery.
explanation: The second sentence explicitly offers a causal explanation ("because the science has long held an aura of mystery") for the observed phenomenon in the first sentence (many applications), thus forming an argument.
main_claim: Many men applied to cryptography at the war’s start because cryptography’s aura of mystery attracted them.

argument_text: He assures all would-be cryptographers that the era of secret inks is over. The important requirement now is the love of plain and simple office work.
explanation: These statements imply a contrast between romanticized expectations and the current reality of the work; the first sentence undermines the "secret inks" mystique, supporting the second sentence’s normative/descriptive claim about what is now required, without an explicit "because".
main_claim: Contemporary cryptography work primarily demands a love of plain, simple office tasks rather than romantic “secret inks.”

argument_text: Codes, always worked manually are slow and tedious. That is why military cryptography deals mainly in cyphers.
explanation: The second sentence draws an explicit inference ("That is why") from the premise that codes are manually worked and slow, concluding that military practice favors cyphers.
main_claim: Military cryptography mainly uses cyphers because codes are manually worked and slow.

argument_text: The situation is complicated by the position of the letter in the message and the number of letter substitutions used. However, almost all encoding and decoding is done by the use of machines which makes the process very speedy and poses a difficult problem indeed for an interceptor of a secret message.
explanation: The second sentence gives an explicit causal link ("which makes") from machine use to two conclusions: speed and increased difficulty for interceptors; the "However" contrasts prior complexity with the practical outcome.
main_claim: The use of machines makes encoding and decoding very fast and creates serious difficulties for interceptors.

argument_text: The “goodies” were obviously necessities to those who got them, and although only about one third of Foggia’s children were fed, at least some of them had a festa, American style.
explanation: This evaluative sentence advances two linked claims: that the gifts were necessities (not luxuries) and that, despite limited reach, the events were still a positive success for some. The word “obviously” signals a judgment, and the concessive “although... at least” structure implies a reasoning: even if only a third were fed (premise), it was still worthwhile that some had an American-style celebration (conclusion). The necessity claim is implied by context of hunger and crowding described elsewhere.
main_claim: The children's gifts were necessities, and despite feeding only a third of the children, the events were still worthwhile for those who benefited.

argument_text: I spoke to Mary Dolliver in the midst of it all. She supervised every-thing, and kept the atmosphere calm and efficient in the school in comparison to the roar outside. Nothing excited her, and she laughed in her motherly way, "I'm used to this." Two days later, when the last of her parties were over, she still laughed, but it was a wearier and heavier laugh. Feeding over four thousand hungry children in three days is work; but she was the happiest person in Foggia. The Red Cross had done a marvelous job.
explanation: This passage presents premises—Dolliver’s capable supervision under pressure, sustained effort over several days, and the scale of feeding “over four thousand hungry children”—that lead to a stated evaluative conclusion: “The Red Cross had done a marvelous job.” The contrast between calm efficiency inside and chaos outside, along with acknowledgment of hard work, functions as evidence supporting the concluding appraisal.
main_claim: The Red Cross did a marvelous job managing and delivering the children’s Christmas aid efforts.

argument_text: I felt like a heel. I didn’t need that candy.
explanation: These lines assert a moral evaluation of the author’s own need relative to the child’s, implying a normative claim: the candy was better given to the needy child. The feeling of guilt (“heel”) is presented as a reason grounded in perceived lack of need (“I didn’t need that candy”), signaling a value-laden argument about rightful allocation.
main_claim: Compared to the children, the author did not need the candy and thus it rightly belonged with them.

argument_text: The Christmas dinners were a tribute to the mess sergeants, depending on the particular piece of turkey you happened to get.
explanation: This is an evaluative claim praising mess sergeants for the quality of Christmas dinners, with a caveat about variability (“depending on the particular piece of turkey”). The implied reasoning is that the dinners’ quality reflects well on mess sergeants, even if outcomes varied, hence they deserve credit.
main_claim: Overall, mess sergeants deserve credit for the Christmas dinners despite some variability in quality.

argument_text: The American's celebrations were no milder, even if perhaps a bit nostalgic. Franck DeGrazia and his orchestra were seen and heard all over town, from the night spots to the serenades of Christmas Eve.
explanation: The first sentence makes a comparative claim that Americans celebrated just as vigorously, tempered by nostalgia. The following sentence provides supporting evidence (ubiquitous orchestra performances). The argument is implicit because the evidence is presented narratively without explicit connective language like “because.”
main_claim: Americans celebrated just as energetically as anyone else, though with some nostalgia.

argument_text: The children were outstandingly well behaved and one of them sang the Star Spangled Banner in Italian.
explanation: This asserts an evaluative claim about behavior and gives an illustrative example (singing the anthem) as evidence. The structure implies that exemplary conduct is demonstrated by such respectful actions.
main_claim: The orphaned children at the party behaved exceptionally well, as illustrated by one child singing the U.S. anthem in Italian.

argument_text: Major Berg tried to pull his rank on some of the noisier little guys, but they just said, "O. K., Sarge."
explanation: The contrastive “but” signals that military rank failed to command deference from the children. The anecdote implies the broader claim that hierarchical authority is ineffective in this context; the kids’ response downgrading “Major” to “Sarge” serves as evidence.
main_claim: Military rank carried little persuasive or controlling power over the children in the party chaos.

argument_text: After two years in and out of the war zones, after dangerous service freely offered, we find it almost insupportable to have to bear up with the inanities of those fresh from training camps, men whose sole contact with the brutal war now ended was through the medium of United States newspapers in comfortable clubs and dayrooms.
explanation: This passage criticizes the complaints of inexperienced soldiers by contrasting the author's combat experience with the “inanities” of those who only knew the war through newspapers. The evaluative language (“inanities,” “comfortable clubs and dayrooms”) implies the main claim that such complaints lack legitimacy, without stating the conclusion directly. The premise is the speaker’s extensive, dangerous service; the implied conclusion is that the complainers’ views are trivial and burdensome.
main_claim: Complaints from fresh, non-combat-experienced soldiers are inane and illegitimate, especially to those who served in war zones.

argument_text: Well-paid, easy-living, griping — these are the men from whom emanate the most torrid condemnation of their lot as occupation troops. They can do no good here, they say; they must return immediately to their native villages and cities, they cry, or their nerves, their dispositions, their country’s economy will suffer irreparably. To all of you short-sighted complainers, gentlemen, let it be said that by means of conduct and dignified service to your country you can not only earn your money, but do our nation a substantial credit as well.
explanation: This sequence presents the complainers’ claims as premises to refute (“They can do no good here... must return... or else harms will occur”) and concludes with a directive and positive alternative (“by means of conduct and dignified service... you can not only earn your money, but do our nation a substantial credit”). The structure moves from characterization of the complainers to a clear recommendation and stated benefits, forming an explicit argument.
main_claim: Instead of complaining and demanding to return home, occupation troops should serve with dignity because they can earn their pay and bring credit to the nation.

argument_text: The people you pass by on the street look to you as representatives of the greatest nation on earth; and by your actions you give them either vicarious pride in your birthright, or else you generate odium and sully the flag that flies over our comfortable quarters.
explanation: This sentence asserts a causal link between soldiers’ behavior and national reputation (“you give them either vicarious pride… or else you generate odium and sully the flag”). It implies the normative conclusion that soldiers ought to behave properly to produce pride rather than odium, although the “ought” is not stated. The premise is that soldiers are seen as national representatives; the implied conclusion is a recommendation about their conduct.
main_claim: Because soldiers’ actions shape how others view their nation, they should act in ways that inspire pride rather than generate odium and sully the flag.

argument_text: That is OK Ma, be they wanted to start a little band. Now, I have heard they are selling them at the usual markup in prices.
explanation: The juxtaposition sets up a conditional approval (buying to form a band is acceptable) contrasted with the new information that the instruments are being resold at a markup. The contrast implies a normative conclusion that reselling at a markup is wrong/objectionable, even though it is not directly stated. The evaluative “OK” versus “Now, I have heard…” cue the implicit stance.
main_claim: Buying up PX instruments is acceptable only if for a band, but reselling them at a markup is wrong.

argument_text:
I always thought that the men are few and far between who would take such a much desired commodity from the PX and then sell it to the Italians, thereby doing dirt to their buddies. I play an instrument and could really have used one.
I don’t know who these men are. I don’t want to know. But they know who they are and they also know what vermin they are.
explanation: The passage presents premises and a conclusion. Premises: the instruments are a “much desired commodity,” some men took them from the PX and resold them to Italians; the writer needed one. Conclusion: such behavior is “doing dirt to their buddies” and those responsible are “vermin.” The causal connector “thereby” explicitly links the action to the harm, supporting the evaluative conclusion.
main_claim: The men who bought up PX instruments and resold them to Italians harmed their fellow servicemen and are contemptible.

argument_text: (The PX informs us that there are still two instruments left. One, A Buscher Sax at 239 dollars and one Trombone at 119 dollars. They also hope to get some more instruments in around the 8th of January. Don’t be too harsh on those guys because after all they are only byproducts of a rotten system that never stopped the whole black market when it originally started: Ed)
explanation: The editor advances a prescriptive conclusion—“Don’t be too harsh on those guys”—and provides reasons: they are “byproducts of a rotten system” that failed to stop the black market at its inception. The “because” explicitly connects the systemic-causation premises to the normative recommendation.
main_claim: Readers should moderate their condemnation of the resellers because systemic failure to curb the black market is chiefly to blame.

argument_text: "Peace on earth, good will toward men" — democracy must cling to that message. For it is my deep conviction that democracy cannot live without that true religion which gives a nation a sense of justice and of moral purpose. Above our political forums, above our market places stand the altars of our faith — altars on which burn the fires of devotion that maintain all that is best in us and all that is best in our Nation.
explanation: This passage argues that democracy must adhere to a religious message because democracy depends on “true religion” to supply justice and moral purpose, and because religious devotion sustains what is best in the nation. The connective “For” introduces the reason, and the final sentence elaborates how religion functions as a sustaining cause, making the premise–conclusion structure explicit.
main_claim: Democracy must cling to the religious message of “peace on earth, good will toward men.”

argument_text: We have need of that devotion today. It is that which makes it possible for government to persuade those who are mentally prepared to fight each other to go on instead, to work for and to sacrifice for each other.
explanation: This passage claims we need devotion now, and gives a causal reason: devotion enables government to persuade potential antagonists to cooperate and sacrifice. The second sentence provides an explicit “because”-type justification for the first.
main_claim: We need religious devotion today because it enables government to turn potential conflict into cooperative work and sacrifice.

argument_text: That is why we need to say with the Prophet: "What doth the Lord require of thee — but to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with thy God?"
explanation: “That is why” signals an inferential link to prior reasons about devotion’s social benefits, concluding that we ought to endorse and repeat the Prophet’s ethical injunctions. It is a normative recommendation justified by earlier premises.
main_claim: We should affirm the Prophet’s call to justice, mercy, and humility.

argument_text: That is why the recovery we seek. In it are included justice and love and humility, not for ourselves as individuals alone, but for our Nation.
explanation: The phrase “That is why” marks a conclusion drawn from previous reasons: the recovery being sought is defined to include justice, love, and humility at a national level. Despite the elliptical syntax, the structure is a claim about what recovery must comprise, justified by the preceding appeal to devotion and moral requirements.
main_claim: The recovery we seek must include justice, love, and humility for the nation as a whole.

argument_text: That is the road to peace. That is the road to peace.
explanation: This asserts that the previously described path (devotion, justice, mercy, humility in national recovery) leads to peace. The support is implied by the earlier premises; here no reasons are restated, so the argumentative force relies on prior context.
main_claim: Following the path of national devotion to justice, mercy, and humility leads to peace.

argument_text: The news that a showdown among the Army, the Treasury, and the State Department is brewing over the subject of the responsibility for American policy should not come at a surprise.
explanation: This sentence asserts a normative-evaluative claim (that the brewing showdown is unsurprising) without explicit reasons in the same sentence. It implies that inter-agency conflict over policy responsibility is predictable, drawing on the context of differing agency roles and preferences mentioned immediately after. The stance is implied through evaluative phrasing (“should not come at a surprise”).
main_claim: Inter-agency conflict over responsibility for American policy is to be expected and thus unsurprising.

argument_text: The situation which faces the United States is this: How are the Allies to assure the German people a standard of living equal to that of any other people of Europe (with an exception of England and Russia) without permitting them to rebuild an industrial economy which might again threaten the peace of Europe and the world?
explanation: This rhetorical question frames a dilemma—simultaneously ensuring German living standards and preventing reindustrialization that could threaten peace. It implies the claim that the policy challenge is difficult and requires a carefully balanced approach. The argumentative force comes from the contrast (“assure ... without permitting”), signaling a tension that guides policy conclusions later.
main_claim: Reconciling German economic welfare with preventing a renewed industrial military threat is a difficult policy dilemma for the Allies.

argument_text: Any economic program for Germany must consider these items: One, the destruction of German industry, which deprived that country of its military power, can be easily reclaimed if raw materials are supplied from abroad. Two, while there is no disagreement between the four occupying powers regarding the elimination of war industries, there is difference of view over the question of the types and sizes of industries to be retained in Germany for peacetime needs. Three, the creation of four administrative zones and the cession of Germany’s most productive agricultural areas to Poland, which lacks the mechanical implements and the technological knowledge to continue their development, was a grave administrative error. As a result, the Allies may be forced to continually furnish Germany with food and make her dependent upon the United States and Great Britain for handouts.
explanation: The passage explicitly argues that any economic program “must consider” three points, which are then provided as premises: (1) German industrial capacity could be regained with raw materials; (2) inter-Allied disagreements about permissible peacetime industries; (3) zonal division and territorial cessions to Poland were an administrative error causing likely dependence on Allied food aid. The conclusion (what programs must consider) is supported by these concrete considerations and the causal consequence (“As a result”).
main_claim: Any economic program for Germany must account for the ease of industrial revival via raw materials, Allied disagreements over peacetime industries, and the harmful consequences of zonal division and territorial cessions that may force ongoing Allied support.

argument_text: There is still another fact to be considered by those who would analyze Allied policy in Germany. The work of the four powers reflects national differences. The British use a small number of well-trained administrators to direct German activities. The Americans, with their zest for speed, are annoyed at the German slowness to speed their economic and political recovery. The Russians have removed from their zone all the industrial equipment and consumer goods they need, considering them legitimate reparations for Russian losses. The French have not been far behind the Russians in removing foodstuffs and consumer goods from their zone.
explanation: The passage advances the claim that Allied administration reflects national differences and supports it with concrete examples for each occupying power’s behavior. The initial sentence sets a normative frame (“fact to be considered”), making the examples premises that justify the conclusion about divergent national approaches shaping policy outcomes.
main_claim: Allied occupation practices in Germany reflect distinct national differences, which must be taken into account when analyzing policy.

argument_text: The political revolution fostered unwittingly and unwillingly by the Allies is one which will leave Germany with a political regime left of center and an economy replete with extensive governmental controls.
explanation: This sentence makes a causal prediction that Allied actions are fostering a left-of-center regime and a heavily controlled economy. The argument is implicit: it attributes causation (“fostered … by the Allies”) and projects an outcome without detailing evidence in this sentence, relying on the prior discussion of occupation practices to imply the basis.
main_claim: Allied policies are inadvertently producing a left-of-center political order in Germany with extensive economic controls.

argument_text: The establishment of such an inter-departmental control would be favorable to the United States and the United Nations because it is only the left elements which are positively anti-Nazi and would be anxious to work with the Allies. Because the powers represented at Versailles in 1919 failed to support these elements, the Weimar Republic fell.
explanation: This advances a policy recommendation (establish inter-departmental control) and provides two explicit premises: (1) only left elements are definitively anti-Nazi and cooperative, and (2) historical precedent (failure to support left elements after WWI) led to Weimar’s fall. The “because” clauses link premises to the conclusion, forming a clear argument.
main_claim: An inter-departmental control favoring cooperation with left elements should be established because these groups are reliably anti-Nazi and history shows failing to support them leads to regime failure.

argument_text: It is not a question of a War Department policy or a State Department policy or one emanating from the Treasury Department.
explanation: This negation implies that the correct approach is not siloed by individual departments, suggesting the need for a unified, cross-departmental policy. The argument is implicit in rejecting alternatives, thereby advancing a contrary preferred approach (unity/inter-departmental policy).
main_claim: U.S. policy toward Germany should not be driven by individual departmental agendas but by a unified approach.

argument_text: What should be America’s role? The United States should decide to participate in the Allied occupation of Germany as long as necessary. Second, an agency dealing with occupation affairs representing all agencies of the government should be created to expedite occupation decisions. Third, a corps of qualified civilians should be sent to Germany to administer the American zone for a number of years and replace military administrative personnel.
explanation: This sequence poses a policy question and immediately provides three recommendations (continued participation, creation of a cross-agency occupation body, and deployment of qualified civilians). The “should” language marks normative claims; the rationale is implied by prior discussion of inter-agency conflict and administrative shortcomings, but not restated here, making the argument implicit.
main_claim: The U.S. should remain in the occupation, create a unified occupation agency across government, and replace military administrators with qualified civilians for several years.

argument_text: It should be a policy enunciated and developed by the United Nations, a policy which would approach the German people not in a spirit of revenge or sentimentality. In cooperation with the German people, the United Nations should uproot those causes which lead a nation to use modern technology for destructive purposes and remedy those flaws so that industry can be used for the benefit of the world community.
explanation: This recommends that policy be UN-led and non-revengeful, with a stated goal: uproot causes of destructive uses of technology and fix flaws “so that” industry serves global benefit. The “so that” provides an explicit consequentialist justification for the recommended approach.
main_claim: A UN-led, non-revengeful policy should cooperate with Germans to remove the causes of destructive militarism so that German industry benefits the world community.

argument_text: De Grazia’s ‘Occupators’ Take Place Of Carolers
explanation: The headline frames the band as substituting for traditional carolers, implying they fulfilled the communal/caroling role during Christmas. The claim is suggested via the metaphor “Take Place Of,” which presupposes a lack or need for carolers that the band met.
main_claim: De Grazia’s band fulfilled the role of Christmas carolers for the community.

argument_text: The music came closer and many leaned out of their windows to listen. GIs smiled in their sleep, as if hearing the music in a dream. For a moment they were home.
explanation: The passage uses observational details (people listening, smiling) to imply a causal conclusion that the music produced feelings of being “home.” The evaluative phrase “For a moment they were home” functions as the tacit conclusion drawn from the preceding descriptive premises.
main_claim: The band’s music gave the GIs a comforting sense of being at home.

argument_text: This bit of Christmas happiness was spread by Frank De Grazia and his Occupators. Not satisfied with playing at dances and parties, they went out on a serenade. After a long days work they took their horns and spread the Spirit of Christmas with their music.
explanation: These sentences assert a clear causal and evaluative claim: the band actively spread “Christmas happiness” and the “Spirit of Christmas,” supported by reasons about their actions (going on a serenade after a long day’s work). The premises (effort, initiative) lead to the conclusion (they spread Christmas spirit).
main_claim: Frank De Grazia and his Occupators spread Christmas happiness and the Spirit of Christmas by serenading after a long day’s work.

argument_text: A happier Foggia thanked them.
explanation: This sentence implies that Foggia’s increased happiness resulted from the band’s actions and that the community’s gratitude is evidence of this positive impact; the causal link is suggested rather than stated with “because.”
main_claim: The band’s serenade made Foggia happier and prompted public gratitude.

argument_text: In their songs they try to present a story which will bring to light a message from the scriptures that will tend to broaden the spiritual side of life as well as improve our everyday living.
explanation: This passage advances a causal-normative claim: that conveying scriptural messages through song tends to broaden listeners’ spiritual life and improve everyday living. The premises are implied (scriptural messages presented in story form), and the conclusion is the beneficial effect on spirituality and daily life. The argument is implicit because it is framed as a description of the quartet’s aim and expected effect, without explicit argumentative markers like “therefore” or direct evidence; it assumes the positive efficacy of scriptural messages.
main_claim: Presenting scriptural messages in song tends to broaden spiritual life and improve everyday living.

argument_text: Next, Joe learned to his woe that he was over his head in paperwork. In applying for veteran benefits, he discovered, he had to have handy his serial number, discharge papers, pension ‘C’ number, draft classification, GI insurance policies, social security card, birth certificate and marriage certificate. Without these he’s lost.
explanation: This recommends that veterans keep specific documents handy because they are required to apply for benefits. The conclusion (keep documents) is implied by the listed requirements and the evaluative statement “Without these he’s lost,” which functions as the reason-consequence cue.
main_claim: Veterans need to keep required documents ready because without them they will be unable to secure their benefits.

argument_text: Former servicemen who want to keep their National Service Life Insurance policies should check through their discharge papers to find out when the next premium is due, and before that date send a check or money order to Collections Sub-division, Veterans Administration, Washington, D. C., and make it payable to the Treasurer of the United States.
explanation: This gives a prescriptive course of action tied to a goal: to keep the insurance policy. The implied premise is that timely payment is necessary to maintain coverage; therefore, one should check the due date and pay before it.
main_claim: To keep their NSLI policies in force, veterans should verify the premium due date and pay it before that date.

argument_text:
Since National Service Life Insurance is presently limited to an 8-year term, a policyholder may want to convert before that period expires to government ordinary life, 20-payment life, or 30-payment life. This can be done by filling out VA Form 1535. The new policy will have a cash value
after a year and vets may borrow on it if necessary, but conversion will sharply increase premium costs.
explanation: This presents reasons (the term limit, cash value, borrowing ability) and a counterconsideration (higher premiums) to support the recommendation that a policyholder may want to convert before expiry. The recommendation is not phrased as a strict conclusion but is clearly advised based on the stated pros and cons.
main_claim: Veterans should consider converting their NSLI term policy before it expires because conversion offers cash value and borrowing options, despite higher premiums.

argument_text: All persons who arranged to postpone payment on private insurance when they entered the service must bring their payments up-to-date within 2 Years after discharge, if they wish to continue the insurance. If in a position to do so, ex-servicemen may want to keep both NSLI and private insurance.
explanation: The first sentence provides a conditional requirement to maintain private coverage; the second offers a recommendation to keep both types of insurance if feasible. The advice is implied to be beneficial due to maintaining multiple coverages; the requirement provides the practical premise supporting the recommendation.
main_claim: Veterans should update deferred private insurance payments and, if they can, keep both NSLI and private policies to maintain coverage.

argument_text: Want to make a few post-war improvements on your mental faculties? One of the best features in the G.I. Bill of Rights is its educational provisions. Vets who have been in active duty 90 days or more, regardless of their age at time of enlistment, are eligible for a year in the classroom, or its all-time equivalent, all expenses paid to the tune of 500 dollars a school year, and 50 dollars monthly for living expenses for an unmarried person. A wife, husband, or other dependent rates an additional 25 dollars.
explanation: This implicitly argues that veterans should take advantage of GI Bill education because it is a valuable benefit. The evaluative claim (“One of the best features…”) and the listed financial supports function as reasons supporting the desirability of using the educational provisions.
main_claim: Veterans should consider using GI Bill educational benefits because they are generous and support post-war self-improvement.

argument_text:
"Points" will be important to a GI after he is discharged, too. To be eligible for Civil Service, it is necessary to take and pass a Civil Service examination—and a veteran gets 5 extra points added to his grade, as bonus. Disabled vets receive 10 points.

Since Civil Service applicants are placed on a list from which they are hired in order of grade, the extra points mean that veterans go higher on the list. And when vets and non-vets receive the same score, the job goes to those who have been in the armed forces. In all Civil Service jobs, except scientific and professional jobs where the starting salary is over 3000 dollars, disabled vets who pass the examination automatically find their names right at the top of the list.
explanation: This states a conclusion (“‘Points’ will be important”) and provides explicit reasons: extra points on exams raise veterans’ rankings and tie-breaks favor veterans; disabled vets get even higher preference. The premises clearly lead to the conclusion about importance.
main_claim: Civil Service preference points will be important to discharged GIs because they raise rankings and give veterans hiring priority.

argument_text: Soldiers would do well to list on a sheet of paper their education, pre-war experience, hobbies, skills acquired in Army, USAFI courses, and any other pertinent information. This list might be presented to the I&E officer, an appropriate veteran’s counselor, or any qualified officer or EM who conceivably might be of help. If a man would like to open a haberdashery, he would do well to visit several local ones, if any, and ask the proprietor his advice: how much experience is necessary; what hours he works; what capital is required; what income might be expected; and so on. A soldier overseas could—and should—write General Electric, for example, if he would like to become a dealer in electrical appliances, stating his qualifications and requesting information.
explanation: This recommends specific actions (compile a skills list, seek advice from practitioners, write companies) to improve job or business prospects. The reasons are implied by the usefulness of presenting the list to counselors and obtaining practical information from industry sources.
main_claim: Soldiers should proactively inventory their qualifications and seek targeted advice and information to improve their job or business prospects.

argument_text: The important thing is for men to act NOW to find their niche, and not wait until they are discharged.
explanation: This prescriptive claim urges immediate action, with the rationale implied by the surrounding guidance that preparation and early inquiries aid placement and planning.
main_claim: Veterans should start planning and seeking opportunities immediately rather than waiting until discharge.

argument_text: In general, sections of the country where the population is on the increase are most prosperous. Men who are free to move around should take advantage of this fact. The Missouri Valley, for example, should become such an area when the power-electrification-flood control projects there get going.
explanation: This presents a general premise (growing-population areas are more prosperous), gives a specific example (Missouri Valley due to forthcoming projects), and draws a prescriptive conclusion that mobile men should move to capitalize on prosperity.
main_claim: Veterans who can relocate should target growing-population areas, such as the Missouri Valley as projects commence, to benefit from greater prosperity.

argument_text: Soldiers with a hankering to buy their own farms or set up their own businesses, should proceed with caution. Right now, they’re likely to have to have to pay a war-inflated price. Men should not go in for either project without considerable experience and study of local conditions affecting success. The Department of Agriculture, on the one hand, and the Smaller War Plants Corp. and Department of Commerce, on the other, can provide helpful information.
explanation: This argues for caution in buying farms or starting businesses, providing reasons: war-inflated prices and the need for experience and local knowledge, and it offers sources of information to mitigate risks. The premises support the conclusion to proceed cautiously and research first.
main_claim: Veterans considering farms or businesses should proceed cautiously and conduct substantial research due to war-inflated prices and the need for experience and local knowledge.

argument_text: Outside of the ARC Club was an excited mob of gift-seekers drawn by the promise of a Christmas party.
explanation: This sentence advances a causal claim: the promise of a Christmas party caused (drew) an excited mob of gift-seekers. The argumentative cue is the causal phrasing “drawn by,” which attributes the crowd’s presence to the promise. Although presented as a description, it implicitly argues that the announcement was effective in attracting people.
main_claim: The promise of a Christmas party attracted a large, excited crowd outside the ARC Club.

argument_text: Inside, joy reigned supreme. Jock Jordon watches Santa (Bob Olivigli) give a present to a Foggia child.
explanation: This two-sentence passage presents an evaluative conclusion (“joy reigned supreme”) followed by a scene that functions as implicit evidence (Santa giving a present to a child being watched), implying that the joyous atmosphere is demonstrated by the festive gift-giving moment. The evaluative language and the juxtaposition of evidence indicate an implicit argument.
main_claim: The atmosphere inside the ARC Club was very joyful.

argument_text: Well, see the town. Probably New York. I’ve never been there.
explanation: The speaker states an intended action (see the town, probably New York) and immediately provides a reason (“I’ve never been there”), which functions as a premise supporting the conclusion about the choice of destination. The causal relation is clear even without a connector like “because.”
main_claim: He will go see New York first because he has never been there.

argument_text: Due to the success of the Occupators on past remote broadcasts, it was decided to make their weekly appearance at the Fortress Club a regular feature on the air.
explanation: This sentence presents a clear causal justification (premise: past broadcasts were successful) for the decision (conclusion: make the appearance a regular on-air feature). The phrase “Due to” signals explicit reasoning from cause to decision.
main_claim: The show was made a regular on-air feature because past remote broadcasts were successful.

argument_text: The outstanding number will undoubtedly be George Gershwin's "Rhapsody in Blue." They have a specialty arrangement made by Marty Dell, a former member of the band who at one time worked with Fred Waring.
explanation: This passage asserts a judgment (“outstanding number”) and immediately provides credentials about the arrangement and arranger, implying justification. The support is suggested by juxtaposition and prestige cues (specialty arrangement; arranger’s notable background) rather than an explicit “because,” making the argumentative link implicit.
main_claim: “Rhapsody in Blue” will be the standout piece of the program.

argument_text: The half-hour broadcasts usually run about seven numbers, but they only intend to announce three or four before the show. That leaves a little element of surprise for those listening in.
explanation: This gives a policy (announce fewer selections) and explicitly states the intended consequence/justification (“That leaves a little element of surprise”), forming a straightforward reason-conclusion relationship.
main_claim: Announcing only some selections preserves an element of surprise for listeners.

argument_text: Like every other section, the band has been hit by redeployment. They just recently lost Sgt. John Maxwell, assistant solo clarinetist; Cpl. Early Kern, third trombone in the Occupators; Cpl. Rowe Scott, tenor sax in the Jive Bombers; and Pfc. Steve Mizerak, bass man in the Occupators. "Even if all the men with over forty-five points left, we could carry on," said De Grazia, who has forty-two points. "We're doing our best to keep things rolling until the last man is out of Foggia."
explanation: The losses due to redeployment are detailed and followed by De Grazia’s claim that the band can “carry on” and their commitment to keep things rolling. The argument is that despite losses (premise), the band remains capable and committed (conclusion). The causal or resource-based sufficiency is implied rather than spelled out.
main_claim: Despite redeployment losses and potential further departures, the band can continue performing and is committed to doing so.

argument_text: CID Very Active In Recovery Of Stolen Military Equipment Between fifty thousand and seventy-five thousand dollars worth of United States Government equipment has been recovered by the Foggia branch of the Civilian Investigation Department in the past 30 days.
explanation: The headline asserts a positive evaluative claim (“CID Very Active”) and the following sentence provides quantitative evidence (the dollar amount recovered in 30 days). The structure is that the large recovery figure functions as an unstated reason supporting the conclusion that CID activity has been robust.
main_claim: The CID has been very active in recovering stolen military equipment recently.

argument_text: Most stolen vehicles are recovered in the vicinity of Naples or Avellino. The town of Avellino near Naples is known as a center of crime for deserters and Italian gangsters. A great many of the recovered vehicles were found while engaged in black market operations.
explanation: The juxtaposition of recovery locations with the characterization of Avellino as a crime center, plus the association with black market operations, implicitly argues that criminal hubs and black-market activity are the locus of stolen vehicles and explain why recoveries occur there. The causal/explanatory link is implied by selective facts and evaluative labeling (“center of crime”).
main_claim: Stolen military vehicles tend to be tied to criminal hubs like Naples/Avellino and to black market operations.

argument_text: The CID men emphasize the necessity for care of equipment. Keeping things from being stolen is easier than getting them back.
explanation: This presents a normative recommendation (“necessity for care of equipment”) supported by a stated reason (“keeping things from being stolen is easier than getting them back”). The premise directly justifies the conclusion about what ought to be done.
main_claim: Personnel should take care to prevent theft of equipment because prevention is easier than recovery.

argument_text: To be emphasized are very heavy bombers, which were largely responsible for the strategic bombing of Japan.
explanation: The sentence advances a policy recommendation (emphasize very heavy bombers) and provides a reason (they were largely responsible for the strategic bombing of Japan). The causal clause functions as an explicit premise justifying the proposed emphasis, forming a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The peacetime air program should emphasize very heavy bombers.

argument_text: To save expense, it is planned to operate units at 100 percent of the authorized table of organization, instead of 100 percent as during the war.
explanation: The phrase "To save expense" provides an explicit rationale for the operational plan, linking the intended action (operating units at a specified level) to the goal of cost savings. This is an explicit purpose/means argument: the policy is justified by the cost-saving objective. Note: the text’s identical percentages introduce ambiguity but the argumentative structure remains clear.
main_claim: Operating units at the authorized table of organization is planned in order to save expense.

argument_text: A Veterans Administration spokesman said the number of veterans who have been turned down "are relatively small".
explanation: This sentence advances an evaluative claim (“relatively small”) implying a comparison to the much larger number of approvals reported earlier in the article. The underlying premise (many more approvals than rejections) supports the conclusion that rejections are few. The premise is not stated within the sentence itself but is supplied by the preceding statistics, making the argument implicit.
main_claim: The share of veterans’ loan applications that are rejected is small relative to the total.

argument_text: "By far the greatest number of rejections have not been the fault of the applicant but of inflated real estate values," he said. He explained that under the bill, loans cannot be granted unless the property to be purchased can be obtained at "a reasonable normal value". "Reasonable normal value has been the joker. Real estate prices have gone sky high and what was a reasonable price when the bill was passed can hardly be found now."
explanation: This passage presents a causal argument: Conclusion—most rejections are due to inflated real estate values, not applicant fault. Premises—(1) the law forbids loans unless properties are at a “reasonable normal value”; (2) real estate prices have “gone sky high,” so such values are hard to find. The rule plus the market condition together explain (and justify) the stated conclusion.
main_claim: Most loan application rejections result from inflated real estate prices rather than any fault of the applicants.

argument_text: Miss Antonietta was chosen as the 'Queen of the Dance' at the regular Red Cross Enlisted Men's Club dance last Thursday night. Votes were taken from all the men present, and she won by a good margin.
explanation: This passage justifies the selection by appealing to the process and outcome of voting. The premise (votes were taken from all men present and she won by a good margin) supports the implied conclusion that her selection as Queen was legitimate/appropriate. The justificatory sequencing indicates an argument even though the conclusion is not explicitly stated.
main_claim: Maria Antonietta’s selection as Queen of the Dance was legitimate because she won by a clear vote among all men present.

argument_text: Miss Starbuck was asked by the MPs to christen one of the cars because of her help in the contest to name them.
explanation: This sentence provides a reason (“because of her help in the contest to name them”) for the action (“was asked by the MPs to christen one of the cars”), forming a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Miss Starbuck was selected to christen one of the cars due to her assistance with the naming contest.

argument_text: These vehicles, once dogs of war, are now watch-dogs of peace. That is why, as a symbol of co-operation, they are being christened by one Italian girl and one American girl.
explanation: The first sentence asserts a status change (from instruments of war to guardians of peace), and the second uses “That is why” to draw a conclusion about the appropriate symbolic act (having one Italian and one American christen them). The premises explicitly support the conclusion.
main_claim: They are being christened by one Italian girl and one American girl as a symbol of cooperation because the vehicles now serve as watch-dogs of peace rather than dogs of war.

argument_text: Miss Mary was no happier to leave than Foggia was to see her go. "This is the first time in my life that I've been in a club that was small enough to feel 'homey'," she told us. "I'm sorry to leave just as I'm beginning to know so many of the boys."
explanation: The passage advances a claim that the community valued her and did not want her to leave. The writer’s framing (“no happier to leave than Foggia was to see her go”) implies mutual reluctance and esteem; her quotes provide supporting cues (calling the club “homey” and expressing sorrow to leave), which function as premises suggesting the conclusion about being well-regarded and missed, without stating it directly.
main_claim: Foggia did not want Miss Mary to leave and she was sincerely missed by the community.

argument_text: "There is only one thing that I have set a record for in all my time overseas," she said. "That is that I have spent more hours playing the piano for GI Sings than any other woman. At times in Iceland, I played almost steadily for five or six hours."
explanation: This contains a clear conclusion (“I have set a record… more hours… than any other woman”) supported by a reason/example (“At times in Iceland, I played almost steadily for five or six hours”), which functions as evidence of extraordinary time spent at the piano.
main_claim: Miss Mary holds a record for the most hours a woman has spent playing piano for GI Sings.

argument_text: She neglected to mention another "first." She was part of the first Red Cross unit to come overseas in this war.
explanation: The passage implies a character evaluation: that she is modest. The premise is that she omitted mentioning a notable “first,” and the implied conclusion is that she downplays her achievements. The evaluative phrasing “neglected to mention” signals the implied judgment.
main_claim: Miss Mary is modest about her significant achievements.

argument_text: There, one of her hobbies was getting scholarships for boys to go to college. While she was there, the first boys ever to attend a university from some of these towns graduated from college.
