explanation: The juxtaposition of moving vehicles out and the imminent derequisitioning implies a causal/justificatory relation: the area is being cleared because the land will be derequisitioned. Although phrased as sequential facts, the sequence and policy context suggest an argument that vacating is warranted by derequisitioning.
main_claim: Vehicles are being moved out because the land is about to be derequisitioned.

argument_text: Cardinal-designate Stritch, a short white-haired man with a fatherly smile, reminisced about the time he was in Rome in 1907 when Orville Wright had demonstrated the airplane. He laughed as he said that Wright had prophesied that the airplane probably would never have commercial value.
explanation: The anecdote, delivered with laughter, contrasts Wright’s past prophecy with the present context of the cardinals arriving on commercial TWA Constellations. The irony implies a claim that the prophecy was wrong and that airplanes do have commercial value now. The argument is suggested rather than stated directly, relying on evaluative tone and situational contrast.
main_claim: Airplanes have proven commercial value today, contrary to Wright’s earlier prediction.

argument_text: LIFE's cameraman, Ralph Morris, tried to challenge the right of the military police to prevent his entrance, but he succeeded in getting pictures only of the angry faces and fists of determined MPs. Sam Schulman (INS) added to the tumult by reminding the police that he was trying to make a living, and by that time all the newsmen, deciding that they could do it with numbers, broke through the barrier and got their pictures and recorded the statements made by the unruffled cardinals.
explanation: The passage frames MPs as overzealous (“angry faces and fists”) and highlights journalists’ professional justification (“trying to make a living”), culminating in collective action that achieved news coverage. This sequencing implies the claim that the MP restrictions were unreasonable and that press access was warranted to fulfill journalistic duties. The argument is implied through evaluative descriptors and causal narration rather than an explicit conclusion.
main_claim: The MPs’ restrictions on press access were excessive, and journalists were justified in pushing through to do their job.

argument_text: The MPs were taking no chances this time with all these dangerous people around.
explanation: The phrasing is sarcastic: calling reporters “dangerous people” implies the opposite—that they are not dangerous—and critiques the heightened security as overreaction. The argumentative force relies on irony and evaluative framing, not on an explicit premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The MPs’ heightened precautions toward reporters were an overreaction because reporters are not dangerous.

argument_text: At the press conference, Cardinal Glennon sat, and Cardinal Spellman stood at his side, while Cardinal Thomas Tien was surrounded by adoring Chinese worshippers who boasted that "he is the first cardinal China has had."
explanation: The boast foregrounds “firstness,” implying significance and pride in Cardinal Tien’s elevation. The evaluative term “adoring” and the emphasis on being the first suggest a claim about the historical and symbolic importance for Chinese Catholics. The argument is embedded in the quoted celebration rather than explicitly stated as a conclusion.
main_claim: Cardinal Tien’s elevation is historically significant and a point of pride for Chinese Catholics.

argument_text: Bob Buffington, radio announcer on station ARC "The Earphone Ballroom" at the 55th Station Hospital, broadcast a novel play-by-play account of General C. H. Lee's visit to the hospital Monday morning. From the ARC studio atop the hospital front, Buffington described the entrance of the General's entourage and all the formalities of the reception as they happened, while the hospital's patients listened with their bedside earphones. Buffington commented on the caliber of the salutes, and when the visiting party disappeared from his view, he played popular recordings until the General reappeared.
explanation: The evaluative term "novel" is a cue that the report advances a positive assessment of the broadcast’s format. The subsequent details (real-time descriptions, patient listenership, filling gaps with popular recordings) function as reasons supporting that assessment, implying the claim that the coverage was innovative and engaging. The argument is implicit because the text does not explicitly conclude "therefore it was innovative/effective," but the framing and evidence suggest that conclusion.
main_claim: Buffington’s real-time coverage of the general’s visit was innovative and engaging.

argument_text: Station ARC, built by a signal company in the spring of 1944, plays as a supplement to Foggia AES. Whenever the local AES is off the air, either during the regular 9 AM to 11 AM break or because of mechanical failures, station ARC takes over.
explanation: The passage presents a functional justification: ARC supplements AES and assumes broadcasting when AES is off the air. This causal framing implies the evaluative claim that ARC is useful/necessary because it ensures coverage during breaks and failures. The argument is implicit, as the value judgment ("useful/necessary") is not explicitly stated but is suggested by the described role.
main_claim: Station ARC provides a necessary service by ensuring broadcast coverage whenever Foggia AES is off the air.

argument_text: During the morning broadcasts, Bob Buffington plays a request program for the patients and interrupts the music with advertisements of hospital significance.
explanation: The description that programming is tailored to patient requests and includes "advertisements of hospital significance" implies the normative claim that the content serves patient needs and hospital purposes. The supportive detail (customization and relevance) functions as reasons, though the evaluative conclusion is unstated, making this an implicit argument.
main_claim: The station’s morning programming is designed to serve patients’ needs and hospital priorities.

argument_text: The consolidation of the units has necessitated a shuffling of living quarters for officers and enlisted men.
explanation: This states a causal necessity: because the units are being consolidated (premise), a shuffling of living quarters is necessary (conclusion). The verb “has necessitated” makes the inference explicit.
main_claim: The consolidation requires a reallocation of living quarters.

argument_text: This reorganization will not affect units such as the 55th Station Hospital, 1898th Engineers, 1585th Ordnance, AES, 1921st since they are under separate commands.
explanation: Provides a conclusion (these units will not be affected) with a stated reason introduced by “since” (they are under separate commands), forming a clear premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Units under separate commands will not be affected by the reorganization.

argument_text: (Ed's Note: This is written as of Tuesday, February 19, and cannot be considered final and authoritative. Like all military activities, it is subject to last-minute changes.)
explanation: The editor asserts the article is not final (conclusion) and justifies it by the general premise that military activities are subject to last-minute changes (“Like all military activities...”), making the causal reasoning explicit.
main_claim: The information should not be treated as final because military activities can change at the last minute.

argument_text: In selecting the officer personnel for this flight section, consideration will be given to those individuals who are capable of functioning in other duties.
explanation: This prescribes a selection criterion implying a value claim: officers capable of multiple duties are preferable/beneficial for the unit. The rationale (operational flexibility/efficiency) is unstated but suggested by privileging multi-capable individuals.
main_claim: Multi-capable officers should be prioritized for selection for operational advantage.

argument_text: Five officers left Foggia this week, but they did so with mixed feelings—they have to come back!
explanation: This sentence presents a conclusion (they have mixed feelings about leaving) and a reason (because they have to return). The causal dash directly links premise to conclusion, making the argument explicit.
main_claim: The officers feel ambivalent about leaving because they must return after their temporary duty.

argument_text: "And coming back won't be so bad. I expect to feel fine about the whole thing. Besides, with that new Army Regulation limiting overseas service to thirty months, I'll be going home anyway six months after I get back. I feel pretty good."
explanation: The speaker argues that returning will be acceptable, providing a clear supporting reason: the new regulation caps overseas service at 30 months, so he will go home six months after returning. The connective "Besides" signals the premise supporting the conclusion.
main_claim: Coming back won’t be so bad because the 30-month cap means he’ll go home six months after he returns.

argument_text: "Now that I know I'm going, I don't feel any different, but I hate to think what I'll feel like when I come back. Well, the best thing, I guess, is not to think about it."
explanation: This recommends a course of action (not to think about it) based on an implied reason (thinking about returning causes distress). The evaluative phrase "I hate to think" suggests the negative effect of thinking about it; the advice "the best thing... is not to think about it" draws a conclusion from that implication.
main_claim: It’s best not to think about the impending return because thinking about it will make him feel bad.

argument_text: "And then I guess I won't mind coming back. I'm in the Regular Army anyway, and anxious to finish up with this overseas stuff."
explanation: The conclusion is that he won’t mind returning, supported by two premises: he is in the Regular Army and he is eager to complete his overseas duty. The “anyway” and “and” link reasons to the conclusion.
main_claim: He won’t mind coming back because he’s Regular Army and wants to finish his overseas service.

argument_text: "Boy if that isn't typical of the Army. Yesterday morning they tell me the whole deal is off, and now they say I'm leaving tomorrow."
explanation: The speaker asserts a generalization about the Army’s typical behavior (being changeable/contradictory) and provides immediate evidence: conflicting orders within a day. The structure is a claim followed by supporting facts.
main_claim: The Army typically handles things in a contradictory last-minute way, as shown by reversing his orders within a day.

argument_text: "Well, it is, but I've been away from there ever since I was drafted in 1941, and I guess I'm not up on things. This 'rest and recuperation' stuff will brush me up on the place, though."
explanation: The conclusion is that R&R will reacquaint him with his hometown; the reasons are that he has been away since 1941 and isn’t up to date. The “but” and “though” indicate contrast and inference from the premises.
main_claim: R&R will help him get up to date on his hometown because he’s been away since 1941 and isn’t current on things there.

argument_text: "But I guess you know I was top man on this list with 32 months overseas. St. Louis will really look good after that."
explanation: The speaker implies that a long stretch overseas makes one appreciate going home, concluding that St. Louis will look good. The causal "after that" ties the premise (32 months overseas) to the evaluative conclusion without explicitly stating the rule.
main_claim: After 32 months overseas, going home to St. Louis will seem especially appealing.

argument_text: They related the sad tale of how they had left the States in December and had arrived in Le Havre on Christmas Day. "Not much of a damn Christmas present," was Ernie's comment.
explanation: Evaluative language frames arriving in Le Havre on Christmas Day as undesirable; the premise (arrival on Christmas Day after leaving home) implicitly supports the conclusion that this was a poor Christmas experience. The conclusion is implied by the sarcastic remark.
main_claim: Arriving in Le Havre on Christmas Day after leaving the U.S. was a bad Christmas experience.

argument_text: "Cheese, you should see how they live up there. Those pre-fabs, and the outside latrines and showers, ugh." "Kinda reminded me of Shepherd Field," Red put in.
explanation: The speakers imply that living conditions at Istres (and by comparison Shepherd Field) are substandard, citing prefabricated buildings and outside latrines/showers as evidence; the evaluative interjection "ugh" signals a negative judgment.
main_claim: Living conditions at Istres (and similarly at Shepherd Field) are poor.

argument_text:
"Well, we ain't had a chance to get around much yet, only been here four days. But I heard some of the fellows say they liked that Top Hat Club, and Red here went out and got drunk there the other night, so I guess it must be pretty good." "Yeah, and you can put down that we got a good reception when we came here, everybody was glad to see us, if you know what I mean. We're in the 96th Squadron, and Capt. Skinner gave us a little talk when we arrived, but that's all. Now we're just working out here on the line."

"What I like is the good service you get in the mess hall.
explanation: They present positive indicators (popular club, warm reception, good mess hall service) as reasons implying a favorable evaluation of Foggia’s amenities and reception for newcomers.
main_claim: Foggia offers a good reception and decent amenities for new arrivals.

argument_text: "What do you think about the point system, think it was fair?" They didn't answer as quickly as before; then Red came out slowly with, "Well, I guess it was pretty fair. We really haven't got anything to gripe about there. We just got in on things too late. But according to the MTO plan that's up on the bulletin board, I'll be home in June."
explanation: Explicit conclusion ("it was pretty fair") is justified by the premise that their late entry, not the system itself, explains their low points; reference to the MTO plan supports the fairness and projected outcome.
main_claim: The point system for return is fair, and their situation results from joining too late.

argument_text: But what gripes me is that we have been in the army all that time and we're still privates, and then we got a guy with us who's only been in eight months and already he's a Pfc. What about us?
explanation: The contrast between longer service with lower rank and shorter service with higher rank implies the claim that the promotion system is unfair; the rhetorical question underscores grievance.
main_claim: The promotion system is unfair because longer-serving soldiers remain privates while newer ones are already PFCs.

argument_text: Lt. Al Gutgesell, Engineering Officer of the 96th Squadron, was enthusiastic about the towns he had seen. "And you should have seen that Wiesbaden," he said. "What a place! They really live right up there. Nice hotels, good food. What a place. Of course, the fact that it's USAFE Headquarters might have something to do with it."
explanation: He evaluates Wiesbaden as having superior living conditions and suggests a causal explanation—its status as USAFE HQ—as the reason, using “might have something to do with it” as a causal hedge.
main_claim: Wiesbaden’s superior living conditions are likely due to its status as USAFE Headquarters.

argument_text: "Boy, you should see it," he exclaimed. "For instance, they have a big taxi service all over the town. Any time you want to go someplace, you just call up and get a jeep with a German driver. Or, you can hail them on the street. Terrific. You can go any place you want. And the beer up there is out of this world. You can get a keg of it for a buck ten, or these big mugs full for two and a half marks. That's a nickel. You don't hear any complaints up there."
explanation: He lists conveniences (taxi service) and cheap, plentiful beer as evidence to support an overall positive conclusion about living conditions and satisfaction (“You don’t hear any complaints”).
main_claim: Living conditions and morale in Wiesbaden are excellent due to convenient services and cheap beer.

argument_text: Since it was USAFE Headquarters, we wondered if there was much rank there. "Oh, hell yes. On one street near main headquarters, I counted fifteen staff cars, and all of them had one to three stars on them. This one guy I was talking to said he saw one car pull up and five full colonels pile out. But," he went on, "I didn't notice that it was very chicken up there. We had to wear blouses at dinner, but that was about all."
explanation: The premise is that high-ranking officers are abundant; the conclusion is that despite this, the environment is not overly strict (“not very chicken”), with minimal dress requirements as evidence.
main_claim: Despite the heavy presence of senior officers, Wiesbaden is not overly strict or fussy.

argument_text: "We were in Germany five days, and you should see that weather. I think the whole time I was in Germany I was on instruments."
explanation: By stating he flew on instruments the whole time, he implies the weather was consistently poor; instrument flying serves as evidence for bad weather conditions.
main_claim: The weather in Germany during his visit was consistently poor.

argument_text: "Did you come back with anything?" "Yes, I traded six packs of cigarettes for an Iron Cross. Got the ribbon with it, too. It's red, black, and white. Pretty nice. Souvenir." The cigarette market, as you can see, has hit bottom.
explanation: The narrative provides a premise (an Iron Cross obtained for six packs of cigarettes) and then draws an explicit evaluative conclusion (“has hit bottom”), signaled by “as you can see,” about the state of the cigarette market.
main_claim: The cigarette market has deteriorated severely.

argument_text: Somehow, as we entered the building, we turned left instead of right and came upon a hallway that had a line of very imposing signs, and for a second we thought we had hit on a new airline terminal in the making. We saw "Briefing Room," "Pilot's Locker Room," "Store Room," "Weather Office," and it all seemed like a great setup. Then, our interest aroused, we wandered down the hallway. The signs were no mirage, but the rooms were empty. The proposed briefing room had a great map of all Europe and North Africa on one wall. There was nothing else there. In the waiting room, there was only a desk, no chairs, or any of the other usual accoutrements.
explanation: The contrast between “imposing signs” and empty rooms implies criticism that the facilities are incomplete or more appearance than substance. The details (only a map; only a desk) serve as evidence.
main_claim: The new Base Operations setup is unfinished or hollow—impressive in signage but lacking actual equipment and furnishings.

argument_text: When we walked into the store room, we came across Lt. H. D. Kelley, Second Bomb Group wit and also Base Operations Officer. He was looking solemnly at the four blank walls. We asked him what he was thinking. "Hell, I was just wondering if this place is ever going to get finished. Would really be pretty nice, except the Weather Officer took the warmest room in the whole place.
explanation: The statement questions whether the facility will ever be completed (implying it is delayed) and suggests an improper allocation (“Weather Officer took the warmest room”), implying mild criticism. The rhetorical wondering functions as an argument about incompletion.
main_claim: The facility remains unfinished and is being allocated in a questionable way (e.g., the Weather Officer taking the warmest room).

argument_text: we entered a bright, airy floor that looked like it would be excellent for such use, although we must admit that we know very little about such things.
explanation: The passage advances an evaluative claim that the floor is excellent for obstetrical use, suggested by the descriptive cue “bright, airy.” The hedge about limited knowledge undercuts authority but still implies the conclusion from the positive features. The premises (brightness/airiness) are used to support the implied claim of suitability.
main_claim: The obstetrical floor is well-suited/excellent for its intended use.

argument_text: In the entire department, the hospital has given him the best cooperation, and he is quite pleased with his pleasant surroundings and likes the complete equipment.
explanation: This praises institutional support and resources as evidence of quality in obstetrical care. The evaluative phrases “best cooperation,” “pleasant surroundings,” and “complete equipment” function as reasons that imply the positive conclusion about the department’s performance.
main_claim: The hospital’s obstetrical service is strongly supported and well-equipped, indicating high-quality care.

argument_text: In the post-delivery ward, the wives seem to be aware that they were getting care that compares to anything in the States. When we walked in, they were chatting happily, and the bright sunlight streaming through the large windows on the green tile walls made a pleasant scene.
explanation: The passage argues that the care is on par with U.S. standards, using observed indicators (patients chatting happily, bright, pleasant environment) as evidence. The comparison to “anything in the States” is the implied conclusion supported by these contextual cues.
main_claim: The post-delivery care is comparable to top-quality care in the United States.

argument_text: "And that isn't all," Ginny said, as if she were trying to rent out one of the rooms, "there is also a pre-natal clinic that is conducted every Saturday afternoon. We have from ten to fifteen wives who come here between two and four in the afternoon to get all sorts of advice and treatment."
explanation: The “that isn’t all” framing and listing of a weekly clinic with attendance and services imply a persuasive claim that the hospital’s maternal care is comprehensive and proactive. The details about frequency, numbers, and services function as reasons for that evaluative conclusion.
main_claim: The hospital provides comprehensive prenatal services that enhance the quality of maternal care.

argument_text: "And when the wives are under the doctor's prescription," she added, "they can draw seven cans of milk and fourteen ounces of sugar a week at the PX we have set up for them here. Oh, I think we treat them fine."
explanation: Explicit conclusion “we treat them fine” is supported by the concrete benefit of prescribed access to milk and sugar via a dedicated PX. The structure presents a reason (provisioning) leading to the evaluative claim about treatment quality.
main_claim: The hospital treats expectant mothers well.

argument_text: And we agreed; they really do.
explanation: This sentence affirms the prior claim that the hospital treats the wives well. While it lacks internal premises, it functions as a conclusion that relies on the preceding listed services and conditions as implied support.
main_claim: The staff indeed treat the wives well.

argument_text: "Now, look, Vic," he was saying, "you've got to put a ledge on them so the fellows can put their drinks down."
explanation: The statement gives a conclusion (you've got to put a ledge on the dice tables) supported by a reason introduced by "so" (so the fellows can put their drinks down). This is a straightforward premise-to-conclusion design argument.
main_claim: The dice tables need a ledge to hold players’ drinks.

argument_text: "Boy, you are really going to have a club here; come here, let me tell you about it. This is going to be the best club in Italy. The bar is all done up in a red and black checkerboard pattern that is really 'reet.' There's even indirect lighting coming right from the glass bricks in the bar itself. Then there are soft seats, like couches and divans and stuff, with maroon upholstery. There's a gambling room, a ladies' powder and restroom. It's gonna be terrific. I figure somebody will be using this place for quite some time."
explanation: The speaker asserts the evaluative conclusion that it will be “the best club in Italy” and “terrific,” and supports it by listing multiple features (decor, lighting, seating, amenities) and a prediction of enduring use. The features serve as premises for the claim of superiority and quality.
main_claim: The renovated Fortress Club will be outstanding—indeed the best club in Italy—because of its superior design and amenities.

argument_text:
Ladies Man

An Italian woman came into the room suddenly, exclaiming her complaint loudly. Mac nodded slowly and sympathetically. When she had run herself out of words, he matched her in patter as he smiled and pinched her cheek. She walked out of the room, beaming.
explanation: The heading “Ladies Man” functions as a claim about McKnight’s skill with women; the subsequent anecdote (calming a complaining woman who then leaves “beaming”) serves as evidence. The argument is implied through framing and illustrative evidence rather than stated deductively.
main_claim: McKnight is adept at handling and charming women.

argument_text: Languages! we thought, mulling over the jive talk in our minds. "This fellow makes up his own."
explanation: The narrator juxtaposes McKnight’s interest in studying languages with his heavy use of “jive talk,” implying the conclusion that he effectively invents his own language. The irony and contrast cue an implied evaluative claim rather than an explicit argument form.
main_claim: McKnight already invents or uses his own kind of language.

argument_text: We had seen him around the Fortress Club, supervising the renovation of the large club. But it ran in the family, Mac said. His father is an engineer and does construction work, but that wasn't for Mac.
explanation: The passage offers a causal/explanatory link—“it ran in the family”—to account for McKnight’s supervision of renovations, using his father’s engineering and construction background as the reason. The claim is suggested rather than formally argued, and partially complicated by the caveat that construction “wasn't for Mac.”
main_claim: McKnight’s involvement in supervising the club renovation is connected to his family background in engineering and construction.

argument_text:
"Say," we said, "that's bad. Why don't you get it published?"

"Nope, not that. That's a personal one."
explanation: McKnight provides a clear reason for not publishing the poem (“That’s a personal one”), which justifies the decision not to publish in response to the suggestion that he should.
main_claim: He will not publish that poem because it is personal.

argument_text: Although this sum has provided seven hundred workdays for the laborers of the province, it has, until this time, proved inadequate to solve the pressing problem.
explanation: This sentence presents a concession (some workdays were provided) and a conclusion (the funds are inadequate) linked by "Although," which signals an explicit argument: despite the limited benefit, the measure fails to solve the larger unemployment problem.
main_claim: The appropriated funds have been inadequate to solve Foggia’s unemployment problem.

argument_text: Lack of raw materials has been the chief cause of Foggia's failure to get back on its feet. The main industries of the city remain closed because of a lack of electrical power. An idle cement factory, one of the largest in Italy, and a great bauxite plant, which remains closed, are testimonies to the fact that, at the present time in Foggia, raw material is far more important than money.
explanation: This passage advances a causal claim (chief cause is lack of raw materials) and supports it with evidence (industries closed due to lack of power; idle cement and bauxite plants), culminating in an explicit conclusion that raw materials are more important than money right now. The structure links premises to a stated conclusion.
main_claim: In Foggia’s current situation, raw materials are more important than money because shortages are the chief cause keeping industries idle.

argument_text: There is a need for cement and steel which will provide materials with which Foggia can rebuild and aid in solving its unemployment problem.
explanation: This is a prescriptive/causal claim implying that supplying cement and steel will facilitate rebuilding and reduce unemployment. The argument relies on prior context about raw material shortages; the necessity claim implies the conclusion without detailing premises within this sentence, making it implicit.
main_claim: Supplying cement and steel is necessary to rebuild Foggia and help reduce unemployment.

argument_text: One of the key causes of the increase in the number of unemployed is the pulling out of Allied Forces units. In February of 1945, approximately 22,000 persons were in the employ of the armed forces. At the present time, that number has dropped to 2,000.
explanation: The passage states a causal claim (withdrawal of Allied units caused unemployment to rise) and immediately provides quantitative evidence (drop from 22,000 to 2,000 employed), forming an explicit argument.
main_claim: The withdrawal of Allied Forces units is a key cause of increased unemployment in Foggia.

argument_text: Insofar as a substantial number of persons were being employed in agricultural fields at that time, the number was low.
explanation: This sentence explains the low unemployment figure in June by giving a reason introduced by "Insofar as," explicitly linking the premise (many employed in agriculture) to the conclusion (the number was low).
main_claim: Unemployment was low in June because many people were working in agriculture then.

argument_text: However, at the present time, because of the seasonal nature of agricultural work, unemployment in that field has risen from 2,427 in June to 13,724 in December.
explanation: This sentence asserts a causal explanation—seasonality—explicitly introduced by "because," and supports it with comparative figures, forming a clear argument.
main_claim: Due to the seasonal nature of agricultural work, agricultural unemployment has risen sharply from June to December.

argument_text: However, the exceptional nature of the present crisis is trying the funds of the nationwide organization, and additional measures are necessitated.
explanation: This sentence presents a premise (the crisis is straining the organization’s funds) and an explicit conclusion (additional measures are needed), linked by "and," making the argument explicit.
main_claim: Because the crisis is straining the institute’s funds, additional measures are necessary.

argument_text: Unemployment, however, at the present time is of such an extended nature that the Instituto Nazionale Previdenza Sociale is unable to cope with the problem.
explanation: The "such...that" construction explicitly ties the premise (unemployment is extensive) to the conclusion (the institute cannot cope), forming an explicit causal argument.
main_claim: Unemployment is so extensive that the Instituto Nazionale Previdenza Sociale cannot cope with it.

argument_text: Foggia looks forward to the receipt of the raw materials it needs to begin its reconstruction program, which will cut down its problem of unemployment.
explanation: This sentence asserts a forward-looking causal claim that receiving raw materials and beginning reconstruction will reduce unemployment; the "which will cut down" clause explicitly states the predicted effect.
main_claim: Receiving needed raw materials to start reconstruction will reduce Foggia’s unemployment.

argument_text: "I was just thinking about going home, but when will they get down to 28 points?"
explanation: This is an argument because the rhetorical question implies a critique of current demobilization policy and a normative preference for lowering the points threshold. The premise is his desire to go home; the implied conclusion is that authorities should reduce the points requirement to 28 promptly. Cues indicating implicitness include the rhetorical question, the contrastive "but," and the presupposition that lowering to 28 points is both anticipated and desirable.
main_claim: The points threshold for demobilization should be lowered to 28 soon so that servicemen like him can go home.

argument_text: "I was just thinking about what I was going to say on the 'Around the Town' broadcast this morning. Got to keep trying to make this place sound intriguing."
explanation: This advances a normative claim without explicit support: that he ought to frame the locale as "intriguing" on the broadcast. The premise is his role in preparing broadcast remarks; the implied conclusion is that, to fulfill that role (e.g., sustain interest or morale), he must keep making the place sound appealing. Cues include the deontic "Got to" and the presupposition that portraying the place as intriguing is necessary/beneficial.
main_claim: He ought to keep portraying the place as intriguing on the broadcast to fulfill the program’s aims (e.g., audience interest or morale).

argument_text: School officials in Foggia, working hard to bring battered buildings and disorganized courses back into operation, have raised some 1,090,000 lire in a province-wide drive for the schools of Foggia.
explanation: The evaluative phrase “working hard” combined with the reported fundraising success implies a positive claim about officials’ diligence and effectiveness. The premise (they have raised 1,090,000 lire while working to restore battered buildings and disorganized courses) suggests the conclusion that their efforts are commendable and effective, even though that conclusion is not stated explicitly.
main_claim: School officials are diligently and effectively restoring the school system, as evidenced by substantial funds raised.

argument_text: Heads of schools, working with the school superintendent, have organized several money-raising projects, with the aim to acquire 4,000,000 lire as their first goal. This sum, which will pay for a thousand student benches and forty desks, is part of the total of 250,000,000 lire that is estimated to be the amount needed to bring the entire school system back to pre-war condition.
explanation: The passage links a concrete first goal (4,000,000 lire) to specific outputs (benches and desks) and a larger need (250,000,000 lire to restore the system). This functions as an implicit justification: because the funds have concrete uses and contribute to a large, necessary target (pre-war condition), the goal is appropriate and warranted. The evaluative necessity is implied by the framing of “needed to bring” the system back.
main_claim: The 4,000,000-lire fundraising goal is justified as a necessary first step tied to concrete needs within a much larger requirement to restore schools to pre-war condition.

argument_text: Cooperation from many parties is responsible for the good results thus far. Volunteers have taken up a house-to-house canvass, soliciting funds in the name of the drive. Receipts are given in all cases, and names of the donors are available with the amount each has contributed. Some 10,000 lire is attributed to GIs and officers so far.
explanation: The first sentence makes an explicit causal claim that cooperation caused the “good results.” The following sentences provide supporting evidence: volunteer canvassing, transparency practices, and contributions from GIs and officers. The structure is explicit: conclusion (cooperation led to success) supported by facts about cooperative actions and outcomes.
main_claim: Broad cooperation has caused the fundraising drive’s success so far.

argument_text: Receipts are given in all cases, and names of the donors are available with the amount each has contributed.
explanation: These practices imply an unstated conclusion about accountability and trustworthiness. The premises (universal receipts and public donor lists) are standard transparency mechanisms, which suggest the drive is honest and reliable, though the evaluative conclusion is not explicitly stated.
main_claim: The fundraising drive is transparent and trustworthy.

argument_text: Perhaps a third of the money has been raised by a voluntary tax that shopkeepers have been willing to impose on themselves and customers.
explanation: The wording emphasizes voluntariness and willingness, implying normative approval and suggesting broad community endorsement and sacrifice for the cause. The implicit claim is that the drive has legitimate, willing support from shopkeepers and customers, inferred from their acceptance of a self-imposed levy.
main_claim: The fund drive enjoys broad, willing community support, as shown by shopkeepers’ self-imposed voluntary tax.

argument_text: Paper for forms, tickets, and receipts has been donated free, and printing plants have offered their services also without charge.
explanation: The in-kind donations imply that local businesses deem the cause worthy and are supporting it materially. The implicit conclusion (community endorsement and the drive’s worthiness/legitimacy) is suggested by the willingness to donate services without charge.
main_claim: Local businesses’ in-kind donations indicate that the school fund drive is a worthy cause with strong community backing.

argument_text: Committeemen report that the first purchase of the desperately needed benches has already been made.
explanation: The adjective “desperately needed” carries evaluative force, implying urgent necessity; coupled with the report of purchase, it suggests the conclusion that funds are being effectively directed to urgent priorities and that the drive addresses real needs. The normative assessment is implied rather than asserted directly.
main_claim: The fundraising is effectively meeting urgent needs, as shown by the purchase of desperately needed benches.

argument_text: His life story was dramatized over "Cookie Time" the other day. It was a bit sketchy, but it covered the subject!
explanation: The passage evaluates the adequacy of the dramatization. The concessive "a bit sketchy" functions as a premise acknowledging a potential shortcoming, while the conclusion "but it covered the subject" asserts sufficiency despite that shortcoming. The evaluative language and the contrast cue "but" signal an implicit argument that the coverage was adequate overall.
main_claim: Despite being sketchy, the dramatization adequately covered Mustache's life.

argument_text: Speaking of "Mustache," that program "Midnight in Foggia" is still going strong. (Due to conditions beyond our control)
explanation: The parenthetical phrase ascribes a causal reason for the program's continued success or persistence ("Due to conditions beyond our control"), implying that external circumstances, not necessarily merit, explain why it "is still going strong." The causal attribution without specifics, plus a likely ironic tone, makes this an implicit argument linking cause to outcome.
main_claim: Midnight in Foggia continues strongly because of external circumstances beyond the studio’s control.

argument_text: The new studio production "Slim the Milkman" is being turned over to Slim's assistant, now that demobilization has hit "Slim." That same demobilization hit your A.E.S. but good lately. Within the space of one month, we have lost 45% of our personnel.
explanation: This is a causal-explanatory argument: demobilization (premise) has affected individuals and the unit, leading to concrete outcomes—handover of a production and a 45% personnel loss (evidence). The phrasing "now that demobilization has hit" and "That same demobilization hit your A.E.S." explicitly link cause and effects, supporting the conclusion that demobilization significantly impacted AES operations.
main_claim: Demobilization has seriously affected AES operations and staffing.

argument_text: Incidentally, Frank said that he was through traveling for quite a while, for since he has been in the army, he's made six trips across the states... a pretty good record for a three-year man.
explanation: The sentence presents a conclusion ("he was through traveling for quite a while") supported by a stated reason introduced by "for": he has already made six cross-country trips in three years. The causal connector makes the argumentative structure explicit.
main_claim: Frank is done traveling for a while because he has already traveled extensively during his three years in the army.

argument_text: Frank said his only difficult problem came one time out at the transmitter when he searched for two hours and a half for trouble in the set and then suddenly spied the tail of a mouse deep within the transmitter. It had shorted out a tube from plate to ground and was literally burned to a crisp.
explanation: The narrative concludes with an explicit causal explanation: the mouse "had shorted out a tube," accounting for the transmitter trouble that took hours to diagnose. The second sentence provides the cause of the malfunction, supporting the claim about the source of the problem.
main_claim: The transmitter trouble was caused by a mouse shorting a tube.

argument_text: There is one question that remains unanswered here at the studio... How did G.I. Jill sneak in on Cookie Time the other night?
explanation: The rhetorical question implies a claim about an irregular or unauthorized appearance by G.I. Jill, suggesting a lapse or unexpected access. The framing "remains unanswered" and the verb "sneak" carry evaluative and presuppositional cues that something improper or surprising occurred, hence an implicit argument about studio control/scheduling.
main_claim: G.I. Jill’s appearance on Cookie Time was unexpected or improper, indicating a lapse in studio control or scheduling.

argument_text:
It was hard for Sgt. Barbour to give any specific instance of something interesting that has happened. It was like asking a fireman if he has seen a fire.

"Goodness, we could write a book," she laughed.
explanation: The simile and the quip imply the conclusion that many noteworthy events occurred at the club. The premise is that asking for a single instance is futile because there were so many (like a fireman seeing many fires), reinforced by “we could write a book.” The conclusion (abundance of interesting happenings) is suggested rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: The club experienced so many interesting events that it’s hard to single out any one instance.

argument_text:
Similar to Our ARC

NAAFI-EFI, which stands for Navy Army-Air Forces Institute - Expeditionery Forces Institute, performs for British Forces many of the services that the American Red Cross does for American troops. The spacious NAAFI canteen in the Palazzo Del Studi housed a dance hall, restaurant, store, snack bar, game room, lounge, and other nooks where weary troops found relaxation and entertainment.
explanation: The heading and first sentence assert functional similarity to the American Red Cross, and the subsequent listing of facilities and their purpose (relaxation and entertainment for troops) serves as supporting evidence. The reasoning is: because NAAFI provides these ARC-like services and amenities, it is similar to the ARC. The inferential link is implied through juxtaposition rather than stated with explicit connectives.
main_claim: NAAFI-EFI is functionally similar to the American Red Cross for British forces.

argument_text: The club, which was established a year after the British Army liberated Foggia, has been busy until recently and has seen times when a turnover of 5,000 troops a day was commonplace.
explanation: The sentence makes a claim (“has been busy until recently”) and immediately supports it with evidence (“turnover of 5,000 troops a day was commonplace”). The premise directly substantiates the conclusion about busyness.
main_claim: The club was very busy until recently.

argument_text: The British WVS (Women's Voluntary Services), represented by Mrs. Vera Haigh of Wakefield in Yorkshire, gave English boys that sought-after touch of home. In NAAFI, the WVS did much to provide entertainment and look after the social welfare of the men.
explanation: The first sentence claims WVS provided a “touch of home”; the second provides reasons (entertainment and social welfare efforts) that imply why it felt like home and why their contribution was significant. The evaluative conclusion is suggested through these functions rather than argued with explicit logical markers.
main_claim: The WVS effectively provided British troops with a comforting “touch of home” through entertainment and social-welfare support.

argument_text: "All I do is answer the phone," he told us when we asked how he handles all those jobs. "Mario Di Padua and Tony Mangano do all the work."
explanation: The passage offers a direct reason for how he manages many jobs: he only answers the phone while Mario and Tony do the work. The premise (subordinates do the work) supports the conclusion (he can handle all those jobs).
main_claim: He is able to handle many jobs because his subordinates do the actual work.

argument_text: He said that Tony takes care of the blank forms and has made a complete numerical file of every one. Now, when someone asks for a form, they can have it in a minute.
explanation: The passage implies a causal argument: the creation of a complete numerical file enables rapid retrieval of forms. Although not explicitly framed with “therefore,” the sequence and outcome suggest the claim that the filing system improves efficiency.
main_claim: Tony’s complete numerical filing system makes form requests much faster.

argument_text: "Mario is my chief assistant," he went on. "He does all the typing, makes up letter orders with no help from me, and runs the mimeograph. I just made staff sergeant on the strength of his work, so I got him a raise."
explanation: This provides reasons (Mario’s extensive work and its contribution to Fields’ promotion) leading to the conclusion/action (he gave Mario a raise), signaled by “so.”
main_claim: Mario deserved and received a raise because his work was substantial and helped Fields get promoted.

argument_text: "I just talk to a lot of people every day and get information that way," he explained. "Nothing official about it."
explanation: He presents a reason (informal conversations as the source of information) to support the claim that the “rumor center” is unofficial, explicitly linking behavior to status.
main_claim: The so-called rumor center is unofficial because his information gathering is informal conversation.

argument_text: "No," he said. "When an officer suggests that, I just tell him that Mario doesn't have a spare minute now. They always understand."
explanation: He gives a justification for refusing additional jobs: Mario’s lack of spare time. The premise (Mario is fully occupied) supports the conclusion (he declines further tasks), evidenced by officers’ acceptance.
main_claim: He refuses to take more jobs by citing Mario’s full workload as a sufficient reason.

argument_text: The replacements scheduled to arrive in Foggia will probably get a pleasantly rose-colored picture of life in Valley Foge. As the tired young low pointers step off onto the station platform at 2 AM Sunday morning, all of Uncle Joe Hamilton's Red Cross girls will be there to welcome them with hot coffee, doughnuts, popcorn, and cigarettes. Freak De Grazia's orchestra will serenade the men,
explanation: This presents a conclusion (“will probably get a pleasantly rose-colored picture…”) followed by concrete reasons (the welcoming reception with coffee, doughnuts, cigarettes, and serenade) that explain why newcomers would form such an impression. The premises causally support the evaluative conclusion, forming a clear argument even without an explicit “because.”
main_claim: New arrivals will form an overly positive initial impression of life in Foggia due to the orchestrated warm welcome and entertainment.

argument_text: and a large crowd of well-wishers is expected to be at the station to yell, "You're gonna be sorry!"
explanation: The reported chant implies a conclusion about the experience awaiting newcomers: that they will regret being there. The statement functions as a warning, using irony to suggest a negative evaluation of life in Foggia. The claim is not stated by the narrator as a proposition but is conveyed through the quoted crowd reaction.
main_claim: The newcomers will regret their assignment in Foggia.

argument_text: After that, they see Foggia.
explanation: Placed after the depiction of a rosy reception, this short line implies a contrast: the reality of Foggia is disappointing or harsh compared to the welcome. The argument relies on presupposition and contrast to suggest the evaluative conclusion without stating it outright.
main_claim: The actual conditions in Foggia are much worse than the initial welcoming spectacle suggests.

argument_text: The outstanding detriment to Italy's educational system is the fact that the people cannot afford to go to school. The educational plan itself suffers little, if at all, in comparison with that of any other nation.
explanation: This juxtaposition contrasts affordability with the quality of the plan to imply that poverty, not the system’s design, is the main problem. The evaluative terms “outstanding detriment” and “suffers little, if at all” function as premises supporting the implied conclusion about where reform should focus.
main_claim: The chief problem with Italian education is economic access rather than the educational plan itself.

argument_text: The Italian laws, which provide compulsory education for children through the ages of 6 to 14, are enforced with greatly varying degrees of efficiency. As in the United States, it is the southern rural areas that suffer the greatest laxity and accompanying illiteracy.
explanation: By linking uneven enforcement to “southern rural areas” suffering “laxity and accompanying illiteracy,” the passage implies a causal argument: variable enforcement leads to illiteracy concentrated in rural south, paralleling the U.S. The conclusion is suggested rather than stated with a connective like “therefore.”
main_claim: Weak enforcement of compulsory education particularly in southern rural areas causes higher illiteracy there.

argument_text: Though the level of this school compares to the top three grades of an American grade school or the first years of a junior high school, the child receives a lot of practical instruction in woodworking, farming, and other manual arts.
explanation: The concessive “Though” signals an argumentative move: despite lower academic level, the practical instruction provides compensatory value. The structure implies a defense of the vocational track’s worth.
main_claim: Even if the vocational school’s academic level is lower, it offers valuable practical training.

argument_text: The child of a poor man or farmer is likely to attend the scuola professionale or vocational school as he is ready to go to work after three more years.
explanation: The causal connector “as” provides a reason for the likelihood: because he can start working after three years, poor/farm children tend toward vocational school. Premise leads directly to the conclusion about educational choice.
main_claim: Poor or farming families’ children tend to choose vocational school because it enables quicker entry into work.

argument_text: Girls in this course learn home economics and other subjects fitting them for the career of housewife.
explanation: By stating that these subjects are “fitting them for the career of housewife,” the sentence implies a normative alignment between girls’ education and the role of housewife. It suggests appropriateness/intent without explicit argument markers.
main_claim: The vocational curriculum for girls is designed to prepare them for being housewives and is suited to that role.

argument_text: The student who enters the science school studies in that institution for five years. His courses are similar but lean heavily toward mathematics, physics, chemistry, and are lighter in the classical studies. However, at completion, he enters the same university with the academic student and may take any major except philosophy or law.
explanation: The contrastive “However” counters a presumed objection that a lighter classical load limits prospects; the passage argues that despite differing emphasis, science students retain nearly equal university access. The structure implies a defense of parity between tracks.
main_claim: Despite having fewer classical studies, science-track students still gain nearly the same university access as academic-track students.

argument_text: This is a skeleton of the Italian educational system as it is today. With rebuilt schools, new books, competent teachers, and law enforcement, this system is capable of raising Italy's children to a position of high educational standing in the world.
explanation: The conditional-like statement provides reasons (rebuilding, materials, teachers, enforcement) that would lead to the conclusion that the system can elevate Italy’s educational standing. It is a clear recommendation-oriented causal argument.
main_claim: If resourced and enforced properly, the existing Italian education system can achieve high international educational standing.

argument_text: Sgt. Bill Gray could be called an "apple-knocker" if his middle name wasn't "whistle-punk." And the reason it is "whistle-punk" is that during his career as a lumberjack, he was a "high-rigger," "choke-setter," "loader," "bucker," "faller," in fact, almost everything but a "whistle punk." So, that, logically, became his nickname.
explanation: This passage presents a conclusion (his nickname is “whistle-punk”) supported by reasons: he worked nearly every job except “whistle punk,” so by a tongue-in-cheek logic, that became his nickname. The connective “So, that, logically,” marks the inferential structure.
main_claim: Bill Gray’s nickname “whistle-punk” follows logically from his having done almost every lumberjack job except that one.

argument_text: Gray, who has been playing a lot of tournament basketball lately, only went in for two sports at Yakima High. They were basketball and tennis. But sports to him are more the great outdoors than the ball courts, for his hometown — Wickersham, Washington — boasts a population of 60 (counting hawgs).
explanation: The claim is that sports, to Gray, are “more the great outdoors than the ball courts.” It’s supported causally by the reason that he comes from a tiny rural hometown; the word “for” signals the premise-conclusion relation.
main_claim: For Gray, sports mean outdoor activities rather than organized court sports because of his rural background.

argument_text:
He debunks the movie sequences that show "high riggers" being crushed by their ropes as the trees they are climbing split apart.

"Never saw or heard of anything like that," he says. "I did once see a wind knock the top off a big tree that twisted around and knocked the rigger off. He fell a hundred and twenty feet into a pile of logs and scratched his forearm a little."
explanation: The passage asserts a conclusion—movie depictions of high riggers being crushed are false—and supports it with testimony and counterevidence: he’s never seen or heard of it, and provides a contrasting anecdote of a severe fall resulting in minimal injury. “He debunks” explicitly frames it as refutation.
main_claim: Film portrayals of high riggers being crushed by splitting trees are unrealistic and inaccurate.

argument_text: Logging isn't a business that has modernized very much. The trees are still cut down by "fallers" who swing the axe in the old tradition of logging men.
explanation: The conclusion that logging hasn’t modernized is directly supported by the premise that trees are still felled by axe-wielding “fallers,” indicating continuity with old practices. The second sentence serves as evidence for the first.
main_claim: Logging remains largely unmodernized because trees are still felled by traditional axe-wielding fallers.

argument_text:
It's the old-timers in this business that Bill admires.

"They can set a can on the ground, and then smash it by dropping a tree right on it," he declares.
explanation: The claim is evaluative—Bill admires old-timers—and the quoted example functions as implicit evidence of their extraordinary skill (precision felling). The passage suggests the argument that old-timers deserve admiration because of such skill, though it’s not framed as a formal premise-conclusion with markers.
main_claim: Old-time loggers merit admiration because of their exceptional precision and skill.

argument_text: At this point, it began to be apparent that besides their other accomplishments, lumberjacks are also somewhat adept at tale-telling.
explanation: This is an evaluative generalization implying that the preceding anecdotes reveal exaggeration or storytelling prowess. The argument relies on the context of preceding stories as implicit evidence; the phrase “it began to be apparent” cues an inferred conclusion rather than a stated premise chain.
main_claim: Lumberjacks tend to be good at telling tall tales.

argument_text: The Second Bomb Group Gymnasium is undergoing a series of changes to keep it in step with changing conditions, Sergeant Russell of Special Services said Wednesday night.
explanation: This ties the justification (changing conditions) to the action (undergoing changes), implying that updates are warranted to remain current. The purpose clause "to keep it in step" signals a normative rationale without formally laying out premises and conclusion.
main_claim: The gym must undergo changes to stay aligned with changing conditions.

argument_text: "We've lengthened the basketball court twenty feet, so that now it is a much better court than it was before."
explanation: Premise: the court was lengthened twenty feet. Conclusion: the court is now much better. The causal connector "so that" explicitly links the premise to the evaluative conclusion.
main_claim: Lengthening the basketball court by twenty feet has made it much better than before.

argument_text: "Then, we have put in eight more showers, a larger water tank, and a new stove, so that those facilities are much better too."
explanation: Premise: added showers, larger water tank, new stove. Conclusion: facility quality is much better. The phrase "so that" explicitly signals the inferential relationship.
main_claim: Adding showers, a larger water tank, and a new stove has improved the facilities.

argument_text: "After basketball season is over, we're going to inaugurate indoor tennis, volleyball, and badminton on the main floor, so that there'll be plenty to do for all the fellows who come down to the gym."
explanation: Premise: multiple indoor sports will be inaugurated. Conclusion: there will be plenty to do for attendees. "So that" marks the intended effect as a reasoned outcome of the planned actions.
main_claim: Introducing multiple indoor sports will ensure plenty of activities for gym visitors.

argument_text: "And also, we have a new coal heating system, as well as having all our formerly opened windows covered over, so that the gym will be warm."
explanation: Premises: new coal heating system and covered windows. Conclusion: the gym will be warm. The causal connector "so that" indicates the conclusion drawn from the listed premises.
main_claim: Installing a new heating system and covering windows will make the gym warm.

argument_text: MEMBERS OF THE RAILROAD GANG Standing trial for alleged criminal conspiracy and complicity in the theft of Allied Military property are, reading from left to right: Pasquale Garruto, Attilio Stridi, Francesco Bruno, Raffaele Scalera, Salvatore Stridi, and Mario Carella.
explanation: The headline labels the pictured individuals as “MEMBERS OF THE RAILROAD GANG,” which presupposes criminal affiliation. The accompanying sentence notes they are “standing trial for alleged criminal conspiracy and complicity in the theft of Allied Military property.” The juxtaposition functions as a premise (they are on trial for alleged conspiracy/theft) supporting an implied conclusion (they are indeed gang members/criminally culpable). The evaluative label “gang” and the presuppositional framing imply guilt beyond the neutral fact of being on trial, making this an implicit argument.
main_claim: The named individuals are members of a criminal “railroad gang” responsible for theft of Allied Military property.

argument_text: Packed courtrooms stood in the tribunal, once the headquarters of the Federazione Fascista, as the leading lawyers of Puglie eloquently charged the local police with coercion in obtaining the confessions.
explanation: This advances the claim that police coerced confessions; although no premises are provided here, the courtroom accusation functions as an argument in context, implying that coerced confessions are invalid and should undermine the prosecution. The evaluative verb “charged” signals a stance against police methods.
main_claim: The local police coerced confessions from the defendants.

argument_text: Giovanni Longo, impressive by his constant hammering at the operations of the police, declared that his defendant, Pasquale Garruto, was an assistant to the thefts but had no jurisdictional obligation to forbid them. "There was no association of thieves," Longo declared, "but rather unguarded temptations to men living in inflationary Italy to improve their way of life by taking the goods that were in the railroad cars."
explanation: This is a defense argument aiming to reduce culpability: premises include that Garruto only assisted and had no duty to prevent theft, and that thefts were opportunistic due to inflationary hardship rather than an organized conspiracy. The implied conclusion is mitigation or non-liability for conspiracy. The normative and causal framing (“temptations,” “living in inflationary Italy”) indicates an implicit argument for leniency or lesser charges.
main_claim: The defendants, including Garruto, should not be treated as members of an organized criminal association and Garruto bears limited responsibility because he had no duty to stop the thefts.

argument_text: The highlight in the defense was the speech of Vittorio Malcangi of Bari, defending the missing Nicola Lioce, who asked for an independent Italian trial due to the presence of Allied interference. The court, he declared, is without exact and accurate report or proofs. He charged that the evidence was obtained by violent police methods and by the use of informers.
explanation: Clear conclusion is requested (“an independent Italian trial”) with supporting premises: alleged Allied interference, lack of accurate reports or proofs, and tainted evidence from violent methods and informers. The “due to” establishes causal reasoning from premises to conclusion.
main_claim: There should be an independent Italian trial because Allied interference and unreliable, violently obtained evidence undermine the current proceedings.

argument_text: Carlo Ruggero, editor of the local Avanti Daunia, asked the court to consider the human interpretation of crime and not the judicial interpretation. "The psychological effects of this war with its lack of materials for civilians, with the lack of discipline among the people, with the high cost of living, with the extreme poverty, perpetuated the activities of people who were not mentally strong enough to resist the cars of plenty," declared Ruggero. "These men are not habitual criminals."
explanation: Ruggero makes a normative recommendation (consider “human” rather than “judicial” interpretation) and provides causal premises (war’s psychological and material effects) to support a conclusion about the defendants’ character (“not habitual criminals”), implying leniency or reclassification of their actions.
main_claim: The court should judge the defendants with a humanitarian lens because wartime deprivation led them to offend and they are not habitual criminals.

argument_text: In February 1945, Salvatore Stridi quit his job on the railroad and went to work for Captain Pietracaprina, CC RR, Foggia, as an informant and chauffeur. This was the same Stridi who, on his wages as a railroad worker, was able to buy a Fiat, motorcycle, house, and pass out thousand lire notes for compensation to others.
explanation: The juxtaposition implies that Stridi’s lifestyle exceeded legitimate earnings, suggesting illicit income from thefts or corruption. The argument relies on the presupposition that a railroad worker’s wages could not fund such purchases, thus insinuating wrongdoing.
main_claim: Stridi likely had illicit income inconsistent with his railroad wages.

argument_text: There were too many people involved to get them at the railroad station. It would be much better to use a net and catch them all. Where to start? Who to get first? Who could one trust when one of the leaders was even employed by the carabinieri? There was only one way. Let the "little fish" swim in the pond. The "big fish" would be right after them. For bait, find some military clothing that had been sold.
explanation: This sequence argues for a specific investigative strategy. Premises: too many suspects, trust issues, infiltration among carabinieri. Conclusion: conduct a sting letting minor actors operate to catch leaders, using military clothing as bait. Rhetorical questions and prescriptive statements structure the reasoning.
main_claim: A sting using “little fish” as bait with military clothing was the best way to catch the gang’s leaders given the scope and infiltration.

argument_text: Precautionary measures had to be taken to ensure the success of the raid. Stridi was too friendly with Italian carabinieri.
explanation: Conclusion: precautions were necessary; premise: Stridi’s close ties to carabinieri risked compromising the operation. The causal necessity (“had to be taken”) is justified by the stated risk.
main_claim: The raid required special precautions because Stridi’s connections to carabinieri could jeopardize it.

argument_text: The operations of the gang had been long and successful. Money had bought out eyewitnesses; money had bought soldiers on sentry duty. This was to be just another successful operation.
explanation: Premises (bribery of eyewitnesses and guards, history of success) imply the conclusion that the gang expected this operation to succeed as well. The evaluative phrasing “had been long and successful” and causal attribution to money support the inference.
main_claim: The gang anticipated another successful theft because bribery had ensured prior successes.

argument_text: It would seem improbable that thefts on such a large scale could continue daily with many workers present. Were all the railroad workers involved? Did they all share in the take? Why hadn't this been reported to the police? What were the Italian guards doing all the time? Some of the railroad workers had criminal records. Other railroad workers, barely existing with the high cost of living, took their share, whatever the principals would give them (sometimes 1,000 lire, sometimes 6,000 lire) to keep quiet. Others were threatened with bodily harm. To have told the Italian soldiers on duty about these thefts would have been of no value since they themselves were involved.
explanation: The passage poses rhetorical questions and then provides multiple premises (criminal records, hush payments due to poverty, threats of violence, complicity of guards) to answer them, concluding that large-scale thefts could continue and go unreported because many were complicit or intimidated.
main_claim: Large-scale, ongoing thefts persisted and went unreported because many workers and guards were complicit, some were paid or threatened, and reporting would have been futile.

argument_text: One railroad worker who did not participate in any of the thefts, however, admitted receiving 5,000 lire on one occasion, 6,000 lire on another, and 4,000 lire another time, since he was on night duty at these times. That was his compensation for keeping quiet.
explanation: The premise (payments received while on duty) supports the conclusion that the payments were hush money. The causal connector “since” and the clarifying sentence explicitly state the purpose of payment.
main_claim: Even non-participating workers were paid hush money to remain silent about the thefts.

argument_text: Raio, Suriani, and De Benedittis deny any knowledge that the caustic soda was stolen property.
explanation: This is a defensive claim implying innocence or lack of culpable intent regarding receiving stolen goods. The denial functions as an argument that they should not be held responsible because they lacked knowledge; the premise is simply their assertion of ignorance.
main_claim: Raio, Suriani, and De Benedittis should not be considered knowingly involved because they did not know the caustic soda was stolen.

argument_text:
They're Buying It On Faith

Henry J. Kaiser, master shipbuilder, is going in for auto manufacture at the giant Willow Run B-24 works. He showed his two forthcoming vehicles, the Kaiser, above (1,000 dollars, 6 cylinders, 6 passengers, front wheel drive), and the Frazer (1,400 dollars, similar to the Kaiser, but larger), at the Waldorf Astoria, New York, recently. Some 155,000 people came to see them in 5 days, and cops had to control the crowds. Although the price is tentative, subject to OPA approval, and no cars were available for a test spin, 11,000,000 dollars' worth were ordered.
explanation: The headline makes a claim that buyers are acting on faith; the body provides evidence: massive attendance, police crowd control, tentative pricing subject to OPA approval, and no test drives, yet $11 million in orders. These facts function as premises supporting the implied conclusion that purchases are being made without typical assurances, i.e., on faith. The argument is implicit because the conclusion is suggested by the framing and the concessive “Although…yet…” structure rather than stated explicitly.
main_claim: Buyers are ordering these new Kaiser-Frazer cars on faith rather than on tested, confirmed information.

argument_text: Some 155,000 people came to see them in 5 days, and cops had to control the crowds.
explanation: This sentence supplies evidence (large attendance and need for police control) that implies a claim about exceptional public interest or demand for the cars. The conclusion is not stated, but the evaluative cue of police crowd control signals unusual popularity, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Public interest in the new cars was extraordinarily high.

argument_text: Although the price is tentative, subject to OPA approval, and no cars were available for a test spin, 11,000,000 dollars' worth were ordered.
explanation: The concessive structure lists reasons one would normally hesitate (uncertain price and no test drives) yet reports substantial orders, which implicitly argues that buyers showed remarkable confidence or faith. The conclusion about trust/remarkable demand is implied rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: Buyers placed substantial orders despite price uncertainty and lack of test drives, indicating strong confidence or faith in the cars.

argument_text: FOOD PROBLEM becomes more severe as India appeals for more rice, and England states her food situation is worse now than during the days of Dunkirk.
explanation: This sentence advances the claim that the food problem is worsening and gives two reasons: India’s appeal for more rice and England’s statement that its food situation is worse than during Dunkirk. The connective “as” explicitly links premises to the conclusion.
main_claim: The global food problem is becoming more severe.

argument_text: U.S., ARGENTINA RIFT expected as the result of the publication by the State Department branding the Argentine government and its predecessors back to the time of Pearl Harbor as active supporters of Nazism.
explanation: This sentence claims a diplomatic rift is expected and cites a causal reason: the State Department’s publication branding Argentina’s government as supporters of Nazism. The phrase “as the result of” explicitly connects premise and conclusion.
main_claim: A U.S.–Argentina rift is expected because of the State Department’s publication accusing Argentina of supporting Nazism.

argument_text: THE NAVY asked Congress to approve the peacetime transition force of 558,000 officers and men pending the outcome of atomic bomb tests on warships and United Nations efforts to stabilize world conditions.
explanation: While phrased as a report of a request, it embeds a rationale: approval is sought “pending the outcome” of tests and UN stabilization efforts, implying that maintaining a sizable force is necessary until uncertainty is resolved. This implies the normative claim that Congress should approve the force for prudential reasons.
main_claim: Congress should approve maintaining a 558,000‑person peacetime transition force until atomic tests and UN stabilization efforts clarify conditions.

argument_text: REPUBLICAN PARTY CONGRESS calls for the Party to put itself in the vanguard of an anti-monarchist front formed by the unification of all republicans in the country.
explanation: This is a prescriptive call for action (to lead an anti-monarchist front), which implies the claim that such leadership is desirable or necessary. The recommendation functions as a conclusion; the implied premise is that unifying republicans against the monarchy is beneficial or strategically important.
main_claim: The Republican Party should lead a unified anti-monarchist front.

argument_text: FERRUCCIO PARRI, former Premier of Italy, commented on the results of the Congress of the Republican Party and remarked that the popular forces want a republic, for only if the monarchy is overthrown can they start to rehabilitate the institutions and economy of the country.
explanation: Parri asserts that popular forces want a republic and provides a reason: overthrowing the monarchy is a necessary condition to rehabilitate institutions and the economy. The connector “for” makes the premise–conclusion relation explicit.
main_claim: The popular forces want a republic because only overthrowing the monarchy will allow rehabilitation of Italy’s institutions and economy.

argument_text: The forces that support the monarchy consist mainly of former supporters of fascism and of landowners who are trying to save their estates.
explanation: This is presented as a characterization of monarchy supporters, but functions as an ad hominem/delegitimizing premise implying the conclusion that the monarchy’s support is self-interested and suspect, and thus the monarchy should be opposed. The evaluative implication is not stated but suggested by associating supporters with fascists and self-interested landowners.
main_claim: Support for the monarchy is largely illegitimate and self-interested, so the monarchy should be opposed.

argument_text: To keep the monarchy would mean civil war, for it would be against the will of the working masses, the leftist parties, and part of the rightists too.
explanation: This sentence makes a predictive claim (keeping the monarchy would mean civil war) and provides a causal reason: it would oppose the will of major social groups. The connector “for” signals the explicit premise–conclusion link.
main_claim: Retaining the monarchy would lead to civil war because it defies the will of most political and social groups.

argument_text: The conservative middle class had better think about that.
explanation: This admonition implies a recommendation: given the preceding warning about civil war, the conservative middle class should reconsider their stance on the monarchy. The imperative phrasing cues a prescriptive conclusion without restating premises.
main_claim: The conservative middle class should reconsider support for the monarchy to avoid the risk of civil war.

argument_text: VITO MARCANTONIO will ask the American Congress to withdraw the Allied troops and the Allied Commission from Italy in order to re-establish the full sovereignty of the Italian Government on the entire peninsula.
explanation: This sentence links the proposed action (withdrawing Allied troops/commission) to a purpose (“in order to re-establish” sovereignty), providing a clear reason for the recommendation and thus an argument for withdrawal.
main_claim: Allied troops and the Allied Commission should be withdrawn from Italy to re-establish full Italian sovereignty.

argument_text: COMMITTEE FOR A JUST PEACE FOR ITALY, with members Charles Poletti, Edward Corsi, and Joseph Di Fede among others, outlined the following measures to be taken in favor of Italy: the Wilson line should be confirmed, the frontier between Italy and Austria should be left unchanged, Italy should retain all colonies acquired before the Fascist Government took power, Italy should not pay reparations, Italy should be given back her merchant fleet and, finally, she should be granted membership of the UNO.
explanation: This lists prescriptive measures framed as “to be taken in favor of Italy,” implying they are justified and ought to be adopted for Italy’s benefit. The reasons are implicit in the “in favor of Italy” framing and the committee’s authority, functioning as an argument for these policy outcomes.
main_claim: The international community should adopt the listed policies (borders, colonies, no reparations, return of fleet, and UNO membership) to favor Italy.

argument_text: — "The Dirty Blonde," the culmination of many hours of fond labor, is the handiwork of Lt. A. L. Buddin.
explanation: The evaluative phrasing "the culmination of many hours of fond labor" functions as a reason implying that the model is noteworthy and deserving of recognition; coupled with identifying the maker ("handiwork of Lt. A. L. Buddin"), it suggests merit and craftsmanship. The conclusion (that the model is commendable/significant) is implied rather than stated explicitly, making this an implicit argument based on evaluative cues.
main_claim: The model is a noteworthy, commendable piece of craftsmanship by Lt. Buddin.

argument_text: (it's a P-39 Airacobra in case you've forgotten aircraft rec.)
explanation: The aside presupposes that readers are expected to know aircraft recognition and uses a lightly ironic prompt ("in case you've forgotten") to imply a normative claim about shared knowledge. The implicit reasoning is that because readers are (or should be) familiar with aircraft rec, simply naming the type suffices; the rhetorical cue signals a stance about expected competence.
main_claim: Readers are expected to know (or remember) aircraft recognition well enough to identify a P-39 Airacobra.

argument_text: is one of many that has been built with kits supplied by Special Service.
explanation: This clause attributes the proliferation of models to the provision of kits by Special Service, implying a causal relationship: because Special Service supplied kits, many models were built.
