The causal wording ("built with kits supplied by") suggests an argument about Special Service enabling model-building.
main_claim: Special Service has enabled the construction of many models by supplying kits.

argument_text: (ANS) — There's a band of unscrupulous educational racketeers throughout the country who are anxious to grab off some of the 500,000,000 dollars set aside for veterans' schooling under the G.I. Bill of Rights.
explanation: This asserts that unscrupulous actors exist and intend to seize veterans’ education funds. The phrase “who are anxious to grab off some of the 500,000,000 dollars set aside” implies a causal motive (the existence of large funds attracts racketeers), functioning as an implicit premise supporting the conclusion that a predatory threat exists.
main_claim: Unscrupulous educational racketeers are targeting the sizable G.I. Bill funds for veterans’ schooling.

argument_text: Educators declared that many quack, fly-by-night colleges, totally inadequate and educationally unsound, are springing up in many parts of the country to gyp veterans of millions of dollars.
explanation: The evaluative language (“quack,” “totally inadequate,” “educationally unsound”) and purpose clause (“to gyp veterans”) imply a normative judgment and causal claim: because these schools are inadequate and opportunistic, they will defraud veterans. This is an argument against such institutions, though not laid out with formal premises.
main_claim: Many inadequate fly-by-night colleges are emerging with the aim of defrauding veterans.

argument_text: Reports disclosed that "racketeer" institutions, taking advantage of overcrowded conditions in legitimate colleges and universities, have already been organized or were being planned.
explanation: By attributing their emergence to “taking advantage of overcrowded conditions,” the passage implies a causal argument: overcrowding creates an opportunity that enables racketeer institutions to form. The premise (overcrowding) supports the conclusion (the formation/planning of racketeer schools).
main_claim: Overcrowding in legitimate colleges is enabling racketeer institutions to form or be planned.

argument_text: The college heads warned that in some states the officials were lax and that often second-rate and poorly equipped schools and even the "quack" type were accredited.
explanation: This warning links the accreditation of second-rate or “quack” schools to official laxity. The implied reasoning is that accrediting poor-quality institutions evidences lax oversight; thus officials are lax. The causal relation is suggested rather than formally stated.
main_claim: Lax state officials have allowed poor-quality and quack schools to gain accreditation.

argument_text: This applied particularly in the case of new commercial schools or colleges, frequently established for the sole purpose of getting on the Veteran's Administration list and offering all kinds of inducements and making false promises to the veterans to get them to enter.
explanation: By asserting that such schools are created “for the sole purpose” of listing with the VA and using inducements and “false promises,” the passage implies these institutions are illegitimate and exploitative; the motive and tactics serve as premises supporting the negative judgment.
main_claim: Many new commercial schools are illegitimate enterprises created to get VA listing and lure veterans with false promises.

argument_text: All signs indicate that the "shady" institutions will become more numerous within the next few years, the educators said, warning that the schools were advertising in metropolitan newspapers.
explanation: “All signs indicate” plus the cited evidence (advertising in metropolitan newspapers) constitute an inference that the number of shady institutions will grow. The advertising is offered as an indicator, functioning as a premise for the prediction.
main_claim: The number of shady institutions is likely to increase in the coming years.

argument_text: A committee had been established to attempt to track down and put out of business all illegitimate institutions.
explanation: Reporting the creation of a committee to shut down illegitimate institutions implies the normative claim that such institutions are harmful and should be eliminated. The necessity of tracking down and closing them functions as a conclusion derived from their perceived illegitimacy.
main_claim: Illegitimate institutions ought to be identified and shut down.

argument_text: To reduce the danger further, it was recommended that more community colleges be established with an overall plan to include cooperation among all the agencies within the State concerned with veteran problems.
explanation: The structure is explicit: goal/premise (“To reduce the danger”) leads to the recommended actions (establish more community colleges and coordinate agencies). The premise provides the stated reason for the policy conclusion.
main_claim: Establishing more community colleges and coordinating state agencies is recommended to reduce the danger posed to veterans.

argument_text: Overcrowded colleges and universities were urged to refer veterans to junior colleges or smaller four-year institutions where facilities were still available.
explanation: This is a direct policy recommendation tied to the premise of overcrowding and available facilities elsewhere; the remedy (referral) is urged because it addresses the stated condition.
main_claim: Overcrowded institutions should refer veterans to junior colleges or smaller four-year schools with available facilities.

argument_text: We say that it is inexpensive, because only if you try hard enough you can make it expensive. There are free admission theaters, clubs that cost you nothing or a very small sum, and a radio station that has no advertisements. But there are also black market restaurants and transient prostitutes who drain you of every cent you have if you let them.
explanation: The passage advances the claim that living/entertaining in Foggia is inexpensive, giving a “because” clause with supporting evidence (free theaters, low-cost clubs, ad-free radio). It also warns that costs rise only if one chooses exploitative options (black market restaurants, transient prostitutes) that “drain you,” reinforcing the conclusion. The explicit causal connector “because” makes the argument structure clear.
main_claim: Foggia can be an inexpensive place to live and find entertainment unless you choose costly black-market or vice options.

argument_text: There are no prostitutes from the City of Foggia itself. The woman who propositions you is a camp follower from other parts of Italy, and she knows more about sex than you do. Why not? She learned from German soldiers, French soldiers, Italian soldiers, Indian soldiers, Polish soldiers, from the 5th Army, from the 8th Army, from the 12th Air Force, from the 15th Air Force, from the RAF, and from your own countrymen. These girls do not make men; they only louse them up. Whether you are single, virgin, married, or senile, you can live much better without stuff like that, and if you have any excess energy, work it off at the gym.
explanation: Although framed narratively and evaluatively, the passage argues that soldiers should avoid prostitutes: premises assert they are outsiders, sexually experienced from many armies, and harmful (“they only louse them up”); conclusion is a prescriptive recommendation to abstain and “work it off at the gym.” The normative language and final directive indicate an embedded argument.
main_claim: You should avoid engaging with prostitutes and instead channel your energy into alternatives like the gym.

argument_text: Restaurants in town, all of which are off limits, cater to a certain type of military personnel who will pay exorbitant prices for food of inferior quality than is served in the mess halls. Aside from the fact that this food does not pass any tests for cleanliness and often is diseased, it takes food from the civilians who are as close to starvation as any people in the world. The racketeers who run these restaurants are serving you because you pay them more than any Italian will, and they care little for the welfare of their countrymen.
explanation: This paragraph argues against patronizing off-limits restaurants by citing multiple premises: they overcharge for inferior food, lack cleanliness and may be diseased, deprive starving civilians, and are run by racketeers who exploit soldiers. The conclusion (do not frequent these establishments) is implied by the negative consequences and moral framing.
main_claim: You should not patronize the off-limits town restaurants because they are exploitative, unsafe, and harm civilians.

argument_text: At the present time, there are a series of change-overs occurring, which makes an accurate listing difficult. Ask someone who knows the town to show you around.
explanation: The first sentence gives a premise (ongoing changes make accurate listings difficult), and the second provides a directive conclusion (ask a knowledgeable person to guide you). The causal relationship is explicit.
main_claim: Because listings are unreliable during change-overs, you should ask someone familiar with the town to show you around.

argument_text: The Post Exchange is the place where you will do practically all of your buying. Operated by Lieutenants DeVogelaere and Skeele, it offers you cigarettes, candy, soap, toilet articles, clothing, and even locally made jewelry and trinkets for souvenirs. The PX is the General Store of Foggian Americans, and although it has been hard hit by redeployment, you will find nothing to compare with it for fair dealing and bargain prices in Italy.
explanation: The passage promotes the PX as the primary and best place to buy goods, supporting this with premises about its broad offerings and superior fairness/prices. The prescriptive force (“the place where you will do practically all of your buying”) functions as a recommendation, with evaluative claims as reasons, making it an embedded argument.
main_claim: You should make the PX your primary place to shop because it offers broad selection, fair dealing, and the best prices.

argument_text: For laundry, you will have to find a civilian establishment. Ask some of the men who have been here for a while, and they will recommend a reliable place.
explanation: The need to use civilian laundry services is given as the premise, and the conclusion is a clear recommendation to consult experienced men to get a reliable place. The inferential connection is straightforward.
main_claim: Since laundry must be done at civilian establishments, you should ask experienced men to recommend a reliable place.

argument_text: At regular intervals, we will cover every topic of interest to you new residents. Look for them, and if you have any questions, don't hesitate to ask us.
explanation: The claim that the publication will cover topics of interest serves as a reason for the directive to “Look for them” and to ask questions. The recommendation is inferred rather than presented with an explicit logical connector, making it an embedded argument.
main_claim: You should watch for these regular articles and ask the staff questions because they will cover topics relevant to new residents.

argument_text: Without the assistance of a single stateside hep-cat, the gymnasium at the NAAFI building rocked under the flying feet of more than 800 prancing Foggiana Sunday night, as UNRRA got its benefit dance off to a fine start.
explanation: This uses a concessive frame (“Without the assistance of a single stateside hep-cat”) to imply that the dance’s success and liveliness did not depend on American expert dancers. The premise is the absence of “stateside hep-cat” assistance; the conclusion implied is that the event was still highly successful and lively regardless.
main_claim: The dance was lively and successful even without any stateside hep-cat assistance.

argument_text: and did the ritmo svelto, which may not be as smooth as the lindy hop but has it outclassed in energy output.
explanation: The concessive contrast (“may not be as smooth… but has it outclassed in energy output”) advances a comparative evaluation: ritmo svelto excels in energy compared to the lindy hop. The premise acknowledges a shortcoming (less smoothness); the conclusion asserts superiority in energy.
main_claim: The ritmo svelto surpasses the lindy hop in energy, even if it’s less smooth.

argument_text: Everything considered, observers were quick to admit it was one of the liveliest and most enjoyable dances held in Foggia.
explanation: This is an evaluative claim supported by appeal to testimony (“observers were quick to admit”). The implied reasoning is that because observers readily attested to its quality, the event indeed ranked among the liveliest and most enjoyable.
main_claim: The dance was among the liveliest and most enjoyable held in Foggia.

argument_text: Some 35,000 lire was raised for UNRRA, which will be used to help establish kitchens where hot meals will be distributed.
explanation: The sentence links the funds raised to a beneficial outcome (“used to help establish kitchens where hot meals will be distributed”), implying the event’s worthiness. The premise is the amount raised; the implied conclusion is that the fundraiser meaningfully contributes to relief efforts.
main_claim: The funds raised by the event will meaningfully support establishing kitchens to distribute hot meals.

argument_text: The gymnasium had its face lifted so well that it seemed a different place.
explanation: The causal phrasing (“so well that”) implies that the quality of decoration transformed the gym’s appearance. Premise: effective “face lift”; conclusion: the gym effectively became a different-seeming place.
main_claim: The decorations transformed the gym so much that it felt like a different venue.

argument_text: We were reminded that it was the gymnasium only when we saw Sgt. John Russel there, a little weary but joining in the festivities.
explanation: This follows and reinforces the transformation claim: only the presence of a familiar gym figure reminded them it was a gym. Premise: the sole reminder was seeing Sgt. Russel; implied conclusion: the transformation was otherwise complete.
main_claim: Aside from seeing Sgt. Russel, nothing about the space felt like a gym, underscoring the transformation.

argument_text: The liquor and sweets were excellent, and everyone was treating. However, though the atmosphere became perceptibly livelier as the evening progressed, all stayed happily above the weather.
explanation: The premises note abundant, high-quality refreshments and a livelier atmosphere; the contrastive “However” leads to the conclusion that attendees remained sober/properly behaved (“above the weather”). This argues that festivity did not lead to excess.
main_claim: Despite plentiful drink and rising liveliness, attendees did not overindulge and remained in good condition.

argument_text: When the hats were sold, the drawing which climaxed the evening was held.
explanation: Labeling the drawing as what “climaxed the evening” asserts a peak moment in the event. The premise is the sequence (hat sales followed by a drawing); the conclusion is evaluative: the drawing was the evening’s high point.
main_claim: The drawing constituted the high point of the evening.

argument_text: The living conditions are below normal for healthy living due to the overcrowding of rooms.
explanation: This sentence presents a conclusion (“living conditions are below normal for healthy living”) and gives a direct causal reason (“due to the overcrowding of rooms”), forming a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Living conditions are substandard because rooms are overcrowded.

argument_text: Food is critically short for several reasons: one, the production of grain in Italy this year was below normal due to the drought and the low level of allotment made by the government due to the general wheat shortage in the world, and the shortage of livestock.
explanation: The statement asserts a conclusion (“Food is critically short”) and explicitly lists causal premises (drought-reduced grain production, low government allotment due to global wheat shortage, and livestock shortage) supporting that conclusion.
main_claim: Food scarcity is severe because production and allotments are low and livestock is scarce.

argument_text: The unemployment situation is grave. Last year, the Allied Forces hired 25,000 civilian laborers; this year, there are less than 2,500 on the payroll. There is no industry to absorb the labor surplus due to the lack of raw materials. Most of the population are farm laborers, and at this time, it is off-season for farm laborers.
explanation: The opening evaluative claim (“The unemployment situation is grave”) is immediately followed by quantitative and causal evidence (decline in hires, lack of industry due to scarce raw materials, seasonal farm work). Although no explicit “therefore” appears, the premises are provided to justify the claim.
main_claim: Unemployment in Foggia is very serious because hiring has collapsed, industry cannot absorb workers, and it is the off-season for farm laborers.

argument_text: The reconstruction of buildings in Foggia is handicapped by a lack of investment capital and materials.
explanation: This is a straightforward causal claim: reconstruction is impeded because of insufficient capital and materials.
main_claim: Building reconstruction is hindered due to a shortage of capital and materials.

argument_text: The high cost of living—15,000 lire a month for subsistence for a family of five—makes living conditions more deplorable. Consider this in the light of a civilian employee of the military forces who averages about 8,000 lire a month.
explanation: The passage argues that high living costs worsen conditions and supports this with a comparative premise (income of civilian employees is much lower than subsistence costs), directly linking evidence to the conclusion.
main_claim: High living costs exacerbate hardship because typical incomes are far below subsistence needs.

argument_text: Your first impressions of the town have probably given you a distorted idea about life in southern Italy, and we will attempt to show you that things are not quite as bad as the place looks or as bad as the flak-happy old timers have led you to imagine.
explanation: This challenges an anticipated negative perception and advances a corrective claim (“things are not quite as bad”). It signals forthcoming justification (“we will attempt to show you”), implying that evidence will follow to support the claim.
main_claim: Conditions in southern Italy are better than initial appearances and veteran tales suggest.

argument_text: There are many recreational facilities and educational possibilities at your disposal here in Foggia. They are open to you, and the wise man will take advantage of them early in the game.
explanation: This is a recommendation framed through evaluative language (“the wise man will take advantage”), with the availability of facilities serving as the reason. The prescriptive “will take advantage” implies an ought-claim supported by accessibility.
main_claim: Soldiers should take advantage of the available recreational and educational facilities.

argument_text: As you will discover before you are in Foggia long, the largest problem confronting the soldiers is one of how to spend his free time best, rather than how to find enough time to spend.
explanation: By contrasting two supposed problems, the sentence claims that abundance of leisure options—not scarcity of time—is the primary issue. The rhetorical contrast implies a conclusion about the adequacy of recreation in Foggia.
main_claim: Soldiers’ main challenge in Foggia is choosing how to use abundant free time, not finding enough of it.

argument_text: Entertainment in Foggia is plentiful and inexpensive, thanks to Special Service, the British, and the American Red Cross.
explanation: The sentence asserts a conclusion about entertainment being plentiful and inexpensive and provides explicit causal attribution (“thanks to” specific organizations).
main_claim: Entertainment is abundant and affordable because of support from Special Service, the British, and the American Red Cross.

argument_text: The Foggia plains, situated south of the Apennine mountains and about ten miles in from the Adriatic, were perfect for airbases for Allied Air Forces. It became the first military target for the 8th Army of the Allied Forces.
explanation: The juxtaposition implies causality: because the plains were ideal for Allied airbases, Foggia became an early military target. The causal link is suggested rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: Foggia’s ideal geography for airbases led to it becoming an early Allied military target.

argument_text: All of these are available to you through your unit Special Service officer, and if there is anything you want that is not in stock, a requisition gets it as soon as a place makes its run to Leghorn.
explanation: This assures access to desired items by stating a condition and causal mechanism: if not in stock, a requisition will secure it upon the next run to Leghorn, supporting the claim of availability.
main_claim: You can obtain any desired items through Special Service because requisitions fill gaps promptly.

argument_text: Timed to be a part of the gala Army Day festivities, the show will be one of the liveliest yet, with Frank De Grazia's new orchestra playing everything from hillbilly to opera. Director and MC M/Sgt. Johnny Bowman says that he has a parade of new acts. Feminine talent from the Red Cross, a skit, and a sizzling harmonica act are a few highlights of the show, which will run between an hour and an hour and a half.
explanation: This passage advances the evaluative claim that the show will be “one of the liveliest yet.” The subsequent details—varied music from a new orchestra, a “parade of new acts,” and specific highlights—function as reasons meant to justify that assessment. The causal connection (variety and novelty imply liveliness) is suggested rather than stated with explicit markers like “because,” making the argument implicit.
main_claim: The show will be one of the liveliest yet.

argument_text: Caused by an extreme shortage of grain in Southern Italy, the raiding began early Saturday afternoon as the building workers paraded through the streets of Foggia yelling for food and work and waving placards and Italian and American flags.
explanation: This sentence attributes a cause (extreme shortage of grain) to an effect (the raiding beginning). The premises are the shortage and the demonstrators’ demands for food and work; the conclusion is that the shortage caused the raiding. The causal connector “Caused by” makes the argument structure explicit.
main_claim: The raiding began because of an extreme shortage of grain in Southern Italy.

argument_text: Men on the train who were transporting black-market food to Bari opened fire on the raiders with pistols and sub-machine guns. In the action, Giuseppe Roberto, 33, of Foggia was killed while trying to enter the train.
explanation: This passage presents a causal chain: the men on the train opened fire, and as a result Roberto was killed while trying to enter the train. The premises (opening fire) support the conclusion (the death occurred in that action), forming an explicit causal argument.
main_claim: Giuseppe Roberto was killed as a result of the train guards opening fire on the raiders.

argument_text: The raiding workers, unmolested by civilian police, removed tons of black-market grain from the train and carried it off to a warehouse in the city in waiting wagons.
explanation: The phrase “unmolested by civilian police” insinuates that civilian police did not intervene when they could have, implying a failure or refusal to act. This evaluative framing suggests a claim about police non-intervention without offering explicit reasons, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Civilian police did not intervene to stop the raiding workers from removing the grain.

argument_text: The grain, camouflaged in luggage and wrapped in old clothes, had been destined for Bari where prices for grain are higher than they are in Foggia.
explanation: This sentence provides evidence (camouflage; destination where prices are higher) that implies a motive of illicit profiteering, supporting the preceding labeling of the shipment as black-market. The causal/economic cues suggest the conclusion without stating it directly.
main_claim: The grain shipment was part of a black-market operation intended to profit from higher grain prices in Bari.

argument_text:
Throughout the day-long demonstrations, the rioters showed a surprising amount of respect for Allied military personnel and equipment. In one instance, the mob stopped at a warehouse in Foggia and began removing boxes of food. When they saw the UNRRA labels on the packages, all the boxes were brought back.

No casualties or damage were reported from Allied sources, and all through the demonstrations an American flag was carried by the building workers. Allied soldiers and military police were cheered whenever they appeared in the vicinity.
explanation: The first sentence states a general claim (rioters respected Allied personnel/equipment). The subsequent sentences supply supporting evidence: returning UNRRA boxes, absence of Allied casualties/damage, carrying an American flag, and cheering Allied soldiers/MPs. This forms an explicit argument with examples supporting the asserted conclusion.
main_claim: The rioters demonstrated respect and goodwill toward Allied personnel and property during the demonstrations.

argument_text: American MPs, who until this time had remained in the background and carefully kept out of the fighting, moved into the crowd and carried away victims of the rioters.
explanation: The description that MPs “carefully kept out of the fighting” and then “carried away victims” implies they acted with restraint and in a protective, humanitarian role rather than as aggressors. The evaluative adverb “carefully” and the sequence of actions suggest the conclusion without directly arguing it.
main_claim: American MPs acted with restraint and primarily intervened to protect and aid victims rather than to engage in the fighting.

argument_text: Scores of G.I.'s deposited American coin and Italian currency just for luck into the foundation of the first flagpole erected in the Foggia Area since the end of hostilities. Lt. Edward Arnett, smiling over the enthusiasm, expected the flagpole to be dug up one of these days.
explanation: This presents an implicit causal argument: since money was placed in the flagpole’s foundation, there is an incentive for someone to dig it up later. The expectation of it being “dug up one of these days” functions as the conclusion, inferred from the premise that coins were deposited “just for luck.” The humorous/ironic tone and lack of explicit “because” signal implicitness.
main_claim: The flagpole will likely be dug up in the future because coins were deposited in its foundation.

argument_text: The first day of spring saw approximately two hundred men witnessing the impressive ceremony at the 529th Air Service Group, as Colonel W. R. Wells raised "Old Glory." M. Sgt. Frank De Grazia's Military Band played the "Stars Spangled Banner" and military marches.
explanation: This advances an evaluative claim that the ceremony was “impressive,” implicitly supported by reasons: high attendance (~200 men), the formal act of the colonel raising the flag, and the presence of a military band performing national music. The evaluation plus supporting details constitutes an implicit argument.
main_claim: The ceremony was impressive.

argument_text: An arsonist coat hanger, which, it is suspected, got a big charge out of the two terminals of a battery last week, caused a mysterious fire to break out in the Special Services storeroom, FAAB Headquarters, and destroyed three football uniforms (the hottest they have been all season) and a radio (which gave a burning account of the entire event).
explanation: This sentence asserts a causal relationship: the coat hanger contacting the two battery terminals caused the fire. Despite the hedge “it is suspected,” the structure presents a clear cause-and-effect claim (X caused Y). The premises are implicit in the description (contact with battery terminals), leading to the conclusion that this caused the fire.
main_claim: A coat hanger that contacted a battery’s terminals caused the fire in the Special Services storeroom.

argument_text: (the hottest they have been all season)
explanation: This parenthetical uses irony to evaluate the football team’s season, implying that the uniforms (and by extension the team) have not been “hot” (i.e., successful or exciting) except when literally burning. The evaluative, sarcastic phrasing signals an implied claim about poor or lackluster performance without stating it directly.
main_claim: The football team has not been “hot” this season.

argument_text: Your quarters at present will be ample, consisting mostly of individual apartments for family units.
explanation: This advances the evaluative claim that quarters will be “ample” and supports it by citing a factual characteristic (“consisting mostly of individual apartments for family units”). The structure implies: because the housing consists mostly of individual family apartments (premise), therefore the quarters will be ample (conclusion). The evaluative term “ample” and the supporting detail indicate an implicit argument.
main_claim: The provided quarters will be adequate for families.

argument_text: A word of caution: There are no cook stoves or refrigerators, hence it is suggested you bring a two-burner electric plate, a roaster to serve as an oven for additional duty, and an icebox as ice is available.
explanation: This contains an explicit premise-conclusion structure: because there are no cook stoves or refrigerators, and because ice is available (premises), therefore you should bring an electric plate, a roaster, and an icebox (conclusion). The causal connector “hence” marks explicit argumentation.
main_claim: You should bring specific cooking and cooling appliances with you.

argument_text: As to recreational facilities, beach clubs, etc., you have no doubt been informed by your husband.
explanation: This sentence implies a justification for not providing details about recreation: since your husband has already informed you (premise), further explanation here is unnecessary (implied conclusion). The phrase “you have no doubt been informed” signals presupposition and functions as an implicit argument for omission.
main_claim: Additional details about recreational facilities are unnecessary because husbands have already informed the wives.

argument_text: To give an opportunity to get acquainted with those destined for this base while en route, the following are names and addresses of those presently requested (listed above).
explanation: This provides an explicit rationale (premise) for the action taken: because the aim is to give an opportunity to get acquainted while en route, the list of names and addresses is provided (conclusion). The purpose clause “To give an opportunity…” functions as a reason.
main_claim: The list of names and addresses is provided to help the wives get acquainted en route.

argument_text: The going will not be as easy as in the United States, but we will make Foggia as pleasant for you as is possible.
explanation: This juxtaposes a difficulty (premise: conditions will be harder than in the U.S.) with a promise of mitigation (conclusion: the command will make conditions as pleasant as possible). It implicitly argues that despite hardships, the base’s efforts will offset them and the wives should feel reassured. The concessive “but” signals a persuasive reassurance.
main_claim: Although life will be harder than in the U.S., the base will mitigate hardships to make your stay pleasant.

argument_text: The families will live in suitable sections of the BOQ#20 building, where forty apartments are available.
explanation: This asserts suitability (“suitable sections”) and supports it indirectly by noting availability of forty apartments, implying adequate capacity and arrangement. The evaluative term “suitable” combined with the factual detail functions as a premise-conclusion structure, though the linkage is not fully spelled out.
main_claim: Housing arrangements in BOQ#20 are appropriate for the incoming families.

argument_text: The new requirement that all wartime government employees must pass civil service examinations in order to retain their jobs is expected to open many positions to veterans. According to the New York Civil Service Leader, which specializes in these matters, the new policy for filling permanent jobs consists of separating the scores into 5-point groups. Thus, if the top scores run from 85 points to 80 points, within this 5-point block the Civil Service Commission will appoint veterans first, war service workers next, and non-veteran, non-war service workers last. When it has placed all the persons from the first 5-point block, the Commission will move down to the next 5-point block. In that manner, the entire list will eventually be covered. In accordance with established practices, veterans who compete with the temporary employees for jobs will receive 5 or 10 point mark-ups on the score of the examinations.
explanation: The passage advances the claim that the new requirement will open many positions to veterans and then supplies mechanisms that imply why: veterans are appointed first within score blocks and receive 5–10 point mark-ups. Although it does not use an explicit “therefore/because” structure, the sequencing of the policy details functions as premises that support the predictive conclusion about increased veteran opportunities.
main_claim: The civil service exam requirement and associated appointment and scoring preferences will open many government positions to veterans.

argument_text: According to the New York Civil Service Leader, which specializes in these matters, the new policy for filling permanent jobs consists of separating the scores into 5-point groups.
explanation: This sentence asserts a description of the policy and buttresses its credibility by invoking the source’s expertise (“which specializes in these matters”). The appeal to authority implicitly argues that the described policy structure is reliable/accurate because it comes from a specialized, knowledgeable source.
main_claim: The policy is accurately described as separating scores into 5-point groups because it is reported by a specialized, authoritative source.

argument_text: In a breakdown of victories based on 330 communities, Il Giornale Del Mattino, Rome, gave the Democrat Christian Party 144 victories on their own efforts and 123 towns to the Left Wing Bloc composed of the Communist, Socialist, and 63 towns to Independent, Republican, and other political parties to indicate that no group enjoyed a clear-cut victory in the first elections.
explanation: The passage presents numerical results (premises) and draws an explicit conclusion: “to indicate that no group enjoyed a clear-cut victory.” The phrase “to indicate that” signals an inference from the distribution of wins across parties to the conclusion that there was no decisive winner.
main_claim: No group enjoyed a clear-cut victory in the first elections.

argument_text: It is significant to point out that in this election, Party leaders in Rome did not wage an all-out campaign to bring victory to their own party but rather permitted their local organization to make any combinations of parties that they desired. In this respect, the campaigns were based to the largest extent on personalities and problems.
explanation: This two-sentence passage states premises (national party leaders did not wage an all-out campaign and allowed local combinations) and draws a conclusion (“In this respect, the campaigns were based to the largest extent on personalities and problems”). The causal connector “In this respect” explicitly links the premises to the conclusion about the nature of the campaigns.
main_claim: The campaigns were primarily based on personalities and problems due to the lack of centralized, all-out party campaigning and the freedom given to local organizations.

argument_text: After evading capture for eight days, two AWOL GIs were apprehended by an Italian guard at the 529th Air Service Group on February 25 and subsequently turned over to the proper authorities for return to the Leghorn stockade from which they had escaped, the CID announced this week.
explanation: This sentence frames the transfer to “the proper authorities” and return to the stockade as the appropriate and justified course of action. The evaluative phrase “proper authorities” and the causal sequence (capture → turnover → return) imply a normative claim that this was the correct procedure for escaped prisoners.
main_claim: Turning the captured escapees over to the proper authorities for return to the stockade was the appropriate and justified action.

argument_text: The two soldiers, privates, were masquerading as Master Sergeants and presented a typewritten authorization to the guard, permitting them to obtain a jeep and stating that they were investigators from a Rome MP detachment. The guard became suspicious and obliged the soldiers to accompany him to the Foggia MP Station.
explanation: The contrast between the deception (impersonation and dubious authorization) and the guard’s response implies an argument that the guard was right to be suspicious and detain them. The causal linkage suggests the premise (they were masquerading and making claims) supports the conclusion (detention was warranted).
main_claim: The guard was justified in detaining the soldiers because their impersonation and claims were suspicious.

argument_text: Investigation by the CID revealed that the men had escaped from the PBS Main Stockade in Leghorn, each having considerable records of jeep stealing and similar crimes.
explanation: By highlighting their escape status and “considerable records” of crimes, the sentence implies that the men were habitual offenders and that their capture/detention was necessary and justified. The evaluative framing of “considerable records” functions as evidence supporting that conclusion.
main_claim: The men’s history and escape status show that their capture and continued detention were necessary and justified.

argument_text: Wide searches for both men had been instituted by the time of their capture.
explanation: This statement implies that authorities considered the fugitives significant enough to warrant wide searches, which in turn supports the conclusion that apprehending them was important and appropriate. The selective detail of “wide searches” serves as evidence of seriousness.
main_claim: The fugitives were important targets whose capture was necessary, as indicated by the wide searches undertaken.

argument_text: With the aid of only a Tech Order and equipment obtained last week to supplement the pilots' four-hour monthly aerial flights, supervised by Lt. Arthur Deering, the Trainer, located next to the A.P.O., was assembled by F/Os George Perrera, Walter Singleton, Raymond McKee, and Calvin Millard.
explanation: The emphasis on "only a Tech Order and equipment obtained last week" and the stated purpose "to supplement the pilots' four-hour monthly aerial flights" implicitly argues that assembling the Trainer under constrained resources was a commendable, necessary initiative to address limited flight hours. The premise (minimal resources and recent equipment; need to supplement limited flight time) supports the implied conclusion that the officers showed resourcefulness and that the setup was justified and beneficial.
main_claim: The officers resourcefully assembled the Trainer to address pilots’ limited flight hours and provide needed supplementary training.

argument_text: Using instruments to maneuver the students enclosed under the canopy, the Link Trainer simulates flying conditions under the instructions of Pvt. Arthur White, a recent arrival in Foggia. The course will initiate the pilot with elementary procedures and from there into advanced work as received in transition school.
explanation: These sentences present premises—simulation of flying conditions and a curriculum progressing from elementary to advanced procedures akin to transition school—that imply the conclusion that the Link Trainer course is an effective and legitimate substitute or complement for real flight training. The evaluative implication arises from the analogy to transition school and the claim of realistic simulation.
main_claim: The Link Trainer course offers realistic, comprehensive training comparable to formal transition school and is an effective way to train pilots.

argument_text: FAAB Headquarters now finds itself with a complete library of three thousand books, which will permit Foggians to widen their literary and scholastic aspects in a quiet and pleasant atmosphere.
explanation: This presents a causal premise (there is now a complete library of three thousand books, with a quiet and pleasant atmosphere) leading to a conclusion (this will permit Foggians to widen their literary and scholastic aspects). The connective “which will permit” explicitly links premise to outcome.
main_claim: The new library will enable Foggians to broaden their literary and scholastic development.

argument_text: Sergeant Lou Claps, Library Chief, finally completing the arrangements for his two rooms on the third floor of the Headquarters Building, has already been swamped with readers' demands for such well-publicized books as "Forever Amber" and "Strange Fruit," which have become the most popular fiction volumes in the I and E Library.
explanation: The sentence offers evidence (being “swamped with readers’ demands” for specific titles) to support the claim that these books “have become the most popular fiction volumes.” The structure links demand (premise) to popularity (conclusion).
main_claim: High reader demand has made “Forever Amber” and “Strange Fruit” the most popular fiction in the library.

argument_text: Between the covers of the three thousand books is the latest in fictional material, and information on every subject of interest to the intelligent Foggian as well.
explanation: The assertion about comprehensive, up-to-date content functions to imply a normative conclusion that the library is valuable and meets readers’ needs. The premise (three thousand books containing the latest fiction and information on all subjects of interest) suggests the implied claim of usefulness and relevance without stating it directly.
main_claim: The library’s collection is comprehensive and up-to-date for the interests of intelligent Foggians.

argument_text: But it is the fact that there are three thousand books that is keeping the staff busy, as they put the books in numerical classification so that they can be easily found on request.
explanation: This sentence contains two explicit causal/teleological links: (1) the large number of books is the reason the staff is busy; (2) the staff classifies books numerically so that (purpose) they can be easily found. The “so that” clause states the justification for the action.
main_claim: Staff are busy classifying the large collection numerically to make books easy to find on request.

argument_text: "I'd sure like to buy some of those overseas bars," he said mournfully, "but they only come in fours and I need eight."
explanation: The speaker uses a concessive structure (“I’d sure like to buy… but…”) presenting a reason that prevents an intended action. Premises: the bars “only come in fours” and he “need[s] eight.” Implied conclusion: he will not/cannot buy the bars as packaged. The conclusion is unstated and suggested through the contrastive “but,” making it an implicit argument. The line may also carry a boastful insinuation about his service length, reinforcing the rationale.
main_claim: He cannot or will not buy the overseas bars because they are sold only in sets of four while he needs eight.

argument_text: There is an odd suspicion of weathermen in the Air Corps, and even though most of us seem to remember their technique of glancing out the window and following with a forecast of what seems most obvious and never remains so, Captain Ed Maiicut, FAAB's chief metro mystic, told us confidentially the other day that what they say about the weathermen is definitely not so. "That isn't guesswork, that's science," he exclaimed.
explanation: This directly advances the claim that forecasting by weathermen is scientific rather than guesswork, explicitly rejecting the common suspicion described. The conclusion (“That isn't guesswork, that's science”) is stated outright in response to the premise that people suspect forecasters just glance out the window.
main_claim: Weathermen’s forecasts are based on science, not guesswork.

argument_text: Did you know that actually we get weather information from all the Mediterranean and European areas? The main trouble is, though, that all our reports come from AACS in Naples over teletype, and mostly for personnel-shortage reasons, communications have not been very good lately.
explanation: This argues that recent communication quality problems are due mainly to personnel shortages, offering a causal explanation for report quality or delays. The “main trouble is… mostly for personnel-shortage reasons” provides an explicit cause for the observed effect (communications not very good).
main_claim: Communications have not been very good mainly because of personnel shortages at AACS in Naples.

argument_text: "Well, as I say, we make use of stations all over Europe and North Africa, but in the Italian area we now have eight stations. Before the war, there were thirty, but the forecasting is still on a high level.
explanation: This contrasts a reduced number of stations (eight now vs. thirty before the war) with the claim that “forecasting is still on a high level.” The “but” signals an argumentative move: despite fewer stations, quality remains high.
main_claim: Despite having fewer stations than before the war, forecasting quality remains high.

argument_text: "It works this way. The reports come into us over teletype, and the Italian weather personnel at Foggia Main draw up complete weather maps. Then, when we clear flights out of the field, our forecasters analyze these maps and make their terminal and route forecasts. In addition to making these forecasts, our staff makes hourly weather observations, which are sent out to all bases through the medium of the Army Airways Communications System.
explanation: While framed as procedure, this functions as an argument that forecasting is systematic and method-driven (maps, analyses, hourly observations, distribution via AACS), countering the earlier stereotype of “glancing out the window.” The detailed process implies the claim without stating it directly.
main_claim: Weather forecasting at the base is a systematic, data-driven process rather than mere guesswork.

argument_text: "But I'll tell you," Captain Maykut added, "forecasting weather during the winter in the Italian theater is really tough. The trouble is that the weather doesn't follow the rules that they teach in metro schools. The main reason for that is the basin-like quality of the Mediterranean area. You see, it's almost completely surrounded by mountains, and the high or low-pressure systems that come across the Atlantic are diverged by the various mountain ranges bordering this region whether they're the Alps, the Pyrenees, the Apennines, or the Atlas Mountains.
explanation: This offers a clear causal argument: winter forecasting is difficult because regional weather doesn’t follow standard rules, and that deviation is caused by the Mediterranean’s basin-like geography and surrounding mountains that deflect pressure systems.
main_claim: Winter forecasting in the Italian theater is difficult because Mediterranean basin geography causes weather patterns to deviate from standard rules.

argument_text: And even though we're on the same latitude as such states as Pennsylvania or Virginia our weather is completely different because the air masses affecting this area come from the south.
explanation: This asserts a difference in weather despite similar latitude and provides an explicit cause: southern-origin air masses. The “because” marks a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: This region’s weather differs from similarly latituded U.S. states because its influencing air masses come from the south.

argument_text: Maybe science has gotten most of weather forecasting under its thumb, but, believe me, there is nothing like experience," Mr. Weather said, glancing out the window as he left us, making his own personal prediction and hoping.
explanation: This advances the evaluative claim that practical experience is crucial, implicitly justified by the earlier-described complexities and unpredictability of the region’s weather. The contrastive “but” opposes reliance on science alone. The narrative detail of “glancing out the window” can be read as ironic reinforcement or gentle self-awareness, making the argumentative intent somewhat ambiguous.
main_claim: Despite scientific advances, practical experience is indispensable for accurate weather forecasting.

argument_text: A college degree might help, but it's not necessary for graduation from the Engineer Officer Candidate School. Figures show that three-fourths of the officers who graduated last year had no more than a high school education, while two percent of the 1,300 new "shavetails" had not even received their high school diplomas.
explanation: This presents a clear conclusion—college degrees are not necessary for graduation—supported by empirical premises: most graduates had only a high school education and some lacked even that. The second sentence provides evidence (“Figures show...”), which directly supports the claim in the first sentence, forming an explicit premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: A college degree is not necessary to graduate from the Engineer Officer Candidate School.

argument_text: There are a couple of terrific sides by the Sammy Donahue Navy Band which show just how wonderful the Donahue cat is. He recently started rehearsing a band in New York. I've seen the outfit and take it from me, it really comes on. He's got a kid on trombone by the name of Eddie Bert, who blew a little for Barnet a few years ago and then went into service. I think this kid Bert is just about the best hot trombone man in the business. And to prevent arguments, wait till you hear him before you start throwing rocks at me. All in all, I think the Donahue Band, if given a decent break, will be among the top bands in the States in about a year.
explanation: The passage advances a clear evaluative and predictive claim about the Donahue Band’s future standing, supported by reasons: recent strong recordings “which show,” the author’s firsthand observation that the band “really comes on,” the presence of standout player Eddie Bert, and an appeal to listeners’ future hearing as corroboration. These premises are marshaled to conclude that, given a fair opportunity, the band will rank among the top within a year.
main_claim: The Donahue Band, given a decent break, will be among the top bands in the United States within a year.

argument_text: I think this kid Bert is just about the best hot trombone man in the business. And to prevent arguments, wait till you hear him before you start throwing rocks at me.
explanation: This advances a comparative quality claim about Eddie Bert, with an implied evidential premise: that hearing his performance will convince skeptics. The argument relies on evaluative language and an appeal to experiential verification rather than explicit reasons, signaling an implicit argumentative structure.
main_claim: Eddie Bert is one of the best hot trombone players in the business.

argument_text: Another band we think is definitely destined for the top of the music heap is the Buddy Rich aggregation. The band, incidentally, is bankrolled by The Voice, Frankie Sinatra, who wasn't too friendly with the hidebeater when they were both with Tommy Dorsey. The band, like leader Rich, is strictly a hep crew with the accent on jump. The vocals are by Dottie Reid and the Maestro. Brooklyn Buddy plays skins all the time, not using a second drummer. Bitsey Mullins takes care of the trumpet riders and George Berg really sends everyone with his fine tenor sax work. There's also a very fine guitarist by the name of Lenny Mirabella. Most of the arrangements are by Billy Moore, who did a lot of those fine old Charlie Barnet numbers. Without a doubt, that is a band to watch. It might as well be swing.
explanation: The passage asserts that the Buddy Rich band is “destined for the top” and “a band to watch,” providing multiple supporting considerations: financial backing by Sinatra, stylistic identity (“hep,” “accent on jump”), specific personnel strengths (vocalists, drummer, trumpet, tenor sax, guitarist), and credible arranging by Billy Moore. These features function as premises to justify the conclusion about the band’s prospective success and noteworthiness.
main_claim: The Buddy Rich band is destined for the top and is a band to watch.

argument_text: New York (CNS) - Golds, yellows, oranges, lemons, and pinks will be the favored colors for men's linen suits come summer, according to Sidney Garfield, men's wear expert.
explanation: This presents a prediction and supports it implicitly by appealing to authority: the claim about favored colors is warranted by the fact that it comes from “Sidney Garfield, men's wear expert.” The expertise functions as the (unstated) premise that experts in men’s wear are reliable predictors of fashion trends, leading to the conclusion that these colors will be favored.
main_claim: Golds, yellows, oranges, lemons, and pinks will be the favored colors for men’s linen suits this summer.

argument_text: The colors will be "out of this world," admits Garfield, who also encourages men not to be afraid of them because they're real male plumage for summer.
explanation: There is a clear normative recommendation (“encourages men not to be afraid of them”) supported by a stated reason introduced by “because” (“they're real male plumage for summer”). The evaluative “out of this world” frames the appeal, but the argument’s structure is explicit.
main_claim: Men should not be afraid to wear these bright colors in summer.

argument_text: Servicemen who haven't been around the last two years to watch the increasing popularity of linen suits are expected to adopt the new colors without protest. Garfield figures that they've been wrapped up in olive drab for so long they'll be glad to put on a pair of pink pants.
explanation: This advances a causal prediction about servicemen’s behavior and provides reasons: (1) they missed observing the rise in popularity of linen suits, and (2) prolonged exposure to olive drab will make them glad to wear bright colors. The second sentence explicitly links the prolonged olive drab to anticipated gladness, functioning as the premise supporting the conclusion that they will adopt the new colors without protest.
main_claim: Servicemen will readily adopt the new bright-colored linen suits.

argument_text:
In your edition of March 10th, Captain Jack Robertson stated that many of these reenlistees have one year or less service. In our case, the undersigned will have, at the date of discharge, approximately two and a half years of service.

We would like to know if the Selective Service Act would pertain to us, and to what extent.

P.S. 69% of us fellows are in the same boat too.
explanation: This challenges a prior characterization by contrasting it with the writers’ own service length and a statistic about their peers. The premise is that 69% of their group have about 2.5 years of service, which suggests the earlier claim (“many have one year or less”) is misleading in their context. The argument is implicit because no explicit conclusion is stated; the evaluative implication arises from contrast and selective evidence.
main_claim: The assertion that many replacements have only a year or less of service does not fit their group, where most have roughly two and a half years’ service.

argument_text: (All men are subject to draft by Selective Service, and veterans must register upon their discharge. As yet, however, very few veterans have been recalled to duty. In the event that drafting of veterans becomes more frequent, men who have served short periods of time would be called before those who have seen extended service.)
explanation: The note provides premises (universal draft liability; registration requirement; current rarity of veteran recalls; order of call-ups favoring shorter-service veterans) that imply a conclusion relevant to the letter writers: veterans with longer prior service are less likely to be recalled now and would be drafted later than short-service veterans. The conclusion is implied rather than explicitly stated, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Veterans, especially those with longer prior service, are unlikely to be recalled soon and would be drafted after shorter-service veterans if recalls increase.

argument_text: T/5 Sylvester McQueen, 893rd Lug - "How my people are doing back in the States - and me with a few more months to sweat out."
explanation: The rhetorical framing expresses a complaint about remaining service time and concern for family, implying the claim that his remaining time is burdensome. The use of "a few more months to sweat out" suggests a negative evaluation of the wait without explicit premises, functioning as an implicit argument about undesirable conditions.
main_claim: Having a few more months left to serve is an unpleasant burden.

argument_text: Jo Balliano, APC - "Just thinking how good this was and wishing I could make it," while munching a biscuit.
explanation: The evaluative phrase "how good this was" advances a positive judgment about the food; the added wish to make it implies it is worth replicating. No explicit reasons are given, but the context of enjoyment while eating functions as an implicit warrant for the positive evaluation.
main_claim: The biscuit is very good and desirable enough to want to make it oneself.

argument_text: Pfc. Steve Enright, 779th AM-1 - "Lend me a hundred lire so I can buy some cigarettes, and make a mint."
explanation: This is a direct persuasive request with stated reasoning: if given 100 lire (premise), he can buy cigarettes and profit ("make a mint") (premise), therefore the addressee should lend him the money (conclusion). The connective "so" makes the inferential structure explicit.
main_claim: You should lend me a hundred lire because it will enable me to buy cigarettes and profit.

argument_text: Gunners Ken Hawpin, Frank Foster, and Derek Dunn, 155/51st HAA Reg. RA - "Uncle Joe's monologue on ghost stories is tops. Wish we could have a canteen of our own."
explanation: The first sentence is an evaluative claim ("is tops") about the monologue, asserting high quality without explicit support. The second sentence expresses a desire for "a canteen of our own," implying a normative claim that having their own canteen would be better or desirable. The pairing suggests a stance that good entertainment and facilities are valued and perhaps lacking.
main_claim: Uncle Joe’s ghost-story monologue is excellent, and it would be desirable for them to have their own canteen.

argument_text: Pfc. William Edwards, 529th QC - "Have just as much chance for promotion as a cog in the streets of Foggia."
explanation: This is an argument by analogy: comparing his promotion prospects to an inanimate "cog in the streets," implying those chances are effectively zero. The figurative comparison functions as a premise supporting the conclusion that his promotion chances are negligible or unfairly low.
main_claim: My chances for promotion are practically nonexistent.

argument_text: 2nd Lt. James Jackson, FAAB - "How long am I going to wait on F/O Townley?"
explanation: The rhetorical question implies dissatisfaction with excessive waiting, conveying the claim that the wait for F/O Townley is unreasonably long. The interrogative form serves as an indirect assertion rather than seeking information.
main_claim: The wait for F/O Townley has been too long.

argument_text: "Another War Bond, Hayworth?"
explanation: This is a rhetorical question that implies a recommendation or social pressure to purchase an additional war bond. The wording “Another” presupposes prior bond purchases and frames buying more as expected or desirable. Addressing “Hayworth” functions as a nudge or prompt, signaling a stance without explicit premises or conclusion.
main_claim: Hayworth should buy another war bond.

argument_text: An approved new Army policy recommended by a board of four generals provides for the organization of Negro troops into units no larger than an infantry regiment or a comparable organization. The decision for small units was based on "experiments and other experiences of World War II," in which the board reported that "the most successful employment of Negro units occurred when they were employed as units closely associated with white units on similar tasks."
explanation: This is an argument because it presents a policy decision (organize into small units) supported by a stated reason (WWII experiments showing success when Negro units were closely associated with white units on similar tasks). The causal justification directly links evidence from experience to the conclusion about organizational size.
main_claim: Negro troops should be organized into small units because WWII experience showed they were most successful when closely associated with white units on similar tasks.

argument_text: Specifically, the new policy calls for the creation of all types of Negro units, both combat and service, based on the 1-10 proportion of Negro to white civilians. In addition, qualified individuals will be used "in appropriate special and overhead units."
explanation: This advances a policy claim with an explicit rationale: unit creation is to be “based on the 1-10 proportion,” which functions as the guiding principle/criterion. The use of “based on” signals a justification for how many and what types of units to create, and the second sentence adds a related allocation principle for qualified individuals.
main_claim: The composition and number of Negro units should be determined proportionally to the civilian Negro-to-white ratio, with qualified individuals also placed in special and overhead units.

argument_text: Negro officers eventually should command all Negro units, it was stated.
explanation: This is a normative recommendation (“should”), which implies an underlying rationale (e.g., leadership by members of the same group enhances effectiveness, equity, or legitimacy), though no explicit premises are provided. The ought-claim signals an argumentative stance.
main_claim: Negro officers ought to command all Negro units.

argument_text: The principle was approved that Negro units of the postwar Army should be stationed "in localities where community attitudes are most favorable and in such strength as will not constitute an undue burden to the local civilian population."
explanation: This is a prescriptive principle containing implicit reasoning: station units where attitudes are favorable and in limited numbers to avoid burdening communities, implying that such placement will improve relations and reduce social strain. The terms “most favorable” and “undue burden” function as justificatory cues.
main_claim: Negro units should be stationed only where local attitudes are favorable and in numbers that do not burden the civilian population.

argument_text: Creation of a broader Negro base in the postwar Army logically includes the organization of appropriate elements of any female component, the board reported.
explanation: The phrase “logically includes” marks an inference from the premise of creating a broader Negro base to the conclusion that the female component should also be organized accordingly. It states a reasoning connection rather than a mere description.
main_claim: Expanding the Negro base in the postwar Army entails organizing appropriate Negro elements within any female component.

argument_text: The board, headed by Lieutenant General Alvan C. Gillem, concluded that the War Department failed to prepare adequate plans for the use of Negro manpower prior to World War II and advised that if "remedial action" were taken now, "many of the apparent deficiencies of the Negro soldier can be eliminated."
explanation: This presents a critique (failure to plan) and a conditional recommendation with causal reasoning: taking remedial action now will eliminate many apparent deficiencies. The “if… then…” structure provides a clear argumentative link between action and expected outcome.
main_claim: Because past planning for Negro manpower was inadequate, taking remedial action now will eliminate many apparent deficiencies of the Negro soldier.

argument_text: The change of command of the Italian unit came as a result of the British removal from the Foggia airfield.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal justification (premise) for an outcome: the change of command occurred because the British removed from the airfield. It follows an explicit X because Y structure, offering a reason for the event, thus constituting an argument (cause supports conclusion).
main_claim: The change of command happened because the British left the Foggia airfield.

argument_text: Acting under the policy announced by higher headquarters concerning the releasing of as many Italian soldiers from duty as possible, Captain Clark is replacing the Italians with as many American replacements as he has available.
explanation: This sentence provides a policy-based justification for an action: because higher headquarters has a policy to release as many Italian soldiers as possible (premise), Captain Clark is replacing Italians with American personnel (conclusion). The causal/justificatory linkage is explicit.
main_claim: Captain Clark’s replacement of Italian soldiers with American personnel is justified by higher headquarters’ policy to release as many Italian soldiers as possible.

argument_text: Mr. Ralph Borah became the new field director of the American Red Cross in the Foggia area on March 18th when Mr. Jake Hoptuer left for further assignment with the International Red Cross in Yugoslavia.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal linkage: Borah’s becoming field director is tied to Hoptuer’s departure. Although phrased with “when” rather than “because,” it implies that Hoptuer’s leaving led to Borah’s appointment, which functions as an argument providing a reason for the change in leadership.
main_claim: Ralph Borah became field director because Jake Hoptuer left for another assignment.

argument_text: Captain Houston J. Zinn is expected to take over command of the 55th Station Hospital this week when Captain Jesse W. Kitchin leaves his duties for the Zone of the Interior.
explanation: This sentence implies a reason for Zinn’s expected assumption of command: Kitchin’s departure creates the vacancy. The “when” construction suggests a causal/conditional relationship functioning as an argument for why Zinn will take over.
main_claim: Captain Zinn will take command because Captain Kitchin is leaving for the Zone of the Interior.

argument_text: Captain Zinn, a former resident of Texas, studied at the Harvard Medical School.
explanation: By highlighting Zinn’s Harvard Medical School background, the sentence implicitly argues for his competence or suitability to command the hospital. The prestige credential serves as evidence supporting an unstated evaluative claim about his qualifications.
main_claim: Captain Zinn is a qualified and credible choice to command the hospital due to his Harvard Medical School training.

argument_text: The stadium is also assuming more importance as summer comes, and with a good turnout track and field will be one of the biggest things for sportsmen.
explanation: This sentence advances a predictive and persuasive claim linking seasonality and turnout to the prominence of track and field. The premise is that summer increases the stadium’s importance; the implied conclusion is that people should turn out so that track and field becomes a major activity. The causal and conditional phrasing suggests an argument without explicit connectives like “therefore.”
main_claim: As summer arrives, increased turnout will make track and field one of the main sports.

argument_text: Track and field athletes are coming into their own at last, now that Foggia Stadium (opposite the 55th Station Hospital on the road to the airfield) is being readied for a big program.
explanation: The claim “athletes are coming into their own” is justified by the stated reason “now that [the stadium] is being readied for a big program.” The “now that” construction provides an explicit causal premise leading to the conclusion.
main_claim: Track and field athletes are finally advancing because the stadium is being prepared for a big program.

argument_text: Bus service makes the track easily accessible; checking service for valuables and hot showers are in operation now.
explanation: The first clause asserts accessibility and gives a cause (“Bus service makes the track easily accessible”). The second clause adds supporting reasons (amenities) that imply the track is convenient and desirable to use. Together they form an argument for the track’s accessibility and user-friendliness.
main_claim: The track is easy and convenient to use because there is bus service and on-site amenities.

argument_text: With a reminiscent eye on the successful boxing matches held in Foggia last year, Sgts. Russel and Gray are calling all men who can lift a glove to start coming down for workouts.
explanation: This sentence presents a call to action (come for workouts) and invokes prior success as the motivating reason. The past success functions as an implicit premise supporting the recruitment appeal, even though no explicit “because” is used.
main_claim: Men should come train for boxing now because last year’s matches were successful.

argument_text: The next tournament sports will be four-wall handball and volleyball. The volleyball court is set up on the basketball floor and can be converted into a badminton court simply by lowering the net. Players or teams contemplating entry in either, especially four-wall handball, are advised to begin training now.
explanation: This block gives forthcoming competitions and facility readiness, then recommends immediate training. The advice relies on the implied premise that upcoming tournaments and available facilities create urgency to prepare, even though the connective “therefore” is not stated.
main_claim: Prospective entrants should start training now because the next tournaments (and ready facilities) are set.

argument_text: Latest announcements about the gym and track will be spotted on the AES radio during Cookie Time (1915 most nights) and Flagella Fanfare (1315 daily). Watch for signs and bulletins which are to appear soon.
explanation: The imperative to “Watch for signs and bulletins” and implicitly to listen to AES programs is supported by the reason that these channels will carry the latest announcements. The advice is justified by information about where updates will appear.
main_claim: You should monitor the AES radio and posted notices to stay informed about gym and track updates.

argument_text: The FAAB athletic program is large now and growing. There is a lot of equipment for the asking and plenty of fun to be had. Just come on down and wade right in!
explanation: The concluding imperative (“Just come on down...”) is supported by reasons given in the prior sentences: the program’s size/growth and the availability of equipment and fun. This forms a clear persuasive argument with premises leading to an action-oriented conclusion.
main_claim: People should participate in the FAAB athletic program because it is expanding and offers ample equipment and fun.

argument_text: The gymnasium is located about two blocks southeast of the traffic circle in a large white building, the Palazzo degli Studi. It can be reached easily by bus or by a ten-minute walk from any part of Foggia proper.
explanation: The second sentence asserts easy reachability and immediately provides reasons (bus access or a short walk). The locational details in the first sentence contextualize the claim. This is an argument establishing accessibility with supporting evidence.
main_claim: The gym is easy to get to because buses serve it and it’s only a ten-minute walk from anywhere in Foggia proper.

argument_text: "Nope, no more boxing for me," said Gus Scharboneau. He unlaced his gloves. "I've got a perfect record." He removed his headguard. "That's the last for me." He climbed down through the ropes. Gus, who beat out two victories at the recent Leghorn matches, views the matter philosophically. He has a medal, is undefeated; might as well leave it at that.
explanation: This presents a conclusion (he will stop boxing) supported by reasons (he has a perfect record, a medal, is undefeated). The phrasing “might as well leave it at that” explicitly ties the premises to the decision.
main_claim: Gus will stop boxing because he is undefeated and wants to leave his perfect record intact.

argument_text: Of course, keeping in condition is another matter. He lost twelve excess pounds in Leghorn and in the spirit of keeping that way, does his eight rounds or so daily.
explanation: There is a clear causal rationale: because he lost twelve excess pounds and wants to maintain that condition, he continues to do eight rounds daily.
main_claim: Gus continues daily rounds to maintain the weight loss and condition he achieved in Leghorn.

argument_text: At Slocum Graf High in Trenton, Michigan, he joined a boxing class presumably to improve on the knowledge picked up in a "more than average" number of street scuffles.
explanation: The sentence attributes a purpose (“to improve”) based on prior experience with street scuffles. The hedge “presumably” signals inference, not a directly stated reason from Gus, making the argumentative link implicit.
main_claim: He joined the boxing class in order to improve the fighting knowledge he had from frequent street scuffles.

argument_text: "I used to love it," he says, "But when we came overseas, my crew went down on their first mission and now, well I don't think I'd like to fly anything but maybe a cub after I leave the Army."
explanation: This is a causal explanation: the loss of his crew led to a change in attitude toward flying, concluding that he would only consider flying a small plane (“maybe a cub”).
main_claim: Because his crew was lost on their first overseas mission, Gus no longer wants to fly anything except perhaps a small plane after the Army.

argument_text:
The travel will be to South America. Why South America?
"Oh, to see some of these Latin women," he says with a smile.
explanation: Direct question-and-answer gives a reason for the choice of destination: the desire to see Latin women justifies traveling to South America.
main_claim: Gus wants to travel to South America in order to see Latin women.

argument_text: It was cadets right away, and then a minor miracle as he went through Basic Training and Classification in eleven days each.
explanation: The evaluative phrase “a minor miracle” implies the conclusion that his progression was unusually rapid or remarkable, supported by the fact that each phase took only eleven days. The argument is suggested rather than formally stated.
main_claim: Completing Basic Training and Classification in eleven days each was exceptionally rapid/remarkable.

argument_text: The heat from the tons of flash powder, described by Captain Adelaide L. Turgeon, Commanding Officer of DP #1, as more intense than anything except atomic energy, singed the faces of observers and destroyed the grass for a radius of 200 yards around the detonation area.
explanation: This passage advances the evaluative claim that the heat was extraordinarily intense, supported by two premises: an argument from authority (the commanding officer’s description) and observable effects (singed faces, grass destroyed for 200 yards). The causal linkage between those effects and the conclusion is implied rather than formally stated.
main_claim: The heat generated by the explosions was extraordinarily intense.

argument_text: Photographers T Sgt. James E. Collier and Lt. Robert L. Warner of FAAB Photo Lab, carrying a Speed Graphic and a K-20 aerial camera respectively, stood 800 yards away as one stack of 22,500 pounds of bombs were detonated.
explanation: By highlighting that the photographers positioned themselves 800 yards away during detonation, the text implies a safety rationale: the blast is dangerous enough to require great distance. The conclusion (distance is necessary for safety) is suggested by the described precaution, not explicitly stated.
main_claim: Observers needed to keep a large distance from the detonation for safety.

argument_text: 2. An American munitions handler fuses a one-pound block of TNT. He lights the fuse, hops into a jeep, and leaves in a hurry.
explanation: The rapid departure immediately after lighting the fuse implies a normative safety claim: one must evacuate quickly due to imminent danger. The behavior serves as evidence for the implied conclusion without being explicitly argued.
main_claim: It is necessary to evacuate quickly after initiating the fuse due to immediate danger.

argument_text: 4. The flames leap aloft and the concussion rocks the walls of the house on the right.
explanation: The physical effects—flames leaping and concussion rocking house walls—serve as evidence for the implied claim that the explosion was powerful. The text presents effects that imply the conclusion without explicitly stating it.
main_claim: The explosion was powerful enough to impact nearby structures.

argument_text: 7. The smoke mushrooms over the house whose plaster walls were cracked by the explosion.
explanation: The cracked plaster walls are presented as a consequence of the explosion, implying its strength. The causal relationship is suggested rather than formally argued.
main_claim: The explosion was strong enough to crack the plaster walls of a nearby house.

argument_text: The heat from the tons of flash powder, described by Captain Adelaide L. Turgeon, Commanding Officer of DP #1, as more intense than anything except atomic energy, singed the faces of observers and destroyed the grass for a radius of 200 yards around the detonation area.
explanation: This sentence advances the claim that the heat was extraordinarily intense.
