It implies support via two kinds of evidence: an appeal to authority (the Captain’s comparison to atomic energy) and observed effects (singed faces, grass destroyed over 200 yards). The causal effects serve as implicit premises supporting the conclusion about intensity.
main_claim: The explosion’s heat was extremely intense, second only to atomic energy.

argument_text: 4. The flames leap aloft, and the concussion rocks the walls of the house on the right.
explanation: This states a causal claim that the concussion from the explosion affected the house’s walls. The causal relationship is directly asserted (“the concussion rocks the walls”), making the argument explicit even though no additional supporting evidence is provided.
main_claim: The explosion’s concussion shook the house’s walls.

argument_text: 7. The smoke mushrooms over the house, whose plaster walls were cracked by the explosion.
explanation: This sentence explicitly attributes the cracking of the plaster walls to the explosion using the causal marker “by.” It asserts a cause-and-effect relationship as the main claim.
main_claim: The explosion caused cracks in the house’s plaster walls.

argument_text: 2. An American munitions handler fuses a one-pound block of TNT. He lights the fuse, hops into a jeep, and leaves in a hurry.
explanation: The sequence implies a causal-normative claim: after lighting the TNT fuse, one must depart quickly due to imminent danger. The phrase “leaves in a hurry” functions as an indicator of risk and necessity, suggesting the conclusion without stating it directly.
main_claim: Lighting the TNT fuse necessitates an immediate, rapid departure because remaining nearby is dangerous.

argument_text: In a world where a brother, a friend of early years, or a friend who lived through the words of the last letter lies buried in the oblivion that is the earth, many of us pause to give thought to the words and deeds of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Humanitarian and Champion of the Dignity of Man that inhabits the universe. This time it is most important that peace loving people throughout the world turn their eyes to the United Nations Organization and raise their voices in unity that those things which he strived for shall bear the fruits of victory.
explanation: This passage advances a recommendation that people should support and rally around the United Nations to realize FDR’s aims. The initial sentence evokes loss and reverence for Roosevelt, which functions as a contextual premise underpinning the normative conclusion that collective action through the UN is “most important.” The causal/ought linkage is implied rather than spelled out step-by-step, signaled by evaluative language (“most important”) and the directive to “turn their eyes” and “raise their voices.”
main_claim: Peace-loving people should unite in support of the United Nations so that FDR’s goals will be achieved.

argument_text: "The structure of world peace cannot be the work of one man or one party or one nation. It cannot be an American peace or a British, Russian, French or Chinese peace. It cannot be a peace of large nations — or small nations. It must be a peace which rest on the cooperative efforts of the whole world.
explanation: This is an explicit argument denying several alternatives (peace made by one actor or by specific nations) and concluding that peace must rest on global cooperation. The repeated negations function as premises eliminating competing possibilities, supporting the positive conclusion that peace requires the cooperative efforts of all.
main_claim: World peace must rest on the cooperative efforts of the entire world rather than any single nation or group.

argument_text: "It will not be easy to win, this people's peace. We delude ourselves if we believe that the surrender of the armies of our enemies will make the peace we long for. Unconditional surrender of the armies of our enemies is the first and necessary step, but the first step only.
explanation: The passage argues that military victory alone is insufficient for lasting peace. Premises: peace is difficult; believing surrender alone suffices is self-deception; unconditional surrender is only the first step. Conclusion: more than surrender is required to achieve the desired peace.
main_claim: Military surrender is necessary but not sufficient to secure the peace people desire.

argument_text: "Peace can be won only by the united determination of free and peace-loving peoples who are willing to help one another, willing to respect and tolerate and try to understand one another's opinions and feelings.
explanation: This sentence provides a conditional necessity claim: peace can be won only if peoples unite and practice mutual assistance, respect, tolerance, and understanding. The list of required attitudes/behaviors serves as premises defining the means to the conclusion that peace can thereby be won.
main_claim: Achieving peace requires united determination grounded in mutual help, respect, tolerance, and understanding among free and peace-loving peoples.

argument_text: "Responsibility for political conditions thousands of miles overseas can no longer be avoided by this great nation. The United States exerts vast influence in the cause of peace throughout the world. It will continue to exert that influence only if we are willing to continue to share responsibility for keeping peace. It would be our tragic loss if we were to shirk that responsibility.
explanation: This argument claims the U.S. must accept ongoing responsibility for global political conditions to maintain its positive influence for peace. Premises: the U.S. has vast influence; responsibility can no longer be avoided; continued influence depends on sharing responsibility; shirking would be a tragic loss. These support the conclusion that the U.S. ought to share responsibility to keep peace.
main_claim: The United States must continue to share responsibility for maintaining peace abroad to preserve its beneficial influence and avoid a tragic loss.

argument_text: "It is our purpose to help the peace-loving peoples of Europe to live together as good neighbors, recognize their common interest and not to nurse their traditional grievances against one another.
explanation: This statement prescribes a policy goal: helping European peoples live as good neighbors, focus on common interests, and abandon old grievances. The normative conclusion is explicit (“It is our purpose to help…”), and the specific behaviors to promote function as supporting content for that goal.
main_claim: We should help Europe’s peace-loving peoples become good neighbors by emphasizing common interests and abandoning traditional grievances.

argument_text: "We can and will achieve such a peace. We shall strive. We may make mistakes - but they must never be mistakes which result from faintness of heart or abandonment of moral principles"
explanation: This passage asserts confidence in achieving peace and issues a normative constraint on how to proceed (do not let mistakes stem from cowardice or immorality). The implied reasoning is that steadfastness and adherence to moral principles are necessary conditions for attaining peace, though the premises are not elaborated; the “but” contrast signals the implied link between method and outcome.
main_claim: We must strive confidently for peace and avoid losing heart or abandoning moral principles, even if errors occur.

argument_text: Major-General L. C. James, (extreme left), Deputy Theater Commander, is shown above, with his staff and Colonel Robert Martin (extreme right), as he addressed the 1898th Engineers last Wednesday, commending the men on the excellence of their work.
explanation: This passage advances an evaluative claim about the 1898th Engineers—namely that their work is excellent—by reporting the commendation from a high-ranking authority. The argument is implicit because the text does not state a conclusion outright but uses the general’s commendation (and his authority) as evidence that the engineers’ work is excellent, signaling an argument from authority through evaluative language (“excellence of their work”).
main_claim: The 1898th Engineers’ work is excellent.

argument_text: "The formations of planes are only an indication of the new training program that is starting this month," said Major Thayer, "to make the men of FAAB more proficient in their positions, both aerial and administrative.
explanation: The passage links the observed low-flying formations to a new training program and states the program’s purpose (to increase proficiency). Implicitly, it argues that the flights are justified and beneficial because they serve the aim of improving proficiency. The causal framing (“are only an indication of”) and purpose clause (“to make the men… more proficient”) function as premises supporting the conclusion that the flights are warranted.
main_claim: The recent B-17 formations over Foggia are part of a justified training effort to improve FAAB personnel proficiency.

argument_text: "In a plan that encompasses a six month period, ground personnel and aircrew members will be given both on-the-job and academic instruction to better qualify them for the jobs they are holding, but which they may not have been trained for before this time.
explanation: The sentence presents a rationale for the training: some personnel occupy jobs they may not have been trained for, therefore they will receive instruction to better qualify them. The evaluative purpose clause (“to better qualify them”) and the contrast (“but which they may not have been trained for”) imply a normative claim that such training is needed and justified.
main_claim: Ground and aircrew personnel should receive on-the-job and academic instruction because some currently hold jobs for which they were not previously trained.

argument_text: In addition, aircrew members will receive both flight training and ground instruction to re-acquaint each man with the duties for which he was originally trained.
explanation: This recommends refresher training, implying that re-acquaintance with original duties is necessary or beneficial. The purpose clause (“to re-acquaint each man”) functions as a justification for the prescribed training, supporting the implicit conclusion that such training ought to occur.
main_claim: Aircrew members should undergo both flight and ground instruction as a refresher to their originally trained duties.

argument_text: In order to maintain this fast service, only one stop in each direction will be made in Leghorn, Rome, Ciampino airfield, Caserta, and Naples.
explanation: This sentence gives a reason (“In order to maintain this fast service”) leading to a policy decision (“only one stop in each direction will be made”). The premise explicitly supports the conclusion by asserting that fewer stops are necessary to sustain speed.
main_claim: The service will make only one stop in each direction to maintain fast service.

argument_text: All mail coming into MTO can be distributed six hours sooner to field Army Post Offices at Leghorn, Caserta, and Naples under the new schedule.
explanation: The sentence asserts a beneficial effect (“six hours sooner”) tied to “the new schedule,” implying the evaluative conclusion that the schedule change is advantageous. The positive outcome functions as the reason for viewing the change favorably, though the evaluative claim is not stated outright.
main_claim: The new schedule improves incoming mail distribution speed.

argument_text: This change of schedule, however, will not affect the theater's outgoing mail.
explanation: The contrastive marker “however” anticipates and addresses a potential objection (that outgoing mail might be affected), implying the conclusion that the change has no negative impact on outgoing mail. The argument is implicit because the concern is unstated and no explicit premises are provided beyond the existence of the change.
main_claim: The schedule change will not impact outgoing mail.

argument_text:
Transportation Hinders Re-opening of Cannes

Foggia - An attempt to reopen rest camp on the French Riviera is now being made, Captain J. Harrison, FAAB Personnel Officer, revealed this week. Chief difficulty has been the inability to arrange for transportation.
explanation: The passage advances a causal claim that transportation problems are hindering the reopening effort. The premise is “Chief difficulty has been the inability to arrange for transportation,” which explicitly supports the conclusion stated in the headline that transportation hinders the reopening. The structure is a clear reason leading to a conclusion.
main_claim: Transportation problems are the chief hindrance to reopening the Cannes rest camp.

argument_text: Because of the inability to have all members of the radio staff appear at the same time, the program is being recorded.
explanation: This sentence presents a clear premise-conclusion structure signaled by "Because." Premise: not all staff can appear simultaneously. Conclusion: therefore, the program is being recorded.
main_claim: The program is being recorded.

argument_text: It will be waxed in fifteen minute portions so that every member will be included in the hour program.
explanation: This offers a means-end justification indicated by "so that." Premise: dividing into fifteen-minute portions enables inclusion. Conclusion: therefore, it will be waxed in such portions.
main_claim: The program will be waxed in fifteen-minute portions.

argument_text: In addition to the voice of General Eaker, the program will include various variety acts known to Foggian veterans, such as Sgt. Sid Del Monte, popular violinist of the AES last year.
explanation: This sentence implies a rationale for including these acts: they are known to veterans and one is described as "popular," suggesting their inclusion is desirable or will appeal to the audience. The evaluative descriptor "popular" and familiarity cue an unstated conclusion that these choices enhance the program's value.
main_claim: Including familiar and popular acts will make the program appealing.

argument_text:
Foggla - In an open letter from Washington to all AUS officers and former officers, General Dwight D. Eisenhower invited them to accept commissions in the Officer's Reserve Corps, National Guard, and Regular Army.

Expressing his appreciation for the job already done by AUS officers, the General hoped that the return to civil life would not be viewed as a "separation from the Service", and cited that it is imperative for the United States to remain strong in the years to come.
explanation: The passage advances a policy recommendation (officers should accept commissions) and provides a reason (the United States must remain strong). The causal/justificatory cue “cited that it is imperative for the United States to remain strong” functions as a premise. However, the text does not explicitly state “therefore accept commissions”; it frames the recommendation as an invitation and a hope, implying rather than directly asserting the conclusion, hence implicit.
main_claim: AUS officers should accept commissions in the Reserve, National Guard, or Regular Army to help keep the United States strong.

argument_text: Expressing his appreciation for the job already done by AUS officers, the General hoped that the return to civil life would not be viewed as a "separation from the Service", and cited that it is imperative for the United States to remain strong in the years to come.
explanation: This sentence presents a normative claim (“the return to civil life would not be viewed as a ‘separation from the Service’”) and explicitly supplies a reason (“it is imperative for the United States to remain strong in the years to come”), yielding a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Returning to civil life should not be regarded as separation from service.

argument_text: Foggia - The Venereal Disease rate in the Foggia area in the month of March declined to 30 percent of what it was in January according to a statement release, by Lt. Leonard B. Polaski, Adjutant of the 55th Station Hospital.
explanation: This presents a claim (VD rate declined to 30% of January) and invokes an authority as warrant (“according to a statement... by Lt. Leonard B. Polaski”). The implicit argumentative move is: because a qualified hospital adjutant reported this, the audience should accept the decline as true. It is not framed with explicit premises/conclusion markers but functions as an argument from authority.
main_claim: The venereal disease rate in March was only 30 percent of the January rate.

argument_text: Man hours lost because of venereal diseases were 524 in the month of January, 354 in February, and 178 in March.
explanation: This sequence of figures implies a trend-based argument: the decreasing man-hours lost serve as evidence that VD-related impact is declining. The normative or inferential step (that VD incidence or its operational burden is dropping) is unstated but suggested by the downward progression of numbers.
main_claim: VD-related absenteeism—and by implication the VD problem—declined sharply from January to March.

argument_text: During Christmas time over 4,000 presents of food and toys were given to Foggia's children by the Red Cross and the various American and British units here. Now with Easter coming, they are trying to meet that quota. It will be hard with the fewer numbers of men in Foggia, but it's up to you. How about it, Jack? Just dump your week's rations in one of the boxes in the ARC's or the PX.
explanation: The passage presents reasons (past success of 4,000 gifts at Christmas; current goal to meet that quota for Easter; fewer men making it harder) leading to a clear conclusion and call to action ("it's up to you... Just dump your week's rations..."). The structure directly links premises to a recommended action, making it an explicit argument.
main_claim: You should donate your week's rations in the ARC or PX boxes to help meet the Easter quota for gifts to Foggia's children.

argument_text:
Foggia - Declaring that they "had been warned about Foggia," manager Al Verdi of the USO show 'Maids And Magic" reported the theft of almost all the clothes and valuables belonging to Miss Marjorie Edwards of the troupe.

The thief entered her room between 9 and 12 PM Wednesday night, when Miss Edwards was at the EM Red Cross, ransacked her closet, luggage, and even personal mail. Clothing, shoes, jewelry, and many small personal items were stolen.
explanation: The quoted warning about Foggia, immediately followed by detailed evidence of a theft, implicitly advances the claim that Foggia is a place where theft is a significant risk and that such warnings are warranted. The narrative structure (warning → incident details) functions as premises supporting the conclusion without stating it explicitly. The evaluative cue is the mention of a pre-existing warning and the selection of theft details that corroborate it.
main_claim: Warnings about Foggia being risky or crime-prone are justified by the reported theft incident.

argument_text: The most ingenious article is a little pendulum wall clock fashioned of wood with plexiglass cogwheels and a can of nails hung on dog tag chains for motive power.
explanation: This sentence makes a comparative evaluative claim ("the most ingenious article") and immediately provides descriptive features (unusual materials and mechanism) that function as reasons supporting that evaluation. The structure implies: because the clock is cleverly made from scarce materials with an inventive power source, it is the most ingenious.
main_claim: The pendulum wall clock described is the most ingenious item in the exhibit.

argument_text: There are two perfectly formed violins, one made completely out of plexiglass.
explanation: The evaluative phrase "perfectly formed" advances a quality claim, and the follow-up detail that one is entirely plexiglass implicitly supports the assessment by highlighting difficulty/skill. The argument is: the violins are of perfect form, as evidenced by the craftsmanship and unusual material.
main_claim: The violins on display are of perfect form and high craftsmanship.

argument_text: A voting system which permits visitors to place candy or cigarettes in the box along with the ballots will determine the creator of the finest piece and his prize.
explanation: This asserts that the described voting mechanism will identify the "finest" piece and award a prize, implying that visitor votes (and possibly their accompanying tokens) are a valid method to determine artistic quality. The underlying reasoning is that popularity or visitor judgment suffices to establish which work is best.
main_claim: Visitor voting via ballots (and tokens) will validly determine the best piece and its winner’s prize.

argument_text: New Books Teach Themselves
explanation: The headline makes a normative, attention-grabbing claim that the books function autonomously for learning. It implies that the books’ design enables self-instruction, but offers no explicit premises within the headline itself; the supporting reasons are provided in the body. The implicitness is indicated by the hyperbolic phrasing “teach themselves,” which relies on the subsequent description to justify the claim.
main_claim: The new textbooks are designed so effectively that learners can use them for self-instruction without a teacher.

argument_text: The new books, written by outstanding experts in their fields are specially designed for use of the Armed Forces with subject material presented so clearly that they are equally useful as self-teaching manuals or classroom texts. Each book contains a complete study guide, exercises, problems, and self-checking tests.
explanation: This passage advances a clear conclusion—“they are equally useful as self-teaching manuals or classroom texts”—and provides reasons: the material is presented “so clearly,” and each book includes study guides, exercises, problems, and self-checking tests. The causal connector “so … that” signals an explicit premise-to-conclusion structure, with the feature list functioning as additional support.
main_claim: The new Army textbooks are equally suitable for self-study and classroom use because of their clarity and built-in study supports.

argument_text: It is expected that I & E and Special Services of many Army units will find it easier to organize off-time study classes with volunteer or inexperienced teachers when supplied with these new textbooks.
explanation: This sentence makes a predictive claim (“will find it easier to organize off-time study classes”) and gives a stated condition that serves as the reason (“when supplied with these new textbooks”). The causal linkage makes the argument explicit: the textbooks’ properties will reduce the difficulty of organizing classes, even with volunteer or inexperienced teachers.
main_claim: Providing these new textbooks will make it easier for Army units’ I & E and Special Services to organize off-time study classes, even with volunteer or inexperienced teachers.

argument_text: From the opening to the closing strains of the Occupators, Spotlight Time was a success Saturday (Army Day) night. With the advantage of a friendly audience willing to meet jokes more than halfway, S/Sgt. John Bowman’s cast got right down to earth and did their parts in a personal manner that was unusual and good in a large stageshow.
explanation: The conclusion “Spotlight Time was a success” is supported by premises about the audience’s receptivity and the cast’s down-to-earth, unusually good performances for a large stageshow. The causal connector “With the advantage...” functions as reasoning for why the show succeeded.
main_claim: Spotlight Time was a successful show.

argument_text: The audience wasn’t strained by having to squirm through any physical stuff or mediocre dance routines. Instead there was a succession of facile musical acts with just enough comedy, and some really fine music throughout the show by Frenck De Grazia’s fine band.
explanation: This passage evaluates the program by negatively contrasting what it avoided (“mediocre dance routines”) with what it offered (“facile musical acts,” “really fine music”). The implied conclusion is that the show was well-designed/enjoyable, supported by selective contrasts and evaluative language.
main_claim: The show’s program was well-judged and enjoyable because it avoided mediocre routines and offered fine music with balanced comedy.

argument_text: Monologue and a hot piano by T/3 Phil Campichairo provided some of the best solo playing and most honest laughs of the evening
explanation: This is an evaluative claim asserting superiority (“some of the best,” “most honest laughs”), implying that Campichairo’s act stood out in quality. The argument relies on the reviewer’s judgment as evidence without explicit premises.
main_claim: T/3 Phil Campichairo’s monologue and piano performance were standout highlights of the evening.

argument_text: After that an obstreperous intruder appeared, obviously under the influence of liquor who interrupted the show. With the deadpan assistance of Sgt. Calvin Bourgeault, the drunk (Pfc. Bob Kerr) engaged MC Bowman in a battle of words and the audience speculated upon the amount of liquor necessary to be able to act that way and still remember lines. Whether Pfc. Kerr was actually tipsy isn't known although popular opinion is that nobody could act that way without a few in him.
explanation: The conclusion implied is that Kerr was likely intoxicated; the supporting premises are the observed behavior, audience speculation about required liquor, and the generalization that “nobody could act that way without a few in him.” The concessive clause acknowledges uncertainty but advances a probabilistic claim.
main_claim: Pfc. Kerr was probably tipsy during the act.

argument_text: The skeleton was a song of South Sea Island love upon which was hung a routine with the best (in a grotesque sort of way) costumes of the evening and a chorus line of ARC beauties who exhibited a stamina and strength of character that strikes a telling blow for the cause of the American Girl.
explanation: The evaluative language (“best…costumes,” “stamina and strength of character”) and the metaphor “strikes a telling blow for the cause of the American Girl” imply the conclusion that the performance affirmatively represented American women. The reasoning is by positive portrayal and exemplary traits.
main_claim: The ARC chorus’s performance positively advanced the image and cause of the American girl through its standout costumes and display of stamina and character.

argument_text: With a little makeup on the actors to soften their faces under the hard lights, some speeding up of the comic lines, and a little more discipline in the orchestra when the acts are going on, Spotlight Time rates a tour of other military camps in Italy.
explanation: The sentence gives specific conditions (makeup, pacing, orchestra discipline) as premises leading to the conclusion that the show merits touring. The conditional “With…” structures the explicit reasoning to a recommendation.
main_claim: If a few production tweaks are made, Spotlight Time deserves to tour other military camps in Italy.

argument_text: "Now the reason we asked you to come out here," he said to us after brushing away several administrative matters, "is that we wanted to tell you about the kind of job your Air Corps boys have been doing, working for the Engineers. It was Colonel Miller’s idea, and that’s why he called you in the first place. When he left to go home he made a speech in the mess hall thanking the Air Corps boys for helping us out now and when that severe manpower shortage got us in the middle of the winter. And, I’m telling you what he said was plenty true. Just look around, and you’ll see what I mean.
explanation: The conclusion is that the Air Corps has done valuable work for the Engineers. Premises include Colonel Miller’s speech of thanks, the context of a severe manpower shortage, and the directive to observe evidence on site (“Just look around”).
main_claim: The Air Corps has been doing an excellent and much-needed job assisting the Engineers.

argument_text: Tall, silent Paul Cole wears pilot’s wings, yet he is now supervising a carpenter’s shop consisting of some heavy machinery and more than a hundred workers. "It isn’t like handling a B-17 and crew but," Major Burke commented, "he’s really turning out what we want and fast."
explanation: The conclusion is that Paul Cole is effective in his reassigned role despite it differing from piloting. The contrastive “yet” and Burke’s assertion that he’s producing what’s needed “fast” serve as premises supporting effectiveness.
main_claim: Pilot Paul Cole is successfully and efficiently supervising the carpentry shop.

argument_text: On our way to the carpenter shop we had passed a large motor pool of engineering vehicles. Over two hundred vehicles were parked in the dust of Foggia Valley. F/O Neale Van Wagner is a rated navigator, but now the problems are more complicated than spinning an E-6-B computer. "You bet they are. He's really got a job on his hands, because Van Wagner's supervising a bunch of PW's who were once slated to go back to Germany, so he's got a morale problem on his hands as well as an administrative one."
explanation: The argument claims Van Wagner’s current job is more complex than navigation; premises include the size of the motor pool and that he supervises POWs, creating both morale and administrative challenges. The “because” clause explicitly provides reasons.
main_claim: Van Wagner’s reassigned duties are significantly more complex than his navigation work due to large-scale logistics and POW morale/administrative issues.

argument_text: “Yeah,” said Lt. Parr, sitting behind an administrative desk, but wearing a leather flying jacket, “when we started to work with the engineers they were so short of men you could have counted them on your fingers. Good thing we were around,” he mused.
explanation: The conclusion “Good thing we were around” is supported by the premise of extreme manpower shortage among the engineers (“so short of men”). The causal relation is implied by the juxtaposition.
main_claim: The Air Corps’ presence was crucial because the Engineers faced an acute manpower shortage.

argument_text: “It sure was,” Engineer Major Burke put in, turning to us. “and I hope they stick with us for a while. These Air Corps guys can sure do more than fly planes.”
explanation: Burke endorses Parr’s claim and generalizes capability (“can sure do more than fly planes”), implying the conclusion that the Air Corps personnel should continue working with the Engineers because they are versatile and effective. The recommendation (“I hope they stick with us”) and evaluative generalization function as premises/conclusion.
main_claim: Air Corps personnel should continue assisting the Engineers because they have proven capable of valuable work beyond flying.

argument_text: USO: Look To Your Laurels
explanation: The headline implicitly argues that the USO should guard its prestige because the featured show sets a high bar or challenges its standing; the idiom “look to your laurels” is a caution to maintain superiority in the face of competition.
main_claim: The USO should be cautious to maintain its standing because this show’s quality is competitive.

argument_text: This Army Doesn’t Pay Any Longer
explanation: The headline asserts a stance that the Army no longer provides advancement or rewards, implying a negative change in benefits or promotions. It functions argumentatively by framing the subsequent facts as evidence; the evaluative phrasing “Doesn’t Pay Any Longer” presupposes that it used to “pay” and now does not, inviting the reader to accept that conditions have worsened. The support is implied rather than stated within the headline itself.
main_claim: The Army no longer provides the promotions or rewards it once did.

argument_text: Anyone who bought all the brass from gold bars to five stars in anticipation of making all the grades would do well to sell his stars and eagles if he has a business mind.
explanation: This is a recommendation implying a conclusion: sell insignia now. The reasoning is suggested rather than spelled out: “would do well” and “if he has a business mind” imply that the market for higher-rank insignia will decline due to fewer promotions/more demotions, so selling now is prudent. The premises are implicit expectations about future demand/value.
main_claim: People who stockpiled officer-rank insignia should sell them now.

argument_text: Latest news from Washington relates that 212 generals have been demoted to the rank of colonel, and now a MTOUSA order just in from Caserta states that no more promotions will be made to the rank of colonel and that as a matter of fact, most temporary officers from the rank of captain upward can expect a one rank demotion soon.
explanation: This sentence advances concrete claims (demotions, promotion freeze, expected demotions) and supports them by citing authoritative sources (“Latest news from Washington” and an “MTOUSA order”). The structure is explicit: because these official reports/orders say X, we should accept X as true.
main_claim: Promotions to colonel are halted and many temporary officers from captain upward will be demoted, as evidenced by recent official reports and orders.

argument_text: "I don't think we should. We are already doing our share by sending over more than any other nation. A sort of voluntary rationing by the people themselves would be all right. But not another compulsory system."
explanation: The speaker opposes compulsory rationing and provides reasons: the U.S. is already contributing more than any other nation, and voluntary rationing would suffice. The premises directly support the conclusion against a compulsory system, making the argument explicit.
main_claim: The United States should not impose another compulsory food rationing system, though voluntary rationing is acceptable.

argument_text: "At first I thought we should. But now I think it would be better to send them farm implements and get them started on producing their own food."
explanation: The speaker contrasts two options and concludes that sending farm implements is better than rationing, offering a reason (to enable self-production of food). The structure presents a clear comparative conclusion supported by a rationale.
main_claim: Instead of rationing in the U.S., it would be better to send farm implements to help others produce their own food.

argument_text: "I think it would be a good idea. People were used to rationing and shouldn't mind another year of it. The rest of the world has to survive too."
explanation: The speaker endorses rationing and gives two supporting reasons: domestic tolerance (people are used to it) and a moral/humanitarian imperative (the rest of the world must survive). The premises explicitly support the pro-rationing conclusion.
main_claim: The United States should ration food again because people can tolerate it and global survival depends on such aid.

argument_text: "It would be a pretty good idea if the extra food resulting from the rationing were then distributed fairly among the needy countries."
explanation: The speaker conditionally endorses rationing, with the condition that extra food be fairly distributed among needy countries. The conditional premise explicitly states the circumstance under which the conclusion holds.
main_claim: Rationing would be a good idea if the extra food were fairly distributed among needy countries.

argument_text: "Of certain commodities, yes. We could ration wheat and vegetables and it wouldn't hurt us in the least. But rationing meat and poultry would hurt us as much as anybody."
explanation: The speaker advances a nuanced position: ration some items (wheat and vegetables) because it would not harm Americans, but do not ration meat and poultry because it would be harmful. The claims are supported by explicit harm/no-harm premises.
main_claim: The U.S. should ration wheat and vegetables but not meat and poultry, since rationing the former would not hurt Americans while rationing the latter would.

argument_text: Why don't we send them all our excess K rations?"
explanation: This rhetorical question implies a policy recommendation: send excess K rations abroad as an alternative or supplement to domestic rationing. The interrogative form suggests rather than states the conclusion, making it implicit.
main_claim: The United States should send its excess K rations to needy countries.

argument_text: "When are they going to close the Stork Club?"
explanation: The rhetorical question implies dissatisfaction with the Stork Club and presupposes that its closure is expected or warranted. The implied premise is that there are reasons to close it; the conclusion is that it should be (and soon). The evaluative stance is conveyed through the expectation embedded in “when are they going to…,” signaling a recommendation without stating it explicitly.
main_claim: The Stork Club ought to be closed soon.

argument_text: "Getting the new replacements recreational facilities."
explanation: This fragment functions as a recommendation/priority, implying that new replacements lack adequate recreational facilities and that obtaining them is necessary. The normative force (“getting … facilities” as a goal) suggests an ought-claim: that such facilities should be provided. The argument is implicit because no explicit premises or conclusion are stated, but the phrasing frames provision as needed.
main_claim: New replacements should be provided recreational facilities.

argument_text: No, it couldn’t be true… but it is. The column is here again. Did you see Deadpan. Bourgeault, of «Skim (not a misprint) the Milkman» fame in Spotlight Time? If you did then you also saw Cookie of Cookie Time. Weren’t they great? Marvelous? Sensational?
explanation: Rhetorical questions and emphatic evaluative language imply the conclusion that the performances were excellent. The passage suggests a judgment without formally stating premises, relying on the reader’s shared experience (“If you did…”) as tacit support.
main_claim: Deadpan Bourgeault and Cookie’s performances were outstanding.

argument_text: They started to play a new arrangement. The trumpets went screetching, and the windows started breaking. Any band that was loud enough to break windows was felt too loud for Roseland. And Kenton was handed back his contract.
explanation: This gives a reasoned causal chain: extreme loudness (premise) implies being “too loud for Roseland” (intermediate conclusion), which explains the contract being rescinded (final conclusion).
main_claim: Kenton’s band lost its Roseland booking because it was judged too loud.

argument_text: He went back to California soon after that, but the band had made a great impression on those who had been lucky enough to hear it. Kenton had his own style of music but the public as a whole wasn't ready for it yet. The six foot four inch Maestro was also very uncompromising. He was going to play the music he wanted to, not what someone else wanted him to. The band was broken up. Re-formed, broken up, and re-formed again. The pianist cooled down a little and started playing a few things that Stan Kenton didn't write. Finally the public began to see what the critics meant and with a few condescensions to commercialism the band was finally on its way.
explanation: This passage argues that early failures stemmed from public unreadiness and Kenton’s uncompromising style; later partial concessions and changing public perception led to success. Premises include the public’s unreadiness and Kenton’s rigidity, with evidence of multiple breakups and eventual “condescensions to commercialism,” leading to the conclusion that these factors explain the band’s trajectory.
main_claim: Kenton’s initial lack of success resulted from an uncompromising, ahead-of-its-time style, and modest concessions plus shifting tastes enabled the band’s eventual success.

argument_text: Right now the Kenton band has a bunch of young brilliant men who are contributing to the future of modern jazz. Ray Wetzel, and Buddy Childers, two of the five trumpeters are fine soloists. Childers is working on a new slide trumpet which he occasionally uses. Freddy Zito plays wonderful trombone as does Boots Musilli play alto, and Bob Varney drums. Eddie Safranski on bass has done a great deal for the band since his addition to the rhythm section.
explanation: The author asserts the band’s significant contribution to modern jazz and supports it by listing standout musicians and innovations (e.g., slide trumpet), implying that such talent and experimentation justify the claim. The argument is implicit because the conclusion relies on evaluative terms (“brilliant,” “wonderful”) and examples rather than an explicit premise–conclusion structure.
main_claim: The Kenton band’s current lineup is advancing modern jazz due to its talented and innovative musicians.

argument_text: Singers June Christy and Gene Howard are both fine; Howard is really a find as he does all his own arrangements, something quite unusual.
explanation: This directly links a reason to an evaluative conclusion: because Howard does all his own arrangements (and this is unusual), therefore he is “really a find.” The causal/justificatory connector “as” makes the structure explicit.
main_claim: Gene Howard is an exceptional singer because he uniquely does all his own arrangements.

argument_text: Now for Kenton himself. The guy is one of the solidest pianists around, and is also a very, very fine arranger with a style completely his own.
explanation: The evaluative claims about Kenton’s pianism and arranging are supported implicitly by the qualifier “with a style completely his own,” suggesting that originality underpins the assessment. The reasoning is suggested rather than spelled out.
main_claim: Stan Kenton is an outstanding pianist and arranger, partly because of his distinctive personal style.

argument_text: But why didn’t the public like it the first time? Those of us who saw the first Kenton band will always remember it. As wonderful as this band is, it is not as good as the magnificent outfit that the public turned down five years ago.
explanation: The author argues that the earlier Kenton band was superior, using an appeal to firsthand experience and a contrast with the current band (“as wonderful as this band is… not as good as the magnificent outfit”). The rhetorical question frames the argument about public misjudgment.
main_claim: The original Kenton band rejected by the public five years ago was better than the current one.

argument_text: The public is beginning to wake up now. Let’s hope that they continue to, so that bands like Kenton’s won’t have to struggle for five years before they get the recognition due them.
explanation: This is a normative, purpose-driven argument: because the public is now recognizing quality, they should continue to do so in order to prevent deserving bands from enduring prolonged struggles for recognition. The “so that” clause states the intended consequence.
main_claim: The public should continue becoming more appreciative so deserving bands receive timely recognition.

argument_text: Keep watching for announcements about our anniversary. April 21 your AES in Foggia will be two years old. So stick around. Sign a waiver if you have to, because it’s going to be worth it. Among other things there will be a dramatic narration with every one taking part.
explanation: The author urges readers to stay for the upcoming anniversary event, implying it will be rewarding; the justification is the promise of worthwhile content (“it’s going to be worth it,” “a dramatic narration with every one taking part”). The jocular “Sign a waiver if you have to” underscores the recommendation via humorous exaggeration.
main_claim: Readers should stay tuned and attend the upcoming AES anniversary because it will be worthwhile and feature engaging activities.

argument_text: Approximately three hundred men flooded the club's three rooms at the Security Section to demonstrate their will power over Italian liquor.
explanation: This sentence uses ironic phrasing ("demonstrate their will power over Italian liquor") to imply a stance about the attendees’ intentions and behavior. The evaluative/ironic tone suggests the claim that the crowd came to drink heavily (or test/indulge their drinking), not merely to attend an opening. The argumentative move relies on insinuation and framing rather than explicit premises and a stated conclusion.
main_claim: The large crowd came intending to drink heavily, highlighting a kind of ironic “will power” over Italian liquor.

argument_text: When the demand for liquor exceeded the supply Cpl. Robert Duwe, supervising the bar, was well prepared for the Latrine Run. Late comers were shown to the door and left in disgust.
explanation: This passage states a causal relationship: because demand exceeded supply, specific consequences followed (preparedness for the “Latrine Run,” latecomers being turned away). The structure presents premises (excess demand) leading to effects, which functions as an explicit causal argument about why those actions occurred.
main_claim: Excess demand for liquor caused management to take contingency measures and turn away latecomers.

argument_text: "It was a premature opening," said one of the guests as he departed. The management vainly attempted to seat and hold its patrons, but for lack of tables and chairs many could not be accommodated.
explanation: The quoted conclusion (“It was a premature opening”) is followed by descriptive evidence about inadequate seating and inability to accommodate patrons, which implicitly serves as premises. The argument is that the opening occurred before adequate preparation; the link between the evidence and the conclusion is inferred rather than formally laid out.
main_claim: The club opened before it was adequately prepared to handle patrons.

argument_text: Acting manager Cpl. Rod Crabb stated, "The club was organized for recreational purposes for the man coming off guard duty. We just didn't expect so many outsiders."
explanation: The manager provides reasons (intended audience: men off guard duty; unexpected outsiders) that imply a justification for the overcrowding and unpreparedness. The implicit conclusion is that the problems were due to unforeseen attendance beyond the intended scope, mitigating management responsibility. The argumentative force comes from causal attribution and explanation.
main_claim: The overcrowding and resulting problems occurred because many unexpected outsiders showed up beyond the club’s intended audience.

argument_text: After enrollment is complete, no new students will be admitted. There is still time to enroll at the I & E Library in Headquarters Building.
explanation: These sentences together imply a recommendation to act quickly: because enrollment will close (premise) and there is still time now (premise), prospective students should enroll promptly (conclusion). The conclusion is not stated but is suggested by the urgency created by the contrast between closure and remaining time.
main_claim: Prospective students should enroll promptly at the I & E Library before enrollment closes.

argument_text: Seventy-two students, many sent by FAAB section heads, will start in two courses, beginner's typing and military correspondence, Monday, April 15th in room 308 Headquarters Building.
explanation: The mention that “many [were] sent by FAAB section heads” functions as an argument from authority/endorsement: the fact that supervisors are sending personnel implies the courses are valued or important. The conclusion (these courses are worthwhile/endorsed) is suggested rather than stated, relying on the authority cue.
main_claim: The typing and military correspondence courses are important and endorsed by leadership.

argument_text: With the stampede at Christmas time still rankling memories, the candy collected at the ARClubs will be distributed this time by delivery instead of at a party, although there may be a party for some orphans of Foggia.
explanation: This sentence gives a clear reason (the remembered Christmas stampede) leading to a policy decision (distribute candy by delivery rather than at a party). The causal connector “With… the stampede… the candy… will be distributed… by delivery instead of at a party” presents a premise-conclusion structure. The concessive clause about a possible party for orphans is an exception but does not undermine the core argument.
main_claim: The candy will be distributed by delivery instead of at a party due to problems experienced at a previous Christmas event.

argument_text: "In pro ball you play only for yourself - for money. Yes you play your best, but it isn't the same as high school ball. That's the only place where you play with spirit - for the team.
explanation: This series of evaluative claims contrasts professional baseball with high school ball, implying that pro ball is inferior or less meaningful because it is motivated by money and lacks team spirit. The premises (pro = for money/self; high school = spirit/team) support the implicit conclusion that pro ball is less desirable. The conclusion is not stated explicitly, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Professional baseball is inferior to high school ball because it is motivated by money and lacks team spirit, making it less desirable.

argument_text: "And it's work. You know how pro sports are. Travel around. Knock yourself out. And all you get is drunk every night."
explanation: The speaker lists burdensome features of professional sports—being hard work, constant travel, exhaustion, and habitual drinking—to imply the conclusion that pro sports life is undesirable and not worth pursuing. The conclusion is implied rather than stated, so this is an implicit argument.
main_claim: The lifestyle of professional sports is grueling and unhealthy, so it is not worth pursuing.

argument_text: That then, was what made Mel abandon what might have been a career and go to work inspecting B-26s at the Martin plant back in '42.
explanation: This sentence asserts a causal conclusion—that the previously listed negatives of pro sports caused Mel to abandon a potential pro career. The premises are provided in the immediately preceding statements, and the sentence draws an inferential link (“That then, was what made...”), making it an implicit argument connecting reasons to the decision.
main_claim: Mel left a potential professional baseball career because the drawbacks of pro sports led him to choose other work.

argument_text:
The coming of Foggia's baseball season doesn't lure him too strongly.

"I'll just keep things running smoothly at the stadium," he said. And that means until his "duration" is over, for more education is what he wants.
explanation: This passage presents a plan (keep running the stadium until his service is over) and gives a reason for it (“for more education is what he wants”). The connective “for” signals an explicit reason-conclusion structure: desire for education justifies not pursuing playing and instead maintaining the stadium role for now.
main_claim: He will avoid returning to play baseball and instead keep the stadium running for the duration because he wants to pursue further education.

argument_text: Not a few former cadets remember the "case of the 36,000" - those trusting lads with their noses in the blue who dreamed of P-38s and got 50 calibre machine guns as their ticket to glory.
explanation: The phrasing “trusting lads... dreamed of P-38s and got 50 calibre machine guns” contrasts expectations with the outcome and carries an evaluative tone, implying criticism of how the cadets were treated (bait-and-switch). The conclusion—that the cadets were misled or unfairly reassigned—is implied through contrast and emotive language rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: The “36,000” cadets were led to expect pilot roles but were instead given gunnery positions, implying an unfair bait-and-switch.

argument_text: With Special Services getting on its feet in the reorganized 529 ASG area, a large construction program of athletics facilities has been inaugurated under the supervision of F/O Calvin Millard, 529 Special Services officer.
explanation: The sentence links the state of “getting on its feet” after reorganization with the inauguration of a large construction program, implying a causal relation. The claim (that a construction program has begun under Millard) is presented as resulting from the premise (Special Services is now organized/operational), signaled by the “With X, Y” construction.
main_claim: The reorganization and operational readiness of Special Services have led to inaugurating a large athletics construction program under F/O Millard.

argument_text: The regulation size field is being built with the aid of German PW’s, next to their soccer field, and there have been as many as forty men working on the field at one time. At present the number has been decreased to ten; however, work continues on the rolling of the smooth infield.
explanation: The contrastive “however” introduces a concession-contrast structure: despite the premise of reduced manpower (from up to 40 to 10), the conclusion is that work is still progressing (continues on rolling the infield). The passage uses selective facts to support the implied claim of ongoing progress.
main_claim: Work on the baseball field is continuing and progressing even though the workforce has been reduced.

argument_text:
Special Services men Sgt. Paul Chaland, Cpl. Wallace Klein, and Pfc’s Bill Carson and Charles Buckley are putting through the job.

Said F/O Millard, “When this diamond is finished it’ll be the best ball field in the Foggia area. Then we’ll start on a softball diamond.”
explanation: The named personnel and their active involvement function as implied support for the evaluative and predictive claim that the diamond will be “the best” and that a subsequent project will follow. The argument relies on implied premises about the competence and effort of the team leading to superior quality and readiness for the next construction.
main_claim: The baseball diamond under construction will be the best in the Foggia area, after which the team will proceed to build a softball diamond.

argument_text: Flying the Big Birds loaded with mail, passengers, and supplies over well beaten sky routes is a pleasantly dull routine compared with last year's combat missions.
explanation: This sentence advances an evaluative comparison that implies a conclusion: courier missions are uneventful and less intense than combat missions. The cues are the comparative framing “compared with last year's combat missions,” the descriptor “pleasantly dull,” and reference to “well beaten sky routes,” which functions as an implicit premise for reduced risk/excitement. Although no explicit “because” is used, the contrast and evaluative language imply the claim.
main_claim: Courier missions are safe and uneventful in contrast to last year's combat missions.

argument_text: Today it's a job and not an adventure. But it's an important job and we like it, we like it, we like it!
explanation: This passage argues that despite lacking the excitement of “adventure,” the courier work has significance and is satisfying. The concessive structure (“not an adventure”/“But it's an important job”) and emphatic repetition (“we like it”) imply a defense of the job’s value. The premises are implied by earlier context (carrying mail, passengers, supplies), rather than stated here.
main_claim: Even though courier flying is not adventurous, it is important and satisfying work.

argument_text: At the flight line Captain Edward Maykut briefs Pung and Radio Operator Jim Panarisi (left) on the weather conditions enroute and at destination. The briefing is short, but vital to the success of the flight.
explanation: This provides a reasoned claim: despite the briefing's brevity, it is essential for mission success. The first sentence supplies the content of the briefing (weather conditions), and the second asserts its importance using a concessive “short, but vital,” forming an explicit argument for the necessity of the briefing.
main_claim: The weather briefing, though brief, is essential to the flight’s success.

argument_text: After breakfast, Pung (center) and Co-pilot F/O Martin Haber (right) climb onto the crowded bus for the flight line. You can see note of cheerfulness on their faces as the morning limps on.
explanation: This suggests a claim about morale: despite an early, dragging morning and crowded transport, the crew remains cheerful. The evaluative observation (“note of cheerfulness”) and contrastive temporal framing (“as the morning limps on”) imply the conclusion without stating it as an argument with explicit premises.
main_claim: The crew maintains good morale even during a tiring early-morning routine.

argument_text: In the course of the program, Colonel Robert K. Martin spoke, emphasizing the values and need of the AES.
explanation: This reports that Col. Martin emphasized “the values and need” of the AES, which functions as an evaluative and normative claim that the station is valuable and necessary. Although the specific premises are not quoted, the phrasing signals advocacy, implying reasons were presented to justify AES’s value/necessity. The argument is implicit because the supporting reasons are not stated in the text; only the conclusional stance is conveyed.
main_claim: The American Expeditionary Station is valuable and needed.

argument_text: Congratulatory messages were received by the station from many persons along with bouquets of flowers from the Red Cross and the 55th Station Hospital, and an anniversary cake from Mess Sgt. John Golden. After the broadcast, the cake was cut by Col Martin and a party followed for the large studio audience.
explanation: The listing of congratulations, gifts, and a celebratory party serves as social proof, implying broad approval and esteem for the station. This framing suggests the station merits celebration and holds community value. The argument is implicit because the text does not explicitly state the evaluative claim; it relies on the evidence of widespread congratulations and institutional participation to imply the conclusion.
main_claim: The American Expeditionary Station is widely valued and deserving of celebration.

argument_text: The breakdown was the final result of a general lack of overhaul and repair that the equipment has long needed.
explanation: This is a causal argument: it asserts that the cause of the breakdown (conclusion) was the long-standing lack of overhaul and repair (premise). The wording “final result of” explicitly links cause and effect.
main_claim: The ice plant broke down because it had long lacked needed overhaul and repair.

argument_text: This job has now been done, and little further trouble with the machinery is anticipated.
explanation: This presents a reasoned forecast: since the needed overhaul/repair has now been completed (premise), the author concludes that little further trouble is expected (conclusion). The conjunction “and” signals the inference from completed work to expected reliability.
main_claim: Because the overhaul/repair has been completed, the machinery is expected to have little further trouble.

argument_text: The military ice plant on the Corso Garibaldi, out of commission for the past month, will be back in operation this week, stated Cpl. Allen Lanier, noncom in charge.
explanation: This uses an appeal to authority: the prediction that the plant will resume operation is supported implicitly by citing the responsible official as the source. The warrant is that the noncom in charge is a credible authority on the plant’s status, so his statement justifies believing the claim.
main_claim: The plant will resume operation this week, as evidenced by the responsible official’s statement.

argument_text: When ice-making is resumed, the plant will produce more than 15,000 pounds of ice every day, which will be distributed to mess halls, meat storehouses, and other military establishments that need ice.
explanation: This implies a normative justification for resuming operations: since many military establishments “need ice,” and the plant will produce and distribute large quantities daily, restarting is beneficial/necessary. The need and planned distribution function as premises supporting the implied conclusion about the value or appropriateness of resuming.
main_claim: Resuming ice-making is warranted because it will supply needed ice to essential military facilities.

argument_text: "The presence of large numbers of bicycles, both civilian and military, and ridden, led, and driven animals on the roads in this theater presents," declared Captain Rollins, "a serious traffic hazard and necessitates special precautions. In order to prevent accidents and display proper road courtesies in the presence of such hazards, drivers of military vehicles must exercise such precautions as the reduction of speed and the yielding of the right of way to slower moving traffic, unless otherwise directed by traffic control personnel."
explanation: This passage states premises (there are many bicycles and animals on roads, creating a serious traffic hazard) and draws a normative conclusion (drivers must take special precautions: reduce speed, yield right of way). The causal and necessity language (“presents a serious traffic hazard and necessitates,” “In order to prevent accidents”) explicitly links the premises to the prescribed actions.
main_claim: Drivers of military vehicles must reduce speed and yield to slower traffic due to the hazardous presence of bicycles and animals, in order to prevent accidents.

argument_text: In city limits, no vehicle should exceed the 20 miles per hour speed limit.
explanation: This is a prescriptive claim without an explicit reason in the sentence. Within the article’s context (“to prevent accidents and ensure safe driving” and the preceding hazard rationale), it implies that limiting speed in the city is necessary for safety. The normative “should” signals an ought-claim supported implicitly by the safety rationale previously given.
main_claim: Vehicles ought not exceed 20 mph within city limits to promote safety.

argument_text: Beyond the city limits, the speed limits for all types of vehicles are as follows: Sedans, jeeps, command cars, and motorcycles, 40 mph; with trailers, 35 mph. Cargo trucks, 35 mph. Cargo trucks in excess of two and a half tons, 25 mph.
explanation: These prescriptive speed limits are presented without an explicit reason in the same passage. Given the article’s stated goal of accident prevention and the identified traffic hazards, the implied argument is that adhering to these specific limits is required to ensure safe driving under local conditions. The list functions as policy prescriptions justified implicitly by safety considerations.
main_claim: Drivers should adhere to the specified speed limits outside city limits to ensure safety.

argument_text: All drivers will obey all traffic signals and personnel engaged in traffic control duties regardless of nationality. The above personnel will be accorded the same respect and obedience as United States Military Police. Violation of their signals or directions will be reported to the Provost Marshall.
explanation: This prescribes obedience to traffic authorities “regardless of nationality,” implying a defense against potential noncompliance toward non-U.S. personnel. The assertion of equivalence to U.S. MPs and the threat of reporting to the Provost Marshal function as implicit premises (authority and sanction) supporting the conclusion that drivers must obey these personnel and signals.
main_claim: Drivers must obey traffic signals and traffic-control personnel regardless of nationality, as they have authority equivalent to U.S. MPs and violations will be penalized.

argument_text: Convoys may continue through intersections against red light stop signals only when employing road guards to stop cross traffic.
explanation: This permits an exception (running red lights) only under a condition (use of road guards to stop cross traffic). The implied rationale is safety: the presence of road guards mitigates the risk of collisions. The conditional restriction serves as an implicit argument that safety considerations justify and limit the exception.
main_claim: Convoys may proceed through red lights only if road guards are used to halt cross traffic for safety.

argument_text: The shortage of meat, which has been apparent in FAAB mess halls during the past month, indicated a situation typical of the entire theater during that period
explanation: This sentence presents an inferential claim: from the observed shortage in FAAB mess halls (premise), it concludes that the situation was typical of the entire theater (conclusion). The verb “indicated” functions as an explicit inferential marker linking premise to conclusion.
main_claim: The local shortage in FAAB mess halls shows that the entire theater was experiencing a similar shortage during that period.

argument_text: The shortage of meat, which has been apparent in FAAB mess halls during the past month, indicated a situation typical of the entire theater during that period and developed as a result of an unexpected delay in shipment from the United States.
explanation: This sentence makes a causal attribution: it asserts that the shortage developed because of an unexpected shipment delay from the United States. The phrase “developed as a result of” is an explicit causal connector linking cause (delayed shipment) to effect (meat shortage).
main_claim: The meat shortage occurred because shipments from the United States were unexpectedly delayed.

argument_text: Now that the meat has arrived, FAAB menus in the immediate future will include the improved fare.
explanation: This provides a premise (the meat has arrived) and a conclusion (menus will include improved fare) connected by the causal/conditional phrase “Now that,” which explicitly signals that the arrival of meat justifies the conclusion about improved menus.
main_claim: Because the meat has now arrived, FAAB menus will soon feature improved fare.

argument_text: Colonel Martin added that further interruptions of fresh meat delivery to this theater are not expected.
explanation: This advances a prediction/assurance without stated evidence, relying implicitly on Colonel Martin’s authority and presumed access to logistical information as the reason to accept the claim. The appeal to authority functions as the underlying warrant for the conclusion.
main_claim: There will likely be no further interruptions in fresh meat delivery to this theater.

argument_text: Oh, we carry on all communications from air to ground. Like giving out weather information, contacting with planes to get their ETAs and distress signals, if there are any. In fact, we used to do everything except take care of the tower on the field, and now we're taking that over. Besides that, we run the homing beacon—that's in this building—and the range station, which is about three miles past Foggia Main. You see, it's not so much.
explanation: The speaker lists a set of routine duties (premises) and then concludes evaluatively, "You see, it's not so much." The evaluative conclusion is supported by the preceding description of tasks as manageable and ordinary, implying that the station's work is not extensive or remarkable. The argument is implicit because the reasoning from the list of tasks to the evaluative judgment is suggested rather than formally stated.
main_claim: The ACS station’s workload and responsibilities are not extensive or remarkable.

argument_text: They're called ILA trucks. If a plane is in the soup, they can bring him right down on the runway by use of the special type of beam these trucks send out. The pilots refer to it as a runway localizer. They're not used very often, but you know they can be plenty important when they are needed.
explanation: The claim that ILA trucks are "plenty important when they are needed" is directly supported by the stated capability to guide a plane down in poor conditions ("in the soup"). The concessive structure ("not used very often, but...") explicitly contrasts infrequency with critical utility, yielding a clear premise-to-conclusion argument.
main_claim: ILA trucks are important despite being infrequently used because they can safely guide planes to the runway in difficult conditions.

argument_text: Several times when bombing objectives in the mountains near Bari, Chacksfield related, three ILA trucks spaced at determined intervals projected beams forward into the enemy line so that the three beams crossed at the known position of the target. Making use of his localizer equipment, the pilot would fly until he received a solid tone, indicating the crossing of the three projected beams. Then, after flying a short time on the same heading, he would salvo his bombs. "From what we heard," Chacksfield went on, "they got good results with the system."
explanation: The concluding assertion—"they got good results with the system"—is presented with an evidential qualifier ("From what we heard") and comes after a step-by-step description of how the system worked. The explicit claim of effectiveness is supported by reported outcomes and by the preceding procedural detail, functioning as premises for the conclusion that the method was effective.
main_claim: The ILA beam-crossing system for target location produced good results in wartime operations.

argument_text: Now that the silence of peace has come to the ACS station, it has settled back to its functional duties of running the communications of Foggia's airfield.
explanation: The sentence implies a causal reasoning: because peace has arrived, the station has reverted to routine functions. The temporal-causal cue "Now that" signals a premise (peace) leading to a conclusion (return to basic communications duties), making the argument implicit.
main_claim: With the arrival of peace, the ACS station has returned to routine communications duties.

argument_text: It was Crandall Chacksfield from the San Bernardino Valley, who has spent a year and a half in the Foggia Valley. He could not imagine anything to be interesting about the ACS station in which he has worked during that time.
explanation: The juxtaposition of Chacksfield’s extended experience at the station (premise) with his judgment that nothing about it is interesting (conclusion) suggests an argument from experiential authority: because he has worked there for a long time, his assessment of its lack of interesting aspects carries weight. The inference is implied rather than explicitly drawn.
main_claim: The ACS station is uninteresting, as judged by someone with long experience there.

argument_text: Captain Dout pointed out the "Siemens" label on his X-ray machine. "Much of this kind of X-ray equipment was exported to America before the war. It is quite good." Lt. Gwartney, an American hospital official attached to the German unit, agreed that it was good equipment.
explanation: The passage advances an evaluative claim that the X-ray equipment is good. The reasoning is implied: citing the Siemens brand and the fact that such equipment was exported to America functions as credibility/quality cues, followed by the evaluation “It is quite good,” and corroborated by an American official’s agreement. The premises (brand reputation, export to the U.S., expert agreement) support the conclusion without an explicit logical connector.
main_claim: The German-made X-ray equipment used in the hospital is of good quality.

argument_text: "And we have to keep getting more and more because the hospital keeps getting bigger."
explanation: This sentence explicitly provides a reason (“because the hospital keeps getting bigger”) for the conclusion/obligation (“we have to keep getting more and more” equipment or supplies). Clear causal structure with “because.”
main_claim: The hospital must continually acquire more equipment due to its ongoing expansion.

argument_text: "You see, we raised the capacity of the hospital because now we have to service 10,000 prisoners-of-war, and we figure on 2 1/4% being in the hospital on an average."
explanation: This is a direct justification of an action (raising capacity) with two reasons: the need to serve 10,000 POWs and an expected inpatient rate of 2.25%. The “because” signals the premises-supporting-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The hospital’s capacity was increased to accommodate 10,000 POWs given an anticipated 2.25% hospitalization rate.

argument_text: We looked at the living quarters of the enlisted men attached to the field hospital unit. Making the best of living in tents, the men have found time to decorate their quarters with wood carvings, pictures, and the like. In one tent, we saw a well-done wooden booth, which could seat six men. The wood had been burnt to bring out the natural design of the grain, and above the seats were hung intricate wood carvings of antlers set in rustic plaques. The tents were, on the whole, neat and plain. And the patients seemed content, and perhaps a bit surprised, at the adequate facilities allowed them by the Americans.
explanation: The descriptive details (decorations, neatness, amenities) serve as evidence leading to the evaluative conclusion that the facilities are adequate and make patients content. The phrase “adequate facilities allowed them by the Americans” expresses the conclusion, while the preceding observations function as unstated premises; the inferential link is implied rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: The Americans are providing adequate facilities that leave POW patients content.

argument_text: "It was a happy day for me," Tinkin said, "because I worked for your airfields afterward as a mechanic."
explanation: This quote states a conclusion (“It was a happy day for me”) and gives a causal reason introduced by “because” (he subsequently worked for American airfields as a mechanic), asserting a positive evaluation of his capture day due to the beneficial outcome.
main_claim: Tinkin views the day of his capture positively because it led to post-capture work at American airfields.

argument_text: In honor of the late Chief Justice Stone, flags will be placed at half-mast until 24 May.
explanation: This sentence presents a reason (“In honor of the late Chief Justice Stone”) leading to a policy action (“flags will be placed at half-mast until 24 May”), forming a clear premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Flags will be placed at half-mast until 24 May to honor the late Chief Justice Stone.

argument_text: Because of the shortage of airplane seat cushions, all such cushions will be turned into the Flight Section Aircraft Engineering Officer or the Base S-3 office.
explanation: This sentence uses a causal connector (“Because of the shortage”) to justify the directive (“all such cushions will be turned in”), explicitly linking premise to conclusion.
main_claim: All airplane seat cushions must be turned in due to a shortage.

argument_text: Officers are reminded that they have been failing to call their respective Orderly Rooms prior to 0800 hours and having their names placed on the Sick Book. In the future, officers not having their names entered on the Sick Book by their Orderly Rooms will not receive medical attention.
explanation: The passage states a pattern of noncompliance and a consequence (no medical attention). While it announces a policy, it implicitly argues that officers ought to call their Orderly Rooms before 0800 to be placed on the Sick Book, with the consequence serving as the practical reason.
main_claim: Officers should ensure their names are placed on the Sick Book by calling their Orderly Rooms before 0800 if they want to receive medical attention.

argument_text: All vehicles of this command leaving this area will have a regulation top, or the top will be removed. Under Peninsular Base Section orders, all vehicles with homemade tops will be impounded.
explanation: The text issues rules and sanctions (removal/impoundment), which implicitly argue that personnel should not use homemade tops and should use regulation tops to avoid these penalties; the enforcement functions as the reason for compliance.
main_claim: Personnel should avoid homemade vehicle tops and use regulation tops to prevent removal or impoundment.

argument_text: All non-organization firearms and souvenirs such as brass knuckles and knives will be collected and kept under lock in company and similar storerooms. Court martial will be mandatory for illegal possession of carrying of arms while not on duty.
explanation: The collection requirement and the mandatory court-martial sanction serve as reasons that implicitly argue personnel should not illegally possess or carry non-organization weapons and should turn such items in for secure storage.
main_claim: Personnel should not illegally possess or carry non-organization firearms and related weapons and must turn them in for secure storage to avoid court martial.

argument_text: Along with the warm blossoming of spring flowers, amateur photographers, now so numerous in Foggia, cast off their winter lethargy and emerge blinking into the sunshine, vibrant with creative ardor! To meet this fine ambition, a representative of the FAAB Photo Lab, S/Sgt. James Collier, is now engaged in the organization of photography clubs.
explanation: The second sentence gives a reason-for-action structure (“To meet this fine ambition”), using the first sentence as the motivating premise (many eager amateurs). The conclusion is that organizing photography clubs is the appropriate response to the amateurs’ ambition.
main_claim: Organizing photography clubs is the right step to meet the ambitions of numerous, eager amateur photographers in Foggia.

argument_text: In order to start proceedings, Sgt. Collier recommends the posting of a roster on the bulletin board for all interested men to sign. Then, with men to do some work, construction of the darkroom is easy. Supplies have a way of appearing.
explanation: This is a recommendation with explicit supporting reasons: posting a roster yields volunteers, which makes darkroom construction easy, and supplies will show up. The premises directly support the advised action.
main_claim: Units should post a sign-up roster to launch clubs because volunteers will make darkroom construction easy and supplies will come together.

argument_text: The 955th club has managed to get enough developer, hypo, and printing paper for a start. At present that is what is recommended for the other clubs.
explanation: The first sentence provides evidence (what the 955th obtained to get started), and the second draws a recommendation from it for others. The precedent is used as a reason for the policy.
main_claim: Other clubs should start with developer, hypo, and printing paper as their initial supplies.

argument_text: Competitions and salons, the medium of expression for the serious amateur, will be emphasized, Sgt. Collier stated.
