explanation: This passage advances a clear claim that mail is "a nice thing to get," and supports it with a reason: it signals that "somebody is thinking about you." The structure is premise (mail indicates someone is thinking of you) leading to conclusion (therefore, mail is nice).
main_claim: Mail is pleasant to receive because it shows that someone is thinking about you.

argument_text: The truth of the matter is that we haven't got the 'guts' to handle a letter like that. If we did, we would say that every time we sit down to prepare the church schedule for next week, a guy comes along and tells you about this fellow and that fellow selling coffee, selling gasoline, selling uniforms, selling everything that doesn't belong to him. So we say, what the hell - put in the movie schedule instead.
explanation: This offers reasons for avoiding church notices: recurring reports of wrongdoing drain resolve, leading them to substitute a movie schedule. The conclusion (they avoid/replace the church schedule) is implied by the causal narrative rather than formally stated as “therefore.” The evaluative confession of lacking “guts” and the causal “every time… so we say” cue an implicit argument.
main_claim: We avoid printing the church schedule because repeated reports of corruption make us choose the easier alternative.

argument_text: Sunday comes along, and we get that religious fervor going again, and we set up the church schedule for next week. In comes a character complaining that "...she is a nice stupid girl who believes in marriage and all her family are stupid because they won't let me at her alone." There goes that church schedule in the basket again!
explanation: This narrates a cause-effect pattern: when they prepare a church schedule, someone’s complaint revealing sexual opportunism prompts them to discard it. The implied claim is that such displays of immorality/hypocrisy discourage or undermine printing religious content. The conclusion is shown by action (“in the basket again!”) rather than argued explicitly.
main_claim: Encounters with others’ sexual cynicism or predation lead us to drop the church schedule.

argument_text: So what do we do? We go down to chat with the Chaplain for a couple of hours. It's like penicillin. It makes you feel new again.
explanation: Through analogy (“like penicillin”) and outcome (“makes you feel new again”), the passage argues that talking with the Chaplain is restorative/beneficial. The therapeutic claim is implied by evaluative comparison rather than a formal premise-conclusion statement.
main_claim: Talking with the Chaplain is therapeutically restorative.

argument_text: This time we are going to put that church schedule in because there are a lot of other guys who ought to listen to that man.
explanation: This is a direct justification: the action (include the church schedule) is supported by a normative reason (many others ought to hear the Chaplain). It follows a clear “do X because Y” structure.
main_claim: We should include the church schedule because many people ought to hear the Chaplain.

argument_text: With renewed vigor, out we go strolling down towards Piazza Settembre, when one of those little things they call 'jeeps,' buzzes by us at a rate of 1000 miles an hour, jerks back to where we are, trying to move out of the place where we were frozen, and an apologetic voice belonging to one of the members of humanity that President Truman said paid 25 cents at a corner drugstore to get his license whispers, "I am really sorry, I thought that you were a civilian when I spotted you crossing the street a mile back." "Brotherly love!"
explanation: The sarcastic “Brotherly love!” after recounting reckless behavior and a contemptuous apology implies a criticism: some servicemen treat perceived civilians with arrogance and a lack of fraternity. The argument is conveyed through irony and contrast between supposed values and observed behavior.
main_claim: Some military drivers display unbrotherly, contemptuous behavior toward those they take to be civilians.

argument_text: And yet, there is that letter staring you in the face. Church schedule, religious discussion. What are you going to do about it? You take the easy way out. You don't write about that Paris affair, and you don't print the church schedule. In this way, you are still one of the 'broad-minded boys,' one of the fence sitters, one of the mob who always take the easy way out.
explanation: This passage argues evaluatively that choosing to publish neither the sensational Paris story nor the church schedule constitutes moral evasion (“the easy way out”) and aligns one with “fence sitters.” The reasoning is implicit: the described choice leads to a negative categorization, implying that such avoidance is cowardly or conformist.
main_claim: Avoiding both controversial religion and sensational stories is an evasive, fence-sitting “easy way out.”

argument_text: It's so much easier to write about the nice things. In that way, we don't have to worry about our conscience. My god, man, you only live once. Get in step, let the next guy print that church schedule!
explanation: Using rhetorical ease, self-justification, and “you only live once,” the passage argues for letting others handle religious content and sticking to “nice things.” The exhortation “Get in step” suggests conformity as a reason. The tone is likely ironic, implying criticism of this rationale even as it states it.
main_claim: We should sidestep moral difficulty by writing only pleasant pieces and leaving the church schedule to someone else.

argument_text: The tire racket is still one of large proportion in Italy, and Foggia comes in for its share. We interviewed CID Agent Harry Manicas this week to get some information about this activity. In both the MP and CID offices, there are large stocks of recovered stolen tires awaiting return to the proper depots—mutilated tires, revulcanized tires, tires in all stages of attempted disguise. At CID headquarters, in a large bin marked "evidence," are kits of tire-disguising tools. There are curved plates with the letters "Pirelli" and "Michelin" cut into them which are used for molds, and crude knives used to cut new treads into military tires. To combat these well-organized rings, the CID and Military Police are constantly on the lookout.
explanation: This passage presents evidence (large stocks of recovered stolen tires; tools for disguising tires) to support two linked conclusions: that the tire racket is large and organized, and that continuous vigilance by CID/MPs is warranted. The prescriptive statement about being “constantly on the lookout” is justified by the preceding evidence of organized criminal activity; the argumentative connection is implied rather than signposted.
main_claim: The tire racket in Italy is large and organized, which justifies CID and MP constant vigilance.

argument_text: Spotting a spurious tire is much like spotting a counterfeit piece of paper money. There is always evidence of the crude job of burning in new trade names, or the scraped places where old names have been cut off; phony treads have sharp lines from the knife instead of molded grooves from vulcanization. And, very often, there is no attempt to cover up military treads.
explanation: This passage advances the claim that altered tires are identifiable and supports it with specific indicators (burned-in names, scraped areas, knife-cut treads, uncovered military treads). The analogy to counterfeit money and the listing of telltale signs provide explicit reasons for the conclusion.
main_claim: Altered or spurious tires can be reliably detected because they show telltale signs.

argument_text: There have been certain 'respites' ordered during which time the CID and MPs did not recover tires. Civilians were notified that they must denounce all their doubtful tires and get permits during that time. After the period was over, the two agencies went back to work again, and again the steady trickle of illegal and permitless ones began. "They are being stolen all the time," explains Manicas.
explanation: The sequence of policy (respites for denouncing/permits), observed outcomes (resumption of a steady trickle of illegal tires), and the concluding assertion by Manicas imply the conclusion that ongoing theft is persistent despite measures. The argument is inferential: the continued appearance of illegal tires after an amnesty indicates continual theft.
main_claim: Tire theft persists continuously despite amnesty periods for legalizing doubtful tires.

argument_text: In his speech, Mr. Saragat discussed the question of the institutional form of government and declared that only a parliamentary and democratic republic can save Italy.
explanation: This passage advances a clear stance on Italy's institutional future, asserting exclusivity (“only”) and a causal/evaluative claim (“can save Italy”) without providing explicit supporting premises in the text. The lack of articulated reasons makes the argumentative structure implicit, inferred from the normative language and exclusion of alternatives.
main_claim: Only a parliamentary and democratic republic can save Italy.

argument_text: The party is composed of three groups: the right wing of clericals who favor the monarchy and the establishment of the Catholic religion as the state religion; the center group, the majority, which favors a democracy and a republic, and also favors the maintenance of the Concordat between Church and State; and the left wing, Christian Socialists or Christian Communists, who remain in the party favoring the religious program of one and the economic program of the other parties. The party favors a program of collectivism and industrial reform. They desire that representatives of labor be placed in the administrative council of industries and propose that workers share in industrial utilities and prepare for future joint-property ownership. The party is extremely flexible, consistently receiving strong support from the Catholic Church.
explanation: The evaluative conclusion that the party is "extremely flexible" is supported by premises describing its ideological breadth (three wings with divergent positions) and its range of policy proposals. The structure implies: because it contains diverse factions and adaptable policies, therefore it is flexible. The language is not framed as "therefore," making the reasoning implicit.
main_claim: The Christian Democratic Party is extremely flexible.

argument_text: Communist Party is the strongest political organization in Italy. It maintains constant control over members with no factions in the group. They draw their total support from the factory workers and farm laborers.
explanation: The main claim that it is the strongest is presented alongside reasons: organizational discipline (no factions, constant control) and a broad working-class support base. The causal/justificatory link is implied rather than explicitly stated with connectives.
main_claim: The Communist Party is the strongest political organization in Italy.

argument_text: During the Fascist regime, they were more active than other parties in the underground fight and hence they had more men and women sent to prison and places of confinement than the others.
explanation: This sentence uses "hence" to explicitly draw a conclusion from a premise: greater underground activity led to more imprisonments.
main_claim: Because they were more active in the anti-Fascist underground, Communists had more members imprisoned than other parties.

argument_text: Embarrassed by Russia's demand for Trieste for Jugoslavia as reparations for Russia, they advocate Trieste for Italy.
explanation: This is a direct causal attribution: the cause (embarrassment over Russia's demand) is given as the reason for the stance (advocating Trieste for Italy).
main_claim: The Communists advocate Trieste for Italy because of embarrassment over Russia’s demand for Trieste for Jugoslavia.

argument_text: Policy is not known due to Russian favoritism towards Jugoslavia and France, which seek reparations from Italy.
explanation: The sentence states a conclusion (policy is not known) and provides an explicit cause ("due to" Russian favoritism toward Jugoslavia and France that seek reparations).
main_claim: The Communist policy is unclear because Russia favors Jugoslavia and France, which are seeking reparations from Italy.

argument_text: Weakness lies in the different factions, which constantly split their strength.
explanation: This explicitly presents a claim about the party’s weakness and gives the reason: internal factions that divide strength.
main_claim: The Socialist Party’s weakness is caused by internal factions that split its strength.

argument_text: Strength lies in the fact that the group is composed of landowners, industrialists, bankers, and other large entrepreneurs.
explanation: This gives a conclusion about the party’s strength and an explicit reason: its composition of powerful socioeconomic groups.
main_claim: The National Democratic Union’s strength comes from its composition of elites like landowners, industrialists, bankers, and large entrepreneurs.

argument_text: It is considered the most dangerous movement in Italy today due to continued clashes between Qualunquists and members of the left parties.
explanation: This sentence asserts a conclusion (most dangerous movement) and provides a stated reason ("due to" the continued clashes).
main_claim: The Uomo Qualunque movement is the most dangerous in Italy because of ongoing clashes with leftist parties.

argument_text: They favor the inauguration of an Administrative State where technically trained men are elected without political affiliation to serve the general well-being of the masses, a program which political analysts compare with the Fascist doctrine which "rejects the doctrine of popular sovereignty for state sovereignty. For government by the whole people, it substitutes government by the chosen few, who are asserted to be capable of ignoring their own private interests in favor of the higher demands of society."
explanation: The juxtaposition of the party's "Administrative State" program with analysts’ comparison to Fascist doctrine (quoted as rejecting popular sovereignty in favor of rule by a chosen few) implies a critical conclusion: the program aligns with anti-democratic, Fascist-like principles. The evaluative stance is implied through comparison rather than an explicit "therefore" statement.
main_claim: The Uomo Qualunque program aligns with anti-democratic Fascist doctrine that substitutes elite rule for popular sovereignty.

argument_text: Republican Party derives its origin from Giuseppe Mazzini, who founded the Republican Party in 1828 in order to unite the different states of Italy.
explanation: This provides a reason for Mazzini’s founding of the party ("in order to unite the different states of Italy"), explicitly linking motive to action.
main_claim: Mazzini founded the Republican Party in 1828 to unite Italy’s different states.

argument_text: Thomas S. Moore, 803 MP's - "Don't know, but it's funny how you can pick out the American wives in the streets of Foggia. They really look good, all the way up."
explanation: The speaker implies that American wives are identifiable in Foggia because of their superior appearance. The evaluative phrase "They really look good, all the way up" functions as the reason that supports the conclusion that one can "pick out" American wives. The argument is implied via evaluative language and causal insinuation without an explicit premise-conclusion marker.
main_claim: American wives in Foggia are easily identifiable because they look especially good.

argument_text: Sgt. Clarence E. Seely, 529 Hdq. & Base Sqdn. - "Just got back from Leghorn, where I attended Cook's and Baker's school. In a way, I hated to come back and in a way, I didn't. The living quarters there are lousy with eighteen men to a six-man tent."
explanation: He advances a negative assessment of Leghorn's living conditions, offering overcrowding ("eighteen men to a six-man tent") as the reason. This supports why he "didn't" hate to return. The causal connection is implied; the overcrowding is presented as evidence for the conclusion that living quarters there are lousy and thus a reason not to miss it.
main_claim: Leghorn’s living quarters are bad, as shown by the severe overcrowding.

argument_text: T/5 Arthur S. Baron, 803 MP's - "Watching the Reds play baseball reminds me of the corpses I've seen dead for two years that look better than those guys."
explanation: Through hyperbolic negative comparison to corpses, he implies the team looks or performs terribly. The rhetorical device suggests a conclusion (the Reds are very bad) without explicit premises; the comparison functions as evidence meant to persuade.
main_claim: The Reds look or play extremely poorly.

argument_text: Lt. Wesley Williams, Op. Unit Personnel - "This place has got the States beat as far as recreation goes, with all these clubs around and the set-up at Siponto."
explanation: He makes a comparative claim ("has got the States beat") and provides explicit reasons ("with all these clubs... and the set-up at Siponto"). The premises directly support the conclusion about superior recreation.
main_claim: Foggia offers better recreation than the States because of the numerous clubs and the setup at Siponto.

argument_text: Pfc. Conrad O. Smith, Billeting - "I'll go thirsty at the beach before I pay twice as much for a Coke."
explanation: He asserts a decision rule implying a value judgment: paying double for a Coke is not worth it. The contrast ("go thirsty... before I pay") functions as an implicit argument that one ought to refuse overpriced goods.
main_claim: It is not worth paying double for a Coke at the beach, so one should refuse to buy it even if it means going thirsty.

argument_text: SO THE PEOPLE MAY KNOW: ON WHAT BASIS ARE THE OFFICERS AND ENLISTED MEN'S CLUBS BEING RUN? IS IT THE PURPOSE OF THE CLUBS TO GIVE EACH INDIVIDUAL THE MAXIMUM OF ENTERTAINMENT AND THE BEST QUALITY IN HIS DRINKS, OR IS THE INTENTION OF THESE CLUBS TO OPERATE ON THE PROFIT SYSTEM TO MAKE AN EARNING ON EACH INDIVIDUAL SOLDIER?
explanation: These are rhetorical questions that frame two contrasting purposes for the clubs, implying that the latter (profit-seeking) is occurring. The evaluative contrast and the framing “SO THE PEOPLE MAY KNOW” signal a challenge to current practices, suggesting the main claim without stating it directly.
main_claim: The clubs are being run to make profit from individual soldiers rather than to maximize their entertainment and drink quality.

argument_text: Late comers to dinner at the Officers' club miss out on dessert, but this same commodity of food may be purchased for a nominal fee later in the evening at the Snack Bar. At certain Enlisted Men's Clubs, as much as five dollars profit is being made on a single loaf of bread. The soldier is charged thirty lire for a sandwich. Such a price is obtained on approximately fifteen sandwiches from a loaf of bread that originally cost the club EIGHT CENTS. The men at the bakery confirm our convictions, stating that, "Too much money is being paid by the G.I.'s for a bite to eat."
explanation: The passage provides concrete premises (pricing, cost of bread, calculation of profit, and corroboration from bakery workers) leading to the conclusion that G.I.s are overcharged and clubs make excessive profit on food items. The claim “as much as five dollars profit” and the corroborating quote make the argumentative structure explicit.
main_claim: The clubs are overcharging G.I.s for food and making excessive profits on items like sandwiches.

argument_text: Why was there no explanation offered in the sudden drop of the monthly beer rations? Surprising, that as much as sixteen cans of beer are allotted monthly at the corner P.X., and this while the month is young. The remainder of the G.I.'s favorite drink is obtainable at the squadron clubs, which in itself is doubtful, as there are nights when the clubs run a "NO BEER TONIGHT" sign. Who drinks these precious rations at a price higher than the P.X. sells them for? What did happen to the original case of twenty-four cans of beer?
explanation: The series of rhetorical questions, contrasts (PX allotment vs. club shortages), and insinuations about higher prices imply mismanagement or diversion of beer rations and a lack of transparency. The claim is suggested rather than directly asserted.
main_claim: Beer rations are being mishandled or diverted and sold at higher prices without transparency.

argument_text: In a few brief weeks, after a change of management and constant drawbacks, an Enlisted Men's club opened its doors to an ever-increasing turnout, but the fatal blight of monopoly hindered as well as destroyed all hopes of a fair enterprise. Working on the American exchange, a two dollar bar book may be purchased for four hundred and fifty lire. This puts a coke, the pause that refreshes and as far as we know the best-selling beverage, in the ten cent category or approximately twenty-two lire. An amount that doubles the price charged by any of the clubs in the town.
explanation: The passage explicitly claims that “the fatal blight of monopoly…destroyed all hopes of a fair enterprise,” and supports this with pricing evidence showing that a Coke costs double town prices under the club’s system. The premises (exchange rate, bar book price, resulting per-drink price) support the stated conclusion about monopoly harming fairness and inflating prices.
main_claim: Monopoly practices at the enlisted men’s club have undermined fair enterprise and led to inflated prices compared to town.

argument_text: Such information reaches our ears, yet it is taken to be understood that these clubs are running on a non-profit basis. This method may be fashionable elsewhere, but we desire to serve notice upon these establishments that it will not go in Foggia. If such WHEELS are to run their clubs in such a fashion, then we will force the issue in denouncing these various deeds.
explanation: The passage juxtaposes reports of profiteering with the claim of “non-profit” status, implying hypocrisy and unacceptability. The normative stance (“it will not go in Foggia”) and conditional threat to “denounce” indicate a prescriptive conclusion grounded in the implied premise that profit-seeking contradicts non-profit claims.
main_claim: The clubs’ profit-seeking practices, despite claims of non-profit status, are unacceptable in Foggia and will be publicly denounced if continued.

argument_text: Ah, yes, there's good news today because a bunch of swell guys are on their way home at last.
explanation: Uses a because-clause to justify the evaluative claim that there is “good news.” Premise: several men are going home. Conclusion: therefore, today’s news is good.
main_claim: Today’s news is good because several men are finally going home.

argument_text: Anita set the country on fire five and a half years ago when she made her debut with the Gene Krupa Band, and the fire hasn't gone out yet.
explanation: Evaluative metaphor (“set the country on fire”) and continuation (“hasn't gone out yet”) imply the claim that Anita O’Day remains highly impactful/relevant. The support is suggestive rather than structured; the language frames ongoing significance without explicit premises beyond the debut timing.
main_claim: Anita O’Day’s popularity and impact remain strong to the present.

argument_text: I was lucky enough to see Anita the first night she hit New York with the Gene Krupa Band. It was a great band—Sammy Danahue, Sammy Musiker, Milt Raskin, Roy Eldridge—and Anita, an unknown, unheralded, redhead, stole the show from all these great musicians. She sang blues, jump, teamed up with Roy for a few unforgettable numbers, and with tears in her eyes had to beg off because the Krupa Band didn't have any more arrangements with her singing. The Krupa Band at that time was very fine. Anita and Roy made it one of the greatest of all time. Even the notoriously un-hip public at that time took Anita to their hearts.
explanation: Presents observations (unknown singer stole the show; memorable performances; public acceptance) as premises leading to the explicit conclusion that Anita and Roy elevated the Krupa band to “one of the greatest of all time.”
main_claim: Anita O’Day and Roy Eldridge made the Krupa band one of the greatest bands of all time.

argument_text: All good things must come to an end, so Anita had to retire because of illness.
explanation: Uses a general maxim as a premise and links it with a specific cause (“because of illness”) to conclude that Anita’s retirement was a necessary end, signaled by “so.”
main_claim: Anita’s retirement was an inevitable end brought on by illness.

argument_text: For a while it was great and then something happened to Mr. Krupa. He began displaying some very poor taste, having Anita sing such inane stuff as "Chickory Chick" and "Jose Gonzales." Having his name mentioned in the lyrics of a song whenever it was possible and even a few times when it wasn't possible. Maybe it wasn't Gene's idea, but still, it was his band, and he could have put a stop to it if he wanted to.
explanation: Offers evidence of “poor taste” (examples of “inane” songs and self-referential lyrics) and explicitly assigns responsibility to Krupa (“his band… he could have put a stop to it”), supporting the conclusion that Krupa is at fault for low-quality choices.
main_claim: Gene Krupa is responsible for poor musical choices that reflected very poor taste.

argument_text: A lot of people are bemoaning the fact that Anita quit. Knowing how much Anita loves to sing, I don't think she wanted to quit. I think she was disgusted, fed up, maybe even tired of wandering about trying to find the right place, so she's cooking bacon and eggs.
explanation: Uses a stated premise about Anita’s love of singing and the prior context to infer she didn’t want to quit; concludes she left due to disgust/fatigue and is now housewifing (“so she’s cooking bacon and eggs”). The reasoning is explicit but inferential about motives.
main_claim: Anita O’Day didn’t truly want to quit music; she left out of disgust and fatigue with her situation.

argument_text: I hope she tires of that soon and comes back. We jazz fans need her, the greatest jazz vocalist of this age—Anita O'Day.
explanation: Presents a recommendation/ought-claim (that she should return) justified by a value claim (jazz fans “need her” because she’s the greatest vocalist of the age). The “need” functions as the premise; the conclusion (she should come back) is implied by the hope statement.
main_claim: Anita O’Day should return to music because jazz fans need her as the greatest vocalist of the age.

argument_text: Talking about greatest things of the age, every Thursday evening at 11:00, you can hear some of the most popular songs of all time done in new light symphonic arrangements by such wonderful musicians as Kostalanetz, Gould, Paige, and so on. It's "Reflections In Music," a relaxing half-hour of the finest in soft, lilting music with some choice words given by Roy Arndt. It's really a lovely show, so don't forget to tune in. Thursday evening at 11:00—Reflections In Music.
explanation: Provides evaluative premises (wonderful musicians; relaxing, finest soft music; lovely show) leading to the directive conclusion (“so don’t forget to tune in”). The “so” marks the inferential step.
main_claim: You should tune in to Reflections In Music on Thursday at 11:00 because it is a lovely, high-quality show by excellent musicians.

argument_text: At this surprise party, eighteen Rebel teammates feasted in an atmosphere that reflected gay youth without the intrusion of some silly, asinine military courtesy and old WHEELS dismal taboos. Here are friendships that are life-lasting and familiarity that does not breed contempt.
explanation: This passage evaluates military courtesies and “old WHEELS dismal taboos” as “silly” and “intrusive,” contrasting them with an atmosphere of genuine camaraderie. The evaluative language and contrast imply a normative claim that such formalities are undesirable and that their absence fosters better, lasting friendships. The argument is implicit because the conclusion (that dropping formal courtesies/taboos is preferable) is suggested rather than formally stated.
main_claim: Dispensing with formal military courtesies and taboos is better because it allows genuine, lasting camaraderie to flourish.

argument_text: Hit hard by the recent shipment of men to the states is the Special Service team. Among those who departed stateside: Mel Burgess, Lou Avila, Jesse Hannon, and Joe Accardo.
explanation: This asserts a causal relationship: the team was “hit hard” because key players shipped stateside. Listing the departed players functions as evidence supporting the claim that the team has been significantly weakened. The structure presents a clear cause (departures) leading to an effect (team adversely affected).
main_claim: The Special Service team has been significantly weakened by the recent departures of multiple players to the United States.

argument_text: ...and here we stop to consider whether the following throws were strikes or walks. Umpire Schwartz carried three men to bases on called walks. Poor visibility or threats could be blamed for the decision. Needless to say, the Reds gained four unearned runs and won the game, 9-8. Why is it that the teams in the American League must play in the absence of official umpires?
explanation: The passage links questionable ball/strike calls to conditions (“poor visibility or threats”) and the game’s outcome, implying that the result was unfairly affected by substandard officiating. The culminating rhetorical question about playing “in the absence of official umpires” suggests the conclusion that official umpires are needed to ensure fair play. The argument is implicit because the text uses insinuation, causal attribution, and a rhetorical question rather than a direct “therefore” claim.
main_claim: Teams should have official umpires because the lack of them leads to questionable calls that can unfairly decide games.

argument_text: In a free vote in which over eighty percent of eligible voters cast their ballots on June 2nd and 3rd to make their choice of a Republic or Monarchy, fifty-four percent of the people chose the Republic.
explanation: This sentence presents turnout and procedure (“free vote,” “over eighty percent”) as evidential support for the outcome, implying the conclusion that the result carries democratic legitimacy and reflects the popular will. The evaluative framing (“free vote” + high participation) functions as premises that suggest, without stating outright, the normative claim about legitimacy.
main_claim: The referendum result establishing the Republic is democratically legitimate and reflects the will of the people.

argument_text: Locally, however, the balloting was more in line with Southern Italy’s traditionally conservative vote. Foggia voted a 66% majority for the Monarchy, and the Christian Democrat Party got a 41% plurality.
explanation: The passage uses a contrast (“however”) and invokes “traditionally conservative” as a causal/explanatory frame, then provides local results as evidence. It implies the conclusion that Foggia’s outcomes are explained by Southern Italy’s conservative political tendencies.
main_claim: Foggia’s pro-Monarchy and Christian Democrat results reflect Southern Italy’s traditional conservatism.

argument_text: The close referendum vote (54% to 46%) came as a surprise to foreign observers who had gone out on a limb before election time to predict an overwhelming defeat for the House of Savoy. Stateside press opinion had been that the Monarchy had only a “slim chance”.
explanation: This asserts a conclusion (the close result was a “surprise”) supported by stated premises (observers and U.S. press predicted overwhelming defeat/slim chance for the Monarchy). The reasoning is explicit: when expectations predicted a landslide, a close outcome is surprising.
main_claim: The closeness of the referendum result was surprising given prior foreign and stateside predictions of a decisive Monarchy defeat.

argument_text: Christian Democrats votes apparently surprised the people when, after having decided by a large majority at the D. C. party convention to oppose the Monarchy, they shifted heavily to the King’s side.
explanation: The passage explicitly argues that the Christian Democrats’ voting behavior was surprising because it contradicted their prior formal decision to oppose the Monarchy; the premise (party decision) supports the conclusion (surprise at their shift).
main_claim: The Christian Democrats’ heavy shift to the King was surprising because it contradicted their convention decision to oppose the Monarchy.

argument_text: If leftist votes went Republican, then only about one third of the D. C. votes were for the Republic.
explanation: This is a conditional inference: given the premise (leftist votes went Republican), the conclusion follows about the proportion of Christian Democrat votes supporting the Republic. It presents a logical relationship rather than mere description.
main_claim: Assuming leftist voters supported the Republic, only about one third of Christian Democrat votes were for the Republic.

argument_text: Yesterday, after final results had been announced and the man on the street was hearing wild rumors that Sicily was thinking of secession because of the King’s defeat, four major parties entered a plea to the people to accept the results and maintain order.
explanation: The reported plea contains an implicit normative argument: people ought to accept the results and maintain order, with the situational context (final results, secession rumors after the King’s defeat) functioning as reasons. The “plea” and the juxtaposition with rumors signal a persuasive aim to prevent unrest.
main_claim: The public should accept the referendum results and keep order to avoid unrest amid secession rumors.

argument_text: Contradictory to a previous order by the Foggia Province Food Office which announced a food ration cut, it was revealed this week that the arrival of the freighter, USS Northwestern Victory, with a load of 8500 tons of UNNRA flour had averted the impending cut in ration and food crisis.
explanation: The passage asserts a clear causal relation: the arrival of a freighter with 8,500 tons of flour (premise) led to averting the ration cut and food crisis (conclusion). The verbs “had averted” and the specific causal setup tie the evidence directly to the outcome, forming an explicit argument.
main_claim: The arrival of a freighter carrying 8,500 tons of UNRRA flour averted the impending ration cut and food crisis.

argument_text: The foodcargo of the American ship was delivered almost totally to the Puglia province, which is the heel of the boot of Italy, and it is now expected that the food situation in this geographical area will be secure until the harvesting of the local wheat crop in a few weeks.
explanation: The sentence advances a prediction that the food situation will be secure (conclusion) and implicitly grounds it in two facts: the cargo’s delivery to Puglia and the near-term local wheat harvest (premises). Although no explicit “because” is used, the coordination (“and”) and temporal reference to the harvest imply the reasoning linking supply and impending local production to security.
main_claim: The food situation in Puglia will remain secure until the local wheat harvest in a few weeks.

argument_text: Colonel Martin further explained that the shift of command was necessitated by the fact that the Foggia Army Air Base consists of mainly a service group and had consequently lost its tactical statis.
explanation: This sentence provides a clear premise-conclusion structure: because the base is mainly a service group and has lost tactical status (premises), the shift of command was necessary (conclusion). The causal language “necessitated by the fact that” and “consequently” makes the argument explicit.
main_claim: The shift of command was necessary due to FAAB being mainly a service group and having lost tactical status.

argument_text: Colonel Martin commented that the reorganization will have little effect on the working and training schedules of the base. Flying schedules will also be continued on the same basis as they have in the past months, and whatever couriers have been running will be mainteined.
explanation: The first sentence advances the claim that the reorganization will have little effect. The following sentences provide supporting indications (continuation of flying schedules and couriers) that imply why effects will be minimal. The link between these facts and the conclusion is not stated with an explicit “therefore,” making the argumentative connection implicit.
main_claim: The reorganization will have little effect on base operations.

argument_text: An officer applying for a commission in the ground forces of the Regular Army has one chance in ten of being appointed. In the Air Forces he has one chance in fifteen, a cable received here from M’TOUSA Headquarters stated recently.
explanation: The passage presents comparative odds (1 in 10 vs. 1 in 15) without explicitly stating a conclusion. The contrast invites the inference that it is harder to get a commission in the Air Forces than in the ground forces. The evaluative conclusion is implied by the numerical comparison and the juxtaposition of the two sentences.
main_claim: It is more difficult to obtain a commission in the Air Forces than in the ground forces of the Regular Army.

argument_text: A total of 108,582 applications for the RA have been received by the WD. After rejections, and withdrawals, 97,550 remain. Of approximatly 23,000 applicants for Ground Arms, there are 4,000 vacancies, but 50,000 applicants for them. In technical and administrative forces there are 27,000 applications for 2,400 vacancies.
explanation: This sequence of statistics contrasts the number of applicants with the number of vacancies, using oppositional phrasing (“but”) to foreground scarcity. Although it does not explicitly state a conclusion, it strongly implies that applicants vastly outnumber available positions and that competition is intense. The implicit claim follows from the numerical disparities presented as premises.
main_claim: Applicants greatly outnumber available Regular Army vacancies, making selection highly competitive.

argument_text: It was added, however, that the change may effect redeployment, in that the group will be able to get rid of some surplus personnel, the Colonel said.
explanation: This passage contains a clear causal structure: the conclusion is that the change may affect redeployment, and the stated reason is that it enables the group to get rid of surplus personnel. The "in that" clause explicitly links premise to conclusion.
main_claim: The change may affect redeployment because it will allow the group to eliminate some surplus personnel.

argument_text: "We are trying also," Colonel Martin concluded, "to return home all Class V category officers as soon as possible."
explanation: This is a policy commitment/ought-claim implying that returning Class V officers home quickly is desirable and should be pursued. While no explicit premises are given, the recommendation/intent signals an underlying evaluative stance that such redeployment is warranted or prioritized.
main_claim: Class V category officers should be returned home as soon as possible.

argument_text: In this last big shipment, Foggia has been allotted a quota of 26 wives, which Miss Andren advised, will be filled without difficulty.
explanation: This advances a predictive claim (“will be filled without difficulty”) supported implicitly by an appeal to the authority/expertise of Miss Andren. The premise is the attribution to an informed source; the conclusion is that the quota will be met easily. The argument is implicit because the text does not state “therefore” or provide explicit reasoning beyond the source attribution, relying on the reader to infer that her advice is a sufficient basis for the prediction.
main_claim: The 26-wife quota for Foggia will be filled without difficulty.

argument_text: To combat the redeployment bugaboo, the OCCUPATOR must now call for new writers.
explanation: This sentence presents a reason (combat the redeployment “bugaboo,” i.e., problem) leading to a conclusion (the OCCUPATOR must call for new writers). The causal “To combat …” signals an explicit premise supporting the necessity claim.
main_claim: The OCCUPATOR needs to call for new writers because redeployment is causing a problem.

argument_text: The hours are not regular. They start at 0800 hours and stop when the work is finished. There probably will not be any Wednesdays and Saturday afternoons off, not to speak off all day Sunday. But a man who likes writing will find plenty of redeeming things about the job.
explanation: The series of statements sets up a concession (irregular, demanding hours) followed by a contrastive “But,” implying that despite these drawbacks the job is still worthwhile for someone who likes writing. The evaluative phrase “plenty of redeeming things” and the contrast cue “But” indicate an implicit persuasive conclusion: the job is worth pursuing if you enjoy writing.
main_claim: For someone who likes writing, the job is worthwhile despite the demanding hours and lack of time off.

argument_text: When the Second Bomb Group moved from the old airfield into Foggia last October and November, the officers were billeted in order of rank, and when the Group filled up the BOQ they discovered that the flight officers were left out in the cold, so to speak.
explanation: This presents a causal chain implying a claim: the policy of billeting by rank led to flight officers being excluded from BOQ accommodations. The evaluative idiom “left out in the cold” suggests unfair disadvantage, functioning as a premise-conclusion structure without stating “therefore.” The causality and evaluative framing indicate an argumentative stance rather than mere narration.
main_claim: Billeting officers strictly by rank resulted in flight officers being unfairly excluded from BOQ accommodations.

argument_text: Apologetically, the FO's were pushed into the Sarti Hotel, a place for transient officers, and only from time to time were their cries heard.
explanation: “Apologetically” signals that decision-makers recognized the move as suboptimal; labeling Sarti as “a place for transient officers” implies it was ill-suited for FO’s long-term housing, and “only from time to time were their cries heard” suggests neglect. These cues support the implicit claim that FO needs/complaints were largely disregarded and their billeting was inadequate.
main_claim: Flight officers were relegated to an unsuitable transient hotel and their complaints were largely ignored.

argument_text: In common misery, a sort of fraternity was established, an amiable group that never excluded friendly lieutenants.
explanation: The phrase “In common misery” functions as an explicit premise leading to the conclusion that a fraternity formed; it asserts a causal explanation that shared hardship produced camaraderie inclusive of friendly lieutenants.
main_claim: Shared hardship led to the formation of an amiable, inclusive fraternity.

argument_text: Thus, the hybrid rank, not commissioned officers and still forbidden to fraternize with enlisted men, made the Sarti their not-so-quiet castle.
explanation: “Thus” marks a conclusion drawn from stated premises (their hybrid rank and fraternization restrictions). The sentence argues that because of their in-between status and rules, they established the Sarti as their social base.
main_claim: Because of their hybrid status and fraternization rules, the flight officers made the Sarti their social stronghold.

argument_text: Transient officers marveled at the comraderie that existed at the Sarti, and USO troops who billeted there met the boys and left to spread the story of their parties and celebrations all over Europe.
explanation: The cited reactions (marveling; stories spread “all over Europe”) are evidence used to imply the conclusion that the Sarti’s camaraderie and social life were remarkable and notable beyond the local context. The claim is suggested through reported effects rather than directly stated.
main_claim: The Sarti’s camaraderie and parties were distinctive enough to gain broader renown.

argument_text: It was agreed that the organization would take the shape of a bar—a healthful place, they planned, in the open where one could drink and sun himself at the same time.
explanation: This sentence presents a claim—calling the bar “a healthful place”—and immediately provides a reason: it will be “in the open where one could drink and sun himself at the same time.” The causal rationale links openness and sunbathing to healthfulness, forming a premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The planned bar is a healthful place because it is outdoors and allows sunbathing while drinking.

argument_text: Visitors who came to gaze on the tranquillity of the fraternal brothers were received by a cool nod, much like that given by combat veterans to quartermaster soldiers.
explanation: The simile implies a normative stance about social hierarchy and justified aloofness: by likening the FO’s behavior to that of “combat veterans” toward “quartermaster soldiers,” the text suggests that the FO’s cool reception of visitors is appropriate or warranted due to perceived status differences. The argument is implied through evaluative comparison rather than stated directly.
main_claim: The FO’s aloof treatment of visitors is appropriate, akin to the deference gap between combat veterans and quartermaster soldiers.

argument_text: But more staid members of the USO - stage hands probably - and officials in Theater Specials Services do not smile at the tradition of the Red Eye. The Sarti Hotel's reputation is to them one of wild parties, trumpeteers playing through the windows all night, and a place where bad girls go worse.
explanation: This passage advances a negative evaluation of the Red Eye by citing its “reputation” for excess and immorality. The premises (wild parties, late-night trumpet playing, “bad girls go worse”) implicitly support the conclusion that staid officials disapprove of the Red Eye’s “tradition.” The evaluative language and reputational framing indicate an implied argument rather than an explicit conclusion statement.
main_claim: The Red Eye is a disreputable and morally problematic scene that staid USO and Special Services officials rightly disapprove of.

argument_text: Recently an embittered USO directive changed the Camps Shows' billets in Foggia to the more moral 55th Station Hospital, and they wondered about one of their girls who deserted the show in Leghorn to revisit one of the Sarti boys.
explanation: This sentence links a policy change (“changed the Camps Shows’ billets... to the more moral 55th Station Hospital”) with concerns about morality and a specific desertion incident. The implied reasoning is that moral risk and corrupting influence associated with the Sarti/Red Eye scene justify stricter, “more moral” accommodations. The causal and evaluative cues (“embittered,” “more moral,” mention of desertion) signal an implicit argument for the change.
main_claim: Concerns about morality and a desertion incident justified moving Camp Shows personnel to a “more moral” billet at the 55th Station Hospital.

argument_text: Red Eye's latest blow came when a number of their tribe was transferred to the 1898th Engineers, "to work", the boys say horrified.
explanation: Calling the transfer a “blow” and quoting “to work” with the boys “horrified” implies that being reassigned to work undermines the Red Eye lifestyle and is a punitive or harmful development. The evaluative framing and irony suggest the conclusion without stating it explicitly.
main_claim: The transfer of Red Eye regulars to the 1898th Engineers for actual work is a damaging setback to the Red Eye crowd’s way of life.

argument_text: The Red Eye is a sad place today. Over their cokes the FO's talk of the good old days, and as a member pours himself another drink, they say, without the former brotherliness, "Mark it on the books, Jack. You're going to have to pay for drinks from now on."
explanation: These observations support an evaluative conclusion that the Red Eye has declined in spirit and camaraderie. The premises (nostalgic talk of “good old days,” loss of “former brotherliness,” and instituting payment for drinks) imply deterioration, forming an implicit argument about current conditions.
main_claim: The Red Eye has lost its former camaraderie and generosity, becoming a sadder, less brotherly place.

argument_text:
Just over from the States, Captain Bluhm got his first award for excellence of command while CO of Fitzsimons General Hospital in Denver, Colorado (July 1942 to June 1944), and the cluster for meritorious service as Chief of Military Personnel at the same hospital (September, 1945 to March, 1946).

"I'm a master sergeant," said the Captain with a smile. In the Regular Army, of course. Actually, I am a master sergeant in the RA and a Captain in the Reserve (since 1935) at the same time. A little awed, we asked how long he had been in service. "Twenty years on the 19th of this month," he answered. As we started to ask the ne question he said, "And I'll probably be a thirty-year man before I quit." We think the man deserves another ribbon.
explanation: This passage culminates in a normative conclusion—“We think the man deserves another ribbon.”—supported by preceding evidence: multiple commendations, dual status (RA master sergeant and Reserve captain), long service (20 years), and intention to serve 30 years. The argument is implicit because the premises are presented as biographical facts and admiration (“A little awed”), without an explicit connective (e.g., “therefore”), but they function as reasons for the evaluative conclusion that he deserves another ribbon.
main_claim: Captain Bluhm deserves another ribbon.

argument_text: Yes, Clubmobile is gone and although it might not sound like anything worrisome, from an easy-chair in the Red Cross of Foggia proper, there has already been many a cry of anguish from the less fortunate in the areas surrounding the town.
explanation: The sentence contrasts an initial expectation (“it might not sound like anything worrisome”) with evidence (“many a cry of anguish”) to imply the conclusion that the Clubmobile’s end is indeed worrisome/harmful, especially for outlying areas. The concessive framing and evaluative language signal an argument moving from premise (cries of anguish) to conclusion (the end is worrisome).
main_claim: The termination of the Clubmobile is a real problem for surrounding areas.

argument_text: The move, it seems, has sprung from a War Department directive, and isn’t the ARC’s idea.
explanation: This causal attribution implies a normative stance about responsibility: the decision originated with the War Department, so the ARC should not be blamed. The structure provides a reason (source of the decision) that supports the implied conclusion (ARC is not at fault).
main_claim: Responsibility for ending the Clubmobile lies with the War Department rather than the ARC.

argument_text: “It’s a disappointment to a lot of men,” says Jean who already is reminiscing about the ‘good old days’. “As soon as we’d drive up they’d drop everything and tear over to the place where we serve the doughnuts and coffee and lemonade. Whenever we were a little late there would be a line formed and they’d make cracks.”
explanation: The main claim (“It’s a disappointment to a lot of men”) is supported by evidence of strong demand and enthusiasm (dropping everything, forming lines, making cracks when late). This is a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Many men are disappointed that the Clubmobile has ended because it was highly valued and in demand.

argument_text: There were two trips daily totaling some eighty miles around Foggia and toward Manfredonia. Between a thousand and thirteen hundred doughnuts were consumed every day. and ‘gallons’ of lemonade and coffee. Then there were also the incidental jobs like bringing airplane models and magazines to the boys who asked for them.
explanation: The enumeration of frequency, distance, quantities served, and extra services functions as evidence implying the conclusion that the Clubmobile provided substantial, needed service; thus its end is a loss. The implicitness comes from presenting statistics without an overt evaluative statement.
main_claim: The Clubmobile performed significant and widely used services, so its discontinuation represents a notable loss.

argument_text: “I hope it’ll come back,” she said sadly. “Maybe, if there’s enough requests…”
explanation: The conditional “if there’s enough requests” implies a causal means to an end: public requests could bring the Clubmobile back. This functions as an indirect recommendation to submit requests to restore the service.
main_claim: People should make requests because sufficient requests might bring the Clubmobile back.

argument_text: We walked into BOQ 20 the other day and came into a mild fit of sneezing when we entered a hallway foggy with DDT.
explanation: This sentence narrates an event in a way that implies a causal relationship: entering a hallway “foggy with DDT” is immediately linked to “a mild fit of sneezing.” The temporal and situational linkage (“when we entered”) suggests the claim that DDT exposure caused the sneezing, even though it is not stated explicitly as a conclusion supported by premises.
main_claim: The DDT-filled hallway caused them to sneeze.

argument_text:
and close by, his head in a mist of DDT, was Lt. Paul Nighswonger, Foggia's inexorable mosquito fighter.

He looked a little weary and we thought that perhaps all that DDT was wearing him down.
explanation: The passage presents an observation (Lt. Nighswonger’s head is in a mist of DDT; he looks weary) and offers a tentative causal inference (“we thought that perhaps all that DDT was wearing him down”). The evaluative/causal phrasing “wearing him down” and the hedge “perhaps” indicate an implied argument rather than a formally stated one.
main_claim: DDT exposure is wearing down Lt. Nighswonger.

argument_text: "No," he explained, "DDT doesn't hurt people. I've done everything but swim in it and I feel okay."
explanation: This presents a conclusion ("DDT doesn't hurt people") supported by a premise (the speaker’s extensive personal exposure without harm). The structure is clear: personal evidence is offered as a reason to accept the safety claim.
main_claim: DDT is safe for people.

argument_text: "The worst of it is all the trouble it seems to cause. A lot of the wives don't like us to spray their rooms. It does make a big mess."
explanation: The conclusion is evaluative ("The worst of it is all the trouble it seems to cause") and is supported by reasons (wives object; it makes a big mess), forming a clear premises-to-conclusion argument about the main problem with spraying.
main_claim: The primary problem with DDT spraying is the mess and resulting trouble it causes.

argument_text: "We only spray it on the walls and ceilings. But of course it gets on everything," he said wearily, "It's just a big mess and I make enemies."
explanation: This argues that spraying leads to social friction and mess because, despite targeting walls and ceilings, the spray gets on everything. The causal link from overspread to mess/enmity is explicitly stated.
main_claim: Spraying creates a mess and makes enemies because the spray inevitably gets on everything.

argument_text: "It'll evaporate soon though and they'll forget about it. At least I hope so. I don't want so many lasting enemies."
explanation: The claim is that the negative effects are temporary, supported by the premise that the substance will evaporate soon; the desire to avoid lasting enemies underscores the intended conclusion about transience.
main_claim: Any resentment from spraying will fade because the DDT will evaporate soon and be forgotten.

argument_text: "Some wives have even refused to let us spray their apartments," he continued, "They don't realize that they're in the middle of Italy."
explanation: The juxtaposition implies a normative claim: refusing spraying is unreasonable given local conditions (“the middle of Italy,” suggesting higher insect risk). The argument relies on implied premises about environmental hazards to conclude they ought to permit spraying.
main_claim: Wives should allow spraying given the local Italian conditions that make it necessary.

argument_text: "I wish they'd all be like Mrs. Palmer and Mrs. Sadler. They were very nice about it and we had to do their apartments twice."
explanation: By praising compliant individuals and expressing a wish others were like them, the speaker implies that cooperative acceptance of spraying (even multiple times) is the appropriate behavior; the positive evaluation functions as a reason.
main_claim: Others ought to emulate Mrs. Palmer and Mrs. Sadler by being cooperative about repeated spraying.

argument_text: Lt. Nighswonger covered the exposed clothes with a blanket, arranged the man's raincoat over some toilet articles and then motioned the laborers to begin.
explanation: The described precautions implicitly argue that sprayers act responsibly to protect personal items, suggesting objections about carelessness are unfounded; the careful actions serve as evidence for the implied claim.
main_claim: The spraying team is careful and takes steps to protect occupants’ belongings.

argument_text: The spraying of BOQ 20, we learned, is one more in the long list of places that the anti-malarial team has cleansed. Eventually every military establishment in Foggia will be in insect-proofed by the spray, even offices. The biggest job, that of spraying all the farmhouses around Foggia has already been largely completed. The teams ran into very little opposition there.
explanation: This passage advances the claim that the anti-malarial spraying campaign is successful, extensive, and accepted. The premises are cumulative: many places already “cleansed,” a plan to cover every establishment, the “biggest job” largely completed, and “very little opposition.” The evaluative term “cleansed,” the completion status, and lack of resistance together imply the conclusion of success and approval, though no explicit “therefore” is used.
main_claim: The anti-malarial spraying program in and around Foggia has been broadly successful, widely implemented, and met with little resistance.

argument_text: "They welcomed us, said Lt. Nighswonger, "Remembered from last year. The foreman of the sprayers would approach the houses and yell 'Ho Fleet' (We have Flit) and they'd come out smiling."
explanation: This quotation functions as evidence for a positive reception to the spraying and suggests a causal reason: prior experience (“Remembered from last year”) led residents to welcome the teams and respond happily to the announcement of “Flit.” The welcoming and smiling reactions imply approval and acceptance of the program, supporting the broader claim of little opposition.
main_claim: Local residents welcomed and approved of the sprayers, likely because of positive prior experience with the anti-malarial work.

argument_text: Foggians voted last Sunday and Monday in the first free election here in over twenty years — for men under forty-five and for all women, it was the first time in their lives to have cast a ballot. The 30,000 people crowded the polls, and many, like the man and woman above had to wait on lines all day to exercise their newly won right.
explanation: The passage presents facts (first free election in over twenty years; first-time voters; 30,000 crowding the polls; many waiting all day) coupled with evaluative framing ("first free election," "newly won right"). These cues imply a positive normative stance toward the election and suffrage expansion. The premises (unprecedented opportunity and high participation/effort) support the implicit conclusion that the election was a significant democratic milestone that citizens valued highly.
main_claim: The election was a significant democratic achievement that Foggians highly valued, as evidenced by the large turnout and willingness to wait all day to vote.

argument_text: In 1848 Victor Emanuel I, from the ruling family of the state of Sardinia-Piedmont, gained popular support of a confused Italian people when he offered his father’s “Statuto” to Italians, which provided for a king, two-chamber parliament, and council of deputies.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal structure: offering the Statuto (premise) explains why Victor Emanuel I gained popular support (conclusion). The use of “when” signals the causal relation, making the argument explicit.
main_claim: Victor Emanuel I secured popular support because he offered the Statuto establishing constitutional institutions.

argument_text: With the aid of the fiery Garibaldi, and (indirectly) even the help of the king-hating Mazzini, the House of Savoy ruled all of Italy, except Venice, by 1870.
explanation: The sentence attributes the House of Savoy’s success in ruling Italy to the aid of Garibaldi and Mazzini, presenting a causal explanation where the assistance (premise) led to national rule (conclusion).
main_claim: The House of Savoy achieved rule over Italy largely due to the aid of Garibaldi and Mazzini.

argument_text: The House of Savoy, associated with the unification of Italy, went on to make its reign far from distinguished in the annals of social or political progress. When the men about the King (Mazzini, Cavour, Garibaldi) died or left public life, the nation floundered externally and developed a case of social sea-sickness internally. King Umberto I, successor to Victor Emanuel, was assinated in 1900 after many attempts at his life.
explanation: These sentences use evaluative language (“far from distinguished,” “floundered,” “social sea-sickness”) and selective evidence (political instability, assassination) to support the negative assessment of the Savoy reign. The premises imply the conclusion without an explicit “therefore,” marking an implicit argument.
main_claim: The House of Savoy’s reign was poor in terms of social and political progress.

argument_text: Internationally, Italy was having trouble with France and its territorial ambitions. Bitter at the French acquisition of Tunis, Italy turned to Germany, and consented to sign the Triple Alliance with Austria, traditional enemy of Italy, as the third signatory.
explanation: The passage explicitly links Italy’s difficulties with France and bitterness over Tunis (premises) to Italy’s decision to join the Triple Alliance, even with a traditional enemy (conclusion), forming a clear causal explanation.
main_claim: Italy joined the Triple Alliance due to its conflict with France and resentment over Tunis.

argument_text: The end of the war left Italy weak; that and the fact that England could not live up to her promises to Italy left the way open for Mussolini.
explanation: This sentence explicitly presents premises (Italy’s postwar weakness and England’s failure to fulfill promises) leading to the conclusion that these conditions enabled Mussolini’s rise, using a clear causal connector.
main_claim: Italy’s post-WWI weakness and Britain’s unfulfilled promises created conditions that enabled Mussolini’s rise.

argument_text: Victor Emanuel III did little to resist the dictator, and eventually the king found himself powerless.
explanation: The structure asserts that the king’s inaction (premise) led to his powerlessness (conclusion), with “and eventually” marking a causal progression, making the argument explicit.
main_claim: Victor Emanuel III’s failure to resist Mussolini resulted in his own powerlessness.

argument_text: Victor Emanuel III abdicated after fourty-five years in power, in a political move designed to strenthen the position of the Monarchy.
explanation: The sentence asserts an inferred motive—abdication was “designed to strengthen” the monarchy—without providing explicit supporting premises in this sentence. It implies the reasoning that abdication before a referendum would bolster monarchist prospects.
main_claim: Victor Emanuel III abdicated strategically to improve the monarchy’s chances.

argument_text:
Memorial Day was observed on the 31st of May. In Italy, three days later, the people went to the polls and chose their form of government and their leaders. Women voted for the first time on a large scale in the country's history. In all, more than eighty per cent of the people cast their ballots.

Following so closely upon the day that we choose to pay tribute to the memory of our men who died fighting for these freedoms, we cannot help but observe that 'they have not died in vain!'
explanation: The passage presents premises—Italy’s high-turnout, inclusive democratic election occurring shortly after Memorial Day—leading to a stated conclusion that the fallen “have not died in vain.” The temporal linkage (“Following so closely upon the day...”) and evaluative inference (“we cannot help but observe”) make the argumentative move explicit: democratic participation is evidence that the freedoms soldiers died for are being realized.
main_claim: The sacrifices of the fallen were not in vain, as evidenced by Italy’s robust, inclusive democratic election held just after Memorial Day.

argument_text: They Have Not Died In Vain...
explanation: The headline asserts an evaluative conclusion that the fallen’s sacrifices were meaningful and justified. While no explicit premises are stated, the surrounding captions describing solemn ceremonies (march, invocation, tribute, wreaths, volleys, Taps) function as implied support: communal remembrance and honor suggest their deaths had purpose and are not forgotten. The use of a value-laden phrase with ellipsis cues an implied argument rather than neutral description.
main_claim: The war dead did not die in vain; their sacrifices had purpose and deserve honor.

argument_text: Major William Berg (left) makes an address paying tribute to men who sacrificed in the war.
explanation: This sentence reports a tribute and presupposes its appropriateness: honoring those who sacrificed implies they merit public recognition. The evaluative act (“paying tribute”) implies the normative claim that such men deserve tribute because of their sacrifice, even though the premises are not spelled out.
main_claim: Men who sacrificed in the war deserve public tribute.

argument_text: "The different attitude of Nights 'Round Foggia was something the Club Managers needed to get off their high horses."
explanation: The speaker criticizes club managers for being on their "high horses" and implies they needed to change their behavior or attitude. The phrase "the different attitude of Nights 'Round Foggia" functions as a reason or trigger for this needed change. The evaluative language ("needed to get off their high horses") signals a normative claim supported by a situational contrast, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Club Managers needed to stop acting arrogantly and adjust their attitude.

argument_text: "Tell that 'I'll-go-thirsty-at-the-beach-before-I-pay-twice-as-much' Smith guy, to go thirsty."
explanation: Through a directive and ironic framing, the speaker endorses the idea that if someone refuses to pay higher prices, they should accept the consequence (going thirsty). This implies a stance that paying the price is reasonable or that complaining about prices is not justified. The argument is conveyed via mockery rather than explicit premises, making it implicit.
main_claim: If someone refuses to pay higher beach prices, they should accept going thirsty rather than complain.

argument_text: "Something should be done about the irregularity of the busses. The other day I waited an hour before I got a ride back to the base."
explanation: This presents a clear conclusion ("Something should be done") supported by a concrete reason ("I waited an hour"). The structure is a straightforward normative recommendation backed by evidence of inconvenience, making it an explicit argument.
main_claim: Action should be taken to fix the irregularity of the buses.

argument_text: "Things didn't seem half as nice as they turned out to be. The town is much better than I expected and I enjoyed the beach. But the surprise of my life was when I saw the living quarters in Foggia!"
explanation: The speaker advances a positive evaluation of Foggia relative to prior expectations, citing enjoyment of the beach and unexpectedly good living quarters. The contrastive framing ("much better than I expected," "surprise") and evaluative language imply the overall claim that Foggia exceeded expectations, functioning as reasons supporting a positive conclusion.
main_claim: Foggia exceeded expectations, with a better-than-expected town, enjoyable beach, and surprisingly good living quarters.

argument_text: And a lot of good wishes from the gang up here go with him because he's been such a swell guy both on and off the job.
explanation: Uses the causal connector "because" to give a reason (he's been "such a swell guy both on and off the job") for the conclusion (the gang's good wishes go with him). Clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The gang is sending him a lot of good wishes because he has been a swell guy on and off the job.

argument_text: While we are on the subject of being on the job, there is a guy up here who is really on said job, Pfc. James Luman Rock, of Flint, Michigan. James has had fifteen months of service so far, five of them overseas. As a civilian Jim graduated from high school and came right into the Army. He went to sheet metal school and then learned all about kitchens the hard way. He came to the A.E.S. and has been working as an engineer ever since.
explanation: Begins with an evaluative claim that Rock is "really on said job," followed by a list of credentials and experience. The biography functions as evidence implying diligence/competence, even though there is no explicit “therefore.”
main_claim: Pfc. James Luman Rock is highly diligent and competent at his job.

argument_text: And now we present the golden trumpet of Randy Brooks... and surprise, surprise! ... it really sounds like a golden trumpet, for Randy Brooks plays a really wonderful horn.
explanation: The conclusion is that it "really sounds like a golden trumpet," supported by the stated reason introduced by "for": "Randy Brooks plays a really wonderful horn."
main_claim: Randy Brooks’s trumpet truly sounds exceptional because he plays a wonderful horn.

argument_text: The band has been in existence now for about sixteen months and is definitely on the way to the top of the musical heap. There was a little tough sledding at first, but it looks like the Brooks style of music has finally caught on.
explanation: Asserts a predictive evaluative claim ("on the way to the top") and implies justification by noting that after initial difficulties the style has "finally caught on." The catching on is presented as evidence of upward trajectory and quality.
main_claim: Randy Brooks’s band is rising toward top-tier status because its style has now caught on after early difficulties.

argument_text: He has a pair of good vocalists in Dorie Vincent and Billy Usher; Willie Baker's tenor sax in the outstanding instrumental feature, and the arrangements of Johnny Brooks (no relation) are really fine on both ballads and jump.
explanation: Lists multiple favorable attributes as evidence, implicitly arguing for the band’s high quality, though the evaluative conclusion is unstated within this sentence.
main_claim: The Brooks band is high quality owing to strong vocalists, an outstanding tenor sax feature, and fine arrangements.

argument_text: Of course, Randy himself is terrific on anything he plays... his tone is clear and brilliant with lovely phrasing and hard driving on the frantic antics.
explanation: The initial evaluative claim ("Randy himself is terrific") is supported by subsequent specific qualities (tone, phrasing, drive). The ellipsis introduces reasons, forming an implied argument.
main_claim: Randy Brooks is an excellent performer because of his clear, brilliant tone, lovely phrasing, and driving style.

argument_text: He has some new ideas both for the band and on his trumpet, and he isn't afraid to use them.
explanation: Highlights innovation and willingness to apply it, implying that these are positive qualities that enhance his and the band’s merit, without an explicit “therefore.”
main_claim: Randy Brooks’s innovation and willingness to use new ideas make him and his band commendable.

argument_text: He has one of the finest ranges in the country, both upper and lower register and has the good taste not to overdo his high-note stuff the way a great many other trumpet men of the day are doing.
explanation: Combines comparative excellence (one of the finest ranges) with a normative contrast (good taste vs. others who overdo), implying that he is superior and musically tasteful.
main_claim: Randy Brooks is superior and tasteful as a trumpeter because of his exceptional range and restraint compared to others.

argument_text: That's about all you can say about the Brooks band. The rest of it has to be heard. So listen to Randy Brooks and his trumpet.
explanation: Provides a reason ("The rest of it has to be heard") leading to the imperative conclusion introduced by "So": "listen to Randy Brooks and his trumpet."
main_claim: You should listen to Randy Brooks and his trumpet because their qualities are best appreciated by hearing them.

argument_text: We go to different ones each week so keep listening and sooner or later you'll hear yours.
explanation: Uses "so" to infer the recommendation "keep listening" from the premise that they feature different bandstands each week, with the promised outcome that the listener’s hometown will eventually be featured.
main_claim: You should keep listening because the show rotates bandstands weekly and you’ll eventually hear your hometown’s.

argument_text: The order evidently resulted from the recent deaths of infants on the wives' ships from intestinal disease and whooping cough.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal claim that the policy change (no further shipments of babies under six months) was caused by infant deaths on ships. The premise (recent deaths from disease) is offered as the reason for the conclusion (the order resulted from this), signaled by "evidently resulted from."
main_claim: The new restriction on shipping babies under six months was instituted because infants recently died on wives' ships from disease.

argument_text: The quota of twenty-six will be filled, however, Miss Andren stated, as there are many wives in categories other than that of April marriages that may be sent with the coming shipment.
explanation: This sentence gives a conclusion (the quota will be filled) supported by a reason (there are many eligible wives in other categories), explicitly linked by "as," which functions as a because-connector.
main_claim: The shipment quota will still be met because there are many eligible wives in other categories besides April marriages.

argument_text:
Calls Promptly Answered By AES

The system on the Jack Early musical show (0700 to 0830) is something new in radio. When a listener wants to hear a number, he can make a telephone call directly to the studio. Jack Early (Johnny Bowman) receives it through his earphones, and less than three minutes later, the request is on the air.
explanation: The headline asserts a claim about promptness, and the body provides evidence: direct studio calls and fulfillment “less than three minutes later.” The structure functions as an argument that AES answers requests promptly, with the time-to-air serving as a reason. The conclusion (prompt response) is implied by the descriptive evidence rather than stated with an explicit “therefore.”
main_claim: AES promptly answers listener calls and fulfills requests.

argument_text: The system on the Jack Early musical show (0700 to 0830) is something new in radio. When a listener wants to hear a number, he can make a telephone call directly to the studio. Jack Early (Johnny Bowman) receives it through his earphones, and less than three minutes later, the request is on the air. And if Jack Early is sure of his requester (there is a strict rule about language over the radio), he can push a button that will beam the voice from the telephone to the microphone, and the requester may even hear himself asking for the number over his own radio.
explanation: The passage advances the explicit claim that the show’s system “is something new in radio” and then provides multiple concrete features as reasons: direct call-ins, sub-three-minute turnaround, and live patching of callers’ voices. These premises directly support the evaluative conclusion of novelty.
main_claim: The Jack Early show’s request system is innovative for radio.

argument_text: And if Jack Early is sure of his requester (there is a strict rule about language over the radio), he can push a button that will beam the voice from the telephone to the microphone, and the requester may even hear himself asking for the number over his own radio.
explanation: This sentence presents a conditional policy and its rationale: only if Early is sure of the requester will he patch the caller through, and the parenthetical “there is a strict rule about language over the radio” functions as the explicit reason for that gatekeeping. The reason-premise directly supports the policy-conclusion.
main_claim: Early only patches a caller’s voice on-air when he is confident about the requester to comply with strict language rules.

argument_text: Opportunity is breaking a hard rule by knocking twice.
explanation: This figurative statement implies that a rare or second chance is being offered, suggesting readers should seize it. The evaluative framing (“breaking a hard rule”) cues an implicit claim about the exceptional nature and urgency of the opportunity, functioning as persuasive encouragement.
main_claim: This is a rare second chance that readers should not miss.

argument_text: Men are still needed for full-time jobs, and right now is the time to apply while positions are still open on the editorial staff.
explanation: This sentence presents an explicit recommendation (“right now is the time to apply”) supported by premises (“Men are still needed” and “positions are still open”). The causal/temporal clause (“while positions are still open”) provides the reason for the urgency.
main_claim: You should apply now because there are still openings and staff are needed.

argument_text: Men who are accepted will be relieved of other duties for full-time work on the Occupator.
