explanation: This offers a benefit as a reason to apply, implying that the job is desirable because it frees applicants from other duties. The persuasive function is implicit: the stated outcome serves as a motivating reason without an explicit “therefore apply” conclusion.
main_claim: The position is attractive because it frees accepted applicants from other duties.

argument_text: Come to the I & E Office, room 311 of the FAAB Headquarters Building, or call Newmarket 32.
explanation: This directive constitutes a recommendation/ought-claim, implicitly arguing that readers should take this action to pursue the opportunity. The imperative mood signals a prescriptive stance, with reasons supplied by the surrounding context (open positions, benefits).
main_claim: You should contact the office now to pursue the opportunity.

argument_text: Cpl. Don Wilmont of the 803rd MP's looks under the wheels of the truck that knocked him off his motorcycle a few seconds before. As the truck turned without signaling, Wilmont, riding on the inside of the truck's turn, saw it coming and jumped clear as the truck and bike hit.
explanation: The passage attributes causality and implies fault: it states the truck “knocked him off” and specifies the truck “turned without signaling,” suggesting negligent driving caused the crash. It also notes Wilmont’s quick reaction (“saw it coming and jumped clear”) as the reason he avoided being run over. These are cues of an embedded argument assigning cause/blame to the truck driver and crediting Wilmont’s action, without explicitly stating a normative conclusion.
main_claim: The truck driver’s unsignaled turn caused the collision that knocked Wilmont off his motorcycle, and Wilmont’s quick jump prevented more serious harm.

argument_text: April's five cases (making the rate 53.5 cases per thousand men per annum) were considered high, although compared to cases in ETO, it was not above the overseas average.
explanation: This sentence advances a two-part evaluative claim: that April’s rate was “high” but still within the overseas average. The “high” assessment is an evaluative conclusion implied from the numeric rate (53.5) without a normative threshold stated; the concession “although compared to cases in ETO, it was not above the overseas average” provides a comparative premise suggesting normality relative to ETO. The contrastive “although” signals a reconciled stance: high in local terms yet average in broader context.
main_claim: April’s VD rate was high locally but not above the overseas average in the ETO.

argument_text: In May, however, the VD rate jumped to 160.9 cases per thousand per annum, with 19 new infections treated, and reached a very serious high.
explanation: The passage asserts that May’s situation was “a very serious high,” which is a normative conclusion supported by the premises that the rate jumped to 160.9 and that 19 new infections were treated. The evaluative term “very serious” is not defined but is justified implicitly by the magnitude of the increase and the case count.
main_claim: May’s VD situation was very serious due to a sharp increase to 160.9 per thousand and 19 new infections.

argument_text: The alarming jump in the number of infections was attributed by Lt. Crider to the influx of new men into Foggia last month. "It seems as though the men who were new in Foggia attempted to make their arrival one big fling and this has been the result," Dr. Crider reported.
explanation: This presents a causal argument: conclusion—new men’s arrival and behavior caused the surge in infections; premises—there was an influx of new men, and they “attempted to make their arrival one big fling,” leading to “this result.” The explicit attribution (“was attributed… to the influx”) and the causal phrasing (“this has been the result”) provide a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The surge in VD infections was caused by the influx of new men who engaged in increased sexual activity upon arrival.

argument_text: These measures, Lt. Rodgers specified, are only the usual precautionary steps taken by the Army when any contagious disease breaks out.
explanation: This sentence advances a normative claim about the nature of the measures (that they are “only the usual precautionary steps”) and justifies it with a general rule/premise (“when any contagious disease breaks out” the Army takes such steps). The structure links the premise (Army’s standard practice) to the conclusion (current measures are routine precaution, not extraordinary response).
main_claim: The restrictions put in place are routine precautionary measures rather than signs of a serious outbreak.

argument_text: There have been no other cases of polio thus far, which indicates that the one that did occur was isolated, a not uncommon occurrence with poliomyelitis.
explanation: This sentence states a premise (“There have been no other cases of polio thus far”) and draws an inference/conclusion from it (“which indicates that the one that did occur was isolated”), further supporting the inference with background knowledge (“a not uncommon occurrence with poliomyelitis”). This is a clear premise-to-conclusion argument.
main_claim: The absence of additional cases indicates the incident was an isolated case.

argument_text: The 55th Hospital orders have already been lifted and close seating is again permissible in the Flagella Theater.
explanation: While presented as factual updates, the lifting of orders and resumption of close seating imply a conclusion about reduced risk/safety. The implicit argument is that authorities would not lift such restrictions unless the situation were safe enough, so the action signals that the threat has subsided. The inference relies on presupposed norms about when restrictions are lifted.
main_claim: Conditions are considered safe enough to resume normal seating.

argument_text: The ban on swimming stands, however, at least until the completion of tests on the water, and possibly until stagnant sewage deposits (discovered in streams emptying into the beaches) are cleared out.
explanation: This sentence justifies maintaining the ban with explicit reasons/premises: tests on the water are not yet complete and sewage deposits have been discovered. The conclusion (the ban remains) is directly tied to these conditions, making it an explicit policy justification.
main_claim: Swimming remains prohibited because water tests are pending and sewage deposits need to be cleared.

argument_text: We might point out that whether we want to admit it or not, that was part of the reason we fought a World War II. Viva was for the new Italian republic, voted in a referendum two weeks ago, and the festa was a celebration of the exit of the King, making Italy more like the US than it has been before.
explanation: This passage links the civilians’ celebration (“viva” for the new Italian republic and the exit of the king) to the stated purpose of fighting WWII, and frames the change as making Italy “more like the US.” The premises (celebration of the republic; end of monarchy; alignment with US model) imply the evaluative conclusion that the festa is good/justified and aligned with Allied war aims, even though the positive evaluative conclusion is not stated with an explicit “therefore.”
main_claim: The festa celebrating the new Italian republic and the king’s exit is a good and justified development aligned with the reasons the Allies fought WWII.

argument_text: We came into Italy and beat the fascists. Now the Italians are trying democratic governing for the first time in a generation. The festa was a victory for us, and we should consider our job well done.
explanation: The passage provides premises (defeat of fascists; Italians adopting democratic governance) leading to a clear conclusion (“we should consider our job well done”), explicitly presenting an argument that the celebration represents Allied success.
main_claim: We should regard the festa as a victory and consider our mission in Italy accomplished.

argument_text: Her biggest worry was how to provide for his education for the one year that they expect to be in Italy. She will teach Jerry the few subjects that the teacher advised before they left Dallas, but in the main, most of his education will have to be what he can learn by seeing Europe and make up the formal education by the art, culture, and travel he gets in Europe.
explanation: These sentences present a plan justified by circumstance: because they will be in Italy for a year and formal schooling is limited, experiential learning (art, culture, travel) will “make up” for formal education. The implied claim is that experiential European exposure is a suitable substitute or complement to formal schooling. The evaluative stance is implied rather than directly argued with “therefore.”
main_claim: For their year in Italy, Jerry’s education should largely come from experiencing Europe’s art, culture, and travel as a practical substitute for formal schooling.

argument_text: We still think being nine years old is a wonderful thing. And education here in Italy? Why, he'll really be able to tell those kids back home some stories.
explanation: The rhetorical question and evaluative language suggest the conclusion that Jerry’s Italian experience will be valuable and enriching, functioning as meaningful “education” that will benefit him (e.g., giving him stories/knowledge to share). The argument is implied via tone and framing rather than stated as a formal premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Jerry’s time in Italy will provide enriching educational experiences worth having.

argument_text: "The nurse gave me these," he said, "When Mother gives me candy, she rations me to one bar a day. These are small anyhow."
explanation: The child justifies consuming the sour balls by contrasting his mother’s rationing of candy bars with the small size of the sour balls, implying that eating more of them is acceptable. The reasoning is suggestive rather than explicit: small candies are taken to not “count” like a bar.
main_claim: It’s acceptable to eat multiple sour balls because they’re small and unlike the rationed candy bars.

argument_text: But being the maestro of the FAAB Band entails more than leading musicians through their cadenzas, and Frenck De Grazia was busy in some of his administrative duties when we disturbed him.
explanation: This asserts a general claim about the scope of the bandmaster’s role and immediately offers observable evidence (he was busy with administrative duties) as a reason, forming a premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: Being the maestro of the FAAB Band involves administrative work in addition to conducting.

argument_text:
Civilians Like Band

The idea of giving public concerts came to the FAAB bandmaster after, oddly enough, he had received several compliments on his band's work from several Foggians.
explanation: The headline makes a claim (“Civilians Like Band”) and the following sentence provides evidence (several compliments from Foggians), creating a direct support for the claim.
main_claim: Civilians in Foggia like the FAAB band.

argument_text: "Oh, they like the band all right, but I can tell that they don't think we can play anything but swing and marches. Now I've been working with these boys for months and I don't think there's another army band that's putting out as much. They're really getting good. They have to, to give out with some of the things, like a fifteen-minute piece from Bizet's Carmen that we have on the book."
explanation: The speaker challenges a perceived belief (that the band only plays swing and marches) and supports the counter-claim with reasons: his prolonged work with the musicians, comparative evaluation against other army bands, and concrete evidence of repertoire difficulty (a 15-minute Bizet Carmen piece). The premises explicitly support the conclusion that the band is capable and versatile.
main_claim: The FAAB band is highly capable and can play more than swing and marches.

argument_text: Frenck De Grazia can talk about musical organizations with authority after spending fifteen years in the music business.
explanation: This is an argument from authority: the conclusion (he can speak with authority) is supported by the stated reason (fifteen years of experience in the music business).
main_claim: De Grazia is a credible authority on musical organizations because of his experience.

argument_text: The FAAB Band has been having its troubles lately. George Keeley, ace reed man, vocalist, and drum major, has been in the hospital, and DeGrazia is still busy making allowances for instrument shortages, but most of all he is kept busy with administrative detail and wishing someone else would take the red tape off his hands.
explanation: The text states a conclusion (the band has been having troubles) and supports it by listing reasons (loss of a key member to hospitalization, instrument shortages, and burdensome administrative duties), forming a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The FAAB Band is currently facing significant difficulties.

argument_text: After he returned the telephone to its cradle, Sergeant DeGrazia turned to us suddenly, exclaiming, "Well, I don't know, one of these days I'll get these concerts going without any trouble."
explanation: The exclamation implies that organizing concerts has been beset by difficulties; the claim is suggested rather than directly argued. The phrase “one of these days” and “without any trouble” presuppose ongoing trouble, functioning as indirect evidence of current obstacles.
main_claim: Organizing the concerts has been troublesome so far.

argument_text: ...but most of all he is kept busy with administrative detail and wishing someone else would take the red tape off his hands.
explanation: This phrasing implies a normative stance that administrative red tape is burdensome and should be handled by someone else; the wish serves as a cue to the underlying recommendation without stating it outright.
main_claim: Administrative red tape is excessive and should be delegated or reduced.

argument_text: He was the Editor, and three officers, two enlisted men, and a whole civilian staff took orders from him in the truest military style, accomplishing his idea of a newspaper that was not "in the truest military style" in unit newspapers.
explanation: This sentence uses contrast and ironic quotation marks to imply a claim: despite operating with strict hierarchical command, Hoffman achieved a newspaper that rejected a rigid “military style.” The premise (staff took orders in the truest military style) is juxtaposed with the conclusion (the newspaper was not in that style), signaling an argument through contrast rather than explicit connective words.
main_claim: Hoffman’s leadership produced a newspaper that was not in a rigid “military style,” even though the staff worked under strict military command.

argument_text: Truth was an obsession for Milton Hoffman, and he let no preconceived prejudices or staff recommendations color his newspaper. Under him, the Occupator tried to be free of libelous stories about civilians as well as soldiers.
explanation: This passage presents premises (Hoffman’s obsession with truth; refusal to let prejudices or staff recommendations influence the paper) leading to a conclusion about editorial outcomes (the paper tried to avoid libel against civilians and soldiers). The causal/justificatory sequence forms a clear argument supporting a claim about the paper’s integrity under his editorship.
main_claim: Under Hoffman’s editorship, the Occupator strove to avoid libel and bias due to his obsession with truth.

argument_text:
Milton Hoffman, as a man, was an outspoken liberal and confident that soldiers from America and civilians from Italy could live together peacefully and happily; and as an editor, he pressed that belief with a zeal that often annoyed less confident soldiers and civilians. Truth was an obsession for Milton Hoffman, and he let no preconceived prejudices or staff recommendations color his newspaper. Under him, the Occupator tried to be free of libelous stories about civilians as well as soldiers.

We were sorry to see Milton Hoffman go.
explanation: The passage lists positive qualities and effects of Hoffman’s editorship (commitment to peaceful coexistence, zeal, obsession with truth, avoidance of prejudice and libel) and then states the evaluative conclusion that “We were sorry to see Milton Hoffman go.” The reasons are supplied before the concluding sentiment without an explicit connective like “therefore,” making the argument implicit but structured: his virtues and editorial standards justify their regret at his departure.
main_claim: The staff’s regret at Hoffman’s departure is justified by his principled leadership and truthful, fair editorial standards.

argument_text: 1) Eliminate off-duty saluting except on Army posts and in occupied areas.
explanation: This is a recommendation (ought-claim) implying that eliminating off-duty saluting will improve Army personnel relationships or practicality/morale. The normative “Eliminate” indicates a policy stance, with the context (“gripe board” on personnel relationships) supplying the unstated reason.
main_claim: Off-duty saluting should be eliminated except on Army posts and in occupied areas.

argument_text: 2) The system of promoting officers by seniority be discarded for a merit system. Officers should serve one year in the ranks.
explanation: Two linked policy recommendations imply that promotions should be based on merit and that officers should gain enlisted experience, presumably to increase fairness and effectiveness. The reasons are not stated but the recommendations signal an evaluative stance.
main_claim: Officer promotions should be based on merit rather than seniority, and officers should first serve a year in the ranks.

argument_text: 3) In courts-martial, the higher the rank, the higher should be the penalty.
explanation: A normative rule is proposed, implying that greater rank entails greater responsibility and thus warrants higher penalties; the justification is implied rather than stated.
main_claim: Court-martial penalties should increase with the rank of the accused.

argument_text: 4) Wholesale distribution of decorations be stopped. The higher a man's rank, the more difficult it should be to get an award.
explanation: These recommendations argue for stricter award standards, especially for higher ranks, implying concerns about fairness, morale, and the value of decorations. The rationale is suggested, not explicit.
main_claim: The Army should stop giving out decorations too freely and make awards harder to obtain for higher-ranking personnel.

argument_text: 5) Identical allowances for food, travel, and quarters be given to all ranks.
explanation: An egalitarian policy recommendation implying that equal allowances will improve fairness and morale; the evaluative basis is implied.
main_claim: All ranks should receive identical allowances for food, travel, and quarters.

argument_text: 6) Rules against social fraternization of ranks be wiped out.
explanation: A policy change is urged, implying that removing anti-fraternization rules will improve relationships or reduce unnecessary barriers; reasons are implied.
main_claim: The Army should abolish rules prohibiting social fraternization between ranks.

argument_text: 7) Army pay be increased to attract high-caliber men from civilian jobs.
explanation: This contains a clear reason-conclusion structure: increase pay (conclusion) because it will attract high-caliber men from civilian jobs (stated purpose/justification).
main_claim: Army pay should be increased to attract high-caliber men from civilian jobs.

argument_text: Municipal councils of two Virgin Islands were "jubilant over this great act of the president."
explanation: The praise “great act” evaluates the President’s appointment decision, implying that appointing William H. Hastie was commendable and beneficial; the evaluative stance functions as an argument by endorsement, though reasons are unstated.
main_claim: The President’s appointment of William H. Hastie as governor of the Virgin Islands was a commendable action.

argument_text: Medicine: A new relief for stomach ulcers was reported recently by Dr. Benjamin Bernstein of N.Y. University. An injection of "histamine" resulted in complete relief of ulcer pain in 69 cases out of 75, in from 4 to 18 days of treatment.
explanation: Empirical results are presented as evidence implying the conclusion that histamine injections are an effective treatment for ulcer pain. The claim is suggested through the success rate and timeframe.
main_claim: Histamine injections are an effective new relief for stomach ulcer pain.

argument_text: Lt. Col. Richard Schumacher - Showed marked executive abilities and maintained a high standard of morale. Second Bomb Group was able to administer the entire Foggia area with the help of his thorough supervision and anticipation of exigencies.
explanation: The passage provides reasons (executive ability, morale maintenance, effective supervision, anticipating exigencies) and links them causally to a successful outcome (administering the entire Foggia area), which implicitly supports the conclusion that Schumacher merits commendation. The causal phrasing “with the help of his thorough supervision” signals reasoning, while the ultimate evaluative claim (that he deserves the commendation) is implied rather than stated.
main_claim: Lt. Col. Richard Schumacher’s leadership and foresight produced effective administration of the Foggia area, warranting commendation.

argument_text: Maj. Harold Thayer - Accomplished the transition from combat operation to occupation and the move from Amendola to Foggia with efficiency in spite of the loss of personnel.
explanation: This sentence gives a reason (efficiently accomplishing a difficult transition despite personnel losses) that implicitly supports the evaluative conclusion that Thayer merits recognition. The concessive structure “in spite of the loss of personnel” strengthens the implied argument for commendability.
main_claim: Maj. Harold Thayer efficiently managed a difficult transition despite reduced personnel, justifying commendation.

argument_text: Maj. William Berg - As executive officer, he administered the Second Bomb Group during the transition from combat operations to occupation. He secured recreational facilities and instituted and consolidated the Unit Personnel system.
explanation: The passage lists actions and achievements (administering during transition, securing recreation, instituting and consolidating personnel systems) that function as premises for an implied conclusion that Berg deserves commendation for effective administration and organizational improvements.
main_claim: Maj. William Berg effectively administered the group and improved organizational and recreational systems during transition, meriting commendation.

argument_text: Maj. William Gilbert - During a time when there was a large decrease in trained personnel, he succeeded in instituting a training school and in maintaining aircraft in a high state of efficiency.
explanation: By presenting achievements accomplished under adverse conditions (establishing a training school and maintaining aircraft efficiency despite a personnel decrease), the passage provides reasons that imply the conclusion that Gilbert is commendable for effective leadership and problem-solving.
main_claim: Maj. William Gilbert successfully built capacity and sustained aircraft efficiency despite personnel shortages, warranting commendation.

argument_text: Maj. William Havard - As Group Communications Officer, he took over a greatly expanded communications system and ran it with great effectiveness.
explanation: The statement advances a positive evaluation (ran an expanded system with great effectiveness) as a reason for the implied conclusion that Havard merits commendation for competent management and effectiveness.
main_claim: Maj. William Havard effectively managed a greatly expanded communications system, justifying commendation.

argument_text: Capt. David Ives - Exercised sound judgment in the disposition of requisitioned property and did excellent work as Foggia Town Major during a difficult period. He helped to avoid undue distress, and under him, Italo-American relations became very much improved.
explanation: The passage offers multiple reasons—sound judgment, excellent performance in a difficult period, alleviating distress, and improving Italo-American relations—that imply the evaluative conclusion that Ives deserves commendation. The causal and evaluative language (“helped to avoid undue distress,” “very much improved”) signals argumentative support for his merit.
main_claim: Capt. David Ives’s prudent administration and improvements in local welfare and Italo-American relations during a difficult period merit commendation.

argument_text: Claimed to be "out of the ordinary" by their press releases, Holiday For Joe is headed by the Flying Buddies, Isobel and Clarence Reuter, who are famous in the States for their amazing roller-skating acts. Also billed are Joe May and Margie Greene ("two slick laugh-makers"), Keane Janis ("songs, sweet and hot"), Peliney and Peggy ("two tap-dancing redheads"), Jerry Bragin ("plays a mean piano"), and Victor Dexter ("a juggler who can juggle"). Scheduled to last one hour and fifteen minutes, the showmen promise laughs and swoony music to suit all.
explanation: This passage uses evaluative descriptors and promotional framing (e.g., "out of the ordinary," "famous," "amazing," "two slick laugh-makers," "plays a mean piano") and a promise of "laughs and swoony music to suit all" to imply a conclusion that the show will be highly entertaining and worth attending. The premises are the reputations and skills of the performers and the promised experience; the conclusion that audiences should expect quality entertainment is suggested rather than stated explicitly.
main_claim: Holiday For Joe will be an especially entertaining show that audiences should want to attend.

argument_text: Although Foggia voted heavily monarchist, republican celebrations occurred entirely without incident.
explanation: The sentence uses a concessive contrast ("Although...") to set up a premise—Foggia’s heavy monarchist vote—that would normally license an expectation of tension or unrest, and then asserts the outcome that defies that expectation—celebrations were incident-free. This framing implicitly argues that the peacefulness is noteworthy and counters anticipated conflict, functioning as an argument by highlighting contrast between expected and observed outcomes.
main_claim: Republican celebrations in Foggia were peaceful despite the city's strong monarchist vote.

argument_text: Previous to the parade, several units of Carabinieri were placed in strategic locations throughout the city in the event of disorders. Although in the national election Foggia Province voted for the monarchy by a majority of more than two to one, the parade wound through the streets of Foggia and into the Piazza XX Settembre without incident.
explanation: This juxtaposes a precautionary deployment of security forces and the local pro-monarchy vote (which could suggest a risk of clashes) with the outcome “without incident,” implying that fears of disorder were unfounded and that the leftist demonstration was peaceful. The contrastive cue “Although” signals an argumentative move countering an anticipated objection.
main_claim: Despite expectations of tension or disorder given Foggia’s monarchist majority, the leftist parade proceeded peacefully.

argument_text: In the featured speech, given by Domenico Fioritti, head of Foggia's Socialist party, the victory of the Republic was evaluated as a victory over fear. "It was claimed by the Monarchists," Fioritti said, "that the Republic would lead to chaos... just as the monarchy conquered Italy through the fear of separation of provinces and later the fear of Bolshevism. But at last, fear has disappeared, and the people have received their freedom and unity."
explanation: Fioritti sets out a clear argumentative structure: premise that monarchists predicted chaos and historically used fear to rule; observation that fear has now disappeared; conclusion that the Republic’s victory is a victory over fear and has delivered freedom and unity. Quotations explicitly state the reasoning and conclusion.
main_claim: The Republic’s victory overcame fear-mongering and has brought the people freedom and unity.

argument_text: On the importance of the victory, Fioritti remarked, "Now that we have given to the whole world this great example of a historical revolution without bloodshed, we can confirm that a people of these moral principles reach out for high destinies."
explanation: This is an explicit inferential claim: from the premise that the nation provided a bloodless revolutionary example, Fioritti concludes that such moral principles indicate a people destined for great achievements. The connective “now that” and “we can confirm” mark premise-to-conclusion movement.
main_claim: The bloodless revolutionary transition proves that a morally principled people are destined for great achievements.

argument_text: In his final proclamation, Umberto stated that he was forced to leave Italy because of the illegal action of his government, which "with a revolutionary gesture" assumed arbitrary power.
explanation: This presents a clear causal structure: premise that the government acted illegally and assumed arbitrary power “with a revolutionary gesture,” leading to the conclusion that Umberto was forced to leave Italy.
main_claim: Umberto had to leave Italy because his government illegally seized arbitrary power.

argument_text: Behind him, he left a proclamation that only increased the agitation which has beset the country since Umberto first indicated that he suspected election fraud in the recent national referendum.
explanation: The passage attributes increased unrest to Umberto’s proclamation and links ongoing agitation to his earlier suspicions of fraud. The causal attribution and evaluative phrasing imply the argument that his statements/actions are exacerbating national unrest.
main_claim: Umberto’s statements and proclamation have contributed to increasing political agitation in Italy.

argument_text: By leaving Italy, De Gasperi declared, "Umberto expiated the past faults and mistakes of his House, which once compromised with the fascist dictatorship."
explanation: De Gasperi asserts a conclusion (Umberto expiated his House’s past faults) and supplies a reason/background (the House “once compromised with the fascist dictatorship”), making it a justificatory argument that the act of leaving serves as expiation for those faults.
main_claim: Umberto’s departure serves as atonement for the House of Savoy’s past complicity with fascism.

argument_text: After adding in his proclamation that he hoped the Supreme Court will express "its free opinion on electoral irregularities,"
explanation: The phrase presupposes that “electoral irregularities” occurred and that a “free opinion” from the Court is needed, implying the argument that the referendum’s integrity is in question and merits independent judicial scrutiny.
main_claim: The referendum suffered electoral irregularities that warrant an independent Supreme Court assessment.

argument_text: "I am sure that we may still continue that cooperation and maintain what is truly required: the unity of Italy."
explanation: Normative language (“what is truly required”) and the call to “continue cooperation” imply the argument that, despite current tensions, Italians ought to prioritize and preserve national unity; the premise is the desirability/necessity of unity.
main_claim: Italians should continue cooperating to uphold the necessary goal of national unity.

argument_text: Governor Thomas E. Dewey of New York addressed a large crowd in Madison Square Garden this week on the occasion of the proclamation of the Italian Republic. Mr. Dewey called for a quick signing of a peace treaty with Italy and the acceptance of Italy into the United Nations.
explanation: The passage advances a normative recommendation (ought-claims) that Italy should quickly receive a peace treaty and UN membership. While no explicit premises are given, the timing “on the occasion of the proclamation of the Italian Republic” provides contextual support implying that Italy’s new republican status and democratic direction justify speedy normalization and inclusion. The argument is thus implicit, relying on the occasion as a reason.
main_claim: Italy should quickly be granted a peace treaty and admitted to the United Nations.

argument_text: General Mark Clark was this week awarded a citizenship ad honorem by Sorrento. The award was granted, it was stated by Italian officials, because General Clark has shown his friendship for the picturesque Italian town and also the friendship of the American people to an Italy that is on its way to democracy.
explanation: This provides a conclusion (the award was granted) with explicit reasons (“because General Clark has shown his friendship…” and as a sign of American friendship toward a democratizing Italy). It presents a clear premise-to-conclusion justification for the honor.
main_claim: Granting ad honorem citizenship to General Clark is justified by his demonstrated friendship to Sorrento and as a symbol of American friendship to a democratizing Italy.

argument_text: All-important grain harvesting is now taking place in Foggia Province and will be completed within a week. It is expected that the harvested crop will come close to pre-war yields. Last year's crop of 600,000 quintiles was bad because of the summer drought. Pre-war levels for the grain harvest have been from three to three and a half million quintiles.
explanation: The evaluative phrase “All-important” asserts the significance of the harvest, and the subsequent data (expected near pre-war yields, last year’s poor yield due to drought, and pre-war benchmarks) implicitly support the claim that this year’s harvest outlook is positive and significant. The premises are offered as contextual evidence rather than an explicit conclusion.
main_claim: This year’s grain harvest in Foggia Province is crucial and is expected to be near pre-war levels, indicating a positive outlook compared to last year.

argument_text: In Taranto, a large southern Italian seaport, last Tuesday's demonstration marking the proclamation of the Republic was broken up by monarchist members of the San Marco battalion (Italian commandos) who threw hand grenades into the crowds of demonstrators. Thirty-six persons were injured. The battalion has been moved out of Taranto.
explanation: The sequence presents a cause (violent disruption with grenades causing injuries) followed by an action (the battalion’s removal), implying an argument that removal was a warranted response to the violence. The normative judgment is not stated but suggested by the causal framing and aftermath.
main_claim: Because the San Marco battalion violently disrupted the demonstration and injured many, removing the battalion from Taranto was an appropriate response.

argument_text: Amici d'America (Friends of America), an Italian non-political organization, is opening up an educational and recreational institution in San Ferdinando for the town's young children. San Ferdinando has long been known as a center for black market activities. Food for the institution will be provided by the Italian government and UNRRA.
explanation: The juxtaposition of opening a children’s institution with the town’s reputation for black market activity and the mention of official support implies a claim that such an institution is a beneficial or needed intervention in a troubled area. The argument is suggested through framing rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: Establishing the children’s educational and recreational institution in black-market-plagued San Ferdinando is a needed, beneficial intervention supported by public resources.

argument_text: The Italian Youth Movement, organized on lines similar to the Boy Scouts, is opening several summer camps throughout Italy, the largest of which will be situated at the east end of the Italian spur, near Manfredonia. A total of 400 hungry youngsters fed by UNRRA will attend the camp during the summer season.
explanation: The comparison to the Boy Scouts signals legitimacy and positive connotations, and noting “400 hungry youngsters” being fed implies that the camps address urgent needs. Together, these elements suggest the claim that the camps are beneficial and necessary for youth welfare.
main_claim: The Italian Youth Movement’s summer camps are a beneficial measure that will help meet the needs of hungry youth.

argument_text: Rioting at the Bari-Milan soccer match last Sunday broke out after the referee refused to call a penalty against the Milan team. The crowd poured onto the field and chased the referee out of the grounds. Milan won the game 3-1 after the crowd was dispersed by the police. As an aftermath, no more soccer matches will be played in the Bari Stadium for an indefinite period.
explanation: The narrative links disorder and violence at the match to the decision to suspend further matches, implying an argument that suspension is necessary to prevent further unrest and ensure safety. The justification is conveyed through causal sequencing rather than explicit reasoning.
main_claim: Given the violent rioting at the Bari-Milan match, suspending future matches at the Bari Stadium indefinitely is a warranted response.

argument_text: With the "Doolittle board" discussing the caste system (See Page 3, column 1) and its effects on Army morale, an officer, Lt. Dan Hickey, and an enlisted man, Pfc. Charles F. Smith from Foggia, decided to have their own discussion at Siponto Beach recently. Tests of culture, breeding, intelligence, and wit ended in pretty much of a tie, and finally, a test of strength was suggested.
explanation: The passage frames an officer–enlisted encounter as a proxy “discussion” of the Army’s “caste system,” then reports parity across valued traits (“culture, breeding, intelligence, and wit ended in pretty much of a tie”). This implies a normative claim that caste distinctions lack merit because rank does not map onto superior qualities. The cues are the linkage to the “caste system,” the evaluative categories tested, and the reported tie.
main_claim: Officer–enlisted caste distinctions are unjustified because the two are equal in culture, breeding, intelligence, and wit.

argument_text: Lt. Dan Hickey (left) started out with a good scissor hold but has discovered too late that Smith could stand on his own.
explanation: Beyond literal wrestling commentary, “could stand on his own” functions as a double-entendre suggesting enlisted independence/competence matching or surpassing an officer’s advantage. This supports a claim that rank does not confer intrinsic superiority, aligning with the “caste system” frame introduced earlier.
main_claim: The enlisted man’s capability matches the officer’s, undermining any presumption of officer superiority based on rank.

argument_text: Around and around they go. At this point, it is pretty much anyone's fight. Charlie Smith is still on top, however.
explanation: By asserting the contest is evenly matched (“anyone’s fight”) while noting the enlisted man is currently “on top,” the passage implies parity of ability and subtly challenges hierarchical assumptions tied to rank. The evaluative contrast supports an implicit claim of equality.
main_claim: The officer and enlisted man are evenly matched, indicating that rank-based hierarchy does not reflect actual superiority.

argument_text: Decision is reached when Charlie Smith finds a hole in the sand. At the other end of those feet is Dan Hickey. Discussion ends.
explanation: The outcome—enlisted man wins through situational awareness or ingenuity—implicitly argues that results hinge on skill and circumstance rather than rank, reinforcing skepticism toward a “caste system.” The closing “Discussion ends” ties the result back to the broader debate.
main_claim: The enlisted man’s victory shows that practical skill, not rank, determines outcomes, casting doubt on the legitimacy of caste-like distinctions.

argument_text: Charlie has gone on for years being one of the most consistently underrated musicians I know of. The guy plays alto and tenor like mad and is one of the very few that can make the soprano saxophone really sound good.
explanation: The first sentence asserts the evaluative claim that Barnet is "consistently underrated." The following sentence provides reasons (exceptional skill on alto, tenor, and soprano sax) that implicitly support the claim that he deserves greater recognition. The argumentative link is implied rather than signposted.
main_claim: Charlie Barnet is unfairly underrated given his exceptional musicianship.

argument_text: He uses a lot of Ellington tunes and a great many more Ellington moods, but he doesn't copy lavishly or imitate Ellington, as a great deal of the public seems to believe. Charlie puts his own phrasings into anything he plays, at times so subtly as to be almost unnoticeable unless you're listening really closely.
explanation: This passage refutes a common belief ("the public seems to believe") by asserting the contrary claim (he does not imitate Ellington) and supplying a concrete reason (he adds his own subtle phrasings). The contrastive "but" and the follow-up evidence make the argument explicit.
main_claim: Charlie Barnet does not imitate Ellington because he infuses his performances with his own subtle phrasings.

argument_text: As far as his band goes, Barnet has always had a great one. He's had several, and none of them have ever been bad or even mediocre. He's an amazing organizer and can have a brand new band sounding good in less time than most other bandleaders would allow theirs to be heard. He is also a great discoverer of talent and has always recognized good musicianship and surrounded himself with it.
explanation: The passage advances the evaluative claims that Barnet’s bands are consistently great and that he excels as an organizer and talent-spotter. The descriptive statements about organizing quickly and surrounding himself with good musicians function as reasons supporting the overall quality assessment. The inferential structure is implied without explicit connectors.
main_claim: Barnet’s bands are consistently excellent because he is an exceptional organizer and discoverer of talent who surrounds himself with good musicians.

argument_text: And to prove it, here are some of the men who have either been discovered by or played with the Mab: Cootie Williams, Howard McGhee, Al Killian, Peanuts Holland, Bobby Burnet, Dizzy Gillespie, Bernie Privin, and many others on trumpet; the wonderful Eddie Bert, Trummy Young, Tommy Peterson, Ford Leary, and more on trombone; Buddy DeFranco and Ray DeGeer played in his reed section; the late Bus Etri, Chubby Jackson, Oscar Pettiford, Chickie Fromm, Cliff Leemans, Bill Miller, Dodo Marmarosa, Ralph Burns were at one time in his rhythm section; Frances Wayne, Gwen Tynes, Lena Horne first sang with Barnet.
explanation: The phrase "And to prove it" explicitly signals that the ensuing list is evidence supporting the prior claim that Barnet discovers talent and surrounds himself with excellent musicians. The argument uses named examples as proof of that claim.
main_claim: Barnet’s record of working with and discovering many notable musicians proves his talent-spotting and bandbuilding excellence.

argument_text: Just one more thing—you'll notice that many of these wonderful musicians are Negro, and it's another thing to the guy's credit that he has courage enough to fight for the music and the way of life he believes in, in that music.
explanation: The sentence presents a reason (many of his musicians are Negro) leading to an evaluative conclusion (this is to Barnet’s credit for courage in upholding his musical values and way of life). The causal/evaluative link is explicit via "it's another thing to the guy's credit that...".
main_claim: Barnet deserves credit for courageous commitment to his musical values, as shown by his employing many Negro musicians.

argument_text: So more power to Charlie Barnet and men like him. I wish there were more.
explanation: The endorsement ("So more power...") and desire for more like him function as normative conclusions drawn from prior presented reasons (his musicianship, band leadership, and courage). The inferential "So" signals a conclusion based on earlier premises, though those premises are not repeated here.
main_claim: Charlie Barnet and similar figures deserve support and should be more numerous.

argument_text: Due to a change of time in the news broadcasts, a few of your favorite shows have been either shortened, had their time changed, or have been eliminated completely. We are really sorry, but there was nothing we could do.
explanation: The first sentence provides a cause (news broadcast time change) leading to effects (program alterations). The second asserts the conclusion that the station had no control over these changes, presented as justified by the external cause. The causal connector "Due to" and the concessive "but" make the argument explicit.
main_claim: Program changes were unavoidable and beyond the station’s control because the news broadcast time changed.

argument_text: Ninth Air Force Service Command's sudden call for the redeployment of the officers (with 37 months or more service as of August 31st) was attributed by Colonel Robert Martin, Commanding Officer of FAAB, to "the pressure that has been put on higher headquarters by FAAB for the past months."
explanation: This presents a causal explanation: the conclusion is that the sudden call occurred; the stated reason (premise) is sustained pressure by FAAB on higher headquarters. The phrase “was attributed … to” and the quoted cause make the reasoning explicit.
main_claim: The sudden redeployment call happened because FAAB had been pressuring higher headquarters for months.

argument_text: Six high-ranking officers, however, are expected to leave before the end of this month because of maximum age requirements as stated in a recent War Department letter.
explanation: This sentence gives a conclusion (the officers are expected to leave) and an explicit reason (maximum age requirements in a War Department letter). The cue “because of” marks the argument structure.
main_claim: Six high-ranking officers will depart this month due to War Department maximum age requirements.

argument_text: Although the shipment of surplus officers left few gaps in staff or other key positions, there was a serious loss of flying personnel.
explanation: The concessive contrast (“Although … there was …”) implies an evaluative claim: despite minimal staffing gaps, the shipment negatively impacted flying capacity. The premise is minimal staff/key position gaps; the conclusion is that the shipment nevertheless caused a serious loss in flying personnel, signaling a problematic outcome.
main_claim: Despite few staff gaps, the shipment significantly harmed flying personnel capacity.

argument_text: "We have only fifty-five flying officers left," said Captain Henry M. Rollins of the S-3 Office, "and only nineteen of these are first pilots. These men will have to do a great deal more flying to keep up the courier runs, and they will have to share the clearance officer and tower officer jobs besides."
explanation: This provides premises (only 55 flying officers remain, only 19 are first pilots) leading to conclusions (they must fly more and take on additional roles). The necessity claims (“will have to”) are directly inferred from the quantified shortages.
main_claim: Because there are very few flying officers and first pilots left, the remaining pilots must increase their flying and also share additional officer duties.

argument_text: The square alongside the Headquarters Building was packed as the civilians heard the orchestra play selections from Carmen, the Barber of Seville, and popular pieces like Stardust, among others. First of its kind in Foggia, the performance was enthusiastically received by the music-loving populace.
explanation: This pairs an observational premise (“The square ... was packed”) with an evaluative conclusion (“the performance was enthusiastically received”). The causal connection is implied rather than stated explicitly; the descriptor “music-loving populace” further signals a stance that generalizes from the turnout and reaction. Together, these cues suggest an argument that the concert was a success because of the large and positive audience response.
main_claim: The performance was enthusiastically received by Foggia's populace.

argument_text: "Wives who recently arrived here from America are visiting the patients at the hospital six times a week in a new and very successful program," said Miss Elizabeth Thornton, Red Cross Director at the 55th Station Hospital. "The wives," said Miss Thornton, "just started coming and accompanied me on tours of the wards as I wheeled the book and refreshment carts through the wards. Now we have it arranged so that two or more wives take the carts through the hospital every day except Sunday. The patients have said they like the idea so much that some of the wives are now trying their hands at leatherwork and doll dressing. Some even want to do wood carving and iron casting with the patients."
explanation: The passage advances the evaluative claim that the program is “very successful,” and supports it with indications of patient approval and increased volunteer engagement. Although not framed with explicit “because” wording, the premises are: patients report liking the idea; frequency and regularity of service have increased; wives are expanding into crafts and activities with patients. These cues implicitly support the conclusion that the program is successful and beneficial.
main_claim: The wives’ hospital-visiting program is very successful and beneficial.

argument_text: The patients have said they like the idea so much that some of the wives are now trying their hands at leatherwork and doll dressing. Some even want to do wood carving and iron casting with the patients.
explanation: This passage argues, via causal and degree language (“so much that,” “even”), that patient enthusiasm is high and has prompted expanded volunteer activities. The implicit claim is that the program is popular/valuable, with the premises being reported patient approval and volunteers undertaking additional crafts as a consequence.
main_claim: The program is popular with patients, prompting wives to expand into additional therapeutic activities.

argument_text: We spoke at length to some of them, officers and enlisted men, and saw how and where they are living. They have some pretty good gripes, too.
explanation: This presents a conclusion (“They have some pretty good gripes, too.”) supported by the preceding premise that the writer personally interviewed personnel and inspected their living conditions. The evaluative language “pretty good gripes” implies the claims are justified without laying out full explicit premises, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: The 442nd’s complaints are justified based on firsthand observation of their living conditions.

argument_text: After one of the finest and cleanest combat records in the European theater, they took their hitch in Leghorn, "which wasn't bad, considering..." They were led to believe that they were going home, but it turned out that only a token force went to the zone of the Interior, and the rest ended up in Foggia.
explanation: The passage contrasts exemplary service and expectations of going home with the outcome of being sent to Foggia. The evaluative framing (“finest and cleanest combat records” and “led to believe”) implies a normative claim that they deserved repatriation or were treated unfairly. The conclusion is implied rather than stated outright.
main_claim: Despite deserving repatriation and being led to expect it, most of the 442nd were unfairly kept in Italy and sent to Foggia.

argument_text: In all fairness to living in tents in that sandy wasteland, we have to say that it is no worse than conditions combat troops endured out there during the war. But the war is over, and while the 442nd never shied away from combat, they can see little reason for living like that now.
explanation: The passage presents a concession (tent life comparable to wartime) and then a contrasting premise (the war is over; the unit did not avoid combat) leading to a stated conclusion (“they can see little reason for living like that now”). The structure is explicit: premises followed by a normative conclusion.
main_claim: There is little justification for making the 442nd live in tent conditions now that the war is over.

argument_text: They look at the sweet condition of the troops living in town: clean and comfortable rooms, good plumbing, clean mess halls, plenty of nightclubs and theaters, and good access to the ARC. Then they see their own quarters: tents, hot and barely furnished, with five men sharing one tent. Drinking and washing water comes from the mess hall or the latrine. Their supply room, where they are to draw clean sheets, is a weak-looking shack with plenty of holes for ventilation and dirt, and the floor is a dusty mass of white chalk that makes it impossible to keep fresh sheets clean.
explanation: The detailed contrast between comfortable in-town accommodations and the 442nd’s poor conditions implies a normative judgment of inequity/unfairness. The passage uses selective evidence and comparison to suggest the conclusion without stating it explicitly.
main_claim: The 442nd’s living conditions are unreasonably inferior and inequitable compared to other troops in town.

argument_text: One of their officers, pointing to the condition of the small mess, said, "The place is too little for feeding over 150 men, and the POWs eat there too. It is impossible to keep clean, and I'm worried about dysentery starting. I tried to build a new mess hall, but I was refused materials and laborers. One reason is that they don't want any permanent building." He went on to explain that lumber for other projects was "on requisition," but not available yet.
explanation: The officer provides premises (overcrowding, shared use with POWs, inability to keep clean, fear of dysentery, refusal of materials due to non-permanent building policy) leading to an implied but clear conclusion that a new mess hall is needed and current policy/denials are endangering health. The argument is explicit in its causal reasoning and problem statement.
main_claim: The 442nd needs a proper mess facility because the current one is unsanitary and too small, and denying building materials on policy grounds risks disease.

argument_text: Said one of the boys, "The German POWs on the field have modern conveniences, running water and all. I saw a Special Service radio in one of those tents, and when I took it away, they made me return it. Special Service refused to give me a radio, however." PBS Special Service has not authorized FAAB to give them equipment.
explanation: The juxtaposition that German POWs have “modern conveniences” and radios while the 442nd is denied similar equipment implies an argument about unfair or inverted priorities. The conclusion—this is unjust or inappropriate—is suggested by the contrast, not stated directly.
main_claim: It is unfair that POWs receive better amenities and access to equipment than the 442nd, who are denied similar support.

argument_text: 442nd men claim to be sticklers for organization, and as they laugh at the way things are being run, they point out another fallacy that no one seems to notice. "All our boys," said a sergeant, "are in the 18 to 24-month category. Now they're taking riflemen and training them to be desk clerks and interior pool attendants. By the time they are trained in these new jobs, they'll go home and we'll have to start all over again."
explanation: The sergeant states premises (short remaining service time; retraining riflemen for non-combat roles) leading to a clear conclusion (“By the time they are trained… they’ll go home and we’ll have to start all over again”), explicitly arguing that the policy is inefficient.
main_claim: Retraining short-term 442nd riflemen for clerical and pool jobs is inefficient because they will leave before the training pays off.

argument_text: All of the discontent explains some of the flare-ups that have occurred in town, surprising in view of their spotless conduct record in Italy.
explanation: This is a direct causal claim: the premise (discontent) is asserted to explain the conclusion (recent flare-ups), with an appeal to their prior spotless record to underscore the explanatory power.
main_claim: The unit’s recent flare-ups in town are due to their discontent, despite their previously spotless record.

argument_text: A few civilians, surprised to see boys of oriental descent, have passed some pretty nasty remarks on the spur of the moment. The boys, who take a fierce pride in their Americanism, have tried whipping a few of the hecklers.
explanation: The sequence suggests a causal and partial justificatory argument: offensive civilian remarks, triggered by prejudice, led proud American soldiers to retaliate. The conclusion—that the altercations were provoked and thus understandable—is implied by the causal framing, not stated.
main_claim: The altercations with civilians were provoked by racist remarks and the soldiers’ pride in their American identity, making their reactions understandable.

argument_text: We've called too many outfits Lost Battalions to tag the 442nd with that, but the Front Office would do well to look out their way once in a while.
explanation: This sentence delivers an explicit recommendation (“the Front Office would do well to look out their way once in a while”), supported by the implied premise that the 442nd should not be neglected like “Lost Battalions.” The argumentative intent is clear: leadership should pay attention.
main_claim: Higher headquarters should pay attention to the 442nd’s situation.

argument_text: Our pipes gleaming with hoar frost in the interior of Foggia's ice plant prove that the place is operating if the whirring of the electric motor and the swish-flap of the spinning fly-wheel belt leave any doubt.
explanation: The sentence offers evidence (hoar frost on pipes, whirring motor, swish-flap of belt) to support the conclusion that the plant is operating, using “prove” to mark the inference. This is a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The ice plant is operating.

argument_text: "Some of the cans still leak, and we haven't got enough RPMs. We ought to be able to turn out a batch every twenty-four hours, but the best we can do right now is one every thirty."
explanation: This links causes (leaking cans, insufficient RPMs) to an outcome (slower production cycle), explicitly contrasting the ideal (“ought... every twenty-four hours”) with the current reality (“one every thirty”). The premises are directly connected to the conclusion about production limits.
main_claim: Due to leaks and low RPMs, the plant can only produce a batch every thirty hours instead of the expected twenty-four.

argument_text:
It doesn't go into drinks, however.

"The medics declared it inedible," said Lanier, showing us the storeroom. He indicated the stacks of sixty-pound blocks. "It looks clean," he said, "but you know you can't judge anything by that. The medics said it's inedible, so I guess it is."
explanation: This is an argument from authority and against appearance: the conclusion (ice is not used in drinks/is inedible) is justified by the premise that medics declared it inedible, with an additional premise that appearance is not a reliable indicator (“you can't judge anything by that”). The “so” marks the inferential step.
main_claim: The ice should not be used for drinking because medics have declared it inedible, regardless of its clean appearance.

argument_text:
We were walking home from the office pretty late one night this week, and as we rounded the corner near the Red Cross, we saw a large civilian truck and trailer halted in front of the MP station. The MP's objection was that the truck was going the wrong way on a one-way street. Although the driver objected that the only one-way sign had been pointing the other way, he was made to back his truck and trailer up the main street.

Three blocks further on, we saw—as we had seen often before—a couple of drunken soldiers staggering down the street, making passes at every civilian who got near them. But here there were no MPs. We suggest that the MPs step out of their station more often at night.
explanation: The narrative juxtaposes strict enforcement against a civilian traffic infraction with lack of response to disorderly soldiers, implying misplaced enforcement priorities. This supports the explicit recommendation (“We suggest...”) that MPs should patrol more at night. The premises (observations of enforcement vs. non-enforcement) lead to a normative conclusion, though the criticism of priorities is implied rather than directly stated.
main_claim: MPs should patrol outside their station more often at night to address disorderly conduct rather than focusing only on minor infractions.

argument_text: Business: Advice to veterans planning to start small businesses is given in a new book by Sidney Margolius, "A Fresh Start." The ex-GI, who is an expert in his field, says that two main factors in the failure of small businesses are (1) lack of adequate financing and (2) lack of technical knowledge.
explanation: This advances a normative/causal claim about why small businesses fail, attributed to an expert. The premise is the author’s expertise; the conclusion is that the two main failure factors are inadequate financing and technical knowledge. The because-structure is implicit via authority, but the claim is stated directly.
main_claim: The primary reasons small businesses fail are inadequate financing and lack of technical knowledge.

argument_text: The big question is not how much it costs to go into business, but "how much does it take to stay there". Funds are needed not only to buy property and equipment but to pay the overhead and promotion costs while a trade is being built up.
explanation: This presents a prescriptive reframing (the real question should be staying in business) supported by reasons (ongoing needs like overhead and promotion). The second sentence provides the premises that support the conclusion that staying-power costs matter more than entry costs.
main_claim: Entrepreneurs should focus on how much it takes to stay in business rather than just startup costs.

argument_text: Says the author, the 3,000 and 5,000 dollars of which many ex-GIs speak when planning businesses are barely enough to cover initial operating funds of most businesses. As an example, the author gives several typical minimum investments (all in dollars): Restaurants, 300 per seat; Clothing Shops, 5,000 to 8,500; Hardware Stores, 6,000; Furniture Store, 8,000 to 12,000; Drug Stores (with fountains) 7,500; Food Markets, 5,000 to 12,000; Cleaning-Pressing, 3,000 to 5,000; Filling Stations (leased) 2,500 to 6,000.
explanation: The first sentence states a conclusion about the insufficiency of $3–5k; the second provides concrete cost figures as evidence. The structure is data supporting the claim that typical businesses require more capital, making the stated sums barely sufficient for initial operating funds.
main_claim: The $3,000–$5,000 many ex-GIs plan to invest is barely enough to cover initial operating funds for most small businesses.

argument_text: Aviation: Skippers in the Pacific Coast "tuna fleet" are planning to employ their own planes to scout the seas and report the movement of schools of fish. Desiring to continue the wartime practice established by Navy blimps which radioed the location of tuna schools spotted from the air, progressive captains are looking for ex-service pilots who specialized in liaison and observation work.
explanation: The passage implies that using aircraft to scout is effective and thus worth adopting, based on the precedent of successful wartime blimp spotting. The premises are the wartime practice and specialized pilot skills; the unstated conclusion is that adopting similar aerial scouting will improve tuna fishing operations.
main_claim: Tuna fleet captains should adopt aerial scouting (by hiring ex-service pilots) because wartime air-spotting proved effective.

argument_text: Merger: Unofficial reports from Washington take a dim view of the possibility of an Army-Navy-Air Force merger in the near future. Hottest objections have been coming from influential Naval personnel, whose chief objection has recently been 'the independence of the Air Force on a merger agreement. Secretary of War Patterson has been insisting on a true merger, while Secretary of the Navy Forrestal would concede only to a Minister of Common Defense with vague powers to "co-ordinate" the effort of the War and Navy Departments. Washington reporters state that the merger bill cannot be passed through the divided Congress while the chairmen of the House and Senate Naval Affairs Committees put the spikes into all bills on the subject. If a bill passes at all, they predict, it will be on the Navy's watery concession.
explanation: This advances a prediction about legislative outcomes. The premises are (a) strong Naval opposition, (b) disagreement between War and Navy leaders, and (c) committee chairs blocking bills in a divided Congress. From these, it concludes that a full merger is unlikely and only a watered-down version might pass. Cues include causal attribution and forecast language.
main_claim: Because of Naval opposition and congressional gatekeeping, a true merger is unlikely and only a watered-down Navy-favored version could pass.

argument_text: Sports: St. Louis fans are optimistic this year. The Cardinals have sold 10,000 advanced ticket books, assuring the owners of seats at the World Series.
explanation: This presents a conclusion (fans are optimistic) supported by evidence (high advance ticket book sales that secure World Series seats). The second sentence functions as a premise explaining the basis for the stated optimism.
main_claim: St. Louis fans are optimistic, as shown by their purchase of 10,000 advance ticket books guaranteeing World Series seats.

argument_text: Employment: The Supreme Court ruled that the Selective Service Act does not confer superseniority on veterans over non-veterans who held jobs while the vets were away. Justice William O. Douglas ruled that the veteran had the same status he would have held if he had not been drafted (time in service counting as time on the job), but that he could not claim greater seniority than a man who had been on the job a longer time than the vet's employment time plus his service time.
explanation: This is a legal argument summarizing the Court’s reasoning: the statute restores veterans to the status they would have had absent service (premise), therefore it does not grant superseniority over longer-serving employees (conclusion). The second sentence articulates how service time counts but does not exceed others’ tenure.
main_claim: The Selective Service Act restores veterans to their pre-service status but does not give them superseniority over longer-tenured non-veterans.

argument_text: Food: A new "E" ration has been developed to replace the famed "K" as a combat field ration. The new food is more compact and is packed like a sardine can, the development being the result of a recent conference in which 75 veterans came from overseas to advise the Quartermaster General on improvements in present rations.
explanation: This implies that consulting veterans led to practical improvements in rations (more compact design), suggesting the value of veteran input. The causal phrasing “the development being the result of” links the conference to the improved ration, supporting the unstated claim that such consultation is beneficial.
main_claim: Involving overseas veterans in advising the Quartermaster General yields improved, more compact combat rations.

argument_text: Commando Card is now being toted by regular visitors to the ARC enlisted men's club.
explanation: This sentence uses social proof framing: by stating that "regular visitors" carry the card, it implies that carrying the Commando Card is the norm or desirable. The implied premise is that practices adopted by regulars are worth emulating; the unstated conclusion is that you should also tote the card. The argument is implicit because no explicit recommendation is stated.
main_claim: You should carry the Commando Card because regular visitors already do.

argument_text: The girls punch your card as you endure each "mission" and a perfect score entitles you to one of the Bloody Ex badges.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal incentive: completing all missions leads to a tangible reward (a badge). By highlighting the entitlement upon a perfect score, it implicitly argues that aiming for or completing the missions is worthwhile. The conclusion (you should participate/strive for a perfect score) is implied rather than stated.
main_claim: It’s worth completing all the missions on the Commando Card because a perfect score earns you a badge.

argument_text: In these hot summer days, a tour of the ARC is not hard to take.
explanation: This evaluative statement implies a recommendation: because of the hot summer weather, visiting the ARC is pleasant or easy to enjoy. The premise is the heat; the conclusion is that touring the ARC is agreeable and thus desirable. The suggestion to visit is implied through positive evaluation, not directly stated.
main_claim: Visiting the ARC is a good/pleasant idea in the hot summer weather.

argument_text: Service men or veterans desiring to enroll in a foreign institution (whether it's listed above or not) should request complete information from the Veterans Administration, Washington 25, D.C. as to whether it is an approved school.
explanation: This passage uses the prescriptive “should,” implying an ought-claim. The underlying premise is that only VA-approved institutions qualify under the GI Bill; therefore, to ensure eligibility/benefits, one ought to verify approval with the VA. The argument is implicit because the reasoning (approval is required to get benefits) is suggested by context rather than stated.
main_claim: Prospective students should contact the VA to verify that a foreign school is approved before enrolling.

argument_text: Men desiring entry in approved organizations must make all arrangements directly with the school, and must arrange with the State Department for necessary visas and passports.
explanation: This directive uses “must,” asserting obligations. The implied reasoning is that enrollment logistics and legal travel documentation are the individual’s responsibility and handled by those entities; therefore, the student must take these actions. The premises are not laid out explicitly, making the argument implicit.
main_claim: Applicants are responsible for arranging school enrollment and obtaining visas and passports through the State Department.

argument_text: The student is entitled to the same benefits granted men studying in American schools, but the Veterans Administration will not pay any additional costs, such as travel expenses.
explanation: The contrastive “but” frames a normative expectation: although benefits are equal, there are limits; thus students should not expect coverage of extras. The implied reasoning is that VA benefits apply equivalently across locations but do not extend to additional costs. This is an implicit argument because the cautionary conclusion (do not expect travel cost coverage) is suggested rather than argued with explicit premises.
main_claim: While students abroad receive the same benefits as in U.S. schools, the VA will not cover additional costs like travel.

argument_text: Umberto II left Italy last week, and in spite of his charges of fraud in the elections and his hints that he had not given up hope of regaining the throne, Italy remained quiet.
explanation: This sentence juxtaposes Umberto’s allegations and aspirations with the public’s quiet reaction, implying a conclusion that his claims did not resonate widely or destabilize the country. The contrastive cue “in spite of” signals an argumentative framing: if fraud charges and monarchist hopes were compelling, unrest would follow; since “Italy remained quiet,” the implied claim is that support is minimal or the transition is stable.
main_claim: The Italian public did not support or act on Umberto’s fraud claims or hopes to regain the throne, indicating political stability or lack of resonance.

argument_text: Premier De Gasperi broadcast to the nation his shame in "the tragedy of that man" Umberto "as part of the national catastrophe," and asked the nation for unity.
explanation: The negative evaluation of Umberto as part of a “national catastrophe” functions as a premise supporting the recommendation that the nation should unite. The “asked the nation for unity” is a normative conclusion, with the evaluative language providing the reason, though the causal link is implied rather than explicitly spelled out.
main_claim: Given the harm associated with Umberto’s situation, Italians should unite.

argument_text: He bemoaned the fact that the world price of grain has climbed from 71 to 90 dollars a ton, and that the Italian Government, which is paying for all that, will have to make up the deficit in exports.
explanation: This presents premises (grain prices have risen; the Italian government must pay) leading to a conclusion/implication (Italy will have to compensate via exports). The causal necessity is explicit in “will have to make up the deficit in exports,” and “bemoaned” adds evaluative force that this outcome is problematic.
main_claim: Rising grain prices will force Italy to cover higher costs by increasing export-driven compensation, creating a burdensome deficit to make up.

argument_text: Mr. Stone also assured the Italians that he was attempting to speed shipments of sugar, dry legumes, fish, evaporated milk, fertilizer, and insecticides.
explanation: The assurance that shipments will be sped implies an underlying problem (insufficient or slow deliveries) and a normative claim that accelerating shipments is necessary or beneficial. The argument is embedded: because current supply speed is inadequate, it is appropriate to accelerate deliveries.
main_claim: Shipments of essential goods to Italy need to be accelerated to meet needs.

argument_text: Lucera had a courthouse fire last week when a man, Angelo Pavone, on a charge of theft, was bribed by other people under indictment to burn the records.
explanation: This sentence provides a causal explanation: the courthouse fire occurred because a defendant, bribed by other indicted individuals, burned records. The structure directly links the event (fire) to its cause (bribery-induced arson), forming an explicit causal argument.
main_claim: The courthouse fire in Lucera was caused by bribery that led Pavone to burn court records.

argument_text: Miss Lace, that bosom buddy of GIs throughout the war years. Her creator, Milton Caniff (a civilian during the war because he was too old for service) who gave his all for the little guy, decided to accept his ruptured duck, and along with him went Lace.
explanation: This passage frames Caniff’s civilian status (too old for service) alongside the evaluative claim that he “gave his all for the little guy,” implicitly arguing that, despite not serving in uniform, he contributed significantly to GIs through Miss Lace (described as a “bosom buddy of GIs”). The pairing of popularity with GIs and the “gave his all” phrasing functions as premises supporting the conclusion that his civilian work amounted to meaningful service.
main_claim: Milton Caniff significantly served and supported GIs through his work, even though he was a civilian too old for military service.

argument_text: We wish her all the best, and (to anyone else who leaves this place) we hope she doesn't have to come back again.
explanation: The expressed hope that she (and others) won’t “have to come back again” implies a normative stance that returning would be undesirable and that departures should be final—implicitly advocating for a future without circumstances (e.g., renewed conflict or recall) that would force a return. The hope functions as a recommendation/ought-claim, signaling a conclusion about what should happen.
main_claim: Those who leave should not have to return, implying that a peaceful, final departure is preferable.

argument_text: leaving the Navy Yard in 1942 to come back in the army to serve with the 19th Tactical Air Command with General Patton's Third Army, and the 29th Tactical Air Command with General Simpson's 9th Army, as a combat intelligence officer. He was one of the people that really knew what was getting on.
explanation: The concluding claim that he “really knew what was getting on” is supported by the preceding credentials and roles as a combat intelligence officer with major commands. The reasoning is implied: extensive, high-level intelligence service entails deep knowledge.
main_claim: Captain Scull was highly knowledgeable about military matters.

argument_text: The Captain wears the bronze star, the A.T.O. ribbon, the E.T.O. ribbon with six battle stars, the Occupation ribbon, the Victory medal, and the Belgium fourragère and two citations awarded to him for the Battle of the Bulge. He also participated in the air invasion of Europe and the Normandy campaign. Captain Scull has been overseas four times. He's been to Hawaii, Panama, and this is his second trip to Europe. Altogether, he has spent twenty-two months overseas. Quite a record.
explanation: The evaluative conclusion “Quite a record” is supported by a catalog of medals, campaigns, and tours. The list functions as evidence for the assessment that his service record is impressive.
main_claim: Captain Scull’s service record is impressive.

argument_text: He doesn't need to copy anyone, as he has a very fine style of his own.
explanation: This uses an explicit causal connector (“as”) to justify the claim: because he has a fine personal style, he need not copy others.
main_claim: Charlie Ventura does not need to imitate other musicians.

argument_text: There is a little of Gillespie in his work but a lot more of Ventura, and there are a lot of young tenor men who are trying vainly to get that Ventura in their own horns.
explanation: The contrast with Gillespie and the observation that others “try vainly” imply the conclusion that Ventura’s style is distinctive and difficult to emulate. The argument is suggested through contrast and reported imitation failures.
main_claim: Ventura’s style is uniquely his and hard for others to imitate.
