argument_text: He seems to be able to do just about everything he wants to with the horn from great section work to inspired, brilliant solo work both on fast or slow stuff.
explanation: The general claim of near-unlimited ability is supported within the sentence by specific examples (section work, brilliant solos, fast and slow), implying versatility and mastery.
main_claim: Ventura can handle virtually any musical demand on the tenor saxophone.

argument_text: Charlie is fine both in big band stuff or small band work. His fine work with the Krupa Trio continually amazes everyone.
explanation: The first sentence claims versatility across ensemble sizes; the second provides evidence (Krupa Trio performances that amaze), implying that his excellence extends beyond large ensembles.
main_claim: Charlie Ventura excels in both large and small ensemble settings.

argument_text: His amazing speed, technique, and ideas make him one of the outstanding musicians of the day.
explanation: This is a direct causal argument: his speed, technique, and ideas are cited as reasons that lead to the conclusion that he is among the outstanding musicians.
main_claim: Charlie Ventura is one of the outstanding musicians of the day.

argument_text: Without a doubt, he is a musician to watch.
explanation: This recommendation is an evaluative conclusion grounded in prior descriptions of skill and innovation; the reasoning is not stated here but presupposed by the preceding evidence.
main_claim: Audiences should pay attention to Charlie Ventura’s career trajectory.

argument_text: A comparative newcomer to the music business, Ventura is already a capable and natural musician.
explanation: The concessive framing (“comparative newcomer” yet “already capable and natural”) implies a contrast-based argument: despite limited time in the field, he demonstrates notable innate ability.
main_claim: Ventura is already a capable, natural musician despite being relatively new.

argument_text: If he ever steps out with his own group, there's going to be a lot more good jazz music to be heard.
explanation: This prediction relies on implied premises about Ventura’s talent and potential leadership; the causal link (forming a group will increase good jazz) is suggested, not elaborated.
main_claim: Ventura leading his own group would result in more good jazz being produced or heard.

argument_text: So hats off to Charlie Ventura and let's hear more of him.
explanation: This is a normative recommendation inferred from preceding praise; the “So” signals a conclusion from earlier evaluative evidence.
main_claim: The audience should celebrate Ventura and seek to hear more of his music.

argument_text: Another guy you're going to hear more of is David Fenton, one of our announcers, who has already taken over such favorites as the Make Believe Ballroom, every afternoon at 4:30, and Reflections In Music every Saturday evening from 9:30 to 10:00.
explanation: The prediction that we’ll hear more of Fenton is supported by the evidence that he has taken over popular shows; the causal relationship is implied within the sentence.
main_claim: David Fenton is on the rise because he is already hosting popular radio programs.

argument_text: So keep listening for two newcomers to their trade, and they're both good too: Charlie Ventura, tenor sax; David Fenton, announcer.
explanation: The directive “keep listening” is a recommendation grounded in the assertion that both are good newcomers; the “So” indicates this follows from prior evidence of their quality.
main_claim: Listeners should keep tuning in because Ventura and Fenton are talented newcomers.

argument_text: USFET Attempts To Nip Black Markets By Tightening Up On Transmitted Funds
explanation: This headline frames a causal and instrumental relation: tightening controls on transmitted funds is presented as a means to reduce (“nip”) black markets. The evaluative verb “nip” and the “by” construction imply a policy justification. The premises (tightening transmitted funds) support the implied conclusion (black markets will be curtailed).
main_claim: Tightening controls on transmitted funds will curb black markets.

argument_text: Large scale black market operations in Germany were suggested by finance officials here as the main reason behind the change.
explanation: This sentence explicitly provides a reason-for relation: because there are large-scale black market operations in Germany, the policy change (new Currency Control Books) is warranted. It states a cause (“main reason”) for the action, forming a clear premise-to-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The change to the currency control system is justified by large-scale black market operations in Germany.

argument_text: "We cannot look to a world of freedom and security in the midst of famine and impoverishment."
explanation: This sentence advances a normative-causal claim: the presence of famine and impoverishment prevents or undermines freedom and security. The structure is explicit because it presents an inference: not being able to “look to” (achieve/expect) freedom and security because we are “in the midst of famine and impoverishment.” The phrase “in the midst of” functions as the reason for the conclusion that freedom and security cannot be realized.
main_claim: Freedom and security cannot be realized while famine and impoverishment persist.

argument_text: June 29 — "To avoid an epidemic and safeguard the health of the military personnel, all men under thirty-five will receive the Diphtheria shots during the month of July, according to a recent War Department circular," stated Capt. Luis Diaz, Base Surgeon.
explanation: This sentence presents a clear reason (to avoid an epidemic and safeguard health) supporting a policy conclusion (all men under thirty-five will receive shots in July). The structure is explicit: the purpose/premise is given first, followed by the mandated action as the conclusion.
main_claim: All men under thirty-five will receive Diphtheria shots during July.

argument_text: during which time they combined business with pleasure, playing at various stops along the way.
explanation: This passage advances the evaluative claim that the trip served both leisure and work purposes (“combined business with pleasure”) and supports it with evidence (“playing at various stops along the way”). The structure implies justification for the vacation’s legitimacy or productivity by citing performances as evidence, though it does not explicitly present a premise–conclusion connector, hence implicit.
main_claim: The band’s Swiss vacation was justified as both leisure and work because they performed at various stops.

argument_text: Colonel Robert Martin, Commanding Officer of FAAB, stated that the suspension of the Saturday morning reviews was due to the absence of the band.
explanation: This is an explicit causal justification: the conclusion is that Saturday morning reviews were suspended, with the stated reason (premise) being the band’s absence. The phrase “was due to” signals a clear premise-to-conclusion relationship.
main_claim: Saturday morning reviews were suspended because the band was absent.

argument_text: Foggia's 'Uncle Joe' Hamilton, ARC Director, will close the refreshment counter on orders from ARC Headquarters in Rome, which cited the "general world food shortages and greatly reduced appropriated funds" as the reason for the closure.
explanation: This sentence presents a clear premise-conclusion structure: the premises are "general world food shortages" and "greatly reduced appropriated funds," and the conclusion is that the snack bar will be closed. The causal connector "as the reason for the closure" makes the argument explicit.
main_claim: The snack bar is being closed because of global food shortages and reduced funding.

argument_text: However, an open letter to local ARC directors from Washington in May had hinted at a cut in food dispensing since the Army, which is now paying for civilian labor in Red Cross clubs, is attempting to nip expenses.
explanation: This sentence explicitly links the Army’s cost-cutting motive to anticipated cuts in food dispensing via the causal connector "since," yielding an argument that cuts are motivated by expense reduction.
main_claim: Cuts in food dispensing are motivated by the Army’s effort to reduce expenses.

argument_text: The local Theater command, in turn, had refused to pay the wages of snack bar employees.
explanation: While phrased as a factual report, it implies that without local funding for wages, operating the snack bar is untenable, thus supporting the closure decision. The unstated conclusion is that this refusal necessitates or contributes to closure.
main_claim: The local command’s refusal to fund snack bar wages helps necessitate closing the snack bar.

argument_text: Local military personnel were taking a pessimistic view of the end of this incentive to visit the ARC, and Mr. Hamilton quoted a Military Police officer as predicting that drunkenness in the Foggia area would rise 10%.
explanation: This presents a prediction that implies a causal argument: removing the snack bar (an incentive to visit the ARC and a sober alternative) will lead to increased drunkenness. The causal link is suggested rather than explicitly spelled out.
main_claim: Closing the snack bar will cause a 10% increase in drunkenness in the Foggia area.

argument_text: Stationed at the hospital since October 1945, they have proven their efficiency and capability in the various duties assigned to them. Maintaining their own hospital with two of their own doctors, they also worked in the American hospital as ward boys, mess attendants, cooks, and in various other capacities.
explanation: This passage advances an evaluative claim (“they have proven their efficiency and capability”) and immediately lists concrete activities (maintaining their own hospital; working as ward boys, mess attendants, cooks, etc.) that function as reasons. Although no explicit connective like “because” is used, the juxtaposition of the claim with supporting examples implies a reasoning structure: their range of competent service demonstrates efficiency and capability.
main_claim: The Austrian POWs demonstrated efficiency and capability in their assigned duties.

argument_text: "We chose to adopt this orphanage in particular," said Elizabeth Thornton, ARC Director at the hospital, "because we felt a responsibility for these babies whose American fathers had deserted them."
explanation: The statement presents a conclusion (choosing to adopt this particular orphanage) supported by a reason introduced by "because" (a felt responsibility for babies deserted by American fathers). The causal connector makes the argumentative structure explicit.
main_claim: The 55th Station Hospital adopted this orphanage because they felt responsible for babies deserted by American fathers.

argument_text: "Conditions are truly tragic," said Miss Thornton. "Some of the babies are just pale, pasty-looking things, and they just lie there. They have come from various sources - many of them were brought in by people who found them in the fields or by the shore, where their mothers had deserted them. Some had been lying unattended for days. There were a few who would not live."
explanation: The claim "Conditions are truly tragic" is immediately supported by concrete observations (babies’ appearance, abandonment, unattended for days, some dying), functioning as premises that justify the evaluative conclusion. Although no "because" is used, the evidence is explicitly marshaled to support the claim, forming a clear argument.
main_claim: The children's conditions at the orphanage are truly tragic.

argument_text: Says Miss Thornton, "People who visit the home now for the first time are shocked at the sight of such poverty in children, but now that I've seen some of the children grow, I can tell of the progress made in some of them. Those tiny starving things have grown, and although they are still pale and small, they sit up now and play around a bit."
explanation: The conclusion is that progress has been made among the children, supported by premises describing observable improvements (growth, ability to sit up and play), contrasted with ongoing poverty that shocks first-time visitors. The "but" signals the argumentative contrast leading to the claim of progress.
main_claim: Despite ongoing poverty, the children have made progress, as shown by their growth and increased activity.

argument_text: The Geneva Convention occupied the busy medics at the Base Dispensary during the last few days, and such a diversion of interest prompted us to pay them a call to satisfy our curiosity.
explanation: This sentence provides a clear reason-conclusion structure: because the Geneva Convention occupied the medics and diverted interest, the authors visited to satisfy curiosity. It advances a claim about their action being justified by a specific cause.
main_claim: We visited the dispensary because the medics’ preoccupation with the Geneva Convention made us curious.

argument_text: A rather sinister smile came from Cpl. Wilmer as he advanced towards us, weapon in hand, "Sweating it out I see, well you should have thought it over before."
explanation: The remark “you should have thought it over before” implies a normative judgment: those now anxious about medical treatment (suggested by the VD posters and injection context) should have considered their prior behavior. The premise is the current discomfort; the implied conclusion is that this discomfort is a deserved consequence of earlier choices.
main_claim: People anxious about receiving treatment for consequences of their conduct should have considered the risks beforehand.

argument_text: The Corporal retreated to his desk, picked up a couple of small glass containers, and began the process of destruction, using a pair of scissors for a hammer. We wasted no time and made a quick departure.
explanation: The juxtaposition creates an implicit reason-conclusion link: because the medic was breaking glass using scissors as a hammer (suggesting unsafe or alarming behavior), the narrators immediately left. The action is justified by the preceding description.
main_claim: Observing potentially unsafe conduct by the medic justified our immediate departure.

argument_text: As we stepped into the waiting room, Pfc. Ed Booth, Assistant Base Sanitation Inspector, with that grin (after effects of extreme indulgence in that potent stuff) shouted, "The Geneva Convention stated so."
explanation: The parenthetical offers a causal attribution: Ed Booth’s grin is due to the after effects of heavy drinking (“that potent stuff”). This is an implied causal argument linking the observed grin to prior indulgence.
main_claim: Ed Booth’s grin is caused by lingering effects of strong drink.

argument_text: Ed Booth, one of the remaining Pfc's on the Base, recognized us. Perhaps it was our magnetic personality that convinced him to inform us about the drastic measures certain people have taken in violating the Geneva Convention according to the Medic's claim.
explanation: This passage reports a claim that “drastic measures” taken by “certain people” violate the Geneva Convention, attributed to the medics. While reasons are not spelled out here, the wording frames an accusation and implies wrongdoing with a legal-normative standard (the Convention) as the basis.
main_claim: Certain actions have violated the Geneva Convention, at least according to the medics’ account.

argument_text: An injustice was done to them, so they claimed when they were notified to stand guard duty at the Headquarters and Base Squadron gate. The Medics felt that they were not called for extracurricular activity of such a nature where firearms were involved.
explanation: This presents a clear argument attributed to the medics: conclusion—assigning them to guard duty is an injustice; premise—medics are not meant for extracurricular activities involving firearms. The second sentence provides the rationale for the injustice claim.
main_claim: Assigning medics to armed guard duty is unjust because medics are not meant to perform firearm-involved extracurricular activities.

argument_text: These ex-gunners and mechanics, now attached to the Base Dispensary, received approximately a hundred and ten hours of basic instructions in the Medical Department from Lt. Frank Crider, Assistant Base Surgeon. The boys are proud and happy in this new venture of theirs in Medicine, be it Sanitation, Malaria Control, First Aid, or Pro Stations.
explanation: By emphasizing their retraining and commitment to medical roles, the passage implicitly supports the earlier claim that their duties should be medical rather than armed guard work. The implied conclusion is that their professional identity and training make non-medical assignments inappropriate.
main_claim: Given their training and commitment to medical roles, these men should be assigned to medical duties rather than tasks like armed guard duty.

argument_text: We learned to our amusement what the Geneva Convention was all about, as far as the Medics were concerned.
explanation: The phrasing “to our amusement” and “as far as the Medics were concerned” implies skepticism toward the medics’ interpretation of the Geneva Convention, suggesting it may be self-serving or exaggerated. This frames an evaluative stance without explicit reasons.
main_claim: The medics’ interpretation of the Geneva Convention is viewed as somewhat self-serving or amusing by the narrator.

argument_text: He was with a crash crew on the line, and we wondered if the corporal treated any of those casualties resulting from air mishaps. "All we got out were either dead or all right," Kelley stated.
explanation: This passage implies a conclusion without stating it directly. The reported wondering poses an implicit question about whether Kelley treated casualties. Kelley's response provides the premise: the people they extracted were either already dead or uninjured. From this, it follows that there were no treatable casualties, supporting the implicit conclusion that he did not treat casualties resulting from air mishaps.
main_claim: Kelley did not treat casualties from air mishaps in his crash crew work because those they rescued were either dead or uninjured.

argument_text: Representative Donald O'Toole (D., NY) demanded that the purses be held up until the fight, which he called a "stinkeroo," be investigated. He wanted an investigation of the arrangements made between Promoter Mike Jacobs and the fighters, the splitting of the purses, and the existence of any debts of the fighters to Jacobs.
explanation: This advances a policy claim (hold the purses and investigate) supported by reasons: the fight was allegedly poor/suspicious (“stinkeroo”) and there may be questionable arrangements (purses splitting, debts). The premises (suspected improprieties) are offered to justify the conclusion (withholding purses and investigating).
main_claim: The purses should be withheld and the fight’s arrangements investigated due to suspected improprieties.

argument_text: According to O'Toole, Jacobs said, "O'Toole was trying to shake me down for fight tickets." And on the strength of that remark, O'Toole is attempting to sue Jacobs for 100,000 dollars.
explanation: This presents a conclusion (O’Toole is suing Jacobs) and its stated basis (Jacobs’ remark), implying the remark is defamatory or injurious enough to justify legal action. The causal phrasing “on the strength of that remark” explicitly links premise to conclusion.
main_claim: Jacobs’ remark justifies O’Toole’s lawsuit for $100,000.

argument_text: A New York specialty store head says that better apparel supply cannot improve materially until more men go into the needle trades field. In some factories, he points out, the workers' average age is as high as 60 because for several years few skilled hands have entered the field during the war. Shortages became more acute.
explanation: The main claim is that apparel supply will not materially improve unless more men enter the needle trades. Supporting reasons are given: an aging workforce due to years without new skilled entrants has led to acute shortages. The premises directly support the conclusion about necessary labor increases.
main_claim: Apparel supply will not materially improve unless more workers enter the needle trades.

argument_text: President Truman recently signed the emergency housing bill, intended to provide 2,700,000 homes for veterans in two years through private construction. The "heart" of the program provides 400,000,000 dollars for subsidies to spur production of bottleneck materials.
explanation: While phrased as reporting, the juxtaposition implies a rationale: to meet the goal of 2.7 million homes, production of bottleneck materials must be spurred, and subsidies are the means to do so. This conveys an implicit argument that subsidies are necessary/effective to achieve the housing targets.
main_claim: Subsidies to spur bottleneck material production are needed to achieve the veterans’ housing goals.

argument_text: XP-81, one of the hottest of the Army's new fighters, is shown diagrammatically above. Built by Consolidated Vultee, it is the first plane ever to fly with a gas turbine engine designed for propeller drive.
explanation: The evaluative claim "one of the hottest" implies superiority or exceptional status. The following sentence provides a reason: it is the first to fly with a propeller-drive gas turbine, signaling technological innovation. The structure is: claim of excellence implied, supported by uniqueness/first-of-its-kind evidence. The argument is implicit because the conclusion (that it is among the best/newest/most advanced) is suggested rather than spelled out as "therefore."
main_claim: The XP-81 is among the top/most advanced of the Army’s new fighters.

argument_text: Powered by a General Electric gas turbine engine in the nose and a jet engine in the tail, the trim fighter will fly at a speed of more than 500 mph.
explanation: This sentence presents a causal premise leading to a performance conclusion: because it has both a GE gas turbine in the nose and a jet engine in the tail, therefore it will exceed 500 mph. The cue “Powered by ... the ... fighter will” explicitly links reasons to the outcome.
main_claim: The XP-81 will fly at more than 500 mph due to its dual engine configuration.

argument_text: Grain, the lifeblood of Europeans, is finally ready for harvesting.
explanation: The appositive “the lifeblood of Europeans” is evaluative and functions as a premise suggesting grain is vitally important to European survival, thereby implying that its readiness for harvest is significant and positive news. The sentence thus embeds an argument: because grain is essential, its being ready matters. The reasoning is implied rather than stated with explicit markers.
main_claim: Grain is finally ready for harvesting.

argument_text: Foggians, who had planted every yard of soil for their precious grain, have been cutting it this past month, and the crop looks good.
explanation: The description of planting “every yard of soil” and calling the grain “precious” frames the crop as urgently needed and extensively cultivated; followed by “the crop looks good,” it implies a positive outcome that will meet needs. The evaluative “precious” and the causal-chronological buildup (planting extensively, then cutting, leading to a good-looking crop) suggest an argument that their intensive effort is yielding a favorable harvest. The reasoning is implied rather than explicitly structured.
main_claim: The grain harvest in Foggia is turning out well.

argument_text: Did you know you were drinking water out of the longest aqueduct system in the world?
explanation: Rhetorical question implying the claim that the aqueduct supplying the reader’s water is the longest in the world. It functions as an argument by asserting a notable status to frame subsequent information, with the implied premise that comparisons establish this superlative (later supported by comparative data).
main_claim: You are drinking water from the longest aqueduct system in the world.

argument_text: Or that the direction of a mountain stream had been changed in order to get good water here at all?
explanation: Rhetorical question implying causal necessity: to obtain good water locally, the stream’s direction had to be altered. The phrase “in order to” signals purpose/justification for the action, suggesting a premise (quality need) leading to the conclusion (stream was redirected).
main_claim: The stream was redirected because that was necessary to secure good water here.

argument_text: The water for most of these Pugliesi all comes from the same place: an underground source in the mountains at Caposele, 48 miles south-southwest of Foggia, which provides an excellent brand of H2O at the rate of—take a good breath—from 3 to 6 tons a second.
explanation: The evaluative phrase “provides an excellent brand of H2O” advances a quality claim, implicitly grounded in the source being an underground mountain spring and its impressive flow rate. The quality assessment is not argued explicitly but is suggested by these attributes.
main_claim: The Caposele source provides excellent-quality water.

argument_text: It was not until 1915 that the main source at Caposele was captured—a procedure that involved some smart engineering because the water, while plentiful, was all running out the wrong side of the mountain.
explanation: Explicit causal reasoning: “because the water… was all running out the wrong side of the mountain” serves as the premise explaining why capturing the source required “smart engineering,” supporting the evaluative conclusion about engineering skill.
main_claim: Capturing the Caposele source required smart engineering due to the water flowing out the wrong side of the mountain.

argument_text: Since it would have taken considerable time and effort to turn the mountain around, the engineers decided to cheat nature in another way and made the water come out on the Puglia side of the mountain.
explanation: “Since” introduces a reason (turning the mountain would take considerable time and effort/impractical), leading to the decision (to divert the water to the Puglia side). This provides a premise-to-conclusion rationale for the chosen engineering solution.
main_claim: Because turning the mountain was impractical, engineers diverted the water to emerge on the Puglia side.

argument_text: But that wasn't easy. From Caposele to Villa Castelli (10 miles east of Taranto), a total of 152 miles of the main had to be laid, branching north and southeast at Venosa (40 miles south-southeast of Foggia). The main trunk from Caposele passes through 99 tunnels, one of which, near Spinazzola, is 12 miles long and 675 feet underground, 93 bridges, and 6 siphons.
explanation: The claim “that wasn’t easy” is immediately supported by detailed evidence of the undertaking’s scale and obstacles (miles of mains, tunnels, bridges, siphons). The details function as premises demonstrating difficulty.
main_claim: Constructing and routing the aqueduct across Puglia was difficult.

argument_text: Some U.S. systems carry more water, but none, the Acquedotto says, is as long as that right here in Puglia, which is 1,196 miles long. (Catskill, N.Y. 92 miles; Los Angeles 240 miles; Coolgardie, W. Australia 350 miles).
explanation: Contrastive structure (“Some… but none…”) presents a comparative argument: although other systems may exceed in volume, the Puglia system is longest. The parenthetical figures serve as supporting evidence, and the attribution to the Acquedotto adds a source.
main_claim: The Puglia aqueduct is the longest in the world even if some systems carry more water.

argument_text: were in the States during the war in order to be sure that no food leaks into the Black Market.
explanation: This sentence offers a purpose-based justification for measures (presumably rationing/controls): the aim is to prevent leakage to the Black Market. The implicit claim is that such measures are warranted or appropriate because they prevent black market diversion. The causal “in order to” signals the rationale supporting the implied policy.
main_claim: Controls like those used in the States during the war are justified because they prevent food from leaking into the Black Market.

argument_text: The quantity of food, however, will assure adequate diets and nutritional values.
explanation: The contrastive “however” implies a response to a concern (that controls/rationing might cause shortages). The passage advances the reassuring claim that, despite restrictions, there will still be enough food to maintain adequate nutrition, implying the policy is acceptable.
main_claim: Despite controls, there will be enough food to maintain adequate diets and nutrition.

argument_text: 'If all men who desire cards,' concluded Lt. Metzler, 'will make application with the Banking-Ration Officer well in advance, it will make our and their jobs much easier.'
explanation: This is a conditional causal argument: the premise is that men apply well in advance, and the conclusion is that doing so will make both officials’ and applicants’ jobs easier. It also functions as a recommendation based on the stated consequence.
main_claim: Men who want cards should apply well in advance because doing so will make everyone’s job easier.

argument_text: He appealed for reconstruction and peace all over the country and said that Italy would be unable to accept impossible decisions from the Paris Conference.
explanation: This advances a normative stance that Italy should not accept “impossible decisions.” The premise is embedded in the evaluative term “impossible,” implying such decisions are unreasonable or untenable; therefore, they cannot/should not be accepted. The causal/normative link (“impossible” → “unable to accept”) is implied rather than argued with explicit evidence.
main_claim: Italy should not accept untenable (“impossible”) decisions from the Paris Conference.

argument_text: Amnesty was granted to thousands of Italian political prisoners in the first act of the new Council of Ministers. The action granted complete amnesty for political prisoners convicted between the day of Italian Liberation up to June 18 of this year. Death sentences were commuted to life imprisonment and life sentences to 30 years. Many men were released entirely. The act was the first in line to solidify the nation on the eve of a new government.
explanation: The final sentence claims a purpose/effect (“to solidify the nation”) and implies that granting amnesty contributes to national consolidation. The preceding details about the scope and leniency of the amnesty function as contextual premises suggesting how it could foster reconciliation. The argument is implicit because the causal link between amnesty and national solidarity is asserted without explicit reasoning.
main_claim: Granting amnesty to political prisoners will help solidify the nation as a new government forms.

argument_text: Italian Committee for Supply in Rome has requested UNRRA to increase the bread ration to 250 grams per day. (Now it is 200 grams.) This year the total grain production is expected to be 57 million quintiles, but the number of calories for Italian consumers is still inferior to most European countries. UNRRA has not answered the request yet.
explanation: This passage presents a policy request (increase ration) alongside supporting considerations: higher expected grain production and relatively low consumer caloric intake. The juxtaposition implies the argument that, because supply prospects are better and Italians’ calories are low compared to other Europeans, UNRRA ought to raise the bread ration. The conclusion (raise the ration) is implied, not formally stated as “therefore.”
main_claim: UNRRA should increase Italy’s daily bread ration to 250 grams given production levels and comparatively low caloric intake.

argument_text: Weather recently—the high temperatures followed by stiff breezes—were described by Professor Redia, a famous Italian meteorologist, as characteristic of June and determined by Atlantic sea currents.
explanation: This advances a causal explanation: recent weather is determined by Atlantic currents and is typical for June. The appeal to authority (“a famous Italian meteorologist”) functions as the implicit warrant supporting the causal claim, but no explicit empirical evidence is provided, making the inferential support implicit.
main_claim: The recent pattern of high temperatures with stiff breezes is normal for June and caused by Atlantic sea currents.

argument_text: As the ARC changed to an all-ranks club, it changed its signs to match.
explanation: This sentence provides a reason (premise) and an action (conclusion): because the ARC changed status to an all-ranks club, it therefore changed its signs. The causal connector “as” signals an explicit justification for the change in signage.
main_claim: The ARC’s change to an all-ranks club warranted changing its signs to match.

argument_text: AES, whom we all take for granted, decided to do some advertising on its own and put up a new sign, which now hangs in front of its door.
explanation: The evaluative clause “whom we all take for granted” implies a critique that AES is underappreciated, and the subsequent action (putting up a sign) functions as an implied response to that problem. The implicit reasoning is: because AES is taken for granted, it is reasonable/necessary that AES advertise to gain recognition.
main_claim: AES is underappreciated, so its decision to advertise with a new sign is warranted.

argument_text: Vincent Siano's weird Castle Bar is a place to behold with its eerie cave-like fixtures, and spiders and devils hanging from the ceiling to warn drinkers when they have had enough.
explanation: Descriptive and evaluative language (“weird,” “a place to behold”) implies that the bar merits attention/visit. The purpose clause “to warn drinkers when they have had enough” suggests the decor functions as a caution against overdrinking. The implicit claims are that the bar is worth seeing and that the decor serves a regulatory purpose, inferred from the evaluative framing and teleological phrasing.
main_claim: The Castle Bar is notably worth seeing and its decor playfully functions to discourage overdrinking.

argument_text: Captain Fritz Bluhm of the 55th Station Hospital was awarded the new Army Commendation Ribbon and a cluster to go with it, for his excellent work at Fitzsimons General Hospital in Denver, Colorado.
explanation: This sentence states a conclusion (Bluhm received the award) and provides an explicit reason (“for his excellent work”). The causal “for” clearly connects the premise (excellent work) to the outcome (award), constituting a straightforward justificatory argument.
main_claim: Captain Fritz Bluhm received the commendation because he performed excellent work at Fitzsimons General Hospital.

argument_text: Pfc Joseph Tackett — Special Services: "Just wondering on what basis all this rank was given out."
explanation: This utterance uses a rhetorical question to imply a critique: by questioning the basis for rank distribution, it suggests that the promotions may lack a clear, fair, or justified basis. The implied premise is that promotions should be based on transparent criteria; the expressed doubt implies the conclusion that such criteria are unclear or possibly absent.
main_claim: The recent distribution of rank lacks a clear or justified basis.

argument_text: Lt. Nicholas La Rocca — Base Dental Surgeon: "My mind is all cluttered up in knowing that my wife is coming over in the next month or so. It's a great pleasure as I'll have to stay over here another eighteen months."
explanation: The second sentence presents an explicit causal connector (“as”) linking the premise (he must stay in Italy for another eighteen months) to the conclusion (his wife’s impending arrival is a great pleasure). The reasoning is that because he must remain overseas, having his wife join him is especially welcome.
main_claim: It is a great pleasure that his wife is coming because he has to stay in Italy for another eighteen months.

argument_text: More about the people of dusty Foggia, which borders on the dirty in this small space typical of a small town, it "says here in small print.
explanation: This uses evaluative language (“dusty Foggia,” “borders on the dirty”) and a causal framing (“in this small space typical of a small town”) to imply a claim about Foggia’s character. The premise is that small-town “small space” conditions lead to or correlate with dirtiness; the implied conclusion is that Foggia is (nearly) dirty because of its small-town nature.
main_claim: Foggia is nearly dirty because it has the cramped, small-town conditions that foster such qualities.

argument_text: Appropriate rivers and ditches to the ItIcky Flyboys who partied their way out of Foggia and who are now sweating out that boat. And once they embark, look out New York!
explanation: The passage implies a causal-predictive claim: since these “Flyboys” are heavy partiers (“partied their way out of Foggia”) and are about to sail, New York should beware (“look out New York!”). The warning is a rhetorical cue indicating an implied conclusion about anticipated rowdy behavior in New York.
main_claim: Because the Flyboys are hard partiers and are heading to the U.S., New York should brace for their arrival.

argument_text: As promised, 'tis the brightest spot in town, so best you check out a pair of sunglasses from Supply,
explanation: This presents a premise (“’tis the brightest spot in town”) leading to a recommendation (“so best you check out a pair of sunglasses”). The connective “so” marks an explicit inference from the venue’s brightness to the advised action.
main_claim: You should get sunglasses from Supply because the Stork Club is the brightest spot in town.

argument_text: and since these days are so sunny in sunny Italy, an extra pair of eyes are recommended for those mornings after.
explanation: The phrase “since these days are so sunny” provides an explicit reason for the recommendation that follows (“an extra pair of eyes are recommended”), which humorously suggests needing help coping with bright mornings after nights out.
main_claim: Because the days are very sunny, you should have extra “eyes” for the mornings after.

argument_text: Noticeable empty spot in town is that formerly occupied by the 803rd M.P.'s, who have returned to Naples where they probably like it better anyway.
explanation: The clause “where they probably like it better anyway” implies a comparative evaluative claim about preference, using hedged certainty (“probably”) to suggest the MPs prefer Naples over Foggia. The return to Naples serves as the contextual basis for the inference.
main_claim: The 803rd MPs likely prefer Naples to Foggia.

argument_text: Kincade, Father of Kincadism, was in bed all day Sunday after Saturday night's campaign.
explanation: The temporal connector “after” implies a causal relation: Kincade’s all-day Sunday bedrest was due to the previous night’s “campaign” (a euphemism for heavy partying). The implied conclusion is that the partying caused the need to stay in bed.
main_claim: Kincade had to stay in bed all day Sunday because of Saturday night’s partying.

argument_text: Jim "Newmarket" MacDonald is most convenient as he knows all the right telephone lines to Leghorn. Why, he's hardly had any Bloody Ex time all week.
explanation: This pairs a premise (he knows “all the right telephone lines”) with an implied causal consequence (he’s been too occupied to spend time at the Bloody Ex bar). The contrastive “Why” emphasizes the inference that his connectivity keeps him busy and away from leisure.
main_claim: Because Jim MacDonald is skilled at connecting calls to Leghorn, he’s been too busy to spend time at the Bloody Ex.

argument_text: Sad times are ahead as we lose Jeannie Copp to the 88th Division where she's expecting to jump into a foxhole and where she'll be missing the Air Corps, doncha bet?
explanation: Predictive evaluatives (“Sad times are ahead”) and the rhetorical question (“doncha bet?”) imply conclusions: the loss of Jeannie will negatively affect the local community, and Jeannie will regret leaving the Air Corps. The anticipated transfer provides the reason for the predicted sadness and missing.
main_claim: Jeannie’s transfer to the 88th Division will make times sad here and she will miss the Air Corps.

argument_text: And hungry times are ahead for all when the Bloody Ex will be squeezing snacks only on Saturday mornings and Wednesday and Sunday nights. But that's life in the Army as only Willie and the rest of us know.
explanation: The first sentence makes a causal prediction: restricted snack hours will cause “hungry times.” The second sentence generalizes normatively (“that’s life in the Army”), implying the conclusion that such hardships are typical and to be accepted. Together they form an argument about expected scarcity and resignation.
main_claim: Because the Bloody Ex is restricting snack hours, everyone will face hunger, and such inconvenience is just standard Army life.

argument_text: After reading your editorial entitled "Justice," I see that you too must be affected by the shortage of skilled personnel. If not, what is your excuse for letting such an editorial appear in the Occupator?
explanation: The writer implies that only a shortage of skilled staff could explain allowing a poor editorial to be published; otherwise there is no acceptable excuse. The evaluative question and dilemma structure (either shortage or incompetence) support a critical conclusion about editorial judgment without stating it directly.
main_claim: The editor showed poor judgment in publishing "Justice," likely due to a shortage of skilled personnel.

argument_text: It seems that this particular writer has taken on the role of a self-appointed crusader.
explanation: Evaluative labeling (“self-appointed crusader”) implies the writer is overzealous and lacks legitimate authority or balance. This suggests a negative claim about the writer’s stance and methods without explicit premises-conclusion language.
main_claim: The author of "Justice" is acting as an overzealous, self-appointed moralizer rather than a fair commentator.

argument_text: If "Justice" had taken it upon himself to find out the true conditions, I'm sure he would have thought twice before writing such an article.
explanation: The conditional asserts that knowledge of “true conditions” would have prevented the article, implying it was written without adequate facts and is therefore misguided. The premise (ignorance of conditions) supports the conclusion (article should not have been written).
main_claim: The "Justice" article was written without understanding the real situation and thus should not have been written.

argument_text: At the present time, there are 11 M.P.s available for general duty in Foggia, whereas the 803 M.P. Co. had more than 50 men to pull duty. I'm certain that "Justice" would feel as if he were persecuted if asked to work more than 8 hours a day, but some of our boys are pulling 16 hours duty every day.
explanation: The passage presents evidence of staffing levels and long hours to imply that MPs are overburdened and that criticism from "Justice" is unfair or uninformed. The premises (11 vs. 50 men; 16-hour days) support the unstated conclusion about the fairness and feasibility of expectations placed on MPs.
main_claim: MPs in Foggia are severely understaffed and overworked, so criticism like "Justice" is unfair or unrealistic.

argument_text: I'm sure that after writing such a fine and stirring article, the writer will probably make staff or tech, while the only rating the thankless job of M.P. gets is that of First Class.
explanation: Sarcasm (“such a fine and stirring article”) and contrast in promotions imply the writer is rewarded for grandstanding while MPs are underappreciated. The insinuation supports a critical conclusion about misplaced incentives and unfair recognition.
main_claim: The "Justice" writer will benefit career-wise from sensational criticism while MPs remain under-rewarded for difficult work.

argument_text: So "Justice," please have pity on the M.P.s and save us from the fury and wrath of your mighty pen.
explanation: This recommendation implies that the writer’s attacks are excessive and harmful to MPs, and therefore should cease. The directive (“have pity” and “save us”) signals a conclusion about what ought to be done, based on the implied premise of undue harm.
main_claim: The "Justice" writer should stop or moderate his harsh criticism of MPs because it is excessive and harmful.

argument_text: Thanks to the efforts of S/Sgt. John Russel, aided by Cpl. Ed Lencowski and Pfc. Skelly, swimming enthusiasts no longer need to make the long trek to Manfredonia to indulge in their favorite sport.
explanation: This presents a causal reason (the efforts of specific individuals leading to a new pool) supporting the conclusion (no need to travel to Manfredonia). The "Thanks to" construction signals premise leading to conclusion.
main_claim: Because the new pool has been created through these efforts, swimmers no longer need to travel to Manfredonia.

argument_text: Located directly across the street from 803 M.P.'s, five minutes' walk from town, the pool is easily accessible to all and sundry.
explanation: The premises about location and proximity support the evaluative conclusion that the pool is "easily accessible." The sentence explicitly links reasons (location, walking time) to the claim.
main_claim: The pool is easily accessible due to its close location to town and a known landmark.

argument_text: A pile of steel girders and other debris outside of the building is mute testimony of the labor involved in resurrecting the place.
explanation: Physical evidence (pile of debris) is presented as proof of the extent of labor, using the phrase "is mute testimony" to assert a conclusion drawn from observable facts.
main_claim: The debris evidences how much labor was required to restore the pool.

argument_text: A scarcity of necessary materials added to the difficulties of the job.
explanation: This is a causal assertion: the premise (scarcity of materials) explains or increases the conclusion/state (the job’s difficulty).
main_claim: The job was made more difficult because necessary materials were scarce.

argument_text: The water is pumped in from the same source the Foggia drinking water comes from, but due to the former sabotage of the chlorinating system, chlorination has to be attended to after the water is in the pool.
explanation: The sentence gives a reason (prior sabotage of the chlorinating system) for a procedural conclusion (chlorinate after filling). The "due to" construction marks causal reasoning.
main_claim: Because the chlorinating system was sabotaged, chlorination must occur after the pool is filled.

argument_text: Water will be changed once a week, probably the latter part of the week to ensure fresh water over the weekend when the biggest crowds are expected.
explanation: It states a policy and provides its rationale: anticipated peak usage on weekends justifies scheduling water changes later in the week to ensure freshness then.
main_claim: The pool will change water later in the week so that it is fresh for the expected weekend crowds.

argument_text: At the present time, the pool will be open from 10 A.M. until 6 P.M. As soon as nylon netting is obtained for screening to comply with Malaria Control regulations, the hours will be extended to 10 P.M.
explanation: The second sentence provides a condition and rationale (obtaining netting for regulatory compliance) for the conclusion (extending hours), making a clear conditional argument.
main_claim: Once nylon netting is obtained to meet Malaria Control rules, pool hours will be extended to 10 P.M.

argument_text: THE WATER'S FINE Leonard Peterson — Josaph Sisson try out the water in the new FAAB swimming pool located opposite the old 803rd MP area. Photo by Bufalo
explanation: The headline makes an evaluative claim (“THE WATER'S FINE”), and the accompanying caption provides situational evidence (“Leonard Peterson — Josaph Sisson try out the water”). The juxtaposition implies a causal/confirmatory relationship: because people are trying out the water at the new pool, the water is fine/safe/pleasant. This is an implicit argument since the reasoning is suggested rather than explicitly stated with connective language.
main_claim: The new FAAB swimming pool’s water is fine and suitable for swimming.

argument_text: More Civilian Employees To Be Fired; Security Sqdn., Officer Mess To Move 700 To 800 Employees To Be Dismissed As Budget Is Slashed
explanation: The headline links the mass dismissals to budget cuts via the phrase “As Budget Is Slashed,” implying a causal argument: the reason for firing employees is the slashed budget. The claim is suggested through framing rather than laid out with explicit premises and a stated conclusion.
main_claim: Employees are being dismissed because the budget has been slashed.

argument_text: The cut, which had been anticipated early last month, will leave less than one thousand people employed here and came as a result of a reduced budget for the months of July, August, and September.
explanation: This sentence explicitly asserts a causal relationship (“came as a result of”) between the reduced budget and the employment cut. The premise is the reduced budget; the conclusion is that this caused the cut.
main_claim: The employment cut is caused by a reduced budget for July–September.

argument_text: "FAAB has requested an appropriation of 165 thousand dollars for the next three months," said Lt. Kirby, "15 thousand dollars of which is earmarked for American War Department employees. That leaves 50 thousand dollars per month for other civilian help."
explanation: The figures are presented to imply that only limited funds remain for civilian employees, suggesting that cuts are necessary. The arithmetic serves as evidence; the conclusion (need to reduce civilian payroll or staffing) is implied rather than directly stated.
main_claim: The limited remaining funds for civilian help necessitate reductions in civilian payroll/staffing.

argument_text: "Our present number of employees is 1700, and we paid them 40 thousand dollars during the last pay period (2 weeks). If our present rate of expenditures is maintained, we will be spending 30 thousand dollars over our budget."
explanation: This passage presents premises (number of employees and current pay) and draws a stated conclusion about overspending relative to the budget if the current rate continues. The structure is explicit: given these expenditures, overspending will occur.
main_claim: Maintaining current payroll levels will cause spending to exceed the budget by 30 thousand dollars.

argument_text: The new budget request is an emergency one caused by a mix-up during the transfer of Foggia units from MTOUSA to the 40th Bomb Wing and then to the Ninth Air Force Service Command. In the process of transfer, MTOUSA notified Washington to cancel proposed funds for Foggia, but ETO heads did not take over the request. Although the 40th Bomb Wing, when notified of the error, began emergency measures for Foggia funds, Ninth Air Force did not continue them.
explanation: This paragraph advances a causal argument explaining why an emergency budget request was necessary: a “mix-up” in transfers and subsequent failures by specific organizations. It also implicitly assigns responsibility by detailing who did and did not act, but the primary causal claim (“caused by a mix-up”) is explicit.
main_claim: The emergency budget request was necessitated by a transfer-related mix-up and lapses in continuing funding measures by responsible commands.

argument_text: announced today two scheduled changes in FAAB organization that were brought about in part by the reduction of civilian employees to take place early next week.
explanation: This sentence provides a causal justification: the premise is that there will be a reduction of civilian employees early next week; the conclusion is that two scheduled organizational changes were brought about in part because of that reduction. The cue “brought about in part by” explicitly links cause to effect.
main_claim: The scheduled organizational changes at FAAB are (at least partly) due to the impending reduction of civilian employees.

argument_text: The club, said the Colonel, will be open to all enlisted men and their guests, since new regulations forbid women to enter 779th AMS and 955th AES clubrooms in the Squadron areas.
explanation: This sentence justifies a policy decision with a reason: the premise is that new regulations forbid women from entering certain squadron clubrooms; the conclusion is that the club will be open to all enlisted men and their guests. The connective “since” explicitly signals the reasoning.
main_claim: The club will be open to all enlisted men and their guests because women are forbidden from entering certain squadron clubrooms under new regulations.

argument_text: Major Berg served first as an enlisted man with the 11th Infantry at Fort Benjamin Harrison, Indiana, from 1936 until 1939. After two years as a civilian, he re-enlisted in January 1942, and in March 1943, with the rating of M/Sgt, he was sent to the Adjutant General OCS. After graduating in June, Lieutenant Berg was assigned to the newly activated 455th Bomb Group at Fort Washington, Maryland, and five months later he was transferred, with the 455th, to the Mediterranean Theater. Stationed at Cerignola for 18 months, the major has been in Foggia for the past year.
explanation: The passage lists a sustained record of service, advancement, and deployment, which functions as evidence to imply that the nomination is merited. The article does not state the conclusion explicitly, but the selective inclusion of career milestones and continuity of service after re-enlistment acts as premises supporting an evaluative conclusion about his qualifications or worthiness.
main_claim: Major Berg’s Regular Army nomination is deserved because of his extensive and progressive military service.

argument_text: Major William W. Berg, Executive Officer of Foggia Army Air Base, was included in the list of those nominated for appointment to the Regular Army by President Truman last Friday. Major Berg is the only officer in the Foggia area to receive the nomination, one of thirty-eight in the Mediterranean Theater.
explanation: By emphasizing that he is the only officer in the local area and one of a small number in the entire theater, the passage frames the nomination as rare and prestigious, implying that Berg is distinguished. The contrastive quantification serves as an implicit premise for the evaluative conclusion of exceptional status or merit.
main_claim: Major Berg’s nomination signifies exceptional distinction relative to his peers.

argument_text: The critical food shortage prevalent throughout the world inaugurated an intensive drive on food conservation in the Foggia area this week. All mess sergeants have been instructed to institute a program for the elimination of waste, and every effort is being made to save food for the starving people of the world.
explanation: This passage presents a policy (a conservation drive; instructions to eliminate waste) and links it causally to a global condition (a critical food shortage and starving people). The justification is implied: because there is worldwide scarcity and starvation, intensified conservation and waste elimination are appropriate. The evaluative framing (“starving people of the world”) signals a moral rationale without stating “therefore we should,” making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: The food conservation drive and waste-elimination measures are justified by the worldwide critical food shortage and starvation.

argument_text: In order to give an incentive to individuals to increase their efforts, competitive actions will be taken to credit those messes which have achieved success and to bring failures to the attention of those messes which have failed in developing the spirit of this program.
explanation: The sentence states a clear reason (“In order to give an incentive...”) leading to a policy decision (“competitive actions will be taken”). The premise-conclusion structure is explicit: competition will be implemented because it incentivizes increased efforts, with mechanisms of reward and accountability specified.
main_claim: Competitive actions will be implemented as an incentive mechanism to increase efforts in the food conservation program.

argument_text: The general scheme for organizing this competition will be to have all messes compute the monetary value of rations authorized in comparison to those consumed.
explanation: While descriptive, this proposes a specific metric for the competition, implicitly asserting that comparing the monetary value of authorized versus consumed rations is an appropriate and fair way to measure conservation performance. The normative suitability of this method is assumed rather than argued overtly, making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Using the monetary comparison of authorized versus consumed rations is an appropriate method to organize and assess the competition.

argument_text: Capt. Louis Diaz (medics), who is organizing a drive to stamp out VD, said, "Through the medium of orientations, movies, and posters we hope to stop the dangerous rise."
explanation: This advances a prescriptive claim that deploying orientations, movies, and posters will (and thus should) be used to stop the rise in VD. The evaluative phrase "dangerous rise" and the proposed means imply an argument that educational/media interventions are an effective and warranted response, though the premises (e.g., that such media change behavior) are not explicitly stated.
main_claim: Educational and media interventions (orientations, movies, posters) should be used because they can stop the dangerous rise in VD.

argument_text: There has been an alarming increase in the past three months. The April rate of 54.5 cases per thousand men per annum leaped to 160.9 in May. Fourteen new infections during June are alarming medical personnel and are the cause of the latest drive.
explanation: This presents evidence (rapidly rising rates, fourteen new infections) with evaluative language ("alarming") and a causal link ("are the cause of the latest drive") to imply that initiating a VD-control drive is necessary and justified. The conclusion (the drive should occur) is suggested rather than explicitly argued in premise-conclusion form.
main_claim: The sharp and alarming recent increase in VD cases justifies and necessitates launching a new control drive.

argument_text: It later turned out that the money was not needed, and they sent letters to all of the subscribers informing them of their refund. Only twenty-two dollars worth was picked up, and thus they have seventy dollars worth of money orders uncashed. They would appreciate it if the claimants would appear;
explanation: This passage presents reasons (refunds are due; notices were sent; most funds remain unclaimed) that support a normative request (claimants should come forward). The request “would appreciate it if the claimants would appear” implies the conclusion that claimants ought to pick up their refunds, supported by the preceding facts about unclaimed money and prior notification. The argument is implicit because the normative conclusion is suggested rather than formally stated as “therefore, they should appear.”
main_claim: Claimants should appear to pick up their refund money orders.

argument_text: or maybe someone has a bunch of blank dog-tags?
explanation: This rhetorical question insinuates a causal explanation for the unclaimed refunds: that fraudulent or fictitious identities (enabled by “blank dog-tags”) might be involved, hence no legitimate claimants to retrieve the money. The implicit claim is suggested via irony rather than directly asserted, using insinuation as the argumentative cue.
main_claim: The unclaimed refunds might be due to fraudulent or fictitious enlistments/identities created with blank dog-tags.

argument_text: After spending our entire army career envying the lot of the mail clerk ("All he ever does is hand out mail"), we finally got around to delving into the mysteries of what makes an Army Postal Unit tick and we emerged with a definitely changed attitude on the situation. The boys have a lot of work to do, put in a lot of hours to accomplish it, and the result is a very efficient job.
explanation: This passage counters a prior belief and provides reasons: the clerks have a lot of work and long hours, leading to “a very efficient job.” The causal phrasing “and the result is” explicitly links premises (workload, hours) to the conclusion (efficiency), forming a clear premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The Army Postal Unit clerks work hard for long hours and produce very efficient results, contrary to the stereotype that they “just hand out mail.”

argument_text: A word about the packages: they cannot be accepted unless they are properly wrapped and packed securely enough that they won't rattle, and the boys would appreciate it if you would make sure that these conditions are complied with before bringing your packages in.
explanation: This issues a recommendation (“make sure that these conditions are complied with”) grounded in the rule that improperly packed items “cannot be accepted.” The appreciation appeal implies a practical reason (avoid wasted effort/delays). The normative “would appreciate it” and the acceptance condition indicate an implicit argument urging compliance.
main_claim: You should ensure your packages are properly wrapped and securely packed before bringing them to the Post Office.

argument_text: In order to facilitate early delivery and keep up our morale, the mail is sorted immediately so it will be ready for delivery the following morning.
explanation: The purpose clause “In order to” provides explicit reasons (facilitate early delivery, keep up morale) for the action (sorting immediately), linking premises to the conclusion that immediate sorting is warranted.
main_claim: The mail is sorted immediately because it promotes early delivery and maintains morale.

argument_text: The boys generally finish sorting the mail by 8 or 9 PM and decide to call it a day, and from where we sit it looks like a fair day's work.
explanation: The evaluative conclusion (“a fair day's work”) is supported by the factual premise of working until 8 or 9 PM. The judgment is not stated as a formal therefore, but the juxtaposition of long hours with the evaluation signals an implicit argument that the workload merits the assessment.
main_claim: Given their long hours, the postal unit’s daily workload amounts to a fair day’s work.

argument_text: But in spite of the fact that our Editor got one of the first Traffic Violation Tickets handed out this week, we think the tightening up of traffic controls is a good thing.
explanation: This is an argument because it advances a normative claim (“tightening up of traffic controls is a good thing”) while acknowledging a potential counterconsideration (the Editor received a ticket). The premise functions as a concession to possible bias, implying that despite personal inconvenience, stricter enforcement is beneficial—implicitly relying on assumed reasons such as safety or order, which are not stated explicitly.
main_claim: Tightening up traffic controls is beneficial.

argument_text: The charge against him was "accelerating at forty miles per hour," and he is particularly broken up because he had gotten his driver's permit only a few hours before and he swears he was in second gear behind a truck.
explanation: This passage implies that the speeding/acceleration charge was unwarranted or implausible. The stated facts (new permit, being in second gear behind a truck) serve as reasons suggesting he could not have been accelerating at 40 mph, leading to the implied conclusion that the charge was unjust or inaccurate. The conclusion is not stated outright and relies on the reader inferring it from the circumstances.
main_claim: The charge of “accelerating at forty miles per hour” against Shorty was unfounded or implausible.

argument_text: A projectionist may, upon permission from his Commanding Officer, receive such training at any convenient time at the Film Exchange," stated Ben B. B. Lewis, Acting N.C.O. "One visit is usually required to train the operator," Lewis continued, "and each man that passes our standards will receive the required Projection Operator's Permit."
explanation: This passage lists benefits and low barriers (convenient timing, only one visit needed, guaranteed permit upon passing standards), which function as premises implying the conclusion that projectionists should pursue training at the Film Exchange. The evaluative/efficiency cues (“any convenient time,” “one visit,” “will receive the required … Permit”) suggest a persuasive intent without stating an explicit “ought.”
main_claim: Projectionists should get their training at the Film Exchange.

argument_text: The Film Exchange, located on the third floor of the Headquarters building, has also on release the latest and most complete training films in this area, and services are available for repair and the rental of projectors and equipment to all squadrons and organizations. The Film Library covers training and education films on every branch of the services, including the Air Corps, Engineers, and Medics.
explanation: The superlatives (“latest and most complete”) and breadth of offerings and services (repairs, rentals, coverage of every branch) serve as reasons implying that units should use the Film Exchange for training and equipment needs. The persuasive stance is embedded via evaluative language and selective feature listing rather than an explicit recommendation.
main_claim: Squadrons and organizations should use the Film Exchange for training films and equipment services.

argument_text: The angels of mercy picked up our scent and assailed us. Twisting our arms, they marched us to a partitioned area where we caught a glimpse of a giant-sized hypodermic needle (actually a spinal injection needle as we were later informed) attached to a sign:
explanation: This passage uses ironic, adversarial metaphors (“picked up our scent and assailed us,” “Twisting our arms, they marched us”) to portray medics as coercive and aggressive. The implicit claim is that the process is not purely benevolent but forceful. The cues are hostile verbs, militarized imagery, and the contrast with “angels of mercy.” These rhetorical choices imply a stance about undue coercion without stating it explicitly.
main_claim: The medics administer shots in a coercive, heavy-handed manner.

argument_text: We sweated it out as a medical technician toyed with his hypodermic, "Notice the hook on this one," he explained with gleeful pleasure. An electrical shock paralyzed our arm. We knew then that the medics' deed was done. Assisting us to a nearby chair, the technician prepared for his next victim, "Step right up gentlemen; all the shots you want, free of charge."
explanation: The narrative frames the technician as taking “gleeful pleasure,” “toyed,” and calling the next person a “victim,” alongside a barker-like invitation. These evaluative and ironic choices imply the claim that medics enjoy dispensing painful injections and are overly eager to administer them. The pain (“electrical shock”) serves as evidence; the carnival-barker tone suggests zeal rather than reluctant necessity.
main_claim: Medics take enthusiastic pleasure in giving painful injections and eagerly seek more recipients.

argument_text: The sense of humor of our medics touched us. It did more than that, it penetrated us. "And what do we get out of this," they questioned their patient, pointing to a lonely stripe on their arm.
explanation: The concluding quip shifts from humor to a pointed remark about rank (“a lonely stripe”), implying that despite their burdensome, invasive work, medics receive little recognition or reward. The rhetorical question functions as an ought-claim by insinuation: they deserve more than they currently get. The irony and the visual cue of the single stripe signal the argument without explicitly stating the conclusion.
main_claim: Medics are underrecognized and underrewarded for their work and deserve greater rank or acknowledgment.

argument_text: Said T-5 Harry Grabske (Security Section): "I prefer the snack bar because there's more to eat."
explanation: This is an explicit argument: a conclusion (preference for the snack bar) supported by a stated reason (there’s more to eat). The “because” signals the premise-conclusion structure.
main_claim: The snack bar is preferable because it offers more food.

argument_text: Pfc. Sol Flaks (1898th Engineers) said: "Keep the Coca Colas."
explanation: This is a recommendation (ought-claim) implying that continuing to serve Coca Colas is desirable. The stance is asserted without explicit reasons in the same sentence, so the support is implicit (e.g., implied satisfaction or demand).
main_claim: The Red Cross should continue serving Coca Colas.

argument_text: Pfc. James Metty agreed with the first man: "The Red Cross isn't what it used to be minus the snack bar."
explanation: This implies that removing the snack bar has degraded the Red Cross offering. The evaluative comparison (“isn't what it used to be”) functions as a critique, suggesting the change was negative and thus should be reconsidered.
main_claim: The Red Cross is worse without the snack bar.

argument_text: Pfc. Geraud Minnehan (529 ASG) quoted the company: "An iced cold Coca Cola hits the spot."
explanation: This asserts that Coca Cola is satisfying, which implicitly supports continuing to serve it. The evaluative phrase “hits the spot” functions as a positive reason, though the recommendation is not explicitly stated.
main_claim: Serving Coca Cola is good because it is satisfying.

argument_text: And Pvt. Alva Woodall (812 Signal) told of how he "made a habit of catching a snack every morning before dinner."
explanation: By noting a regular reliance on the snack bar, this implies the snack bar met ongoing needs and that its removal is a loss. The argument is inferred from the described habit rather than explicitly stated.
main_claim: The snack bar was valuable because people regularly relied on it for needed snacks.

argument_text: The first two, however, objected to having to pay for the drinks.
explanation: This reports objections to paying, which implies a normative stance that charging for drinks is undesirable or inappropriate. The evaluative verb “objected” signals a negative judgment functioning as an argument against the policy.
main_claim: Charging for drinks is objectionable and should not be done.

argument_text: "Services" were held last Saturday for the end of the snack bar at the Foggia ARC. Among other things, the "Bloody Ex" people marched through town with a band playing a funeral march.
explanation: The passage uses ironic scare quotes around “Services” and invokes a funeral metaphor (a band playing a funeral march) to frame the closure of the snack bar as akin to a death. This evaluative framing implies, rather than states, that the closure is a significant and lamentable loss. The implicit premise is that funerals mark the passing of something valued; by staging a “service” and “funeral march,” the text suggests the snack bar’s end warrants mourning, thereby advancing a negative evaluation of the closure.
main_claim: The closure of the snack bar is a significant loss that merits mourning.

argument_text: U.S. Army policies, however, call for chlorine in any case, just to be safe either in the main supply or at the point of consumption.
explanation: This sentence advances a prescriptive claim (chlorination in any case) and provides its reason (“just to be safe”), forming an explicit premise-to-conclusion structure: to ensure safety, policy mandates chlorination.
main_claim: Chlorination should be used in any case to ensure safety.

argument_text: (There are certain areas, such as for the time being that to the northeast of Foggia, which are supplied from wells. Such water should always be chlorinated, and that in the area mentioned has always been so treated ever since Allied troops first settled there.)
explanation: This passage recommends that well water “should always be chlorinated,” with the preceding sentence identifying the water as coming from wells; the risk associated with wells is implied as the reason. The rationale is suggested rather than stated with “because,” making it an implicit argument.
main_claim: Water supplied from wells should always be chlorinated.

argument_text: The Acquedotto engineers are justly proud of their achievements. And why not? Do you know how Foggia got water before the Acquedotto? By train, from near Naples.
explanation: The passage argues that the engineers’ pride is justified by contrasting present achievements with the inferior past practice of hauling water by train. The rhetorical question and contrast function as implicit premises supporting the evaluative conclusion.
main_claim: The Acquedotto engineers are right to be proud because conditions before the Acquedotto were much worse.

argument_text: There used to be a saying in southeastern Italy that what it needed was water and justice. To date, they figure, they've got the water.
explanation: This uses a proverb about lacking “water and justice” to imply that at least the “water” need has been fulfilled now. The evaluative conclusion about success is implied by invoking the saying and asserting it has been met.
main_claim: The Acquedotto has successfully provided the water that the region long needed.

argument_text:
The reduced quantity of water and the recommendation to avoid waste, which may bring a still further limitation, has caused many consumers to ask: Why is there a lack of water after a rather rainy winter season? "We must go back a little to the origins of the springs of the Acquedotto and to the subsoil phenomena which bring about these variations, in order to explain the present shortage."

"The mountain mass which feeds the springs of Caposele consists of large banks of limestone, sometimes fissured, sometimes compact, and almost entirely surrounded by impermeable rock, so as to create a huge reservoir into which the complex network of underground streams pours their waters. The fissured rocks at the surface absorb the rain and the melting snow and thus furnish abundant water to this natural reservoir, from which the overflow leaks out of the mountain where the permeable layers come in contact with the impermeable ones. This is the origin of our springs (so-called outcrop springs). The case is similar for the acqueducts of Naples and Palermo and the 'Acqua Marcia' of Rome."
explanation: This passage explicitly poses the question of why there is a shortage despite rain and answers it by providing geological mechanisms (limestone reservoir, impermeable boundaries, absorption and overflow points) as premises that explain supply variability. These premises support the conclusion that current shortages (and thus reductions and anti-waste recommendations) are justified by the hydrogeology.
main_claim: The current water shortage despite a rainy winter is due to the hydrogeological nature of the limestone reservoir and spring system, which justifies reductions and avoiding waste.

argument_text: 11 Portavoce, enlarging its activities all the time, came out this week with photographs of employees on the Siponto flatbed and with "photocartoons" of its editors. The photos are printed on the pages whereas the rest of the paper is mimeographed.
explanation: This passage makes an evaluative claim that 11 Portavoce is “enlarging its activities all the time” and supports it by citing new initiatives (adding photographs and “photocartoons”) and a technical distinction in production (photos printed vs. the rest mimeographed). The causal/justificatory connection is implied rather than explicitly signaled with “because,” so the evidence functions as support for the growth claim.
main_claim: 11 Portavoce is actively expanding its activities.

argument_text: International Paris Foreign Ministers Conference agreed on French demands for the Tenda and Briga area on the French-Italian border, with the stipulation that Italy continue to receive hydroelectric power from plants in the area.
explanation: The inclusion of a stipulation functions as an implicit justification: it signals that ensuring Italy continues to receive hydroelectric power is a necessary condition that mitigates or legitimizes conceding territory. The causal/conditional framing (“with the stipulation that…”) implies the claim that the concession is acceptable or balanced because Italy’s power supply is protected.
main_claim: The territorial concession to France is acceptable or justified provided Italy’s access to hydroelectric power continues.

argument_text: The Italian press greeted the news bitterly and as a unit condemned the proposal.
explanation: This sentence conveys a unified, evaluative reaction (“bitterly,” “condemned”) that implies a normative claim: the proposal is wrong and should be opposed. The unanimity of the press functions as an appeal to consensus as evidence that the proposal is objectionable.
main_claim: The proposal is objectionable and should be opposed.

argument_text: Arturo Toscanini, scheduled for a concert performance in Paris on July 8th, canceled the program in protest of the agreement.
explanation: By reporting a high-profile cancellation “in protest,” the passage signals a stance that the agreement is unacceptable; the act of protest serves as an indirect reason to view the agreement negatively (appeal to authority/moral witness).
main_claim: The agreement is unacceptable and merits protest.

argument_text: His Naples birthplace figured largely in his nomination, as the Italian government needed a strong inducement to appease the monarchistic South.
explanation: This sentence provides a causal justification: because the government needed to appease the monarchistic South, De Nicola’s Naples origin was a major factor in his nomination. The structure “X figured largely … as Y” lays out premise (need to appease South) leading to conclusion (birthplace influenced nomination).
main_claim: De Nicola’s Naples birthplace was a major factor in his nomination because the government needed to appease the monarchistic South.

argument_text: Production in Italy has been going up according to recent reports on silk and electric power. This year's production of natural silk in Calabria amounted to 509,300 pounds (pre-war world production was 135 million pounds), and in the first four months of this year, 4,328 million kilowatts were produced in Italy in comparison to last year's corresponding production of 3,329 million kilowatts.
